paragraphs: The Senate had passed the amendment in April 1864, but it stalled in the House until Lincoln pushed for a second vote after his re-election. On 31 January 1865 it cleared the House 119 to 56, a margin so tight it needed several Democrats to cross the aisle, and the chamber erupted when the result was read.

Ratification followed within the year: the required twenty-seven of thirty-six states approved it by 6 December 1865, and it was proclaimed law twelve days later. It abolished slavery and involuntary servitude nationwide except as punishment for crime, a clause still argued over in prison labour cases today.

When the amendment was ratified on 23 January 1964, five states still charged a tax at the ballot box for federal elections: Alabama, Arkansas, Mississippi, Texas and Virginia. The fee itself was often small, but registrars paired it with literacy tests and other hurdles that fell almost entirely on poor and Black voters.

The amendment's reach stopped at federal races; it said nothing about state and local elections, where several of those states kept charging the tax. It took a Supreme Court ruling two years later, Harper v. Virginia State Board of Elections in 1966, to strike poll taxes down everywhere else on equal protection grounds.

Shah Abbas inherited a Safavid throne propped up by Qizilbash tribal chiefs who could unmake him as easily as they had made him. He answered by building a new army loyal only to the palace: ghulams, enslaved Georgians, Circassians and Armenians, formed into musket and cavalry regiments that owed nothing to any tribe.

In 1598 he moved his capital from Qazvin to Isfahan and rebuilt it around Naqsh-e Jahan Square, ringed with mosques, a bazaar and the Ali Qapu palace. He also resettled deported Armenian merchants there and let them keep trading silk, turning a conquered population into the engine of Safavid trade revenue.

The revolt that ended Umayyad rule in 750 was not led by an Abbasid at all. Abu Muslim, a commander of uncertain origins operating out of Khurasan in what is now northeastern Iran, raised an army under the black banner and marched west, defeating the last Umayyad caliph at the Battle of the Zab.

The Abbasid family took the throne Abu Muslim had won for them and, within a few years, had him killed as a threat to their own authority. Their capital did not move to Baghdad immediately either: the caliph al-Mansur founded that city in 762, twelve years after the dynasty itself began.

The agreements took their name from the patriarch shared by Judaism, Christianity and Islam, a framing chosen to present the normalisation as broader than a narrow diplomatic deal. Neither the UAE nor Bahrain had fought a war with Israel, so the accords formalised trade and travel ties rather than ending open conflict.

Representatives signed on the Truman Balcony of the White House on 15 September 2020: Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu, UAE foreign minister Abdullah bin Zayed Al Nahyan, and Bahraini foreign minister Abdullatif bin Rashid Al Zayani. Morocco and Sudan reached similar arrangements with Israel in the following months.

The story gives no reason for the move beyond a command: to leave his country, his kindred and his father's house. Terah had already taken the family as far as Haran, in upper Mesopotamia, before dying there. Abram, then said to be 75, continued south with his wife Sarai and his nephew Lot, ending the journey at Shechem in Canaan, where he built an altar.

No document, inscription or excavation from this period names Abraham; the account survives only in Genesis, written down long after the events it describes. What it records is a promise rather than a conquest: land for descendants not yet born, sealed later by circumcision when Abraham was said to be 99. Three faiths trace their founding claim to that promise rather than to any battle or treaty.

Sultan Iskandar Muda came to Aceh's throne in 1607 and set about breaking the merchant nobles who had shared power with earlier sultans, keeping them dependent on a royal monopoly over the pepper trade instead. He backed the policy with a fleet of galleys carrying up to eight hundred men each, a cavalry mounted on imported Persian horses and an army of war elephants.

Between 1612 and 1625 his forces took Deli, Johor, Pahang, Kedah, Perak and Nias, giving Aceh control of the Strait of Malacca's northern approaches and its spice trade. The limit of his reach showed in 1629, when a huge assault on Portuguese Melaka failed outright and ended any hope of ruling the strait's far side as well.

Cyrus began as king of a minor Persian territory answering to his grandfather Astyages, the Median king. In 550 BC he turned that relationship over, defeating Astyages and folding the larger Median realm into his own, which is the point historians mark as the empire's founding rather than any single coronation.

He kept expanding for three more decades, taking Lydia from Croesus, pushing east to the Indus, and finally entering Babylon in 539 BC. There he issued the Cyrus Cylinder, describing himself as a restorer of temples and displaced peoples, and let conquered populations keep their own laws and gods, a policy later rulers rarely matched.

Scotland came to the table poor. A failed colonial venture on the isthmus of Panama, the Darien scheme, had swallowed roughly 150,000 pounds of Scottish investment, and England had just barred Scottish exports under the 1705 Alien Act unless Edinburgh negotiated union. Scotland's Parliament had also threatened, in 1704, to pick a different monarch than England's chosen Hanoverian heir.

Union came with a price tag: a payment of about 398,000 pounds, called the Equivalent, covered Scotland's share of a joint national debt and reimbursed Darien's investors, while pensions and offices went to peers and MPs whose votes carried the Act. From May 1707 the two parliaments became one, sitting at Westminster under Queen Anne, and Great Britain existed as a single kingdom for the first time.

The 1798 Irish rebellion, backed by a French landing that came close to succeeding, convinced London that a separate Irish parliament was a standing invitation to future revolt. A first attempt to merge the parliaments failed in the Irish Commons by five votes; a second vote in 1800 passed 158 to 115 after the government distributed peerages and honours to buy support.

The merged Parliament of the United Kingdom first sat on 22 January 1801. Many Irish Catholics had backed union on the understanding that full emancipation would follow quickly, but George III blocked it, and Catholics did not gain equal political rights until 1829, nearly three decades later.

Where Yusuf Adil Shah came from is genuinely disputed. Some accounts make him a Georgian slave bought by a Bahmani statesman, others give him Persian or Turkmen roots, and the chronicler Firishta claimed he was a smuggled-out son of the Ottoman sultan Murad II, a story most historians now doubt.

What is agreed is what he did with the governorship of Bijapur he was given: as the Bahmani sultanate crumbled, he declared himself an independent ruler there in 1490. In 1503 he made Shia Islam his state religion, reversed the decision once under pressure from neighbours, then reinstated it, before dying in 1510 fighting the Portuguese over Goa.

Cave deposits at the Bandiagara escarpment in Mali held strips of cloth dating back to at least the eleventh century, among the oldest surviving evidence for the narrow strip weaving technique that came to define much of West African textile making, before it spread outward across the region over the following centuries.

Woven on portable looms and stitched into wider cloth, the strips carried indigo dye that Mandinka and Yoruba specialists produced through fermentation rather than a single dip. Finished cloth became valuable enough to function as a form of currency in parts of West and Central Africa by the fourteenth century.

The body it replaced, the Organisation of African Unity, had spent nearly four decades focused on ending colonial rule and apartheid. Once both goals were achieved, its member states judged it too weak to tackle poverty, conflict and trade, and set about drafting a successor with real institutions.

The African Union launched on 9 July 2002 in Durban, with former South African president Thabo Mbeki as its first chairperson. It borrowed structural features from the European Union, including a rotating summit chair and an assembly of heads of state, aimed at closer economic and political integration across the continent.

A farmer who once grew grain to feed his own household began growing it to sell at a town market instead, and that single change rearranged the countryside. Landowners in England and the Low Countries enclosed common fields, drained marshes and specialised in whichever crop or livestock returned the best price rather than the safest mix of food.

Cities were the reason. As populations in Antwerp, London and Amsterdam grew too large to feed themselves, surrounding regions turned into supply zones, some given over entirely to dairy, others to grain or flax. Farming stopped being a way of feeding a household and became a way of earning a wage.

OpenAI released GPT-4 on 14 March 2023, four months after ChatGPT had turned the underlying technology into something millions of people used daily. Unlike its predecessor it could read images as well as text, held a far longer memory of a conversation, and passed a simulated bar exam near the top of the field rather than the bottom.

OpenAI declined to publish how the model was built or how large it was, breaking with the field's usual practice and drawing criticism from researchers who wanted to check its safety claims independently. Weeks later, more than a thousand technologists and researchers, including Elon Musk, signed an open letter calling for a six month pause on training anything more powerful.

Akbar ranked every officer in his army on a single ladder of thirty three grades, the mansabdari system, each grade fixed to a set number of cavalry that officer owed the empire. It spread military power across many nobles instead of concentrating it in a few great families, and it let Akbar promote on merit rather than birth alone.

His finance minister Todar Mal paired that with a new way of taxing farmland: revenue set at a third of the average harvest over the previous decade, paid in cash rather than in kind, with remission built in for peasants hit by flood or drought. Between them the two reforms gave the Mughal state a steadier income and a more predictable army than either had offered separately.

No other kingdom south of the Sahara struck its own coinage in the ancient world; Aksum, on the Ethiopian highlands, is the sole exception. Its king Endubis issued coins in gold, silver and bronze, inscribed in Greek, the language of trade with the Roman and Byzantine world Aksum dealt with across the Red Sea.

The coins showed the king's profile flanked by stalks of barley, with a crescent and disc above representing the moon and sun. Their weight followed the reformed Roman gold standard introduced by Diocletian in the 290s, a detail that ties Aksumite coinage directly into the wider late Roman monetary world rather than treating it as an isolated invention.

Aksum's decline was not a sudden collapse triggered by the rise of Islam alone. Minting of coins had already stopped by the seventh century, a sign of strain before the Arab conquests cut off Roman and Byzantine trading partners across the Red Sea.

Beja nomads pushed into the Eritrean highlands as the empire lost the strength to hold its frontier, cutting Aksum off from the Red Sea ports its economy depended on. The city of Axum itself shrank, and by around 960 the empire had faded from written record for reasons that remain unclear.

The earliest outside record of Aksum comes from a Greek merchant's handbook, the Periplus of the Erythraean Sea, written around the middle of the first century AD. It describes a kingdom in the highlands of modern Ethiopia and Eritrea already exporting ivory, tortoise shell, gold and emeralds to buyers on the Red Sea.

Aksum's rulers backed that trade with their own currency, striking gold, silver and bronze coins inscribed in Geez and Greek, among the earliest coinage issued by any African state. The kingdom also developed its own script, Geez, later adapted into an alphabet that marked vowels, used on royal inscriptions and religious texts alike.

Aksum's power ran through a port it did not sit on: Adulis, on the Red Sea coast, reached by a caravan road that ran inland five days to the ivory market at Coloe and three more to the capital itself. Through Adulis passed Ethiopian ivory, tortoiseshell, gold and emeralds outbound, and silk and spices arriving from India and beyond, with Aksum taking its cut at both ends of the exchange.

By the early fourth century the kingdom had its own gold, silver and copper coinage, a mark of an economy confident enough to mint rather than only trade in others' money. The Persian prophet Mani, writing around this period, ranked Aksum alongside Rome, Persia and China as one of the world's four great powers, an outsider's judgement of a kingdom most of its trading partners never saw.

The traditional story credits Fatima al-Fihri, a merchant's daughter whose family had settled in Fez after leaving Kairouan, with founding the mosque that became al-Qarawiyyin in the mid ninth century, funding the building from her own inheritance after her father's death.

A later inscription found during renovation instead names Dawud ibn Idris, a local ruler's son, as founder in 877, and the chief medieval source for Fatima's story is considered unreliable by historians. Either way, the mosque grew into a centre of law and theology that drew students from across North Africa.

Morocco in the mid seventeenth century had no single ruler: the Saadi dynasty had collapsed into competing regional strongmen. Into that vacuum stepped Mawlay al-Sharif, declared sultan of the oasis region of Tafilalt in 1631, whose family claimed descent from the Prophet Muhammad. It was a claim that mattered more in Morocco than an army did, at least at first.

His son Al-Rashid did the fighting the claim needed, taking control of the family's cause in 1664 and reuniting most of Morocco within a few years. The decisive moment came in June 1666, when Al-Rashid secured the surrender of Fez, the country's leading city, and made it his capital. The dynasty he secured there has ruled Morocco, with interruptions, ever since.

Alaric did not live to see the Visigoths settled on Roman land. He died in 410, the same year he led them in sacking Rome, and leadership passed to his brother-in-law Ataulf and then to Wallia before Emperor Honorius granted the Goths territory in Aquitaine in 418.

The arrangement made the Visigoths federates rather than conquerors on paper: they received land and tax rights around Toulouse in exchange for nominal loyalty to Rome. In practice their kingdom answered to no one else, and it became the first such Germanic state to take root inside the empire's old borders.

Alaska's path to statehood ran through a Senate stalemate: southern Democrats had blocked it for years over the seats it would add, until a coalition tied its fate to Hawaii's application to move both through together. Eisenhower signed the Alaska Statehood Act in July 1958, and the territory formally entered the union on 3 January 1959 as the 49th state.

Hawaii followed on 21 August 1959, becoming the 50th. The two admissions closed the long era of the contiguous United States expanding across a single landmass, since both new states sat entirely outside it, one an arctic territory and the other a mid-Pacific island chain.

Russia wanted to sell before Britain could simply take Alaska in some future war, and found a willing buyer in US Secretary of State William Seward. The two sides signed a treaty on 30 March 1867 for 7.2 million dollars, about two cents an acre, and the Senate ratified it within days.

Newspapers mocked the deal as Seward's Folly or Seward's Icebox, dismissing the territory as a frozen waste. The mockery has outlasted the facts: most American papers at the time actually backed the purchase, expecting Alaska to open trade routes toward Asia.

Alfred took the throne of Wessex in April 871 because his brother Aethelred had just died worn down by fighting the Danes, not because anyone had planned it. His nephews were too young to rule, and with Viking armies already loose in the kingdom, no one contested his claim.

The early years gave little sign of greatness. Alfred lost at Wilton that same spring and had to buy peace, and in January 878 a Danish force under Guthrum caught him off guard at Chippenham, driving him into hiding among the marshes of Athelney. He rallied local levies from there and defeated Guthrum's army at Edington that May.

Germany forced the conference by objecting loudly to the 1904 Entente Cordiale, which had quietly handed France a free hand in Morocco in exchange for British influence in Egypt. Kaiser Wilhelm II landed at Tangier and declared support for Moroccan independence, hoping a public conference would split Britain and France apart and demonstrate Germany's weight in African affairs instead.

Delegates from twelve countries met at Algeciras in southern Spain in early 1906 and produced the opposite of what Germany wanted: French and Spanish officers were given control of a new Moroccan police force and a state bank, effectively confirming French primacy. Britain backed France throughout the talks, and the episode drew London and Paris closer together rather than apart, hardening the alignment that became the Triple Entente.

France had governed Algeria as an integral part of the republic, not a colony to be relinquished, which is why the war that began in November 1954 lasted almost eight years and toppled a French government along the way. Estimates of the dead range from roughly 400,000 by French historians' counts to over a million by Algerian ones, a gap that itself reflects how contested the war's memory remains.

The Evian Accords were signed in March 1962, and French voters ratified them with 91 percent in favour the following month. Algerians then voted for independence on 1 July 1962, with over 99 percent in favour, ending 132 years of French rule and prompting the departure of most of Algeria's one million pieds-noirs settlers within months.

Ibn Tumart returned from studying in Baghdad convinced that Almoravid Morocco had grown lax in its faith, and around 1121 he declared himself the Mahdi, the divinely guided figure Islamic tradition expects to restore true religion. Driven from the cities, he built a fortified base at Tinmel in the High Atlas by about 1124.

His movement's early battles went badly, including a heavy defeat in 1130 that came shortly before his death. His successor Abd al-Mu'min proved the better general, and by 1147 the Almohads had taken Tlemcen, Fez and finally Marrakesh itself, ending Almoravid rule across the western Maghreb.

Abdallah ibn Yasin preached a strict, Quran-first Islam to Saharan Berber tribes from a fortified retreat, and his allies among the Lamtuna, led first by Yahya ibn Umar and then by Abu Bakr ibn Umar, turned that preaching into an army that seized the Saharan trade town of Sijilmasa in the 1050s.

Marrakesh, founded around 1070 as the Almoravids' new capital, anchored a conquest that reached across Morocco and, after the 1086 victory at Sagrajas, into Muslim Spain. Their strict Maliki orthodoxy unsettled the rulers of the fractured Andalusi kingdoms they went on to absorb.

Iceland's Althing met outdoors, not in a chamber, on a rift plain called Thingvellir that settlers chose because it belonged to no single chieftain's estate. Free men travelled from across the island each summer, and the gathering doubled as market and social event as much as legislature.

At its centre stood the Law Rock, where the Lawspeaker recited the country's laws from memory once a year, since none were written down. A council of thirty nine chieftains, the Logretta, settled disputes and passed new statutes, making the assembly one of the oldest on continuous record.

Jeff Bezos first registered the company as Cadabra, and changed the name within months after a lawyer misheard it as cadaver. Working from a rented house in Bellevue, Washington, in July 1994, he had chosen books from a shortlist of five products because they were cheap to ship and existed in more titles than any warehouse could stock.

He picked the name Amazon out of a dictionary for the river's size, reasoning that the biggest river in the world suited the biggest bookstore in the world, and that a name starting with A would sit near the top of any alphabetised list. The site did not open to the public until July 1995, a year after the company existed only as an idea and a garage.

Pueblo Bonito grew in stages between roughly 850 and 1150, eventually covering three acres and rising four or five storeys in places, with something close to eight hundred rooms enclosed by walls three feet thick. Later excavators assumed a structure that size housed thousands of people permanently.

The evidence says otherwise. Only fifty to sixty burials were found across the whole complex, and the trash deposits expected from year-round habitation are largely missing. More than thirty kivas point instead to a ceremonial centre, used seasonally by a small resident population and filled by visitors when Chaco Canyon's gatherings called for it.

Four men led the meeting in Bloemfontein on 8 January 1912: lawyer Pixley ka Isaka Seme, writer Sol Plaatje, minister John Dube and Walter Rubusana. All came from South Africa's small class of educated, mission-schooled professionals, and their new congress drew together chiefs and delegates from across the country's Black communities.

Its early strategy was petitioning colonial and imperial authorities rather than confrontation. That shifted around 1920, when the organisation, renamed the African National Congress in 1923, turned to passive resistance campaigns against pass laws that controlled where Black South Africans could live and travel.

F.W. de Klerk had led South Africa for less than four months when he stood before Parliament on 2 February 1990 and announced that the ANC, the Communist Party and other banned organisations would be legalised, and that prisoners held solely for membership in them would go free. He told MPs that the door to a new South Africa was open.

Nelson Mandela walked out of Victor Verster Prison about a week later, after 27 years in custody. The unbanning did not itself end apartheid. It opened the negotiations that would, over the next four years, dismantle it and lead to South Africa's first fully democratic election in 1994.

Before she held any elected office, Angela Merkel spent over a decade as a research chemist, earning a doctorate in quantum chemistry in East Berlin. Politics only reached her through the collapse of the state she had grown up in: she joined a party formed during the 1989 revolutions and briefly worked as a spokesperson for East Germany's first freely elected government.

The 2005 election settled nothing cleanly. Her CDU took 35.2 percent to the SPD's 34.2, too close for either bloc to govern alone, so the two rivals formed a grand coalition on 22 November with Merkel as chancellor. What began as an awkward compromise between opposing parties lasted sixteen years.

Twelve countries had spent 1957 and 1958 running research stations across Antarctica for the International Geophysical Year, and none wanted the goodwill that cooperation had built to collapse into territorial argument once the project ended. Several, including Britain, Argentina and Chile, already held overlapping claims to the same ice.

Signed in Washington on 1 December 1959, the treaty set those claims aside rather than settling them, banning new claims, nuclear tests and military bases while reserving the continent for scientific work. It has since grown to dozens of signatories, and the freeze it placed on sovereignty questions has held for over sixty years without a claim being pressed.

Joachim von Ribbentrop and the Japanese ambassador Kintomo Mushanokoji signed the pact in Berlin on 25 November 1936, naming the Communist International as the shared enemy. A secret protocol attached to it was aimed more narrowly at the Soviet Union, committing each side to consult if the other were attacked by Moscow and to avoid agreements that would help the USSR.

Italy joined the following year, turning a bilateral deal into the outline of what would become the Axis, and Spain and Hungary signed on in 1939. During the war itself Finland, Romania, Bulgaria, Slovakia, Croatia and the Japanese-backed Nanjing government all acceded, by which point membership had become less an anti-communist pledge than a declaration of allegiance to Berlin and Tokyo.

Antwerp's older exchange on Hofstraat had simply become too small for the volume of trade passing through the city, so a new building went up in 1531, designed by the architect Domien de Waghemakere in the ornate Gothic style favoured in the Low Countries. Unlike the informal meeting places merchants had used before, this one was built for the purpose from the ground up.

Its open gallery design was copied directly by London's Royal Exchange and by exchanges in Amsterdam, Rotterdam and Lille, earning Antwerp's bourse a reputation as the model every later stock exchange followed. That dominance did not last: the Siege of Antwerp in the 1580s pushed the city's trading position north to Amsterdam within a few decades.

Australia and New Zealand had spent the peace talks ending the Pacific war pressing for a guarantee against a rearmed Japan, and their price for accepting a lenient peace treaty with Tokyo in 1951 was a separate security pact with Washington. The treaty they signed that September named no shared command and no joint force; each government kept the right to decide, through its own constitutional process, whether and how to respond to an attack.

That looseness set it apart from NATO's language of automatic collective defence, echoing instead the old Monroe Doctrine's promise merely to treat an attack on one as a danger to all. The pact left Britain, the region's former colonial power, outside a Pacific security arrangement it had helped negotiate the peace for.

Two years before anyone landed on it, the moon already had legal protection. The Outer Space Treaty was opened for signature on 27 January 1967 in London, Moscow and Washington simultaneously, and entered into force that October, months before any crewed mission left Earth orbit.

Its core clauses bar signatories from placing nuclear weapons or other weapons of mass destruction in orbit or on any celestial body, and they forbid any state from claiming sovereignty over the moon or planets by occupation or use. The framework has held for decades without a major violation, even as more nations gained the means to launch.

Congress drafted the Articles while still fighting the Revolutionary War, finishing in November 1777, but getting all thirteen states to ratify took more than three years. Maryland held out longest over western land claims and did not sign until February 1781, just months before Yorktown ended the fighting the confederation had been formed to manage.

The document it produced deliberately kept the new central government weak. Congress could ask states for money but not tax anyone directly, could not regulate trade between states, and any amendment needed every single state's consent. Those gaps left Congress unable to pay its own soldiers reliably and pushed delegates toward the Constitutional Convention six years later.

For forty years ASEAN operated without a founding legal document, run on informal consensus among its members rather than binding rules. Decisions came from summit communiques, not treaty text, which let disputes over sovereignty and non-interference simmer without any mechanism to force a resolution.

Leaders signed the Charter on 20 November 2007 in Singapore, and it entered into force the following December once Thailand deposited the last ratification. It gave ASEAN its own legal personality for the first time, letting the organisation sign agreements and hold institutions accountable in its own name.

Cold War anxiety, not economic ambition, brought five foreign ministers to Bangkok's Saranrom Palace on 8 August 1967. Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore and Thailand signed a short declaration meant partly to keep communist influence and outside powers from filling any vacuum in the region.

The Bangkok Declaration committed the five to accelerate economic, social and cultural cooperation and to settle disputes peacefully among themselves. What began as a loose grouping without a headquarters, budget or binding legal structure grew over the following decades into a bloc that now includes ten Southeast Asian states.

Takauji had fought to restore Emperor Go-Daigo to power in 1333, ending the Kamakura shogunate, but the emperor's attempt to govern like a Heian-era monarch left the samurai who had backed him unrewarded and resentful. A rumour that Go-Daigo's son planned to have Takauji killed led Takauji to arrest the prince in 1334; the prince was executed the following year.

Open war followed, and Takauji's decisive win at Minatogawa in 1336 drove Go-Daigo from Kyoto to set up a rival court in the south. Takauji installed a new emperor in the capital and in 1338 took the title of shogun for himself, opening the Muromachi period and a split between northern and southern courts that lasted decades.

Assyria had been a power before and had shrunk before, its territory contracting under weak kings and outside pressure. What restarted its growth from 911 BC under Adad-nirari II was not a single victory but a policy: campaign every year, and treat reconquered land as permanently Assyrian rather than a source of seasonal tribute. His successors kept the pattern going for decades.

The clearest beneficiary was Ashurnasirpal II, who by the 870s BC had pushed Assyrian power to the Mediterranean coast and moved the capital to Nimrud to run it from. Kingdoms that resisted were made examples of, and word of that treatment travelled ahead of the army, which was itself a form of conquest. The empire this built would outlast any one king by more than two centuries.

The Navajo and Apache trace their languages to a homeland far to the north, among Athabaskan speakers of northwestern Canada. Around a thousand years ago, some of those speakers began moving south, eventually settling as far as Arizona, New Mexico and neighbouring parts of the American Southwest.

Little direct record survives of the route or pace of that journey, only its endpoint: a Southern Athabaskan, or Apachean, branch distinct enough from the northern homeland languages to mark centuries of separation. Navajo is now the most widely spoken indigenous language north of Mexico, a legacy of settlers who arrived as strangers in an already inhabited region.

Cleisthenes did not come to power as a reformer. He lost a factional fight to Isagoras, who called in a Spartan army to expel him, then tried to dissolve Athens's governing council. Ordinary citizens resisted, besieged Isagoras and his Spartan backers on the Acropolis, and forced them out, which is how Cleisthenes returned and got the chance to redesign the constitution.

His main change broke the power of the old aristocratic clans: he replaced four family-based tribes with ten new ones grouped by residence, mixing citizens from coast, city and inland into each. He expanded the governing council to five hundred members chosen by lot, and introduced ostracism, a vote that could exile a citizen for ten years without trial.

Athens's fleet, its one advantage through most of the war, was destroyed at Aegospotami in 405 BC by the Spartan commander Lysander, who then blockaded the grain route through the Dardanelles that the city depended on to feed itself. Starvation, not battle, forced the surrender that followed in April 404 BC, after Corinth and Thebes had already argued for razing the city and enslaving its people.

Sparta refused that demand, citing Athens's part in earlier wars against Persia, but still tore down its fortifications, seized what remained of its navy and dissolved the empire it had built. A Spartan-backed oligarchy known afterward as the Thirty Tyrants took over the city's government, ruling by terror for less than a year before Athenian exiles under Thrasybulus overthrew it and restored democracy in 403 BC.

Roosevelt and Churchill met aboard warships in Placentia Bay, off Newfoundland, in the second week of August 1941, four months before the United States entered the war. What emerged on 14 August was not a treaty either man signed but a jointly telegraphed statement of principles, drafted and redrafted between London and Washington rather than put on paper in one room.

It renounced territorial gain for either country, backed the right of peoples to choose their own government, and called for freed trade, disarmed aggressors and, eventually, a world free of want and fear. Roosevelt would later admit no signed copy of the charter existed anywhere, yet its language shaped the later Declaration by United Nations and the postwar order that followed it.

Portuguese and Spanish colonists in the Americas needed a workforce for the sugar plantations they were carving out of newly claimed land, and the indigenous population they had first relied on was collapsing under European disease. From the 1460s Portugal had already built forts along the West African coast to take on captives, and by around 1560 a regular slave trade was running directly to Brazil to meet plantation demand.

What had been a smaller, older traffic across the Mediterranean and into Iberian households turned, over these decades, into a transatlantic system built specifically to supply forced agricultural labour. That shift in scale and purpose set the pattern the trade would follow for the next three centuries.

Philipp Melanchthon, not Martin Luther, wrote the document Lutheran princes brought before Charles V at Augsburg, since Luther was still under imperial ban and could not attend in person. On 25 June 1530 a chancellor read the German text aloud in the bishop's palace, a reading so clear that people outside could hear every word, while the emperor kept the general public shut out.

Charles took months to respond, then rejected the confession that September and gave the Lutheran princes until the following April to submit to Rome's counter-statement. They did not, and Melanchthon wrote a defence of the confession instead, leaving a division between the churches that the meeting had been meant to settle.

Austria-Hungary had occupied Bosnia-Herzegovina under an 1878 treaty that never settled who would finally own it. In October 1908 Vienna simply declared the provinces annexed outright, catching its own negotiating partners off guard and leaving the Ottoman Empire to be bought off afterward with a payment of 2.2 million Ottoman lira for the public land.

Serbia mobilised its army and demanded the annexation be reversed or compensated. Russia's foreign minister, who believed he had been promised a quid pro quo over the straits and instead got nothing, backed down under German pressure by March 1909. The humiliation hardened Serbian nationalism and Russian resentment that resurfaced in 1914.

Ten years of stalled negotiation ended in a single afternoon at Vienna's Belvedere Palace on 15 May 1955, when the foreign ministers of the Soviet Union, the United States, Britain and France signed alongside Austria's Leopold Figl. Molotov's agreement to withdraw Soviet troops came only after Austria offered a concession the other three had not been willing to give: permanent neutrality.

The treaty itself does not use the word neutrality; that promise came a day after the last occupying soldiers left, on 26 October 1955, when Austria's parliament separately declared it would join no military alliance and host no foreign bases. The withdrawal ended a decade in which Vienna, like Berlin, had been carved into four occupation zones.

Uthong did not conquer his kingdom so much as marry and inherit it. He already held Phetchaburi and Ayodhya by descent, and a marriage brought him Suphannabhum and Lavo, so that founding Ayutthaya on 4 March 1351 mostly meant declaring, on an island in the Chao Phraya river, that four separate centres now answered to one ruler.

The new city sent tribute missions to the Yuan court and later the Ming, a relationship that marked it as a recognised trading power in Chinese eyes. Ayutthaya went on to demand tribute from Malay principalities as far as Temasek, and the kingdom it founded lasted 417 years before a Burmese siege destroyed the city in 1767.

The alliance that became the Aztec Empire was born out of a succession dispute, not a plan for conquest. When the Tepanec ruler Tezozomoc died in 1426, his heir Maxtla seized power and turned on his own allies, blockading Tenochtitlan and demanding heavier tribute from neighbouring cities. Tenochtitlan, Texcoco and Tlacopan answered by going to war against his capital, Azcapotzalco, and won in 1428.

Two years later the three victors formalised their partnership as the Triple Alliance, agreeing to share the spoils of future conquests, two shares to Tenochtitlan and Texcoco and one to Tlacopan. On paper the three cities remained equals. In practice Tenochtitlan's own armies grew so dominant that within decades it was the alliance in all but name.

Moctezuma II inherited an empire already built by others. His uncle Ahuitzotl had made the Mexica the dominant partner in the Aztec Triple Alliance, so when Moctezuma took the throne in 1502 his task was less to expand than to consolidate what earlier campaigns had already conquered.

By then Tenochtitlan sat at the centre of a domain spanning roughly 220,000 square kilometres and reaching as far as Xoconochco near present-day Guatemala, with an early sixteenth century population across the empire estimated at around six million people, run from a lake city most Europeans had not yet heard existed.

Tenochtitlan's exact founding date is unrecorded; 13 March 1325 was fixed only in 1925, to mark a round anniversary. The Mexica were latecomers to the Valley of Mexico and had been pushed to its margins, and the site they settled, a marshy island in Lake Texcoco, was land nobody else particularly wanted.

Legend held that they were meant to build there once they saw an eagle perched on a cactus, devouring a snake. Whatever drove the choice, the island proved defensible and close to fresh water and fish, and by the time Hernan Cortes arrived in 1519 the city had grown to a population historians put in the hundreds of thousands.

Euthydemus I came to the Bactrian throne by overthrowing its previous king, then had to defend it against the Seleucid ruler Antiochus III, who invaded around 210 BCE with a much larger force. Euthydemus lost the opening battle but held the fortified city of Bactra through a siege lasting some three years, until Antiochus gave up and recognised him as king instead.

With the Seleucids gone, the Greco-Bactrian kingdom pushed outward, gaining ground toward Parthia in the west and reaching north past Alexandria Eschate, a city Alexander the Great had founded in the Fergana valley. Greek rule, improbably, had extended itself to the edge of territory the Chinese would later know as the Western Regions.

Baekje held no army to match its neighbours Goguryeo and Silla, so it built influence by sea instead. Its ships carried scholars, monks and artisans to Japan's Yamato court, and later Korean chroniclers described the kingdom as the Phoenicia of the region.

Through Baekje, the Yamato court received Chinese writing, Buddhist texts and bronze and pottery techniques, and Baekje princes spent time at Yamato, though historians still debate whether they went as envoys or as hostages. Baekje also paid tribute to China's Jin court to offset the pressure it faced at home.

Al-Mansur chose an empty stretch of the Tigris in 762, four years after his family had taken the caliphate from the Umayyads, and reportedly saw no better place for a garrison in his lifetime. Construction of the Round City took four years and, by tradition, more than 100,000 workers. Its plan put the caliph's palace and the main mosque at the centre of two concentric walls, a layout meant to echo paradise as described in the Qur'an.

The site was not virgin ground; older settlements and canals from earlier Mesopotamian empires already ran through the area, which is part of why al-Mansur wanted it. Within a generation the new capital had outgrown the old Sasanian city of Ctesiphon nearby and drawn scholars, merchants and translators from across the region, becoming for a time the largest city in the world.

A regent, not a sultan, pushed the Bahmani state to its widest reach. Mahmud Gawan governed in the sultan's name through the 1460s and into the 1470s, reaching maximum territorial extent by 1473 and doubling the number of provinces from four to eight simply to keep the enlarged state administered.

The fragmentation that followed was quick once it started. From 1490, provincial governors under the weak Mahmood Shah Bahmani II began declaring independence one after another, Bijapur and Ahmadnagar first, Bidar in 1492, Golconda last in 1518, until the five Deccan sultanates had replaced the one state Gawan had briefly held together.

The document was a single letter, dated 2 November 1917, from Britain's foreign secretary Arthur Balfour to Lord Rothschild, a peer with no government office who was asked to pass it to the Zionist Federation. It said the government viewed with favour the establishment in Palestine of a national home for the Jewish people, a phrase with no fixed meaning in international law and chosen for that reason.

The same sentence added that nothing should be done to prejudice the civil and religious rights of the non-Jewish communities already living there, without saying how the two commitments could both be kept. Published in the press a week later, it became one of the founding texts of a conflict over the same land that a single letter could not settle.

A Roman knight sent north under Nero reportedly returned with enough fossilised resin to decorate an entire gladiatorial arena, a story that says more about demand in Rome than about the journey itself. The route he travelled ran the length of modern Poland, through Bohemia, to the Adriatic port of Aquileia, and Roman soldiers were posted along stretches of it to keep raiders off the traders.

Amber was the least of what moved along the road. Furs, honey and wax went south from the Baltic coast; in return, Roman glassware, bronze fittings and tin came north. The gem gave the whole network its name only because it was the one good no one else could supply.

Indonesia, Burma, India, Ceylon and Pakistan called the meeting that opened in Bandung on 18 April 1955, and twenty-nine governments sent delegates, together speaking for well over half the world's population. None were the Soviet Union or the United States. Zhou Enlai attended for China and struck a deliberately conciliatory tone, easing fears among smaller delegations about Chinese ambitions in the region.

Delegates left with the Bandung Declaration, ten principles on peaceful coexistence and respect for sovereignty that were aimed squarely at colonial rule and at pressure from both Cold War blocs. Indonesia's Sukarno spoke of a bloc of what he called newly emerging forces. The gathering fed directly into the founding of the Non-Aligned Movement six years later.

Raden Samudra was heir to the small kingdom of Negara Daha in southern Borneo until his uncles seized the throne and forced him out. He built a rival base downriver at Banjarmasin, and on 24 September 1526 converted to Islam, taking the name Sultan Suriansyah. The conversion marked the sultanate's formal start, though it began as a tributary of the Javanese state of Demak rather than a free power.

Independence came later in the century as Demak itself declined, and Banjar's real growth followed in the early 1600s, when it turned into a major exporter of pepper along the Barito river routes. Under Sultan Mustain Billah, who ruled into the 1640s, that trade gave Banjar command of the surrounding seas.

The government needed 1.2 million pounds to rebuild a navy the French had beaten in 1690, and it had neither the cash nor the credit to borrow it outright. The Scottish trader William Paterson proposed a fix: a joint-stock company would lend the crown the money at 8 percent interest, in exchange for a charter and the right to issue notes against the loan.

Charles Montagu steered the plan through Parliament as the Tonnage Act of 1694, and the money came fast: 1.2 million pounds from 1,268 subscribers inside twelve days. The royal charter followed on 27 July, creating the Governor and Company of the Bank of England as a lender to the state rather than a household name for savers.

Genoa's Bank of Saint George, founded in 1407 to consolidate the city's war debts, grew into one of Europe's first institutions taking deposits and extending credit at scale. The Financial Times later called it the world's first modern public bank.

Its ledgers eventually carried the accounts of rulers across Europe, including Ferdinand and Isabella of Spain, and Christopher Columbus corresponded with its governors. Italian banking houses' willingness to lend across borders let merchants and monarchs finance trade and war without moving physical coin.

A merchant in thirteenth century Florence kept two records of every transaction, one on the debit side and one on the credit, so that the books balanced against each other rather than relying on memory alone. The earliest surviving ledger to show the full system in use belongs to a Florentine merchant, dated to 1299 and 1300.

The Farolfi trading firm, run out of Nimes but rooted in Florence, kept comparable accounts even earlier. The habit spread between Italian merchant cities through the fourteenth century before Venice became the centre where the method was written up as theory rather than just practised, turning a bookkeeping trick into a discipline other merchants across Europe could learn from a manual.

Genoa's fortune in this period came less from vaults than from ships. Its fleets broke Pisan and Muslim control of the western Mediterranean, and the trading rights it won by force, in Levantine ports and Byzantine markets alike, gave its merchants the cash flow that moneylending and exchange later grew out of.

The formal banks came afterwards: Genoa's Bank of Saint George was not founded until 1407. What the twelfth century city-states supplied first was the plumbing, merchants who needed to move money between ports without carrying coin, and the money changers and notaries who worked out how to write a promise instead.

Before 1542 an English merchant who could not pay his debts had no formal legal process at all, only whatever a creditor could extract through the ordinary courts or through violence. The Statute of Bankrupts, passed that year under Henry VIII, was the first English law to deal with insolvency directly, giving royal officials power to seize a failed debtor's goods and property for distribution among creditors.

The statute treated bankruptcy as closer to an offence than a misfortune, aimed squarely at merchants suspected of dodging what they owed rather than at ordinary hardship. It was narrow and punitive by later standards, but it set a precedent English law kept building on for the next three centuries as commerce grew more complex than a single Tudor statute could anticipate.

The Bantu expansion was not one migration but thousands of small ones, stretched across roughly four thousand years and splitting into a western stream toward Angola and an eastern stream toward the African Great Lakes, each absorbing or displacing the hunter-gatherer communities already living there.

Farming travelled with them from the start, palm oil, grains and root crops grown around settled villages rather than the mobile camps of earlier populations. Iron only shows up in the archaeological record later, from around 400 BC, and by the first century BC communities near the Great Lakes were forging carbon steel.

The languages spoken across most of sub-Saharan Africa today trace back to farmers in southern Cameroon who began moving outward roughly four thousand years ago. Linguists worked this out before archaeologists did: the hundreds of Bantu languages spoken from Cameroon to South Africa are close enough to share an unmistakably recent common origin.

The migrants spread in two broad streams, one down the Atlantic side of the continent and one through the Great Lakes toward the east coast, reaching what is now South Africa by around 300 AD. Iron-working, once assumed to have travelled with the earliest farmers, shows up in the archaeological record only centuries later, adopted along the way rather than carried from the start.

Qasim Barid was not a general who seized a throne outright. A Turkish noble in Bahmani service, he rose to become the sultanate's de facto ruler while a puppet sultan still nominally sat in Bidar, the power behind the throne rather than on it.

Once Bahmani authority collapsed for good he made the arrangement formal, founding the independent Bidar sultanate under his own Barid Shahi dynasty. It became the smallest and least powerful of the five Deccan successor states that carved up the old Bahmani realm, but its rulers kept effective control of the fortress city of Bidar for generations.

Coin did not vanish after Rome fell, but it grew scarce, and for centuries wealth in Western Europe meant land more than money. Merchants revived the habit of pricing goods in silver only slowly, along routes still considered too costly and dangerous to bother taxing closely.

Italian city-states led the return to coined exchange: Venice and Florence built banking instruments other regions still lacked, and by 1252 Florence and Genoa were minting gold coins again for the first time since antiquity, a currency solid enough to underwrite trade across the Mediterranean.

The Batak reached the highland interior of North Sumatra later than communities settled along the coast, but isolation did not mean disconnection: camphor and benzoin resin from their forests had moved through regional trade networks for a thousand years or more before European traders ever asked for either by name.

Batak society organised itself into patrilineal clans called marga, all tracing descent from a single founding ancestor, Si Raja Batak. Every member was expected to know a genealogy, or tarombo, linking them back through that line; someone who could not was considered to have strayed from the clan entirely, since kinship rather than territory decided most social and ritual obligations.

Philip II led the Macedonian army against a coalition of Greek city states, chiefly Athens and Thebes, near the Boeotian town of Chaeronea in August 338 BC. His eighteen year old son Alexander commanded the cavalry on one wing. The sides were roughly matched, but the Macedonian phalanx broke both flanks of the Greek line, and Thebes's elite Sacred Band, a unit of 300 men, was reportedly wiped out where it stood.

An Athenian orator later said the freedom of the Greeks was buried with the men who fell there. Philip did not destroy Athens but forced the defeated cities into the League of Corinth, a confederation under his own leadership that ended their independent conduct of war and foreign policy. He was assassinated two years later, and it was Alexander who led the League's planned campaign against Persia.

Antigonus was the last of Alexander's marshals still trying to reunite the whole empire under one ruler, and by 301 BC the others had combined against him. At Ipsus in Phrygia, Seleucus, Lysimachus and Cassander's forces met Antigonus and his son Demetrius. Antigonus, in his eighties, was surrounded by allied infantry and killed by javelins thrown from a distance.

Demetrius fled, and the coalition carved up the territory Antigonus had held. Seleucus took eastern Anatolia, Lysimachus the rest of Asia Minor, and Ptolemy kept Egypt, which he had already occupied without joining the actual fighting. No single ruler would come close to reuniting Alexander's empire again, and the battle set the rough borders of the Hellenistic kingdoms for the next century.

Samuel de Champlain did not just trade for pelts, he built alliances to secure a supply of them, binding French traders to the Huron, Algonquin and Montagnais as partners who moved beaver fur from the interior toward the Saint Lawrence. The Huron in particular became the middlemen who made the whole exchange work.

Metal axes, kettles, cloth and firearms replaced tools Indigenous communities had made themselves, and trapping for European markets began displacing older subsistence patterns. Competition for that trade later turned violent: by the 1640s the Iroquois, supplied by Dutch traders, fought a series of wars to seize the middleman role for themselves, scattering entire nations westward.

From the early twelfth century, women in the Low Countries began living alone, praying and doing charitable work without entering a convent or taking the vows that bound a nun for life. Named beguinages followed later, at Mechelen from 1207 and Leuven before 1232, formal enclosures around what had started as an informal way of living.

A beguine promised not to marry only for as long as she chose to remain one, and she was free to leave and marry afterwards. Most supported themselves rather than relying on an endowment, working the wool trade that made the same Flemish cities rich, which let them live communally without either a dowry or a religious order behind them.

The revolt began at an opera. On 25 August 1830 a Brussels audience watching Auber's La Muette de Portici rose at the duet Amour sacre de la patrie and poured into the streets shouting for revolt against Dutch rule. Within days crowds held the Parc de Bruxelles and the royal palace, and Dutch troops under Prince Frederik fought house to house for four days in September before withdrawing to their fortresses.

The great powers met in London that December and, with none of them willing to send troops to restore Dutch authority, recognised an independent Belgium. Leopold of Saxe-Coburg accepted the new throne and took his oath as king on 21 July 1831, a date still marked as Belgium's national day.

Xi Jinping unveiled the plan not in Beijing but at Nazarbayev University in Astana, Kazakhstan, on 7 September 2013, describing a 'Silk Road Economic Belt' of overland trade routes linking China to Europe. A maritime counterpart, the '21st Century Maritime Silk Road', followed weeks later.

The two strands merged into what became known abroad as the Belt and Road Initiative, financing ports, railways and power plants across dozens of countries through Chinese state loans. Recipient governments took on large debts to Chinese banks, and several later renegotiated terms on projects that ran over budget.

Governor Manuel Cerveira Pereira founded Sao Felipe de Benguela on the Angolan coast in 1617, a fort and harbour built for one purpose: moving captives onto ships bound across the Atlantic. Unlike open beaches used elsewhere, Benguela had jetties, so people could be walked directly from holding pens into small boats and out to the waiting vessels.

For two centuries afterward the port sent enslaved people mainly to Brazil and, later, Cuba, its trade running in step with the sugar plantations on the other side of the ocean. The town's entire economy grew around this traffic, and the road inland that fed it became known as one of the longest slaving routes in southern Africa.

Oba Ewuare, who came to power around 1440, pulled authority away from Benin's hereditary chiefs and toward officials who answered directly to him. He paired a council of town chiefs with a separate council of palace chiefs, and created the title of Edaiken for the crown prince, fixing succession to the eldest son instead of leaving it to be contested among relatives.

He also rebuilt the royal palace on a much larger scale and split the capital into a palace quarter and a town quarter, joined by widened streets. Around the whole city he raised the largest of Benin's earthwork walls and ditches, with nine gates guarded by ritual charms, while inside the palace itself, staff were organised into ranked departments covering the wardrobe, attendants and the royal household.

Before the Obas there were Ogisos, and tradition says the last of them, Owodo, was overthrown by his own ruling council. Rather than rule themselves, the council sent to Ile Ife for a replacement, and the prince who came, Oranmiyan, found the town too difficult to govern and handed it to his son instead.

That son, Eweka I, became the first Oba around 1200, the title that Benin's kings would carry for the rest of the kingdom's history. The bronze casting that later made Benin famous in Europe belongs to a much later period of that dynasty, not to its founding generation.

Stalin's blockade was aimed at a currency, not a city. When the Western powers introduced the Deutsche Mark into West Berlin in June 1948, Soviet forces cut every road, rail and canal link to the city to force its withdrawal. Rather than abandon the two million people left inside, Britain and the United States began flying in everything they needed.

The airlift ran for fifteen months, delivering over two million tons of coal, food and fuel across more than 200,000 flights, with a plane landing roughly every thirty seconds at its peak. One American pilot, Gail Halvorsen, began dropping small parcels of sweets to children below, a habit that grew into an organised effort called Operation Little Vittles.

Fourteen states sent delegates to Berlin between November 1884 and February 1885, including the United States and the Ottoman Empire alongside every major European power. Not one African ruler was invited; the Sultan of Zanzibar's request to attend was turned aside under pressure from anti-slavery campaigners who wanted the conference to look otherwise.

The resulting act confirmed King Leopold II's personal claim to the Congo through his International Congo Society and declared free trade along the Congo basin, but its lasting rule was that a claim to African territory needed actual occupation on the ground to be recognised. That single requirement set off a scramble among European powers to plant garrisons across the continent within a matter of months.

Polls closed on 3 November 2020, but the count dragged on for four days as mail in ballots, swollen by a pandemic, were tallied in battleground states. Networks called Pennsylvania and the race for Biden on the morning of 7 November, more than seventy hours after voting ended, setting off street celebrations in several cities.

Biden finished with roughly 81 million votes, more than any presidential candidate before him, a margin of about seven million over Trump and 306 electoral votes to 232. Trump refused to concede and pursued dozens of lawsuits contesting results in several states, all but one of which were dismissed or dropped before Biden's inauguration in January.

A bill of exchange was a written order: a merchant in Florence, the drawer, instructed a partner elsewhere, the drawee, to pay a named third party, the payee, on a set date. Italian houses gave the instrument its lasting shape between the thirteenth and fifteenth centuries, building on earlier practices used by Middle Eastern merchants.

Unlike the letter of credit it grew alongside, a bill of exchange could be bought, sold and passed on before it was even paid, letting merchants settle debts across several cities without one coin changing hands. France later added endorsement to the practice and German states formalised exchange law, but the underlying device stayed Italian in origin.

James Madison had argued against adding a bill of rights at all, calling the Constitution's structure protection enough. He changed course once it became clear that several states would only ratify with a promise of amendments attached, and he ended up drafting most of them himself in the First Congress.

Congress sent twelve articles to the states in 1789. Ten were ratified by 15 December 1791 and became the first ten amendments. One dealt with congressional pay and went nowhere for two centuries before finally becoming the Twenty-seventh Amendment in 1992; another, on the size of the House, has never been ratified at all.

A coin's value was supposed to equal the metal in it, so European mints struck both gold and silver pieces at a fixed exchange rate between the two. The trouble was that gold and silver never moved in price at the same pace on the open market, and a rate fixed by decree could not keep up with one set by trade.

Whenever one metal became worth more than the ratio allowed, people melted or exported the undervalued coins and hoarded the rest, draining circulation of whichever metal was momentarily cheap to mint. Rulers reset the ratios repeatedly rather than solving the problem, and merchants learned to distrust any coin's face value against its weight.

Charlemagne governed a realm too large to run from Aachen alone, so he sent out pairs of inspectors called missi dominici to check on local officials in his name. One of each pair was a layman and the other a bishop or abbot, a deliberate pairing that put churchmen inside the machinery of royal government rather than beside it.

Bishops answered to Rome for their office but to the emperor for the estates and legal authority that came with it, so a diocese was also a unit of secular administration. That double loyalty gave the church a stake in Carolingian rule and gave the emperor clergy he could post to distant regions with more consistency than most counts.

Prussia's parliament had refused to fund the king's army reforms, leaving the government deadlocked over money rather than principle. On 23 September 1862 King Wilhelm I turned to Otto von Bismarck, a diplomat willing to govern without the legislature's consent, and made him Minister President.

A week later Bismarck told the budget committee that the great questions of the age would be settled not by speeches or majority votes but by iron and blood. He meant it as policy, not rhetoric: Prussia would build an army first and argue about the constitution afterward.

The break was procedural before it was personal. Bismarck opened coalition talks with the Catholic Centre Party in 1890 without telling the young Kaiser Wilhelm II first, a breach of the understanding that a chancellor kept his monarch informed of major moves. The two men also disagreed over how to treat socialist agitators, with Wilhelm favouring conciliation toward workers where Bismarck wanted expanded police powers to expel them.

A furious argument at Bismarck's estate over what Wilhelm considered disrespect toward the imperial family ended the relationship outright. Bismarck resigned, and the Kaiser accepted it within days, choosing weaker chancellors afterward so that no one could dominate policy the way Bismarck had for twenty-eight years, from German unification until March 1890.

The plague reached Europe through Constantinople in the summer of 1347 and spread along trade routes for years afterward. Estimates of the dead range widely by region, from under fifteen per cent in parts of Bohemia and Galicia to as much as eighty per cent in Florence within a few months of 1348, with historians settling on something between thirty and sixty per cent of Europeans overall.

So many labourers died that survivors could demand higher wages, and many inherited land and property from relatives who had not survived, weakening the feudal bonds that had tied peasants to their lords. Landlords found taxes and rents harder to collect as fields and houses sat empty, even as inflation ate into the real value of the higher wages workers had won.

Landlords could not get fields harvested. Villages that had lost a third or more of their people found survivors demanding wages nobody would have paid two years earlier, and some tenants began asking for money rents instead of labour service, since a scarce worker could simply walk to the next manor for better terms.

Edward III's government answered in 1351 with the Statute of Labourers, freezing pay at 1346 levels and threatening idle workers with prison. It was widely ignored: farm wages roughly doubled over the following century, and resentment at the attempt fed directly into the Peasants' Revolt of 1381.

On the night of 20 June 1756, British and Indian prisoners were shut into a small guardroom at Fort William after the fort fell to the Nawab of Bengal, Siraj-ud-Daulah. A survivor, the East India Company official John Zephaniah Holwell, later wrote that 123 of 146 men died overnight in the heat and crush.

Historians have never agreed on Holwell's numbers. Stanley Wolpert put the total confined closer to 64, with 21 surviving; other estimates suggest a smaller cell and a lower toll. Most agree Siraj-ud-Daulah had not ordered the imprisonment and was unaware of it. The episode nonetheless entered British memory as justification for Robert Clive's later conquest of Bengal.

The Dow Jones Industrial Average lost 508 points on 19 October 1987, a fall of 22.6 percent that remains the largest single day percentage drop in the index's history. Stocks had looked overvalued for months, the dollar was weak from persistent trade and budget deficits, and rising interest rates had made bonds a more attractive place to put money.

An international currency pact called the Louvre Accord lost credibility that week when the German central bank raised rates and a US Treasury remark was read as tolerating a weaker dollar. Automated trading made the drop worse: portfolio insurance programmes sold as prices fell, feeding the very decline they were built to guard against. Losses worldwide were later estimated near $1.71 trillion.

On 6 September 1970 the Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine hijacked three airliners and forced them down at a former British airstrip in Jordan, then blew up the empty planes in front of television cameras. For King Hussein, who already governed a country where Palestinian fighters operated almost as a state within his state, the hijackings were the provocation that made confrontation unavoidable.

The Jordanian army moved against the fedayeen in the capital that same month, and fighting continued into 1971 before Yasser Arafat's forces were pushed out, many of them into Lebanon. Casualty estimates vary sharply, from the low thousands to Arafat's own claim of 25,000, a gap that itself shows how contested the episode remained among the parties who fought it.

The Conservative Party had governed Britain since 1979, longer than any single party in modern British history, and by 1997 it was exhausted by sleaze allegations and internal splits over Europe. Tony Blair had spent three years rebranding his party as New Labour, dropping its historic commitment to public ownership and courting business voters the party had once treated as opponents.

Labour won 418 seats to the Conservatives' 165 on 1 May 1997, a majority of 177 that was the largest in the party's history. Blair, 43, became the youngest prime minister in over a century, and Labour under him won two further elections before its run in office ended in 2010.

Late in the afternoon of 7 September 1940, nearly a thousand German bombers and fighters turned toward London instead of the airfields the Luftwaffe had been targeting for weeks. The switch in strategy, meant to break civilian morale, gave Royal Air Force squadrons time to recover just as the Battle of Britain reached its critical point.

London was bombed on 56 of the following 57 nights, and the campaign continued against British cities for eight months until May 1941. Between 40,000 and 43,000 civilians were killed and more than a million houses in London alone were damaged or destroyed, yet production and daily life carried on through the raids.

On 30 January 1972 soldiers of the British Army's 1st Parachute Regiment opened fire on a civil rights march in the Bogside area of Derry. Twenty six people were shot; thirteen died that day and a fourteenth died of his injuries months later. None of those killed was found to have been carrying a weapon.

A 2010 public inquiry, after twelve years of hearings, concluded that the soldiers had lost control and that the killings were unjustified. Prime Minister David Cameron apologised in the House of Commons the same day the report was published, saying plainly that what happened should never have happened.

The territory had no name of its own for most of the war, known simply as Upper Peru, a mountainous appendage of the Spanish empire fought over by armies from Buenos Aires and Lima alike. Antonio Jose de Sucre's campaign broke the last royalist resistance there in 1825, and delegates meeting at Chuquisaca that July had a real choice: join Peru, join Argentina, or stand alone.

They chose independence, and signed the declaration on 6 August 1825, naming the new republic after Simon Bolivar, who had led much of the wider South American struggle from the north. Bolivar was declared its first president but left within months to attend to Peru and Colombia, handing the country to Sucre, who governed it for the next several years.

Chinese sources call it Boni; it is better known today as Brunei. In 1225 the customs official Zhao Rukuo recorded a kingdom on Borneo wealthy enough to keep a hundred warships guarding its shipping lanes, trading camphor, pearls and tortoiseshell into the South China Sea network.

Boni sent tribute missions to the Song and later Ming courts and drew merchants from across maritime Southeast Asia into its harbour. Centuries afterward the kingdom converted to Islam and re-emerged as the Sultanate of Brunei, at its height reaching into the southern Philippines.

Theresa May had tried three times to get Parliament to pass her Brexit withdrawal deal and failed each time before she resigned as Conservative leader in the spring of 2019. Johnson, who had campaigned for Leave and quit her cabinet in protest at her deal, won the party's leadership contest and was appointed Prime Minister on 24 July that year.

He arrived promising to leave the European Union by 31 October, deal or no deal, under the slogan Get Brexit Done. Parliament blocked a no deal exit and forced an early election that December, which Johnson won with a large majority. He then reopened talks with Brussels, and the United Kingdom formally left the EU in January 2020.

Emperor Pedro II was in Europe when the law that ended slavery in his empire was signed on 13 May 1888, so his daughter Isabel, acting as regent, put her name to it instead. The Golden Law ran to two short articles: slavery was abolished, and all prior provisions to the contrary were revoked. There was no timetable, no gradual phase-out, nothing left to negotiate.

Its brevity was deliberate, meant to close off any argument that freedom came with conditions attached. Slaveholders received no compensation from the state, and the freed themselves received none either, no land, no wages owed, no assistance. Brazil had held out longer than every other country in the Americas, and when it finally acted it did so with two sentences rather than a plan.

Marshal Deodoro da Fonseca did not want to lead a coup. Republican officers convinced him only by spreading a rumour that his political rival was about to be named prime minister, and on 15 November 1889 he marched troops through Rio de Janeiro against a government that offered almost no resistance; only one person was hurt.

Pedro II initially assumed the soldiers were after his prime minister, not his throne. Told otherwise, he accepted it without a fight, reportedly remarking that he had worked hard enough and was tired. The imperial family sailed for Europe that same night and were not allowed to return to Brazil until 1920, three decades into an exile none of them had chosen.

Pedro was on horseback near a stream called Ipiranga on 7 September 1822 when letters reached him from Portugal, ordering him back to Lisbon and stripping his ministers of authority. He tore the Portuguese colours from his uniform on the spot and told his companions the break was final.

He rode back to Sao Paulo that night to announce it, and was acclaimed Emperor Pedro I within weeks. The declaration did not end the matter: Portuguese garrisons held parts of Brazil for years afterward, and it took until 1825, and a formal treaty, before Lisbon accepted what Pedro had shouted by a riverbank.

For three weeks in July 1944, 730 delegates from 44 allied governments crowded into the Mount Washington Hotel in rural New Hampshire, chosen partly because it was thought secure from wartime sabotage. Britain's delegation was led by the economist John Maynard Keynes, who arrived pushing a plan for a global reserve currency that the Americans, holding most of the world's gold, declined to adopt.

The conference instead pegged member currencies to the US dollar, itself convertible to gold at a fixed rate, and created the International Monetary Fund and the bank that became the World Bank to manage the system and finance reconstruction. That arrangement held until the early 1970s, when the United States stopped exchanging dollars for gold and the fixed rates it depended on collapsed.

The 2016 referendum, decided by a margin of just under four points, only started the process. Article 50 negotiations dragged through three years of parliamentary deadlock in London, two changes of prime minister and a delayed departure date, before the withdrawal agreement was finally ratified.

The United Kingdom left the EU's political institutions at 11pm on 31 January 2020, but stayed inside the single market and customs union under a transition period that ran until 31 December that year. A new trade agreement with the bloc took effect on 1 January 2021.

Colonel Ahmed Urabi had led Egyptian officers in revolt against a khedive he saw as a foreign puppet, and by mid-1882 his movement controlled much of the government. When a riot in Alexandria killed around fifty Europeans on 11 June and Urabi's forces fortified the city instead of standing down, Britain answered with an ultimatum, then a fleet.

The decisive fight came at Tell El Kebir on 13 September, where General Garnet Wolseley's troops crossed open desert at night and struck an entrenched Egyptian army of some 60,000 at dawn. Urabi's forces broke, and British cavalry rode into an undefended Cairo the next day. Britain called the intervention a restoration of order and a defence of the Suez Canal; its troops stayed for seventy-two years.

The Government of India Act received royal approval on 2 August 1858, less than a year after the uprising that began among Company sepoys at Meerut had spread across northern India. It stripped the East India Company of the territories and armies it had ruled for a century, transferring them to the Crown outright. A new Secretary of State for India, answering to Parliament, took over its administration from London.

Queen Victoria was proclaimed sovereign of India the following year, and a viceroy replaced the Company's governor general as the ruler on the ground. The change was framed as correcting the defects in Company government that the rebellion had exposed, rather than as any softening of British authority; Indians remained excluded from the senior ranks of the civil service the act created.

Rioting broke out across Belfast and Derry in August 1969 as clashes between Catholic residents, Protestant loyalists and the local police spiralled beyond the control of Northern Ireland's own security forces. The unionist government at Stormont asked London for military help rather than risk the police losing the streets entirely.

British soldiers arrived on 14 August 1969, sent initially to support the Royal Ulster Constabulary and separate the two communities. The deployment, later codenamed Operation Banner, did not end for almost thirty-eight years, until July 2007, making it the longest continuous operation in British military history.

Chief Justice Earl Warren wanted no dissent recorded, and on 17 May 1954 he got a unanimous 9 to 0 ruling. The Court held that separate schools for black and white children could never be equal, overturning the standard set almost sixty years earlier in Plessy v. Ferguson, which had allowed segregated facilities as long as they were nominally comparable.

The ruling itself set no deadline. A second decision the following year told districts to desegregate with all deliberate speed, a phrase vague enough that many Southern states spent years finding ways around it, from closing public schools outright to funding private academies that admitted only white students.

A storm in 1134 tore a channel through the coast that reconnected Bruges to the sea, and the city spent the next century and a half turning that accident into a fortune. By 1300 it sat at the meeting point of Hanseatic routes from the north and Italian galley routes from the south, with resident colonies of Genoese, Venetian and Basque merchants each governed under their own laws.

Rather than relying on seasonal trade fairs like older commercial centres, Bruges merchants pooled capital and risk in new partnerships borrowed or adapted from Italian practice. That innovation reached its clearest form in 1309, when the city's money market opened as the Bourse, generally reckoned the first institution recognisable as a stock exchange.

A single sultan's naval reach once ran from the coasts of Borneo to Manila Bay and south to the Sulu Archipelago. Brunei's rulers never held these lands as a unified territory in the European sense; they drew tribute and recognition from coastal chiefs who found it useful to say yes to a fleet.

Manila itself, then called Seludong, sat within Brunei's orbit before the Spanish arrived in 1571 and ended that arrangement within a few years. Inland Borneo stayed largely outside Brunei's grasp throughout, since the sultanate's power was maritime: it lived on control of harbours and shipping lanes, not on holding ground.

A dying kabaka's chosen heir was a secret even from the man himself. A council studied the young princes for years, and the reigning king, acting on their judgement, privately handed a piece of bark cloth to the one he had picked. Nobody else learned the name until the king died, when the heir stepped forward and laid the cloth over the body.

One rule was fixed regardless of merit: the firstborn son, always given the title Kiweewa, could never take the throne. Excluding him removed the most obvious target for rivals plotting early, a safeguard against the kind of succession violence that had repeatedly split other Great Lakes kingdoms.
