Buganda's kingship is usually traced to a founder called Kato Kintu, though historians only place him somewhere between the twelfth and fourteenth centuries, a span wide enough to show how thin the record is. Oral tradition, not a document, carries the story forward.

Early Buganda was small, covering little more than the counties of Kyadondo, Busiro and Mawokota, and the kabaka's authority grew out of existing clan leadership rather than being imposed from outside. Neighbouring Bunyoro traditions claim a different origin for the dynasty, a dispute Baganda historians reject.

Buganda began small, a cluster of clans on the northern shore of Lake Victoria under a line of kabakas tracing back to a founder named Kato Kintu in the early fourteenth century. What turned it into a power was the lake itself: by the nineteenth century its rulers had built war canoes over seventy feet long, some carrying a hundred warriors, and used them to dominate the water and the shoreline kingdoms around it.

Under Kabaka Mutesa I the kingdom fought sixty-six wars in twenty-eight years, and one campaign against island communities reportedly mustered over a hundred thousand warriors and more than two hundred canoes. Rather than seeking allies, Buganda mostly coerced them: neighbouring peoples paid tribute under threat of raids, and conquered districts such as Buddu were absorbed outright into its territory.

The retired shogun Tokugawa Ieyasu summoned the country's feudal lords to Fushimi Castle in the seventh lunar month of 1615 to hear thirteen articles governing how a samurai should live. His son, the reigning shogun Hidetada, formally issued them soon after. The rules covered marriage, mandatory attendance in Edo, and even which castles a daimyo was permitted to keep standing.

None of it was really about archery or etiquette. Restricting inter-domain marriages closed off the alliances that had let regional lords challenge the centre in earlier generations, and limits on fortifications meant fewer places from which to make a stand. The code became the legal skeleton of the bakuhan system, the division of authority between shogunate and domains that structured Japan for the next two and a half centuries.

Before it became a byword for Islamic learning, Bukhara was a Buddhist city. The first Arab commander to reach it described a place of Buddhist monasteries ruled by a queen regent, and its conversion to Islam was gradual rather than a single conquest.

Its reputation as a centre of scholarship came later still, under the Samanid dynasty from the ninth century, when the city's position on the Silk Road funded libraries and drew scholars from across Persia. That wealth had begun long before, in the caravan trade the city's location on the route had already secured.

Russia had drawn up a sweeping Bulgarian state in the Treaty of San Stefano, and the other great powers spent the Congress of Berlin taking most of it back. What remained after July 1878 was a vassal principality, still nominally answering to the Ottoman sultan but running its own constitution, flag and foreign policy in practice.

South of the mountains, a separate province called Eastern Rumelia stayed under direct Ottoman administration. Bulgarians reunited the two through a bloodless uprising in 1885, which Constantinople chose to accept rather than fight, well before Bulgaria declared full independence in 1908.

Aung San did not live to see the country he had negotiated free. On 19 July 1947 gunmen burst into a cabinet meeting in Rangoon's Secretariat Building and shot him along with eight of his colleagues, six months before the independence he had spent his life pursuing took effect on 4 January 1948.

Burma also made a choice few other former colonies made at that moment: it left the Commonwealth entirely rather than remain a dominion under the crown. Clement Attlee's government told parliament it regretted the decision, but the Burma Independence Act had already been drafted to allow for a country outside the King's dominions.

It began with a fuel bill, not a slogan. On 15 August 2007, Myanmar's junta abruptly cut fuel subsidies, doubling diesel prices overnight and driving compressed gas prices up fivefold. Small protests followed, but the movement only widened after soldiers beat monks demonstrating in the town of Pakokku on 5 September and the regime refused to apologise.

Monks responded by refusing religious services to the military and its families, a rejection with real weight in a devoutly Buddhist country. Marches swelled to tens of thousands through Yangon by late September, until troops raided monasteries, cut internet access and detained close to three thousand people, ending the protests within weeks.

Pagan's kingdom, which had unified upper Burma for two and a half centuries, broke apart under Mongol pressure around 1297. What followed was not a single successor state but several rival ones jostling in the same territory: the Myinsaing and Pinya kingdoms first, then Sagaing from 1315, all contesting the same central plain.

None of them reunified what Pagan had ruled. That took the Toungoo dynasty, founded further south, whose kings Tabinshwehti and Bayinnaung did not restore Pagan's old borders until the sixteenth century, and then pushed well beyond them, into territory stretching from Assam and Manipur to the Cambodian frontier.

Napoleon expected Moscow's governor to hand him the keys to a stocked, sheltering city. Instead the fires began within a day of the French occupation in mid September 1812, and burned for four days. Historians still argue over how deliberate it was, but the governor, Fyodor Rostopchin, had ordered the fire brigades removed before he left.

Roughly two thirds of the city's residential buildings were destroyed, along with hundreds of churches, though enough structures survived that a French general judged there was still room for the whole army. What Moscow lacked was food and forage. Napoleon waited five weeks among the ruins before abandoning the city in October, starting the retreat that broke his army.

In the hills between Lake Tanganyika and the Nile watershed, a kingdom formed around a single office: the mwami, a sacred king credited with control over rain and fertility as much as territory. Burundi's early rulers built authority less through conquest than through this ritual role, binding hill chiefs to the throne by ceremony and cattle tribute rather than garrisons.

The kingdom's clan structure separated herding and farming groups into layered, sometimes tense social ranks, a division later colonial administrations would treat as fixed ethnicity rather than the fluid political categories they had actually been. The mwami's court, not any written law, was the institution that held the hierarchy together.

Caesar's first crossing in 55 BC nearly failed at the beach. His legionaries hesitated to jump into deep water under British spears until, by one account, the standard bearer of the Tenth Legion leapt in first rather than let the eagle fall into enemy hands. Storms then wrecked part of his fleet, and after a few weeks with little gained he withdrew, though Rome still granted him twenty days of public thanksgiving.

He returned the following year with 800 ships and five legions, pushed inland across the Thames, and beat the British leader Cassivellaunus, who had staked the riverbank against him. Cassivellaunus agreed to pay tribute and Caesar left a client king, Mandubracius, in charge of the Trinovantes. No Roman garrison stayed behind; actual conquest waited another century, for Claudius.

James Marshall spotted flecks of metal in the tailrace of a sawmill he was building for John Sutter on 24 January 1848, and tried at first to keep it quiet. Word got out anyway, and by 1849 close to ninety thousand people had crossed oceans, deserts and mountain passes to reach the diggings, splitting almost evenly between sea and overland routes.

San Francisco grew from roughly a thousand residents to twenty-five thousand within two years, and the territory drafted a state constitution before Congress had even settled how new land should divide over slavery. For the Native peoples of California the migration brought displacement, disease and killing on a scale some historians now call genocide.

Ali ibn Abi Talib was struck on the head with a poisoned sword while leading morning prayers at the Great Mosque of Kufa on 28 January 661. He died of the wound two days later, in his early sixties. His attacker, a Kharijite named Ibn Muljam, was seized at the scene by a bystander before he could escape.

The Kharijites had broken with Ali years earlier and were crushed by his forces at the Battle of Nahrawan in 658, and the killing was revenge for that defeat rather than a spontaneous act. Ali's son Hasan briefly succeeded him but ceded the caliphate to the Syrian governor Muawiya within months, ending the line of rulers later tradition calls the Rightly Guided Caliphs.

A caravan crossing the Sahara typically ran to about a thousand camels, though the largest reported numbers reached twelve thousand animals moving together. None of them carried enough water for the whole journey, so guides went ahead to arrange supplies at each oasis, and highly paid Berber navigators kept the caravan on course and away from raiders.

Gold from West African fields like Bambuk travelled north as dust, bars and blank discs, struck into coin only once it reached cities like Sijilmasa. Salt moved the other way, mined at Taghaza and sold in the south at prices that, at Timbuktu, ran close to weight for weight against the gold it was traded for.

Anwar Sadat and Menachem Begin spent thirteen days at Jimmy Carter's presidential retreat in Maryland, from 5 to 17 September 1978, in talks so tense that Carter reportedly kept the two leaders apart for much of it and shuttled between their cabins himself.

The result was two framework agreements, one sketching a broader Middle East settlement and one specifically for Egypt and Israel, signed at the White House. The bilateral framework led directly to the Egypt-Israel peace treaty the following March. Sadat and Begin shared the 1978 Nobel Peace Prize, though much of the Arab world condemned Egypt for negotiating alone.

Canute's claim to England was not inherited but fought for. He landed at Sandwich in 1015 with roughly 200 ships and spent fourteen months harrying Wessex and Mercia before the decisive Battle of Assandun on 18 October 1016, where an English commander's withdrawal mid-battle helped decide the day against Edmund Ironside.

Canute and the wounded Edmund then met on an island near Deerhurst to divide the kingdom, Canute taking the north and Edmund the south, with the whole to pass to Canute on Edmund's death. Edmund died weeks later, on 30 November, and Canute was crowned in London the following year, later adding Denmark and Norway to his rule.

The Carolingian line had not run out of heirs when Hugh Capet became king in 987. A cousin, Charles of Lower Lorraine, was still alive and had a claim, but he had made himself a vassal of the German emperor and the great lords of France would not accept him. Meeting at Senlis after King Louis V died childless, they chose Hugh instead, on the argument that a throne need not pass by blood alone.

Hugh was crowned twice within five weeks, at Noyon on 1 June and again at Paris on 3 July. That same year he had his own son Robert crowned as co-king, a precaution against exactly the kind of disputed succession that had just put him on the throne. The house he founded held the French crown, through cadet branches, for close to nine centuries.

Timur made Samarkand his capital and filled it with craftsmen forcibly resettled from cities across his empire, spared for their skill and brought in to build and decorate it. The city sat astride the Silk Road linking China, Persia and Europe, and its wealth depended on caravans passing through safely.

Keeping that traffic moving meant maintaining stopping points along the roads into the city, where merchants, animals and goods could rest under guard between stages of a long journey. Samarkand's markets grew rich largely on tolls and resale rather than on manufacturing everything that passed through them.

Junior army officers of the Armed Forces Movement, exhausted by colonial wars in Angola, Mozambique and Guinea, moved against Marcelo Caetano's government before dawn on 25 April 1974. Almost no one fired a shot, and by the following day the dictatorship that Antonio de Oliveira Salazar had built decades earlier was finished.

Restaurant worker Celeste Caeiro handed out carnations from a delivery meant for a café anniversary, and soldiers pushed the flowers into their rifle barrels as crowds filled the streets, which is where the revolution took its name. It was not entirely bloodless: security police fired on a crowd outside their Lisbon headquarters, killing four people, in the coup's only serious violence.

Stalin was invited to the January 1943 meeting at the Anfa Hotel but stayed in Moscow, telling Roosevelt and Churchill that the fighting still raging at Stalingrad needed his attention more than a hotel in French Morocco did. Free French rivals Charles de Gaulle and Henri Giraud were brought together there too, photographed shaking hands for cameras neither man much wanted to face.

It was here that Roosevelt announced the Allies would accept nothing short of unconditional surrender from Germany, Italy and Japan, a policy meant to prevent any postwar claim that the Axis had merely been talked into a truce. Churchill later said he was startled the phrase became public at all, since the two leaders had discussed the idea privately without settling on how, or whether, to say it aloud.

Daniel O'Connell forced the issue by winning a County Clare by-election in 1828 that he legally could not take his seat from, since Catholics were barred from Parliament by oath. His Catholic Association had organised rent collections and rallies drawing crowds in the tens of thousands, and the government feared what refusing him might trigger in Ireland.

The Duke of Wellington, no friend of Catholic rights, pushed the Act through anyway in 1829 and even threatened to resign over it, judging civil unrest the greater danger. Robert Peel, once nicknamed Orange Peel for his opposition, backed him. The same Parliament raised Irish voting property qualifications, cutting the Catholic electorate it had just enfranchised.

Philadelphia's Fairmount Park hosted the exhibition from 10 May to 10 November 1876, the first World's Fair on American soil and timed to mark a century of independence. Close to ten million visitors walked through its halls before it closed.

Alexander Graham Bell demonstrated his telephone across the length of Machinery Hall, and visitors met Heinz ketchup and Hires root beer for the first time. The arm and torch of an unfinished Statue of Liberty stood on display too, with admission fees going toward paying for its pedestal back in New York.

Sweden already had a bank, and it had just failed. Stockholms Banco, founded in 1656 by Johan Palmstruch, had issued far more paper notes than it held in reserve, collapsed, and left its founder sentenced to death, later commuted. The lesson shaped what replaced it.

In September 1668 the Riksdag transferred Palmstruch's banking privilege to a new institution, the Bank of the Estates of the Realm, placed under parliamentary rather than royal control precisely to prevent the abuses that had sunk its predecessor. That accountability to the state, not the size of its vaults, is what later histories point to when they call it the first central bank.

When Genghis Khan died in 1227, his second son Chagatai received a vast stretch of Central Asia running from the Tarim Basin to the Chu and Talas rivers. It looked like a kingdom of his own, one of four carved out for Genghis Khan's sons and grandsons.

It was not fully his to run. Chagatai still answered to the central Mongol court at Karakorum, and the limits of that arrangement showed plainly: when he dismissed a regional governor he judged unfit, the Great Khan simply reinstated the man over his objection. The khanate that bore his name outlived him, but his own authority over it never stopped being borrowed.

Before the Mongol conquests, a merchant crossing Central Asia faced a different toll collector and a different danger every few days, since no single power held the routes for long. The Chagatai Khanate, ruling the stretch between China and Persia by the 1240s, changed that by policing its own section of road.

Mongol control did not create the Silk Road, but it made the roads themselves safer and the tolls along them more predictable, a state of affairs later writers called the Pax Mongolica. Goods, envoys and eventually plague moved through Chagatai lands on their way between the Mongol courts of China and the Mongol courts of Persia and beyond.

Pulakeshin I took the hill fort of Vatapi, now Badami in Karnataka, in 543 and made it his capital rather than building anew. From there his successors pushed the Chalukya frontier from the Kaveri river in the south to the Narmada in the north, absorbing most of modern Karnataka and Andhra Pradesh.

Pulakeshin II carried that expansion furthest and then lost it. In 642 the Pallava king Narasimhavarman marched on Vatapi itself and occupied it, and Pulakeshin II is thought to have died in the fighting. The dynasty recovered under his successors, who eventually pushed the Pallavas back out of Chalukya territory.

Champa's ports on the central Vietnamese coast drew traders moving spices, silk, ivory and aloewood between the Indian Ocean and the South China Sea, and its ships were as ready to raid a rival cargo as to carry their own. Javanese fleets attacked Cham ports repeatedly in the 8th century before being driven off.

The kingdom's deeper rivalry was with its neighbours on land. The Khmer Empire fought Champa repeatedly even as the two traded and intermarried, and Dai Viet to the north pressed steadily southward for centuries, a pressure that eventually broke Champa's northern territories in a decisive invasion in 1471.

No single town held the Champagne fairs. Six of them, including Troyes, Provins, Bar sur Aube and Lagny sur Marne, took turns hosting a cycle of markets that ran almost the whole year, each lasting two or three weeks before the merchants packed up and moved to the next.

Italian money changers followed the circuit and turned it into something more than a market for wool and spices: a clearing house where debts contracted in one town could be settled in another, an early form of the bill of exchange. The cycle held for more than a century, until France annexed Champagne in 1285 and Italian ships began sailing straight to Flanders instead.

A six-metre iron pillar still standing near Delhi carries an inscription praising a king named Chandra for crossing the Indus in battle and defeating a confederacy of enemies. Most historians read that king as Chandragupta II, whose Gupta empire by 380 stretched from the Oxus in the west to Bengal in the east.

His campaigns pushed the Gupta frontier to the Arabian Sea after he defeated the Western Kshatrapa rulers who had held the coast for generations. Court poets, astronomers and grammarians worked under his patronage, though the label 'golden age' for his reign is a verdict later historians attached, not one his own court used.

When Pepin the Short died in 768, the Frankish kingdom did not pass to one heir but to two. Charlemagne was crowned at Noyon and his younger brother Carloman at Soissons on the same October day, and for three years the brothers ruled jointly, each holding separate Frankish territories rather than sharing one throne.

That arrangement ended when Carloman died suddenly in December 771. Charlemagne moved at once to take control of his brother's lands rather than let them pass to Carloman's young sons, and from that point ruled the Franks alone, the position from which he built an empire across most of Western Europe.

When Maximilian I died in 1519, the imperial title went to election by seven German princes rather than by inheritance, and Charles stood against Francis I of France and even Henry VIII of England for it. He won on 28 June 1519, helped by heavy payments to the electors arranged through the Fugger banking house.

Frederick of Saxony, an elector himself and briefly a candidate, turned the contest by declining the crown and speaking for Charles instead, arguing that only a ruler of Charles's resources could resist the Ottomans. The election joined Spain, the Netherlands, Austria and the Empire under one crown, though coronation as emperor still lay ahead.

Charles's claim to Spain ran through his mother, Joanna of Castile, who was still alive when her father Ferdinand II of Aragon died in January 1516. Rather than wait, Charles had himself proclaimed king jointly with Joanna, an awkward arrangement given her legal claim, and the Castilian parliament at Valladolid only grudgingly accepted it in 1518.

He was sixteen and had grown up in the Netherlands, barely speaking Castilian when he arrived to take up the crown. The union of Aragon and Castile his grandparents Ferdinand and Isabella had built now passed to a Habsburg who would, within three years, add the Holy Roman Empire to his titles as well.

Organisers billed the gathering, on 11 and 12 August 2017, as a protest against the city's plan to remove a statue of Robert E. Lee, and drew together white nationalist and neo-Nazi groups from across the country. Clashes with counter-protesters filled the streets around Emancipation Park through the Saturday, before the crowds were ordered to disperse.

That afternoon a 20 year old Ohio man, James Alex Fields Jr, drove his car into a crowd of counter-protesters several blocks away, killing 32 year old Heather Heyer and injuring 35 others. Fields was convicted of first degree murder in December 2018 and pleaded guilty to federal hate crime charges the following year, receiving two consecutive life sentences.

No inscription records a founding day for Chichen Itza. What survives points instead to a gradual rise: local Maya communities in northern Yucatan had built up the site by around 600, well before the group later called the Itza arrived and folded themselves into it around 800.

The name itself carries a trace of that later arrival. Itza is thought to mean something close to those who speak the language imperfectly, a label the earlier inhabitants gave to newcomers who eventually reshaped the city. Its earliest dated hieroglyphic inscription belongs to 832, by which point the core of the site was already taking the shape that would make it a regional power.

Chile's independence was declared on 12 February 1818, but the date on the document mattered less than the army that could defend it. Bernardo O'Higgins had led the Patria Vieja resistance years earlier; it took Jose de San Martin marching an army across the Andes from Argentina to give the declaration any teeth.

That army was tested at Maipu on 5 April 1818, when patriot forces broke the last major royalist push against central Chile. Spain refused to recognise any of it for another quarter century, and pockets of royalist resistance in the south held out until 1827, but Maipu is what made the February declaration stick rather than read as another failed attempt.

For seventeen days after the San Jose mine collapsed on 5 August 2010, nobody on the surface knew whether the 33 men below were alive. Contact came only when a drill bit broke through to a refuge chamber and rescuers pulled it back up to find a note taped to the end: we are well in the shelter, all 33 of us.

Reaching them took another two months of drilling a rescue shaft narrow enough to fit a purpose-built steel capsule, the Fenix 2, barely half a metre across. Each man rode it up alone at about a metre a second, and roughly 5.3 million people worldwide watched the extraction stream live as, one by one, all 33 surfaced after 69 days underground.

Oral tradition gives the Chimu kingdom a single founder, Taycanamo, said to have arrived by raft on Peru's northern coast around 900 and settled the Moche Valley. His descendants built Chan Chan, which grew into the largest city made of adobe anywhere in the Americas.

Chan Chan held roughly thirty thousand people inside ten walled royal compounds, some enclosed by adobe walls nine metres high. Most residents lived in neighbourhoods outside those compounds, a layout that separated the ruling lineages' quarters from the rest of the city.

For over two decades the Republic of China on Taiwan held China's seat at the United Nations, even as the Communist government in Beijing controlled the mainland. Albania led a group of seventeen member states pressing to correct what they called an anomaly rather than a genuine representation of China.

On 25 October 1971, the General Assembly adopted Resolution 2758, recognising the People's Republic of China as the sole legitimate representative of China and expelling the Taipei delegation. Beijing took both the Assembly seat and the permanent seat on the Security Council, a shift several NATO members and non-aligned states had voted to support.

Getting into the World Trade Organization took China fifteen years of negotiation, longer than almost any other member's application. Talks stalled repeatedly over tariffs, state subsidies and market access, and Beijing had to agree to cut import duties on hundreds of categories of goods before members would sign off.

Membership took effect on 11 December 2001. Foreign firms gained new rights to sell directly into Chinese markets and Chinese exporters gained protection from arbitrary tariffs abroad, a trade that reshaped global manufacturing over the following decade far more than either side had projected at the signing.

The law President Chester Arthur signed on 6 May 1882 did more than pause immigration. It barred Chinese labourers, skilled and unskilled, including miners, and required Chinese residents already in the country to carry identity certificates or face deportation. It also closed off naturalisation to Chinese immigrants, making race rather than conduct the test for citizenship.

Congress wrote it as a ten-year measure, but renewed it repeatedly, then made it permanent in 1902. It stayed in force for sixty-one years, longer than anyone who voted for it in 1882 likely expected, until the 1943 Magnuson Act repealed it during wartime alliance with China. Even then the replacement allowed only 105 Chinese immigrants a year.

Paper money began as a private workaround, not a government idea. Sichuan merchants issued promissory notes to avoid hauling the region's heavy iron coins, and only in 1023 did the Song state take the business over for itself, printing standardised notes the following year.

State control did not fix the problem it was meant to solve. Without enough coin reserves behind the notes, their value collapsed. By 1204 a note worth a thousand coins on paper was fetching as few as a hundred, and officials kept stamping fresh seals to slow counterfeiting.

An inscription at Uttaramerur, first cut under the earlier king Parantaka I and maintained under later Chola rule, lays out rules for electing a village council: candidates had to be landowning, versed in scripture, aged between thirty-five and seventy, and disqualified by an unaudited account from an earlier term.

Names went in as palm-leaf tickets inside a pot, and a child drew them out at the assembly while the results were read aloud and confirmed by everyone present, a method called the kudavolai system. The council then split into standing committees overseeing irrigation tanks, farmland and the local gold trade.

Vijayalaya was a minor noble from a branch of the old Chola line that had spent three centuries under the thumb of the Pallava and Pandya kings. Around the mid ninth century he seized the town of Thanjavur, a modest local power grab that later chroniclers treated as the dynasty's rebirth.

The maritime empire came generations later. Vijayalaya's descendants Rajaraja I and Rajendra I built the navy that raided Sri Lanka, the Maldives and the Srivijaya ports of Sumatra in the eleventh century, turning an inland warrior lineage into the dominant sea power of the Bay of Bengal.

Rajendra Chola I did not send his fleet to trade. In 1025 it struck Srivijaya's ports directly, taking Kedah, Pannai and the strategic strait city of Tumasik, now Singapore, and capturing Sangrama Vijayatunggavarman, the last ruler of Srivijaya's Sailendra dynasty, along the way.

Srivijaya survived the raid but not its grip on the sea lanes. Tamil merchant guilds moved into trade routes that Malay traders had long controlled, and the balance of maritime power in Southeast Asia shifted toward Indian influence for the following century.

Before Khosrow I, seven Parthian noble families collected Sassanid taxes locally and kept the empire's income unpredictable. He surveyed the land under his rule and replaced their patchwork with a single land tax based on water rights, plus a graded poll tax on everyone between twenty and fifty who was not noble, soldier or priest.

The same reforms opened the elite cavalry to the lower nobility, the dehqans, multiplying the trained horsemen he could field. In 532 he agreed an Eternal Peace with Justinian that paid Persia 11,000 pounds of gold, but by 540 he had broken it, sacked Antioch, and pulled the two empires into decades more war.

Khosrow II came to the Sassanid throne in 590, lost it within a year to the general Bahram Chobin, and had to be restored to it with Byzantine help. Once secure, he turned that debt into war: from 602 his generals Shahrbaraz and Shahin took Damascus, Jerusalem and Egypt from Byzantium and pushed Persian territory further west than it had reached in centuries.

The reversal came fast. The Byzantine emperor Heraclius rebuilt his army, broke the Sassanids at Nineveh in 627, and marched on the Persian heartland. Facing collapse, Khosrow's own nobles turned on him, and his son Sheroe had him deposed and executed in 628, ending the war on Byzantine terms.

Truman had already dissolved the wartime Office of Strategic Services in September 1945, scattering its intelligence functions between the State and War Departments in an arrangement nobody found workable. The National Security Act he signed on 26 July 1947 rebuilt a peacetime foreign intelligence service from that wreckage and gave it a name, creating the Department of Defense and the National Security Council alongside it.

The new agency's mandate was deliberately vague, authorising it to perform other functions related to intelligence as the National Security Council might direct, a clause later stretched to cover covert operations far beyond the analysis work Congress had mainly discussed. Within a decade it was running coups and paramilitary campaigns overseas that its founding statute never named.

Southern senators held the floor for 54 working days trying to talk the bill to death, Robert Byrd alone speaking for fourteen straight hours. Senator Richard Russell said openly that his side would resist to the end any measure bringing about what he called social equality. On 10 June 1964 the Senate voted 71 to 29 to cut off debate, the first time cloture had ever succeeded against a civil rights filibuster.

President Lyndon Johnson signed the bill on 2 July 1964, weeks after the vote that broke the filibuster. It reached that point only through a bipartisan rewrite led by Senators Mansfield, Humphrey, Dirksen and Kuchel, which pulled in enough Republican votes to survive the Southern bloc. The law banned segregation in public accommodations and schools, and discrimination in hiring.

By 48 BC Cleopatra had already lost a civil war to her brother Ptolemy XIII and fled Alexandria. Julius Caesar arrived in Egypt chasing his rival Pompey, and she saw her opening: rather than send envoys, she went to see Caesar in person, gambling everything on one meeting.

The gamble paid off. Caesar backed her against Ptolemy XIII, and after reinforcements reached Egypt in early 47 BC, her brother was defeated and drowned fleeing the fighting. Caesar then installed her younger brother Ptolemy XIV as her nominal co-ruler, leaving Cleopatra as Egypt's real power.

Cleopatra came to power in 51 BC not alone but as joint heir with her younger brother Ptolemy XIII, as their father Ptolemy XII's will required. The arrangement did not survive contact with either sibling's ambition: within months, official documents had quietly dropped his name and listed her as sole ruler.

That erasure provoked the court faction around Ptolemy XIII, led by the eunuch Potheinos and the general Achillas, into open opposition. The quarrel between brother and sister would eventually draw in Rome itself, but its origin was a will meant to share power that neither party intended to honour.

Bruges, Ghent and Ypres grew rich on wool nobody in Flanders grew. English fleeces crossed the Channel, and Flemish weavers turned them into cloth so consistently fine that the three towns, not the farms that supplied the raw fibre, came to dominate the trade. By the mid 13th century a resident merchant elite ran the business end.

The guilds that organised weavers, fullers and dyers set standards for cloth width and quality and controlled who could train and work in the trade. That grip on production was not uncontested: the decades after 1250 saw repeated unrest among the labourers who did the weaving but had no guild seat, unrest that erupted into general strikes across Flemish cities in 1280 and 1281.

A group of industrialists, scientists and civil servants calling themselves the Club of Rome commissioned researchers at MIT to build a computer model tracking population, food output, industrial growth, pollution and the stock of nonrenewable resources against each other. The resulting book, published in March 1972, modelled these as feeding back on one another rather than growing in isolation.

The team's central finding was that if the trends of the 1970s continued unchanged, the world would run into hard limits within about a century, causing an abrupt fall in both population and industrial output. They were careful to call this a tendency rather than a prophecy, and argued the outcome could still be avoided by deliberately stabilising both population and capital.

The French civil code took effect on 21 March 1804, replacing a patchwork of feudal, royal and regional law that varied from one province to the next. It banned secret and retroactive statutes, required judges to apply the written law rather than invent new rules from the bench, and was drafted in plain French rather than the Latin of earlier codes.

Napoleon carried the code into the territories his armies occupied, and it outlasted his empire: versions of it still underpin the law of France, Belgium, the Netherlands, Louisiana and much of Latin America. Romania kept a Napoleonic-derived code in force until 2011.

Nobody in Europe had eaten a tomato, a potato or a chilli pepper before 1492, and nobody in the Americas had ridden a horse or kept a chicken. Columbus's crossing opened a two-way traffic in crops, animals and microbes that neither continent had ever exchanged before, reshaping diets on both sides of the Atlantic.

Maize and potatoes travelled east and helped feed population growth across Afro-Eurasia for centuries afterward, while horses, cattle and pigs travelled west and remade how Indigenous peoples hunted, farmed and fought. The same ships also carried smallpox and measles, and those diseases killed far more people than the crops ever fed.

Smallpox, measles and influenza needed no soldiers to do their work. Old World pathogens moved ahead of most European settlers, striking populations that had never encountered them and had no accumulated immunity to draw on, so a single outbreak could outrun any army sent behind it.

On Hispaniola alone, a population estimated at half a million or more before contact had fallen to under five hundred people by 1526. Historians put the total loss across the Americas at somewhere between eighty and ninety five percent of the pre contact population within a century and a half, the deadliest sustained die-off on record.

Japan's Tokugawa shogunate had spent two centuries under sakoku, a policy that restricted foreign trade to a single port and a handful of Dutch and Chinese merchants, largely to keep Christianity and outside wealth from unsettling its rule. Perry had first appeared off the coast in 1853 with a show of naval force and left a demand for a reply within the year.

He returned in February 1854 with eight warships, and on 31 March signed the Convention of Kanagawa at what is now Yokohama. Its twelve articles opened two ports to American ships, guaranteed aid to shipwrecked sailors, and promised the United States any terms Japan later granted another power, a small opening that widened fast.

Six separate British colonies, each with its own parliament, tariffs and railway gauge, spent the 1890s arguing over how much power a shared government should hold. Referendums settled the terms, and on 1 January 1901 the Commonwealth of Australia Constitution was proclaimed at Centennial Park in Sydney.

Edmund Barton was sworn in as interim prime minister that day, leading a ministry of nine before any election had been held. Federation kept the colonies as states inside a new bicameral parliament, with a governor-general representing the monarch, rather than dissolving them into one unified administration.

Henry Clay put five bills before the Senate in January 1850, and it was Stephen Douglas who broke them apart and steered each through Congress after Clay's health failed. California entered as a free state, ending Southern hopes of a slave-state belt to the Pacific, while Texas gave up its claim to New Mexico in return for the federal government taking on its debt.

New Mexico and Utah were organised on popular sovereignty, letting settlers vote on slavery rather than have Congress decide, and the slave trade, though not slaveholding itself, was banned in Washington. The compromise's sharpest edge was a strengthened Fugitive Slave Act, which denied accused runaways the right to testify and made helping them a federal crime.

No single document created it. The Concert of Europe grew out of the Congress of Vienna as an understanding among Austria, Britain, Prussia, Russia and later France that the great powers would settle disputes through conferences rather than let any one state upset the borders just redrawn. Its other purpose was blunter: putting down the liberal and nationalist uprisings that kept breaking out across the continent.

It never had fixed rules or a secretariat, just a habit of meeting when a crisis threatened to spiral, and historians argue over exactly when it stopped working. A first phase held roughly until the 1860s; a looser version limped on through rising nationalism and rigid alliance blocs until 1914, when a crisis in the Balkans finally proved too large for any congress to manage.

For fifty years popes and emperors had fought over a single question: who could appoint a bishop. Reformist popes, Gregory VII foremost among them, argued that a secular ruler had no authority to hand a churchman the ring and staff that marked his office. Emperors had done exactly that for generations, treating bishoprics as posts to reward loyal men.

Pope Callixtus II and Emperor Henry V settled it at Worms on 23 September 1122. Henry gave up the right to invest clergy with ring and crosier, leaving that to the Church, but kept a hand in elections and could still grant a bishop his temporal lands with a sceptre, a separate and later ceremony. The papal side put it plainly: the Church would have what belonged to Christ, and the emperor what belonged to him.

Bismarck hosted the other great powers in his own chancellery for a month in the summer of 1878, chairing a congress called to undo a treaty Russia had just imposed on the Ottomans. Delegates from Britain, France, Austria Hungary and Russia argued over a map of the Balkans that none of them agreed on.

The result dismantled the large Bulgarian state Russia had carved out, splitting it into a smaller principality and a separate autonomous province. Austria Hungary took charge of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Britain gained Cyprus, and Balkan nationalists who felt cheated of promised territory carried the grievance for decades.

Delegates from across Europe gathered in Vienna from September 1814 to redraw the map after Napoleon's abdication, and Austria's foreign minister Metternich ran the show. France arrived defeated and largely excluded, yet Talleyrand talked his way into the inner circle anyway, playing the great powers off one another until France had a seat at the real decisions.

Then, in March 1815, Napoleon escaped Elba and marched on Paris. The delegates kept negotiating anyway, and the Final Act was signed on 9 June, nine days before Waterloo settled the matter for good. Between sessions there were enough balls and banquets that one Austrian diplomat is remembered for joking that the congress danced rather than worked.

Until 1982, changing Canada's constitution still meant asking the British parliament to do it. Ottawa and every province but Quebec reached a deal in November 1981, in a late-night meeting known afterward as the Kitchen Accord, on a formula for amending the constitution at home and a charter of rights to go with it.

The British parliament passed the Canada Act in March 1982, ending its own authority over Canadian law, and Queen Elizabeth II signed the Constitution Act into force in Ottawa on 17 April 1982. Quebec's government, under Rene Levesque, never signed on, a refusal that still shapes arguments over the province's place in the federation.

When Muhammad arrived in Medina in 622, the city held Muslim migrants from Mecca, local converts, pagan Arab clans and several Jewish tribes, none bound to the others by blood or prior loyalty. The document he drew up made membership a matter of shared commitment rather than kinship, naming the signatories one community regardless of tribe.

Its terms let each group keep its own faith and law: for the Jews their religion, for the Muslims theirs, while requiring joint defence of the city and peaceful arbitration of disputes rather than the customary tribal retaliation. Muhammad sat as arbiter over the whole arrangement, a role no single clan chief in Medina had previously held.

The delegates who met at Pennsylvania's State House from late May 1787 were supposed to be revising the Articles of Confederation, not replacing them. Within days they had agreed to start over. Windows were nailed shut against the summer heat to keep the debates from leaking out, and no official transcript survives beyond a secretary's sparse minutes.

George Washington presided over roughly fifty-five delegates, though attendance on any given day was closer to thirty. Rhode Island sent nobody. James Madison's own notes, the fullest record of what was argued inside that sealed room, stayed unpublished until after his death in 1836. Thirty-nine of the fifty-five delegates present signed the finished Constitution on 17 September.

Roman jurists sorted binding agreements into four kinds, distinguished by what actually made them enforceable. A verbal contract needed a spoken formula, an exact question and answer called stipulatio. A literal contract rested on an entry in an account book. A real contract required something to actually change hands, as with a loan.

The fourth kind, consensual contracts, needed nothing but agreement itself, and covered the transactions people relied on daily: sale, hire, partnership, and instructing an agent to act on one's behalf. That last category, requiring no ceremony and nothing physical to be handed over, proved the most durable, carrying directly into the contract law of later European codes.

Emperor Constantine convened the bishops at Nicaea in 325 not out of theological conviction but to stop a quarrel splitting his newly unified church. The Alexandrian priest Arius had been teaching that Christ the Son was created by God the Father and therefore not equal to him or eternal, a position that had already caused riots in Egypt.

Roughly two to three hundred bishops attended, and the council sided against Arius, declaring the Son consubstantial with the Father in a creed that anathematised anyone who said there was a time before Christ existed. Arius was exiled, but his teaching outlived the verdict, resurfacing among Germanic kingdoms for centuries afterward.

No bishop from the Western church sat in the Church of Hagia Irene when roughly 150 Eastern bishops gathered there in 381. Theodosius I had called them together to settle disputes Nicaea had left open, and by July they had expanded the Nicene Creed with a fuller statement on the Holy Spirit as giver of life, worshipped alongside Father and Son.

The bishops condemned Arianism, Macedonianism and Apollinarianism in the same sittings, and threw out the contested appointment of Maximus as bishop of Constantinople. One of the council's seven canons also ranked Constantinople's bishop second in honour only to Rome's, a claim that unsettled relations with the older patriarchates for decades.

Cyril of Alexandria opened the council in June 431 before John of Antioch's delegation had even reached the city. Sixty-eight bishops walked in to protest the early start, and Cyril answered by having an imperial decree read out and accepted as covering the proceedings. Nestorius, patriarch of Constantinople, was tried in his absence.

The gathered bishops rejected Nestorius's separation of Christ's human and divine natures and stripped him of his office. They ruled that Mary should be called Theotokos, God-bearer, rather than the narrower title Nestorius preferred. John of Antioch's delegation, arriving late, held its own rival session and condemned Cyril in turn before Rome's legates backed the original council.

Byzantine emperor John VIII Palaiologos travelled to Italy in person, hoping Western military help against the advancing Ottomans could be bought with a reunion of the churches. Negotiations moved from Ferrara to Florence, working through disputes over purgatory, papal primacy and the filioque clause that had divided Rome and Constantinople for centuries.

On 6 July 1439 both sides signed the decree Laetentur Caeli, declaring the schism over. It did not survive the journey home: Constantinople's clergy and public accused the emperor and patriarch of betrayal, and the union was never accepted in the Orthodox east. When the Ottomans took Constantinople fourteen years later, Sultan Mehmed II put anti-union clergy in charge of what remained of the church.

Before 149 BC, prosecuting a Roman official meant convening a special tribunal or bringing the case before the whole popular assembly, a process cumbersome enough that provincial governors who plundered their territories rarely faced it. A tribune named Lucius Calpurnius Piso Frugi changed that with a law creating a standing court just for extortion cases.

The quaestio de repetundis stayed open permanently, and any citizen could bring a charge without waiting on a magistrate to act. The model spread: within a few generations Rome had separate standing courts for treason, election bribery and violence, a system that lasted into the third century AD before falling out of use.

The shells that became money across West Africa had travelled further than almost any coin. Collected off the Maldive Islands, Sri Lanka and the Malabar coast, cowries moved westward along Indian Ocean trade routes for centuries before European ships began carrying them across the Sahara and down the Atlantic coast in bulk.

After the 1500s the volume exploded, driven largely by the slave trade, which used cowries as a currency to purchase captives and goods alike. Their value rested on scarcity and the fact that, until counterfeiters learned to fake them in the nineteenth century, a cowrie could not easily be forged. Some British colonial administrations still accepted them for tax payments into the twentieth century.

Cyprus's National Guard, backed by the military government in Athens, overthrew Archbishop Makarios in July 1974 and installed a president who favoured union with Greece. Turkey, citing its status as a guarantor power under a 1960 treaty, invaded five days later to protect the Turkish Cypriot minority, and by mid August its forces held over a third of the island.

Roughly 160,000 Greek Cypriots fled or were driven from the north and around 51,000 Turkish Cypriots moved the other way, resettling in the territory Turkey now held. A United Nations buffer zone drawn across the island that year still separates the two communities, and repeated rounds of talks have failed to reunify them.

The clay cylinder was buried as a foundation deposit under a temple wall in Babylon and stayed there until Hormuzd Rassam dug it up for the British Museum in 1879. Its cuneiform text is a building inscription in a familiar Mesopotamian form: it damns the deposed king Nabonidus, credits the god Marduk with choosing Cyrus, and describes his entry into the city and his restoration of temples and displaced peoples.

Calling it the first charter of human rights is a twentieth century reading. The Shah's government promoted that phrase in 1971, and a copy still sits at the United Nations, but most specialists treat it as a conventional royal inscription following a much older genre, not a legal or political declaration. What is not disputed is Cyrus's own claim to have returned exiled peoples and their gods to their homes.

A national committee in Prague declared independence on 28 October 1918, days before Austria-Hungary's collapse was even complete, betting correctly that the empire had no capacity left to stop them. Tomas Garrigue Masaryk, who had spent the war abroad lobbying Allied governments for exactly this outcome, returned to become the new state's first president on 14 November.

The republic joined Bohemia, Moravia and Slovak-speaking Slovakia into a single state that had never existed as one before, plus Carpathian Ruthenia in the east. Masaryk's wartime ally Edvard Benes, who had done much of the diplomatic groundwork in Paris, succeeded him as president in 1935.

The kingdom grew out of the Fon people on the Abomey Plateau, an offshoot of the older kingdom of Allada. Tradition credits an early ruler, Dakodonou, with securing land from local chiefs after killing one of them, and it was Houegbadja, ruling from around 1645, who is generally treated as the state's true founder, raiding and absorbing neighbouring towns from his base at Abomey.

Dahomey's real transformation came under King Agaja in the early eighteenth century, whose conquests of Allada in 1724 and the coastal port of Whydah in 1727 gave the kingdom direct access to the Atlantic and to the slave trade routes that ran through it. For decades afterward Dahomey paid tribute to the larger Oyo Empire to its east, not becoming fully independent until 1823.

Dahomey began as a fortified plateau town, Abomey, built up by King Houegbadja in the mid-1600s while he raided the smaller towns around it. His successors kept expanding on the same pattern, and by the time Agaja took the throne in 1708 the kingdom had the base to field a professional standing army rather than levies raised for a single campaign.

That army, some ten thousand strong, carried imported flintlock muskets and steel swords and was organised into wings and reserves rather than a single mass, an unusual level of discipline for the region. It let Dahomey conquer the coastal kingdoms of Allada and Whydah within the following two decades, cutting off their access to the Atlantic trade routes.

Ngo Quyen could not beat the Southern Han fleet in open water, so he planted iron tipped stakes across the Bach Dang riverbed and let the high tide hide them. Small boats then lured the invading warships upstream over the trap before the water began to fall.

As the tide dropped, the Han ships grounded on the stakes and broke apart within reach of the shore. Roughly half the fleet was killed or drowned, including its commander, and the Southern Han emperor abandoned the campaign. The following spring, Ngo Quyen crowned himself king at Co Loa.

Crowds had gathered around the Dalai Lama's summer palace in Lhasa in March 1959, fearing Chinese authorities meant to detain him after inviting him to a theatre performance without his usual guards. As the uprising around the palace turned violent, he left in disguise on 17 March, travelling by night over Himalayan passes toward the Indian border.

He crossed into India on 30 March and reached the town of Tezpur on 18 April 1959, then settled in the hill town of Dharamshala. There he formed a government in exile and rebuilt Tibetan institutions abroad, including monasteries, schools and a 1963 constitution modelled on the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, for a community of roughly eighty thousand refugees who eventually followed him.

Darius's own account, carved into the cliff at Bisotun, says that after Cambyses II died an impostor named Gaumata had taken the throne by posing as Cambyses's brother Bardiya. Darius and six fellow noblemen killed the pretender at a fortress called Sikayauvati in September 522 BC, and Darius took the crown. Historians treat much of that as Darius's justification for what may simply have been a seizure of power from Cyrus's line.

He spent his early reign putting down revolts across the empire before extending it further than any Achaemenid king before him, from Thrace in the west to the Indus valley in the east. His invasion of European Scythia around 513 BC gained little ground, and his attempt to punish Athens for aiding an Ionian revolt ended in defeat at Marathon in 490 BC, six years before his death.

The Bible says the Jebusites who held Jerusalem taunted David that even the blind and lame could keep him out, confident in their walls. He took the city anyway, according to the account by sending men up a water shaft into it. Nineteenth-century excavators found such a shaft and assumed it was David's route in; later study showed it is a natural fissure, not a tunnel dug by anyone.

Jerusalem belonged to neither the northern nor the southern Israelite tribes, which is likely why David wanted it: a captured city with no prior claimant could become his alone. He renamed it the City of David and, by tradition, later brought the Ark of the Covenant there, joining royal and religious authority in one place. Archaeology from this period is thin, so much of the story rests on the biblical text itself.

Signed on 8 February 1887, the law replaced tribal land held in common with individual parcels: 160 acres to a family head, 80 to a single adult, 40 to a minor, each held in trust for twenty-five years before the owner could sell. Congress framed it as a path to citizenship for Native Americans who took up farming, though citizenship itself was tied to abandoning tribal governance.

The parcels rarely matched the land or the people. Whatever acreage was left over after allotment, and there was usually a great deal, was declared surplus and opened to white settlers. Native landholding fell from roughly 138 million acres in 1887 to about 48 million by 1934, a loss of some 90 million acres, and left an estimated 90,000 people without any land at all.

Germany had defaulted on reparations payments, and in 1923 France and Belgium answered by occupying the Ruhr, Germany's industrial heartland, to seize goods directly. The crisis that followed helped drive German hyperinflation to its worst. An American committee chaired by the banker Charles G. Dawes was called in to break the deadlock rather than punish it further.

The plan Dawes produced, adopted in 1924, lowered Germany's annual payments and staggered them upward over five years, while a foreign loan, much of it raised on Wall Street, recapitalised the German central bank. It eased the crisis without settling the underlying sum owed, and by 1929 a second scheme, the Young Plan, replaced it.

Negotiators shut Slobodan Milosevic, Franjo Tudjman and Alija Izetbegovic inside Wright-Patterson Air Force Base near Dayton, Ohio, for three weeks in November 1995, refusing to let them leave until they had a deal. They initialled the agreement there on 21 November and signed it formally in Paris on 14 December, with Bill Clinton, Jacques Chirac and other leaders as witnesses.

The accord split Bosnia and Herzegovina into two entities, a Bosniak-Croat federation and the Serb-led Republika Srpska, joined under a rotating national presidency and a single constitutional court. NATO deployed a sixty thousand strong force to enforce the ceasefire lines it drew, ending nearly four years of war.

The capital's location was settled over dinner, more or less. Alexander Hamilton wanted northern votes for his plan to have the federal government assume state war debts; Thomas Jefferson and James Madison wanted the capital on the Potomac for southern states. The trade became the Residence Act, signed in July 1790, with Philadelphia serving as a ten-year stopgap while the new city was built.

George Washington picked the exact site the following year, a diamond of land straddling the river and taking in Georgetown and Alexandria. Pierre Charles L'Enfant laid out its broad avenues, though he was fired within a year over disputes with the commissioners overseeing the project. The government did not actually move in until 1800.

No press attended when Khrushchev rose before the 20th Party Congress on 25 February 1956. Foreign delegations had already been sent home, and the hall was cleared of stenographers before he began reading a report built on the Pospelov Commission's research into the purges of the late 1930s, when well over a million people had been arrested.

He accused Stalin of shattering the party's tradition of collective leadership and of exaggerating his own wartime judgement while ignoring warnings before the German invasion. Delegates were told not to discuss what they had heard, but copies reached Polish communists within weeks and then the CIA, which had the text in Western newspapers by June, well before most Soviet citizens learned of it through closed party readings.

Alexander died in Babylon on 10 or 11 June 323 BC, the city he intended to make the capital of an empire that stretched from Greece to the Indus. He was 32, and had already been forced to turn his army back at the Beas River in India the previous year when his own troops refused to march further east. He left no adult heir and, according to later writers, no clear instruction for who should succeed him.

Without an agreed successor, his generals, later called the Diadochi, fought a series of wars over the following decades that carved the empire into rival kingdoms in Macedonia, Egypt and across the former Persian territories. His death is usually taken as the start of the Hellenistic period, in which Greek language and culture spread through the lands he had conquered even as his own line was hunted down and destroyed.

Genghis Khan died while still campaigning, in August 1227, during a siege against the Western Xia in what is now northwestern China. Sources disagree on the exact day, giving either the 18th or the 25th, and give no consistent account of the cause. He was around 65.

No successor was named before he died, and the Mongol elite spent two years arguing over the succession while his brother Tolui governed as regent. Not the eldest son Jochi but the third, Ogedei, was chosen in 1229, and it was under him that Mongol campaigns pushed further into China, Persia and eastern Europe.

Augustus had spent decades avoiding the appearance of monarchy while holding power more completely than any king, and he spent just as much care arranging who would follow him. He outlived several chosen heirs before settling on his stepson Tiberius, whom he adopted and had granted powers equal to his own well before the end.

He died at Nola in August of the year 14, reportedly asking those present whether he had played his part well in the comedy of life. Tiberius succeeded him with little disruption, the Senate confirming powers he already held in practice. That smooth transfer, arranged in advance rather than fought over, became the pattern for how the principate would pass from one emperor to the next.

Charlemagne died at Aachen on 28 January 814 and was buried in the palace chapel he had built there. His only surviving legitimate son, Louis the Pious, inherited the whole empire intact, an outcome Charlemagne had not managed for his own father's generation, when Frankish custom usually split land between brothers.

Louis could not hold that unity for his own sons. After years of civil war among them, the Treaty of Verdun in 843 split the empire three ways: Lothair kept a middle strip and the imperial title, Louis the German took the eastern lands, and Charles the Bald took the west, borders that later hardened into Germany and France.

Ali was washing Muhammad's body for burial in Medina when a separate argument broke out at a courtyard called Saqifah. The Muhajirun who had followed Muhammad from Mecca and the Ansar of Medina disputed who should lead the new community, and the meeting turned heated before Umar pledged loyalty to Abu Bakr, who became the first caliph.

Ali's own supporters, including Muhammad's uncle Abbas and companions such as Zubayr, argued he had already been designated at an earlier gathering, Ghadir Khumm, and that Saqifah had bypassed him. That disagreement over legitimacy hardened over the following decades into the divide between Sunni and Shia Islam.

A coin was only worth what a merchant believed it contained, and a king short of cash could quietly reduce that content, striking more coins from the same weight of silver by mixing in cheaper metal. The extra coins covered wars and building projects in the short term without a new tax being announced.

Merchants noticed anyway. Prices rose to match the coin's real silver content rather than its stamped value, and traders began weighing coins or refusing suspect ones outright. Restoring confidence afterwards usually meant recalling and reminting the debased currency, an expensive admission that the original debasement had solved nothing.

Five governors broke from the crumbling Bahmani sultanate within a couple of decades of each other: Ahmadnagar, Bijapur and Berar all declared independence around 1490, Bidar followed close behind, and Golconda came last in 1512. Between the Krishna river and the Vindhya range, one Persianate kingdom had splintered into five rival courts.

Their founders shared little by way of origin, Brahmin converts, a Georgian noble, Turkmen migrants, yet each court patronised the same emerging Dakhani language and the same Deccani miniature painting, and left behind buildings such as the Charminar and the Gol Gumbaz that still define the region's skyline.

On New Year's Day 1942, the United States, Britain, the Soviet Union and China signed a pledge in Washington to fight the Axis with their full military and economic strength and not to seek a separate peace. Twenty-two further governments added their names the next day, and the tally reached forty-seven by the time the war ended.

Roosevelt had coined the phrase United Nations for the wartime coalition, and this declaration is where the name first carried legal weight rather than serving as a slogan. The commitments it wrote down against separate peace and pooled resources became the basis on which the permanent organisation was built three years later in San Francisco.

Seventeen African territories became independent states in 1960, more than in any other single year before or since. Most had been French possessions, including Chad, Gabon, Ivory Coast and the Republic of the Congo, whose independence days clustered through July and August. Nigeria, by far the most populous of the new states, followed on 1 October.

The pace was set less by any single agreement than by exhaustion on the colonial side and organised pressure on the other: France had already granted its territories self-government in 1958 and found full independence hard to refuse once the first few asked. The wave left several new borders, drawn decades earlier by colonial administrators, essentially unchanged.

Protestant nobles confronted four Catholic regents at Prague Castle on 23 May 1618 over the suppression of their religious rights, then put two of the regents and a secretary on trial on the spot for subverting the emperor's promises. Found guilty within the hour, the three men were thrown from a castle window some fifteen metres above the ground.

All three survived the fall. Catholic writers credited the Virgin Mary with catching them; Protestant accounts later claimed a dung heap broke the landing, though no contemporary source mentions one. The incident tipped Bohemia's Protestant estates into open revolt against Emperor Ferdinand II, opening the Thirty Years' War that spread across Europe for the next three decades.

Around 1340 the Delhi Sultanate under Muhammad bin Tughlaq covered more of the Indian subcontinent than at any point before it, a span that governors far from the capital found easier to rule than to answer for. Provinces were entrusted to military commanders who collected revenue and raised troops on the sultan's behalf rather than to a uniform civil bureaucracy.

That distance between Delhi and its outer provinces proved the system's weakness. By 1339 governors in the east had begun declaring independence, and Hindu rulers in the south soon followed, so the same administrative reach that had briefly made the sultanate so large also made it impossible to hold together.

Qutb ud-Din Aibak had begun life enslaved, bought as a boy and raised in the household of Muhammad of Ghor, whose armies he later commanded in northern India. When Muhammad was assassinated in 1206, Aibak, already governing Ghorid territory from Delhi, took the title of Sultan rather than deferring to a distant heir. Contemporaries called him Lakhbaksh, giver of lakhs, for the generosity he showed his soldiers.

He ruled only four years before dying after a fall from his horse during a game of polo. The dynasty he began, later called the Mamluk or slave dynasty for his own origins, was the first of five that governed from Delhi over the next three centuries: Mamluk, Khalji, Tughlaq, Sayyid and Lodi, each seizing the throne from the last rather than inheriting it peacefully.

Alauddin Khalji's death in 1316 left the Delhi Sultanate without a strong hand at the top, and within four years a general named Khusro Khan had seized the throne by force. He held it only briefly: Delhi's Muslim nobility, unwilling to accept him, invited Ghazi Malik, governor of Punjab, to march on the capital.

Ghazi Malik defeated and killed Khusro Khan in 1320 and took the throne himself as Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq, founding a new dynasty on the back of the coup. He rewarded the nobles who had backed him and punished those who had not, a pattern of violent succession that the Tughlaqs themselves would suffer from in turn.

Sparta had led the Greek war effort at Plataea and Mycale, then lost interest in chasing the Persians further. Athens took over, and in 478 BCE delegates from the Aegean city-states met on the sacred island of Delos to found a new alliance, pooling ships and money to keep fighting Persia and to divide whatever spoils came of it. The League's treasury sat on Delos itself, watched over by Athenian officials.

Membership was not really optional once a city had joined: those that tried to leave were besieged back into line. In 454 BCE the treasury moved to Athens, officially for safekeeping, though Pericles then spent some of it on Athenian building projects, the Parthenon among them. By the middle of the century a defensive alliance had become, in practice, an Athenian empire that collected tribute from its allies.

Diocletian did not carve the empire into two halves in a single stroke. He raised Maximian to co-ruler in 286, then in 293 added two junior emperors, Galerius and Constantius, each titled Caesar under a senior Augustus. Four courts, four armies, one frontier problem each: the empire had grown too large for one man to campaign and administer at once.

The system was built to survive its own founders' retirement. In 305 Diocletian and Maximian stepped down together, letting their Caesars rise smoothly to Augustus. It held for one cycle. When Constantius died in 306, his troops proclaimed his son Constantine emperor on the spot, ignoring the succession plan, and the tetrarchy unravelled into rival claimants within a generation.

Thomas Cromwell spent 1535 sending commissioners around England to value every monastery's income and report on its conduct, a survey called the Valor Ecclesiasticus. Parliament then used the results to close any house worth less than two hundred pounds a year, a first pass through roughly 243 smaller communities before the larger abbeys followed.

Monks and nuns were not simply turned out. Most were offered a pension or a transfer to a surviving house, and from 1538 an ordinary monk could expect around five pounds a year for life, a nun rather less. The land and buildings themselves went through a new Crown office, the Court of Augmentations, and much of the proceeds went straight into paying for Henry's wars in the following decade.

Arcadius and Honorius were both minors when their father Theodosius I died in 395, and neither was capable of ruling on his own. The empire passed to them as two halves, the elder taking the east and the younger the west, each propped up by a military strongman, Rufinus and Stilicho, who soon became rivals rather than partners.

No one at the time thought they had created two empires. Romans still spoke of a single state governed from two courts for convenience, not a dissolved union. Only afterward, as the western court weakened and the eastern one endured for another millennium as Byzantium, did the split of 395 read as the one that never healed.

France had renamed the territory the French Territory of the Afars and the Issas in 1967, a decade after a referendum in which it stayed under French rule while neighbouring colonies across Africa were becoming independent states. A further referendum in 1977 finally produced a vote for independence rather than continued association with Paris.

Djibouti became a sovereign republic on 27 June 1977, its small size and position on the Bab el Mandeb strait having made both France and its own population weigh the choice for years longer than most decolonisation votes on the continent took. France kept a military base there under a separate agreement even after the flag changed.

The order went out in Gloucester at Christmas 1085, twenty years after Hastings, because William needed to know exactly what his new kingdom was worth. Royal commissioners rode out to every shire, and in each hundred court twelve local jurors, half English and half Norman, swore to the value of every estate, plough team and mill.

The book got its grim nickname a century later, when a treasury official compared its verdicts to the Last Judgment: once entered, a holding could not be argued away. The name misleads modern ears into hearing disaster, but the Old English doom simply meant law, and no other kingdom in Europe had anything close to this record for another five hundred years.

The British North America Act, passed at Westminster, joined the Province of Canada, split into Ontario and Quebec, with Nova Scotia and New Brunswick on 1 July 1867. Prince Edward Island and Newfoundland stayed out at the time, unconvinced the arrangement suited them, and would join decades later on separate terms.

John A. Macdonald, who had lobbied hard for confederation at conferences in Charlottetown and Quebec City, became the new dominion's first prime minister after elections that August and September. Westminster still controlled foreign policy and constitutional amendment, so the country was not yet independent, a status worked out gradually over the following century.

Dred Scott had been enslaved in Missouri, then taken by his owner into free Illinois and the Wisconsin Territory before being brought back south. He sued for his freedom on the grounds that residence on free soil had already freed him, a claim earlier Missouri courts had upheld for other enslaved plaintiffs.

On 6 March 1857 Chief Justice Roger Taney's opinion went further than the case required: Black Americans, free or enslaved, could never be citizens, and Congress had no power to ban slavery in the territories, which struck down the Missouri Compromise. Two justices dissented at length, and the ruling pushed the country closer to war rather than settling anything.

The evidence against Alfred Dreyfus was a single torn, unsigned document found in a wastepaper basket at the German embassy in September 1894. Handwriting experts of dubious standing, including the police official Alphonse Bertillon, decided it matched his hand and invented a theory of deliberate self disguise to explain where it did not. Seven military judges convicted him that December and sent him to Devil's Island.

The case reopened only after Emile Zola published an open letter, J'Accuse, in the newspaper L'Aurore in January 1898, accusing the army of a cover up and dividing French opinion for years afterward. A second court martial in 1899 convicted Dreyfus again despite mounting doubt, and he was pardoned rather than cleared. Full exoneration and reinstatement as an army major did not come until 1906.

Russia expected gratitude, not isolation. After its army broke the Ottomans in 1877 and 1878, the Congress of Berlin trimmed back the gains St Petersburg had written into the Treaty of San Stefano, and Russian officials blamed Bismarck for the loss. Bismarck answered by signing a secret pact with Vienna on 7 October 1879, the very power Russia had just fought over the Balkans.

The treaty bound Germany and Austria-Hungary to fight together if Russia attacked either of them, and to stay neutral if a third power, understood to mean France, attacked one of them instead. Bismarck had spent a decade trying to keep Russia inside Germany's diplomatic orbit; this agreement chose Vienna over St Petersburg and set the pairing that held through 1914.

The Act of Abjuration, agreed in July 1581, released the Dutch provinces from their oath to Philip II on the grounds that a king who oppressed his subjects and violated their rights had forfeited his claim to rule them. Officials were told to strike his name and seal from coins and legal documents and swear new oaths to their own provincial States instead.

It was not, at first, a bid to rule themselves. The provinces offered the crown to Francis, Duke of Anjou, and later courted Elizabeth I of England, who sent troops but declined the throne. Only after both efforts failed, and after William the Silent's assassination in 1584, did the States General settle into governing as a republic rather than hunting for a new king.

Nothing written by the Dvaravati culture survives as a continuous history; what is known comes from moated town sites, inscribed coins and stone boundary markers scattered across central Thailand. Mon speaking communities, some of them likely seafaring traders, are thought to have carried the culture into the Chao Phraya valley in the early centuries CE.

Radiocarbon dating at sites such as Uthong has pushed occupation back to the fourth or fifth century, earlier than the sixth to eleventh century range once used to define the culture. Its towns left behind Pali inscriptions recording religious donations, evidence that Theravada Buddhism was already embedded in daily life rather than newly arrived.

Long before Swahili city-states like Kilwa and Mombasa reached their medieval wealth, Bantu-speaking farmers were already trading along the East African coast, using natural harbours cut by drowned river estuaries. Monsoon winds did the rest, carrying traders south in one season and home in the next.

Goods moving through these early ports connected the coast to Arabia, southern Asia and, at times, Rome and Greece, centuries before Islam or a written Swahili language existed. The settlements were modest by later standards, but the trading rhythm they set, sailing with the monsoon, outlasted every empire that touched the coast.

Elizabeth I granted the charter on the last day of 1600, to a group of London merchants under the cumbersome title of the Governor and Company of Merchants of London Trading into the East Indies. It gave them a fifteen-year monopoly on English trade east of the Cape of Good Hope, backed by the threat of seizing the ships of anyone who tried to compete with them.

What began as a trading venture grew into something closer to a government. By the mid-1700s it kept its own private army, and after the Battle of Plassey in 1757 it started ruling Indian territory directly rather than just trading in it. The Crown did not take that power back until 1858, and the company itself was not dissolved until 1874.

Indonesia had occupied East Timor since 1975 and offered the territory a referendum only under UN pressure, on the assumption that voters would accept autonomy within Indonesia rather than break away. On 30 August 1999, with turnout near 99 percent, more than three quarters of East Timorese voters rejected that offer outright and chose independence instead.

Militias backed by the Indonesian military responded by burning towns and killing an estimated thousand or more people within weeks, displacing hundreds of thousands more. An Australian-led international force, authorised by the Security Council in September, restored order and the UN administered the territory until full independence in May 2002.

Northern China had fallen to non-Han warlords who captured and killed two Jin emperors in succession, the second, Emperor Min, executed in 316. Sima Rui, a Jin prince who had already moved his household south of the Yangtze, declared himself emperor at Jiankang, near modern Nanjing, the following year rather than surrender the dynasty entirely.

Refugees and displaced gentry families followed the court south in large numbers, and those immigrant clans ended up sharing real power with the throne they had rescued, a pattern historians call gentry politics. Jiankang stayed the seat of southern Chinese government for more than a century, even as the north remained fractured among rival kingdoms the Jin never recovered.

Cassius Dio, writing not long after, thought he knew the real motive: more taxpayers. Only citizens owed certain Roman taxes, so an emperor who made every free man in the empire a citizen also made every one of them liable for revenue that provincials had previously escaped. Caracalla issued the edict in 212 CE, and it applied to free women across the empire as well.

A narrower class, the dediticii, mostly people who had surrendered under treaty or freed slaves branded with a criminal record, were left out.
