Historians also point to a simpler pressure behind the timing: only citizens could serve in the legions proper, so widening citizenship widened the pool the army could recruit from. Roman law itself had to be rewritten piecemeal afterward to fit provincial custom into rules built for citizens alone.

The document agreed at Milan in February 313 did not put Christianity in charge of anything. Constantine and his co-emperor Licinius extended toleration to every religion, ordering confiscated Christian property returned and compensation paid, but stopping well short of an official state faith. That step waited until 380, under Theodosius I, nearly seventy years later.

It was also never quite an edict issued at Milan. Historians now read it as a letter Licinius sent to provincial governors later that year from Nicomedia, after defeating a rival in the east, repeating terms the two emperors had settled on in person. The meeting behind it was real; the paperwork travelled separately.

Henry IV had converted to Catholicism himself to take the throne, but the edict he signed at Nantes in April 1598 let his former co-religionists worship without being harassed for it. Huguenots could hold public office, keep their own courts and universities, and garrison a number of fortified towns at the crown's expense, though Catholicism stayed the official religion and Protestants still paid its tithes.

It held for nearly ninety years. Louis XIV revoked it in 1685, ordering ministers out of France within two weeks and banning most other Protestants from leaving at all. Roughly 400,000 fled regardless, into England, Prussia and the Dutch Republic, taking skills and capital with them that France did not recover for a long time.

Seven states signed the Stockholm Convention on 4 January 1960 and formed the association that May: Austria, Denmark, Norway, Portugal, Sweden, Switzerland and the United Kingdom, nicknamed the Outer Seven against the EEC's inner six. Britain led the push after deciding it would not accept the deeper political union the EEC's founders wanted.

EFTA's members kept their own tariffs against the rest of the world and simply removed them among themselves, unlike the EEC's shared external wall. The looser design suited Britain, Denmark and Norway only for a while: all three later applied to join the EEC instead, and Britain's 1973 departure from EFTA reshaped an organisation that had been built partly around it.

Egypt agreed to something no other Arab state had accepted: recognising Israel outright. The treaty, signed at the White House on 26 March 1979, followed the Camp David framework and set out Israel's staged withdrawal from the Sinai Peninsula, which it had occupied since the 1967 war, in exchange for a demilitarised buffer and normal diplomatic relations.

The peace cost Egypt its place in the Arab League, which suspended the country from 1979 until 1989 over what other members called a unilateral betrayal of the Palestinian cause. Anwar Sadat, who had staked his presidency on the treaty, was assassinated by Islamist militants in October 1981.

On the night of 22 to 23 July 1952, a clique of army officers seized Cairo's key buildings and radio stations without firing on the palace. King Farouk, who had spent the evening at Alexandria's Ras el-Tin palace, was given three days to leave the country and sailed into exile aboard his own yacht on 26 July.

The public face of the coup was General Mohamed Naguib, an older officer whose seniority gave the plotters cover. The actual organiser was Colonel Gamal Abdel Nasser, who had built the secret Free Officers movement over several years and moved against Naguib in 1954 to take the presidency himself, ending the monarchy that the Muhammad Ali dynasty had held since 1805.

Organisers picked 25 January 2011 deliberately: it was National Police Day, and they meant the date as a direct jab at years of police brutality alongside anger over unemployment, food prices and emergency laws that had run for decades. What was planned as a single day of protest instead filled Tahrir Square for more than two weeks.

Hosni Mubarak offered concessions as the crowds grew, then a cabinet reshuffle, then a promise not to seek re-election, none of which ended the occupation. On 11 February his vice president announced on state television that Mubarak had resigned, handing power to the military after thirty years, following a crackdown that had killed several hundred people.

Elizabeth was in Kenya, not London, when she became queen. She and Philip had spent the previous night watching wildlife from a treehouse hotel called Treetops before returning to their lodge on the morning of 6 February 1952, where Philip told her that her father, George VI, had died in his sleep at Sandringham.

She chose to keep her own name rather than adopt a new regnal title, becoming Elizabeth II, and the couple cut short a planned tour of Australia and New Zealand to fly home. There was no coronation for another sixteen months; it took that long to prepare Westminster Abbey and rehearse a ceremony that had not been performed since 1937.

The first person processed through the new federal immigration station on 1 January 1892 was Annie Moore, a seventeen-year-old from County Cork travelling with her two younger brothers to join their parents in New York. Officials marked the occasion by presenting her with a ten-dollar gold coin, a gesture the newspapers covering the opening made much of.

Before Ellis Island, New York had processed arrivals through Castle Garden, a converted theatre at the tip of Manhattan that state officials ran with a reputation for corruption. The federal government took the job over and moved it to an island in the harbour instead. The wooden station she walked through burned down in 1897, and the brick building that replaced it in 1900 handled most of the roughly 12 million people processed there by 1954.

Lincoln issued a preliminary warning in September 1862 and the proclamation itself took effect on 1 January 1863. It applied only to the ten states still in rebellion, naming them individually, and explicitly excluded the loyal border states of Missouri, Kentucky, Maryland and Delaware along with several Union-held counties and parishes in the South.

Lincoln had no authority to free enslaved people anywhere the federal government did not control, so the order reached them only as Union troops advanced; immediate freedom in areas already occupied touched perhaps 25,000 to 75,000 people out of more than three million covered on paper. Roughly 300,000 more, in the exempted areas, gained nothing from it at all.

Freedom did not come with land. Alexander II's manifesto of 3 March 1861 released more than 23 million serfs from bondage to their landlords, but most had to buy the plots they already farmed, often only half of what they had worked before.

The state fronted three quarters of the purchase price to the landowners as bonds, then collected it back from peasants over 49 years of redemption payments plus interest. Household serfs, who had worked inside the manor rather than the fields, gained their freedom but no land at all.

Mediterranean trade was never free of politics. The papacy repeatedly banned Christian merchants from selling timber, iron and weapons to Muslim powers such as the Mamluk sultanate, treating these as materials of war that would only arm an adversary, while galley-owning states like Venice and Genoa depended on exactly those eastern markets for their income.

The bans were issued again and again across the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries precisely because they kept being ignored: merchants paid fines, bought exemptions, or simply smuggled the goods anyway. An embargo that has to be reissued every few years is really a record of how often it failed, not proof that it worked.

Nicolas de Ovando, sent to govern Hispaniola in 1502, began handing conquistadors and officials control over groups of Indigenous labourers as reward for service to the crown. The practice was formalised the following year, when Spain wrote it into colonial policy as the encomienda: a grant of people, not land, tied to a named community rather than individuals.

In theory the grant obliged a colonist to protect his workers and see them instructed in Christianity, in exchange for their labour and tribute in food, cloth or metal. In practice the arrangement left Indigenous communities with almost no recourse, and conditions on many encomiendas differed from slavery mainly in name, a gap Spanish reformers spent decades afterward trying to narrow.

Since 1944 foreign governments had been able to trade their dollars for gold at a fixed rate of thirty five dollars an ounce, a promise that anchored the whole postwar currency system. On 15 August 1971 Nixon announced from the White House that the United States would no longer honour it, alongside a ninety day freeze on wages and prices and a new tariff on imports.

Nixon framed the move as protecting the dollar rather than abandoning it, but suspending convertibility left the fixed exchange rates it had guaranteed with nothing behind them. Within two years most industrialised economies had let their currencies float against the dollar, a shift that fed directly into the inflation of the rest of the decade.

Marcus Aurelius died in March 180, probably at a military camp on the Danube frontier where he had spent much of his reign fighting the Marcomanni rather than governing from Rome. He was the last of five emperors in a row chosen for ability rather than birth, each adopted as heir by the one before him. He broke that chain himself by leaving the throne to his own son, Commodus.

Commodus was around eighteen and had none of his father's interest in the frontier wars or in governing by committee with the Senate. He preferred gladiatorial combat and left administration to favourites, and his reign is generally reckoned the point at which the stability of the previous century began to unwind. Historians still argue over how much of that unwinding was already under way before he took the throne.

The Commonwealth did not collapse under Charles II. It collapsed on its own, once Richard Cromwell proved unable to hold his father's army together and ceded power in 1659. General George Monck marched his forces south from Scotland, forced out the rival commanders, and let a newly convened Parliament settle the succession.

Charles offered concessions from exile in the Declaration of Breda before that Parliament proclaimed him king on 8 May 1660. He landed at Dover on 25 May and reached London on his thirtieth birthday four days later. The Cavalier Parliament that followed sat for over seventeen years and reinstalled the Church of England through the Clarendon Code.

Simon de Montfort had already beaten King Henry III in battle once, at Lewes in 1264, and ruled through a council in the king's name. For his 1265 parliament he went further than any English summons before it, writing to the sheriffs to summon barons and bishops alongside two elected representatives from each county and from a chosen list of towns, ordinary men with no title at all.

It did not save him. Prince Edward escaped custody that May and gathered marcher lords and defectors, among them the powerful Gilbert de Clare. At Evesham on 4 August 1265, a little over a year after the parliament, Edward's men marched under Montfort's own captured banners, and Montfort realised who they were only when it was too late.

William of Orange had already landed and James II had already fled by the time Parliament wrote down what it wanted in exchange for a crown. The Convention Parliament drafted a Declaration of Right in February 1689, offering the throne jointly to William and his wife Mary on the condition it was accepted, then formally enacted it as the Bill of Rights that December.

It barred a monarch from suspending laws or raising taxes without Parliament's consent, from keeping a standing army in peacetime without the same consent, and from prosecuting subjects for petitioning the crown. It also protected free debate in Parliament and required frequent, freely elected sessions, converting a one-off deal over James's throne into a lasting limit on the next one.

Enron's profits were largely a trick of the accounting. The company recorded the projected future value of long-term energy contracts as current earnings and hid billions of dollars in debt inside hundreds of off-the-books partnerships. Its share price, which had reached over 90 dollars, began to unravel in October 2001 once analysts started asking where the debt actually sat.

The company filed for bankruptcy on 2 December 2001, then the largest in American history. Its auditor, Arthur Andersen, was convicted of obstructing justice after employees shredded documents tied to the investigation, a conviction later overturned but not before the firm collapsed. Employees who had put their retirement savings into Enron stock lost most of it almost overnight.

Britain and France had nearly gone to war over African territory as recently as 1898. The 1904 agreement traded recognition: France accepted British control of Egypt, Britain accepted French influence in Morocco, and a separate clause guaranteed free passage through the Suez Canal.

Smaller disputes came with it. France gave up fishing rights off Newfoundland's coast, Britain handed over territory in West Africa, and the two sides split spheres of influence in Siam. The document was not a military alliance, and said so, but it opened the door to joint staff talks between the two armies in the years that followed.

Before 1970, responsibility for air, water, pesticides and radiation was scattered across the Public Health Service, the Interior Department and half a dozen smaller offices, none of which could set a single standard across all of them. Nixon proposed folding them into one agency in July 1970, and the reorganisation took effect that December under a procedure that let Congress veto it and Congress did not.

William Ruckelshaus took the oath as the new agency's first administrator on 4 December 1970. Within months his EPA was suing cities over sewage and banning DDT, an aggressive start that set the pattern for an agency built from other departments' cast-off enforcement powers rather than a single new law of its own.

Augustus made Ephesus the capital of Roman Asia in place of Pergamon, and the city grew to rank behind only Rome and Alexandria in the eastern empire. Modern estimates put its population somewhere between thirty and seventy thousand, smaller than the older, wildly inflated figures but still enormous for the region.

Its wealth rested on a harbour that connected the Aegean to inland Anatolia, and on the Temple of Artemis nearby, a structure so large it was counted among the Seven Wonders. That same harbour was the city's undoing: the river feeding it silted the channel faster than repeated dredging could clear it, and trade slowly moved elsewhere.

The Eritrean People's Liberation Front fought Ethiopian rule for thirty years, from 1961, before it finally overran the Ethiopian garrisons still holding out in May 1991. Fighting on that scale left Eritrea in control of its own territory two years before any country recognised it as a state.

That recognition needed a formal act rather than a battlefield outcome, so a UN-supervised referendum was held in April 1993. Turnout was overwhelming and the result was not close: more than a million voted for statehood against fewer than two thousand opposed. The United Nations admitted Eritrea as a member state that May.

Shang king Di Xin sent an army said to number seven hundred thousand men to meet King Wu's coalition at Muye in 1046 BCE. Many of those soldiers, conscripted labourers or enslaved men, defected to the attackers rather than fight for him, and the Shang line collapsed within a single day.

Di Xin returned to his capital and burned himself to death in the Deer Terrace pavilion rather than face capture. The Zhou dynasty that followed became China's longest-lasting, though for most of its history power sat with regional vassal lords rather than the king directly.

Yekuno Amlak was a regional lord from Amhara, not a member of the ruling house he overthrew. With backing from the Muslim Sultanate of Shewa and fighters raised in Amhara and Shewa, he defeated the last Zagwe king at the Battle of Ansata around 1270; historians still dispute exactly which Zagwe ruler he faced.

Yekuno Amlak justified the seizure by claiming descent from the ancient kings of Aksum, who Ethiopian tradition traced back to Solomon and the Queen of Sheba, casting the Zagwe he had just killed as illegitimate usurpers of that line rather than his own conquest as one. The dynasty he founded on that claim ruled, with interruptions, until 1974.

Emperor Menelik II had spent years buying rifles and artillery from rival European powers before Italy's invasion forced the fight. At Adwa on 1 March 1896 his forces, numbering perhaps 100,000 against roughly 17,000 Italian and colonial troops under General Oreste Baratieri, encircled and broke the Italian line in a single day. Empress Taytu Betul commanded her own contingent in the battle.

Around 6,000 Italian and colonial soldiers were killed and nearly 4,000 captured, against Ethiopian losses estimated at four to seven thousand dead. The defeat brought down Italy's government and forced the Treaty of Addis Ababa, in which Italy recognised Ethiopian sovereignty outright. Ethiopia remained the one African state to defeat a European coloniser and keep its independence, for nearly forty years.

Most of the ten states that joined on 1 May 2004 had spent the previous decade rewriting their laws to match EU standards, a condition of membership that touched everything from food safety rules to competition policy. Cyprus and Malta joined alongside eight former communist states from Central and Eastern Europe.

The accession nearly doubled the EU's membership at once, from fifteen to twenty five countries, and added roughly seventy five million people. Existing members negotiated transition periods before workers from the new states gained full rights to move and take jobs elsewhere in the bloc.

The currency had already existed for three years as an accounting unit before anyone touched it. Banks and stock exchanges had traded in euros since 1999, but the coins and notes that reached tills and wallets across twelve countries only arrived on 1 January 2002, seven years after the name itself was agreed at a Madrid summit.

For a few weeks francs, marks, lire and pesetas were still legal tender alongside the new coins, so cashiers made change in two currencies at once. Vending machines had to be recalibrated overnight, and central banks spent months afterwards exchanging leftover coins that people found in drawers, having briefly become worthless souvenirs of a dozen abandoned currencies.

On 1 January 1999 the euro existed only as an accounting unit. Banks used it to price bonds and settle trades between member states, but no citizen could hold one: francs, marks and lire stayed in wallets and tills for three more years while exchange rates were locked in place.

Notes and coins did not appear until 2002, when eleven countries retired their old currencies within weeks of each other. Vending machines were converted gradually rather than all at once, with roughly two thirds switched over within the first fortnight, while shops kept dual price tags for months so customers could check new totals against something familiar.

Robert Schuman put the proposal in blunt terms on 9 May 1950: pool French and German coal and steel production under one authority, and war between the two countries would become unthinkable, and in material terms impossible. Coal and steel were the raw materials of armies as much as factories, which was exactly why he chose them.

France, West Germany, Italy, Belgium, the Netherlands and Luxembourg signed the treaty establishing the Community the following year, placing their heavy industry under a supranational High Authority rather than national ministries. It was a modest arrangement in scope but a new kind of institution, one that member states answered to rather than merely negotiated with.

The European Community had spent years failing to finish the common market its founding treaty promised, blocked by rules that let any single state veto new rules. The Single European Act, signed by member states in February 1986, extended qualified majority voting to most single market legislation, so one government could no longer stall the rest indefinitely.

It took effect in July 1987 and set 31 December 1992 as the target date for a market with free movement of goods, services, capital and people. The act also gave treaty status to foreign policy cooperation between member states for the first time, laying groundwork the Maastricht Treaty would build on five years later.

Mary had already been Elizabeth's prisoner for eighteen years when letters intercepted in 1586 tied her to the Babington Plot, a scheme to kill Elizabeth and put Mary on the English throne in her place. She was arrested while out riding and put on trial at Fotheringhay Castle, where a court of English peers found her guilty of plotting against the queen who held her.

Elizabeth hesitated for months before signing the death warrant, and even afterward tried to claim it had been sent without her final approval. Mary was beheaded at Fotheringhay on 8 February 1587, and Elizabeth had the man who carried out the order to send the warrant imprisoned in the Tower for acting on it.

By July 1794, members of the National Convention who had once carried out the Terror alongside Robespierre feared they would be next on his lists. On 9 Thermidor, 27 July, they had him arrested along with Augustin Robespierre, Saint-Just and Couthon. During the arrest his jaw was shattered, either by a gendarme's pistol shot or, as most historians now think, by his own attempt to shoot himself.

He was guillotined without trial the next day at the Place de la Revolution, unable to speak from the wound. His death ended the Terror's most radical phase and the Convention that had condemned him soon turned on the machinery of denunciation itself, dismantling the committees that had run it.

A federal open-housing bill had stalled in Congress for two years before Martin Luther King's assassination on 4 April 1968 broke the deadlock. The Kerner Commission had already recommended such a law after the previous year's riots, and Johnson pressed lawmakers to act within days of King's death rather than let the moment pass.

Congress passed the Fair Housing Act, and Johnson signed it on 11 April 1968, barring landlords and sellers from refusing housing on grounds of race, colour, religion or national origin, and from advertising a preference for one group over another. Protection on the basis of sex followed in 1974, and disability and family status in 1988.

Count Joscelin II had moved his court away from Edessa itself and spent his energy feuding with the count of Tripoli rather than guarding his frontier. When the Muslim ruler Zengi turned his army on the city in late 1144, Tripoli refused to send help, and Edessa fell to a siege on 24 December.

It was the first of the four Crusader states to be lost, and news of it reached Europe as a shock rather than a distant border skirmish. Pope Eugene III called for a new expedition, launching the Second Crusade in 1146, but its leaders chose to attack Damascus instead of trying to retake Edessa, and the city never returned to Christian rule.

Samaria held out for three years against Shalmaneser V before it fell, and the Assyrian king who began the siege did not live to finish it. Sargon II, who took the throne in the meantime, claimed the credit and the numbers in his own inscriptions: 27,290 people carried off, a figure later scholarship treats as a partial count rather than the whole population.

Deportation was standard Assyrian practice, meant to break resistance by scattering a people and resettling their land with outsiders. Some Israelites fled south to Judah before the city fell; those who stayed mixed with the newcomers and became the community later known as the Samaritans. The deportees themselves left no continuous record, which is how they became known simply as lost.

Nineveh had walls thick enough to drive a chariot along, but the siege that broke it, by Babylonians under Nabopolassar and Medes under Cyaxares, lasted only three months. It began in May 612 BC and ended in August, when the defences gave way and the city was plundered and burned. King Sin-shar-ishkun died in the fighting; one account blames a diverted river for flooding the walls open.

Assyria did not end with the city. The king's brother, Ashur-uballit II, escaped to Harran and kept a rump state fighting for several more years before Babylonian and Median forces finished it off. Nineveh itself was left in ruins so complete that later Greek travellers who passed the mound did not know a city had ever stood there.

Zhu Wen began as a salt smuggler before rising through the ranks that put down Huang Chao's rebellion, the revolt whose sack of Chang'an and Luoyang had already broken the Tang court's authority. From his base at Kaifeng he seized Chang'an in 901, forced the emperor to Luoyang, and had him assassinated in 904.

In 907 Zhu Wen deposed the last Tang emperor, the boy Ai, and took the throne himself as founder of the Later Liang. No single power replaced Tang authority across China. Rival states split the country for the following half century, a period historians call the Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms, until the Song reunified most of it in 960.

Emperor Min of Jin held Chang'an as the dynasty's last redoubt after Luoyang had already fallen. In 316 the Han-Zhao state, risen from the northern peoples the Jin court had once ruled, took the city and captured him. He was executed soon after, and Western Jin ceased to exist as a functioning state.

Refugees streamed south across the Yangtze rather than accept the new order, carrying the Jin name with them: settlers in Quanzhou named a local river after it. A surviving branch of the imperial family reconstituted the dynasty at Jiankang, today's Nanjing, opening an Eastern Jin period that left the north divided for centuries.

Spanish ships had carried the potato to Europe since the 1500s, but for two centuries it stayed a curiosity, not a crop. Farmers were slow to plant something so unfamiliar in place of grain, and it took until around 1750 for it to become a staple field crop across much of Western Europe rather than a garden novelty.

Once it caught on, it changed how many people the land could feed: one estimate credits the potato with a quarter of the Old World's population and urban growth between 1700 and 1900. That same reliance on one crop later proved dangerous, most starkly when blight destroyed Ireland's potato fields in the 1840s.

Medieval European farming left almost no margin for a bad year. Most peasants worked scattered strips of land with wooden ploughs, no chemical fertiliser and no way to store grain much beyond a single season, so one poor harvest could mean hunger before the next one came in.

A run of cold or wet years, a flooded field, or livestock lost to disease could ripple through an entire village at once, since neighbours farmed the same soil under the same weather. Regional famine returned often enough that chroniclers recorded it as an expected hazard rather than a disaster.

Jean-Baptiste Marchand reached the mud fort at Fashoda in July 1898 with about 130 men, after a march across Africa that had taken more than a year. Herbert Kitchener arrived that September with some 1,500 British and Egyptian troops fresh from victory at Omdurman, and found the French flag already raised over the town on the Upper Nile.

Both commanders reportedly stayed civil in person, but the standoff nearly dragged Britain and France into war over control of the Nile valley. France had no navy to match Britain's and needed British goodwill against a rising Germany more than it needed a garrison in Sudan, so its foreign minister ordered Marchand to withdraw that November. The climbdown was humiliating in Paris, but it cleared the ground for the two countries' 1904 entente.

Abu Abdallah al-Shii spent years among the Kutama Berbers of North Africa before his missionary campaign toppled the Aghlabid rulers of Ifriqiya. In 909 he installed Abd Allah al-Mahdi, who claimed descent from Muhammad's daughter Fatima through her husband Ali, as the first caliph of a new Shia state.

The new caliphate rejected the Sunni caliphs in Baghdad outright, claiming its own line of imams rather than acknowledging theirs. It ruled first from captured Aghlabid territory before building the coastal capital of al-Mahdiyya in 921, and over the following decades pushed east until it took Egypt and moved its court to a new city, Cairo, in 973.

The Fatimid general Jawhar led the invasion of Egypt in 969 against the Ikhshidid rulers, who governed the country while nominally answering to the Abbasid caliph in Baghdad. Resistance collapsed quickly enough that Jawhar's first act as conqueror was to lay out a new capital, al-Qahira, meaning the vanquisher, a name that gave the modern city of Cairo its own.

The Fatimids were Ismaili Shia and had already declared their own caliphate in North Africa decades earlier, rejecting Abbasid religious authority outright rather than merely resisting it politically. Taking Egypt gave that rival caliphate a wealthy, populous base within striking distance of Abbasid territory, and Cairo became its capital for the next two centuries.

Bread queues in Petrograd turned into a general strike on 23 February 1917 by the old Russian calendar, the same day women textile workers marked International Women's Day with protests of their own. Within days the garrison assigned to disperse the crowds mutinied instead, and by 27 February soldiers and workers were forming councils faster than the government could respond to them.

Nicholas II, trying to reach the capital by train, was stopped short at Pskov, where his own generals told him the army could no longer be relied on to restore order in his name. He abdicated on 2 March, ending three centuries of Romanov rule in a matter of days rather than the drawn-out collapse many had expected.

A banking panic in 1907, halted only when the financier J.P. Morgan personally pledged funds to prop up failing trusts, convinced Congress that the country could not keep relying on one private banker to act as lender of last resort. President Woodrow Wilson signed the Federal Reserve Act on 23 December 1913, creating a system of twelve regional reserve banks overseen from Washington.

The design was a compromise between bankers who wanted a single central bank and populists who distrusted concentrated financial power, which is why authority was split regionally rather than housed in one institution. It has been reorganised since, most heavily during the 1930s, but the twelve-bank structure from 1913 still frames how the system is run.

The Sumerian King List names a woman as sole ruler of Kish during its third dynasty, describing her trade beforehand as an innkeeper rather than anything royal. The list gives her a reign of a hundred years, the kind of round, symbolic figure the document uses throughout rather than a literal count of harvests.

She is credited with strengthening Kish's foundations, and one surviving copy of the list even states that there was no king while she reigned, using a female form of the title for a word that otherwise had none. No inscription from her own lifetime has been found, and the list itself was compiled centuries after any such ruler would have lived, so historians treat her as a figure of legend rather than a confirmed monarch.

A diviner told Emperor Wu that horses fit for a god would come from the west, and he sent an army to Fergana to fetch them. The first expedition, in 104 BCE, was turned back and returned empty-handed. Two years later he tried again, with a force reported at over sixty thousand men and thirty thousand horses of their own.

The second army besieged Fergana's capital until its people, threatened with the loss of their own herds, agreed to hand over the best animals. The Han came home with roughly thirty of the prized horses and several thousand of lesser stock, along with alfalfa seed to feed them, at a cost historians put at half the expedition's men.

The Chinese envoy Zhang Qian reported the Ferghana Valley's grain and grape cultivation centuries before this period, describing a settled, urban population unlike the nomadic groups further north. That agricultural base fed the caravans crossing between China and Persia through some of Central Asia's most fought over territory.

By 751 the valley sat at the edge of a collision between empires: Tang China and Abbasid forces clashed nearby at the Battle of Talas, a defeat that ended direct Chinese military involvement in Central Asia. Ferghana's fields kept producing through the upheaval, supplying whichever power controlled the routes past them.

No king or council declared feudalism into existence. As Carolingian central authority broke down, local strongmen who could field mounted soldiers began granting them land, called a fief, in return for military service and loyalty sworn in person before witnesses.

Historians still argue over how uniform this system really was. Francois Louis Ganshof described it narrowly, as obligations among the warrior nobility, while Marc Bloch broadened it to cover clergy and peasants too. Many now treat feudalism as a label historians invented rather than one medieval people used.

Cardinal Wolsey staged the June 1520 meeting near Calais as a festival of excess: a temporary palace of timber and painted cloth covering nearly 12,000 square yards, and feasts recorded as running to thousands of sheep and tens of thousands of eggs across more than two weeks of jousting, banqueting and archery between the English and French courts.

The two kings themselves supplied the meeting's one unscripted moment when Henry challenged Francis to wrestle and lost. Whatever goodwill the spectacle produced did not last: within months Wolsey had brokered an alliance with Charles V instead, who then went to war against France, and the elaborate friendship at Balinghem left no lasting settlement behind it.

The Fourth Republic did not fall to an election but to a mutiny. In May 1958, French army officers in Algiers, backed by settlers who feared losing Algeria, threatened to seize power unless Charles de Gaulle returned to government, and Paris capitulated rather than risk a wider revolt.

De Gaulle used the crisis to demand a constitution built around a strong presidency rather than the shifting coalitions that had toppled twenty governments in twelve years. Voters approved it by over eighty percent in a September referendum, and it took effect on 4 October 1958, giving the president power to dissolve parliament and call new elections directly.

Fijian society before European contact was organised around chiefs, elders and warriors of standing rather than a single crown, and rival settlements competed for land and status over centuries rather than in one recorded campaign. What survives from that period is mostly in the ground: earthworks rather than chronicles.

The clearest evidence is defensive. Important settlements were ringed with ramparts and moats, an engineering effort that only makes sense if raids between rival chiefdoms were a real and recurring threat. The scale of those defences is what tells historians political power was consolidating into fewer, larger hands, even where no written record says so directly.

Fijian communities were never a single kingdom before European contact but a shifting patchwork of chiefdoms, each built around a paramount chief who ranked above village elders and war leaders. Rank was inherited but also contested, and a chief's standing rested on the tribute, in food, mats and labour, that his followers owed him.

Warfare between chiefdoms was constant, fought as much over standing and tribute rights as over land, and alliances between chiefly lines shifted accordingly. The titles recorded by the first European visitors, among them vunivalu, meaning something close to warlord, describe a system that had already been evolving for centuries by the time outsiders wrote it down.

Fijian communities before European contact ran on chiefly rank. Paramount chiefs, elders and bete, spiritual specialists, held authority over particular islands or stretches of coast, and rivalry between chiefdoms was frequent enough that where people built their villages was largely a defensive choice.

Important villages were ringed with ramparts and moats, and the large double-hulled drua gave coastal chiefdoms reach beyond their own shores. Wealth was measured partly in polished sperm whale teeth, tabua, exchanged at ceremonies that sealed alliances between chiefs who were as often rivals as allies.

Mass shooting of Jews by German Einsatzgruppen units began within days of the invasion of the Soviet Union in June 1941, killing an estimated 1.5 to 2 million people in ravines and pits across Eastern Europe over the following months. On 12 December 1941, the day after declaring war on the United States, Hitler told assembled Nazi officials that the annihilation of Europe's Jews was now the necessary consequence of a world war.

In January 1942 fifteen officials met at a villa on Berlin's Wannsee to coordinate the deportation of Jews from across occupied Europe to camps built for killing rather than confinement. Operation Reinhard, the construction and operation of Belzec, Sobibor and Treblinka, ran from March 1942 to November 1943 and accounted for most of the murders carried out that single year.

Crawford Long removed a tumour from James Venable's neck on 30 March 1842 after putting him under with ether, in a small-town Georgia practice with no audience and no announcement. He kept operating quietly for years, wanting to repeat the results before he staked a claim on them.

That caution cost him the credit. William Morton gave a public ether demonstration in Boston in October 1846, four years after Long's operation, and it was Morton's name that spread through the medical press. Only after reading of it did Long start gathering patient affidavits to prove he had done it first.

The Savannah stowed her paddlewheels by eight in the morning on the first day out of Savannah harbour on 24 May 1819, and covered nearly all of the rest of the Atlantic under sail. Her engine ran for roughly eighty hours out of a twenty nine day crossing, closer to a tenth of the voyage than the whole of it.

Liverpool had never seen anything like her arrive on 20 June. Crowds packed the piers and rooftops, and hundreds of small boats came out to look at the smoking ship. She stayed twenty five days while curious visitors, including naval officers, toured her decks, before the novelty proved more profitable as spectacle than as shipping.

Congress chartered the bank for twenty years on 25 February 1791, at Alexander Hamilton's urging, to hold federal deposits and issue a stable national currency. Thomas Jefferson and James Madison opposed it fiercely, arguing that the Constitution gave Congress no power to create a bank and that it would enrich merchants at the expense of everyone else.

Hamilton won that argument, and the bank operated through its full term. When the charter lapsed in 1811, Congress declined to renew it by a single vote in each chamber, and the financier Stephen Girard bought most of its stock and building for his own private bank. A second, larger national bank replaced it in 1816.

Before the Sui dynasty, an official post in China was mostly a matter of family standing. In 587 that started to shift: each prefecture was ordered to put forward three scholars a year for government service, judged on ability rather than birth, and by 599 senior capital officials had to nominate candidates by the same standard.

Emperor Yang went further in 607, creating a new category called the presented scholar, which many historians treat as the true starting point of the examination system rather than the earlier prefectural quotas. The Sui dynasty collapsed before the system matured, and it was the following Tang dynasty that expanded it into the machinery later Chinese governments relied on for centuries.

Herodotus credited the Lydians with being first to strike gold and silver coins, and the metal he had in mind was electrum, a pale gold-silver alloy that occurs naturally in the rivers around Sardis. Lydian mints deliberately added extra silver and copper to it, which meant a coin's true worth was no longer obvious just by looking at it.

That uncertainty is what standard weights and royal stamps were built to solve. King Alyattes issued the earliest of these small, bean-shaped pieces in the decades before 560 BC, and his son Croesus later struck separate pure gold and pure silver coins, creating the ancient world's first bimetallic currency system.

Two of the three envoys Charlemagne sent to Baghdad in 797 died on the journey. Only Isaac, a Jewish merchant chosen for his language skills and contacts across the Jewish diaspora, reached Harun al-Rashid's court and made it home. The mission had set out to open relations between two courts that shared a common rival in the Byzantine Empire.

Harun al-Rashid sent Isaac back with an Asian elephant named Abul-Abbas, along with cloth, perfumes and a water clock. The animal travelled by ship along the North African coast, wintered in Italy, and crossed the Alps to reach Charlemagne at Aachen in the summer of 802, five years after the embassy had left.

ENIAC was dedicated at the University of Pennsylvania's Moore School in February 1946, a machine thirty metres long and three metres deep, built from around eighteen thousand vacuum tubes that failed often enough to require constant attention from its operators. It had been commissioned to calculate artillery firing tables for the Army's Ballistic Research Laboratory, work too slow for human calculators to keep pace with output from new guns.

Before it ever computed a trajectory, ENIAC's first real program modelled the feasibility of a hydrogen bomb, run at the request of scientists at Los Alamos. Reprogramming it meant physically rewiring plugboards and switches for each new task, a process that could take operators, most of them women, several days to complete correctly.

Stalin backdated the plan to October 1928 and then, midway through, raised its own targets by half, so a scheme meant to run five years was declared complete in four. Almost nine tenths of new industrial investment went into heavy industry, steel mills and power plants rather than the food or housing ordinary households needed.

The plan's other half was collectivisation: millions of peasant households were pushed off individual farms and into collective ones, by force where they resisted. Grain was requisitioned to feed the cities and pay for imported machinery, and the resulting famine killed millions, even as the state declared the plan's industrial targets met ahead of schedule.

Eleven ships left Portsmouth in May 1787 carrying roughly 1,400 people, most of them convicts, on a voyage of eight months to the far side of the world. They reached Botany Bay in January 1788, the site James Cook had recommended eighteen years earlier, only for Governor Arthur Phillip to find it open to the sea, short of fresh water and poorly soiled.

Phillip sailed a few kilometres north and found a deep, sheltered harbour he judged one of the finest anywhere. The fleet moved in and raised the flag at Sydney Cove on 26 January 1788, the date Australia now marks as a national holiday, though for the Eora people already living there it began something very different: dispossession followed within years.

Four lodges, three from London and one from Westminster, chose an alehouse for their founding meeting. On St John's Day, 24 June 1717, their representatives gathered at the Goose and Gridiron in St Paul's Churchyard and elected Anthony Sayer as the first Grand Master.

Sayer was a gentleman of modest independent means rather than a figure of rank, and he later fell into financial trouble and had to be supported by the same charity fund his new Grand Lodge of London and Westminster had set up. A blue plaque near the old alehouse site now marks the spot.

Caliph Harun al-Rashid and his vizier Yahya ibn Khalid had a Christian physician, Jibril ibn Bakhtishu, called in to help set up a hospital in Baghdad around 805. Little of the paperwork survives, but by the early ninth century state-funded hospitals were already a recognised feature of Abbasid cities rather than a novelty.

Unlike a monastery infirmary caring mainly for its own community, this institution combined treatment, teaching and the study of medicine under one roof and admitted patients regardless of what they could pay. By the year 1000 Baghdad had five more hospitals built on the same model, and the Baghdad institution itself is known to have still been running two centuries after it opened.

The earliest known canal irrigation was not in the Mesopotamian floodplain itself but nearby, at Choga Mami in what is now Iraq, close to the Iranian border, where channels were diverting river water onto fields by around 6000 BCE. Comparable early systems have been traced to Khuzistan in southwestern Iran around the same period.

Farmers on the Mesopotamian plain proper took up the technique later, from at least the third millennium BCE, building a network of small channels that let them water crops steadily through the growing season rather than relying on seasonal flooding alone. That control over water is what let settlements in the region grow food reliably enough to support cities.

Heinrich Himmler, then police chief of Munich, announced the new camp at Dachau in a newspaper notice on 22 March 1933, describing it plainly as a concentration camp for political prisoners. It opened on the grounds of a disused munitions factory about ten miles from the city, built to hold up to five thousand people.

The first roughly two hundred prisoners came from jails in Munich, mostly communists and social democrats rounded up in the weeks after Hitler became chancellor. Its first commandant lasted only months; his successor, Theodor Eicke, drew up the routines of discipline and punishment that were then copied at every camp built after it.

Constantinople's oldest recorded carer of orphaned children was a priest named Zoticus, later venerated as a saint and remembered simply as Guardian of Orphans. He worked in the decades after Constantine made the city his capital in 330, when church and empire were still working out which of them owed the poor a roof.

No surviving building or charter names an exact founding date, and later writers folded Zoticus into legend, crediting him with founding a hospital as well as an orphanage. What is firmer is the pattern he set: bishops and priests, not the state, ran the empire's earliest organised care for abandoned children for centuries afterward.

A British Antarctic Survey team led by Joe Farman had been measuring ozone over the Halley research station for years, and in 1985 published readings showing losses of up to 70 percent each southern spring. The figures were so far outside expectation that Farman's group initially checked their own instruments for a fault before concluding the depletion over Antarctica was real.

The finding revived a debate about chlorofluorocarbons that had stalled through the early 1980s. Within two years, representatives of 43 countries signed the Montreal Protocol, freezing CFC production at 1986 levels and committing to cut it in half by 1999. Later revisions pushed developed nations to a full phase-out, and the agreement is still cited as the most effective environmental treaty negotiated to date.

Kadesh itself had settled nothing. Ramesses II and the Hittite king Muwatalli II fought to a bloody standstill around 1274 BCE, and each side went home claiming victory. It took sixteen more years, a change of Hittite king to Hattusili III, and shared fear of a rising Assyria before the two empires finally put the argument on paper.

The tablet found at Hattusa and the hieroglyphic copy in Egypt bind both kings to non-aggression, mutual defence against a third party, and the extradition of refugees and criminals. Each version names the other side's gods as witnesses. Ramesses also married a Hittite princess, and the peace held for roughly eighty years, until the Hittite state collapsed.

The idea is credited to Demetrius of Phalerum, an exiled Athenian statesman who pitched Ptolemy I on a collection that would gather every book that existed, but most historians now place the library's actual opening under his son, Ptolemy II. Agents were sent out with state money and a standing order to buy or copy any text they could find, on any subject, in any language.

Ships that docked at Alexandria could have their own scrolls seized and copied by palace scribes, with the copy handed back to the owner and the original kept in the collection, a practice later writers described simply as acquisitions from the ships. Estimates of the final holdings range wildly, from forty thousand scrolls to several hundred thousand, because no inventory from the library itself survives to settle it.

In 1744 a local ruler and a wandering preacher struck a bargain in the small town of Diriyah. Muhammad ibn Saud offered Muhammad ibn Abd al-Wahhab protection and armed force; in return, the preacher's strict Wahhabi reading of Islam gave ibn Saud's rule religious backing it had not had before.

Neither man's domain amounted to much on its own. Together their heirs pushed the alliance's territory across the Arabian Peninsula and into the Levant, reaching the coast near Bandar Abbas and the Bab al-Mandab strait, built on the same division of labour struck at the outset: one family supplied the soldiers, the other the doctrine.

The immediate spark was a soldier who displayed his scars in the forum and described losing his farm to a creditor before being imprisoned for debts run up while he fought for Rome. With harsh debt laws still enforced by the consul Appius, plebeians walked out of the city in 494 BC and camped on a hill outside the walls, the Sacred Mount, leaving Rome without the labourers and soldiers it depended on.

The senate had no army without them and negotiated rather than force a return. Some debtors were released from their debts, and the senate agreed to create a new office, tribune of the plebs, elected by plebeians and legally untouchable while in office. It was the first position in Roman government a plebeian could hold, and the secession, a strike rather than a revolt, became the model for at least four later ones.

Samuel Morse chose the words himself, on the advice of a friend's daughter who had picked them from a Bible verse. On 24 May 1844 he tapped them out in his code from the old Supreme Court chamber in the Capitol, and Alfred Vail received them forty miles away in Baltimore.

The line had been built with a federal grant of 30,000 dollars, after years in which Morse struggled to convince Congress the electric telegraph was worth funding at all. Within a decade a tangle of competing telegraph companies covered the eastern United States, and news that had taken days to travel by rail or post could cross a state in minutes.

A German craft apprentice who finished training did not become a master immediately. He became a journeyman, a Wandergeselle, required to spend years travelling between towns and working in different masters' workshops before he could apply to open one of his own. That travelling requirement, meant to spread technique and standardise skill, also put journeymen from many towns in contact with each other.

Those contacts hardened over time into associations that masters did not control, bodies through which journeymen could press collectively for pay and conditions rather than negotiating alone. The practice left little documentation from its earliest years, but the wandering system itself survived in parts of Germany long after the guild structure that produced it had otherwise faded.

Cyrus Field had already failed twice, losing cable to storms and snapped lines, before his ships finally joined a cable across the Atlantic floor in August 1858. Queen Victoria and President Buchanan exchanged congratulatory messages that took hours rather than the ten days a ship would need, and New York celebrated with fireworks that set City Hall's roof alight.

The celebration was premature. Chief electrician Wildman Whitehouse pushed excessive voltage through the line trying to speed up transmission, ruining its insulation, and by September the signal had failed altogether after barely three weeks of service. A working replacement did not cross the ocean until 1866.

Antiochus III lost the war before he lost the negotiation. Defeats at Thermopylae in 191 BC and Magnesia the following year left him with no army to bargain from, and the terms Rome dictated at Apamea in 188 BC reflected it: he gave up Europe entirely and all of Asia Minor west of the Taurus Mountains.

The bill for defeat was precise. Fifteen thousand talents of silver were due in instalments, twenty hostages were handed over with replacements required every three years, and his war elephants and most of his fleet were surrendered. Rome kept none of the ceded land for itself, parcelling it out to its allies Pergamon and Rhodes instead.

London, not New York, hosted the United Nations' first working session. Delegates from 51 founding nations gathered at Methodist Central Hall on 10 January 1946, a building better known for church conferences than international diplomacy, because no permanent headquarters yet existed anywhere.

The organisation spent its early years without a fixed home, meeting later in a former World's Fair pavilion in Flushing Meadows before Manhattan construction finished in 1951. That itinerant period included one of the Assembly's most consequential early votes, the November 1947 decision to partition Palestine, taken not in London but at the temporary Flushing site.

Theodor Herzl had wanted to hold the congress in Munich, but Jewish community leaders there, uneasy about a political movement built around a homeland in Palestine, pushed him out. He moved it to Basel instead, where 208 delegates from seventeen countries gathered in the Stadtcasino concert hall from 29 to 31 August 1897.

More than half the delegates came from Eastern Europe, and seventeen women attended, though without a vote. The congress adopted the Basel Program, stating that Zionism sought a home for the Jewish people in Palestine secured under public law, and founded the Zionist Organization with Herzl as its president to pursue it.

Nerva became emperor in 96 with a weak claim and no legions of his own, chosen by the Senate mainly because the alternative to him was chaos after Domitian's murder. His fix was to adopt an heir with real military standing, Trajan, rather than risk a son or a relative. It was a stopgap that hardened into a habit.

Four more times in a row, an ageing emperor adopted a capable outsider instead of naming a blood heir: Trajan chose Hadrian, Hadrian chose Antoninus Pius, and Antoninus chose Marcus Aurelius. Historians later credited the run of adoptions itself with the stability, since each successor arrived with backing already built rather than a court to win over. It ended in 180, when Marcus Aurelius broke the pattern and left the throne to his own son.

Flanders had good ports on the Scheldt but no reliable wool of its own, so it built an industry on importing fleece rather than growing it, mainly from England, and turning it into cloth good enough to sell back across the Channel and on to the Rhineland and Italy. Flemish weavers had earlier settled in Norfolk, seeding the very wool trade their home cities came to depend on.

The scale of that trade shows in the buildings it paid for: Bruges and Ghent raised belltowers and cloth halls that still stand, civic monuments funded by drapery rather than by a prince. Under the counts of Flanders, new institutions grew up around the industry, and grain and wine passing through the same ports added a second income alongside the wool.

Nightingale reached the army hospital at Scutari in November 1854 with 38 volunteer nurses and 15 nuns, to find wounded men lying in filth with barely functioning sanitation. Far more soldiers were dying of typhus, cholera and dysentery than of wounds from battle, and she pressed for handwashing, ventilation and clean supplies against a medical establishment that resisted her.

Death rates at Scutari fell sharply after a government sanitary commission overhauled the sewers and ventilation in 1855, though Nightingale herself credited that broader reform rather than her own efforts. She returned to Britain a public figure and used the attention to reform army medical statistics and found a school for nurses in London.

Constantinople's sack by crusaders in 1204 had knocked the Byzantine gold solidus out of circulation as Europe's trusted coin, and for decades no replacement filled the gap. Florence answered in 1252, striking a gold piece of just under three and a half grams that the city guaranteed at a fixed weight and purity, minted the same year as a similar Genoese coin.

The florin's reliability, not its beauty, made it spread. Merchants and bankers from London to the Levant priced contracts in it because they trusted what it contained, and by the following century roughly 150 states and cities were striking their own imitations bearing Florence's lily. A city known for wool and banking had put its name on Europe's benchmark coin.

Woodrow Wilson read his fourteen conditions for peace to a joint session of Congress on 8 January 1918, before the war he was addressing had even ended. They called for open diplomacy, freedom of the seas, self-determination for Europe's subject peoples, and a League of Nations to keep the settlement from unravelling.

Wilson's allies signed on to most of it without sharing his enthusiasm. Britain rejected freedom of the seas outright, and Georges Clemenceau, unimpressed by the whole exercise, is said to have remarked that even God had only ten commandments. The eventual Versailles treaty kept the League but added reparations and territorial terms no point had proposed.

France had been waiting for a chance to weaken Britain since losing the Seven Years' War, and the American victory at Saratoga in October 1777 convinced Paris the rebels could actually win. Benjamin Franklin, Arthur Lee and Silas Deane signed a treaty of alliance with the French minister Conrad Alexandre Gerard on 6 February 1778.

The agreement bound each side not to make a separate peace with Britain, and it opened the door to French ships, money and soldiers that the colonies could not supply themselves. That support proved decisive years later at Yorktown, where a French fleet closed off the bay while French and American troops besieged the British army on land.

It took over thirty years of campaigning against the Saxons alone, punctuated by mass deportations and, after one rebellion, the killing of thousands of prisoners at Verden. Charlemagne also deposed the Lombard king Desiderius in Italy in 774 and removed the Bavarian duke Tassilo in 788, absorbing both duchies directly under Frankish rule.

Not every campaign succeeded: a Frankish force crossing the Pyrenees into Spain was ambushed and destroyed at Roncevaux Pass in 778, a defeat later reworked into legend as the Song of Roland. On Christmas Day 800, Pope Leo III crowned Charlemagne emperor in Rome, the first person to hold that title in the west since 476.

The Congress of Racial Equality sent thirteen riders out of Washington on 4 May 1961 on ordinary Greyhound and Trailways buses, testing a Supreme Court ruling against segregated interstate travel that Southern states were simply ignoring. James Farmer led the first group, planning to reach New Orleans by mid month.

They never made it that far without incident. On 14 May, a mob outside Anniston, Alabama slashed a bus's tyres, forced it to stop, and threw a firebomb through a window, then held the doors shut before the riders escaped and were beaten as they fled. The rides continued through the summer with new volunteers each time a group was arrested, until the Interstate Commerce Commission ordered bus terminals desegregated that November.

Lafayette drafted an early version with Thomas Jefferson, then the American minister in Paris, looking over his shoulder, before the National Constituent Assembly rewrote it into seventeen short articles and adopted it on 26 August 1789. It swept away noble exemptions from taxation and declared that law applies equally to everyone, a direct answer to a monarchy built on inherited privilege.

The articles said little about who counted as a citizen in practice. Olympe de Gouges would answer with her own Declaration of the Rights of Woman three years later, and slavery in France's colonies was not abolished until 1794, then restored under Napoleon. The 1789 text itself survives largely unchanged, now written into the preamble of the French constitution.

War, not ideology, started the Fronde. France's long fight against Spain and its role in the Thirty Years' War had drained the treasury, and when the crown tried to raise money by taxing the bourgeoisie, the Parlement of Paris refused to register the decrees, arguing they violated established rights. The revolt that followed took its mocking name from the fronde, a child's slingshot banned in the city's streets.

The rebellion had two distinct rounds. Judicial officials and the Parlement led the first, from 1648 to 1649; discontented nobles, including the Prince de Condé and the general Turenne, led a bloodier second phase that ran until 1653. Louis XIV, still a boy through much of it, was forced to flee Paris more than once, an experience later historians link to his lifelong insistence on ruling without rivals.

Fujiwara no Michinaga never held the title of regent in the strict sense and did not need to. He married four daughters to successive emperors, including placing his daughter Shoshi as empress alongside an emperor who already had one, giving him a direct hand in choosing every heir to the throne.

He ruled instead through the informal honorific Mido Kampaku, taken from the name of his residence, backed by alliances with the Minamoto military house. Having eliminated a rival nephew through a manufactured scandal and outlived his elder brothers, he governed Japan's court from behind the throne for two decades before retiring as a monk in 1019.

Robert Fulton's North River Steamboat, later remembered as the Clermont, left New York on 17 August 1807 bound for Albany, a distance sailing ships covered unreliably against wind and current. It reached Albany in about thirty two hours of running time, averaging roughly five miles an hour and, by Fulton's own account, overtaking sloops that had been struggling against the wind.

What made the voyage matter was not its speed but its ledger: within its first year the boat turned a profit carrying passengers on a fixed schedule, something no earlier steam vessel had managed. Regular, reliable timing rather than raw novelty was what convinced investors that steam travel on rivers could be a business, not just a demonstration.

Almost nothing about Funan comes from its own writing; most of what is known was dug up at Oc Eo, a port site in the Mekong delta, or recorded by Chinese envoys who visited and wrote it down for their own court. The kingdom's territory ran along the Malay Peninsula and up into what is now Cambodia and southern Vietnam, astride the sea lanes any India-to-China cargo had to pass.

Excavators at Oc Eo found Roman coins bearing Antoninus Pius and Marcus Aurelius alongside Persian, Indian and Greek goods, plus local imitations of Roman currency struck by Funanese craftsmen who had clearly seen the originals. One scholar has argued the port was Kattigara, the easternmost trading point named in Ptolemy's geography, the edge of the known world as a Roman cartographer understood it.

Samurai stipends were paid in rice, not coin, which meant an entire warrior class depended on brokers to turn grain into usable money. The Dojima Rice Exchange in Osaka, licensed in 1697, grew around that need, and by the early eighteenth century its merchants were trading standardised contracts for rice to be delivered later at an agreed price, rather than sacks of grain on the spot.

Brokers effectively ran deposit accounts for daimyo and their retainers, taking in rice, issuing paper claims against it, and extending credit against future harvests. The system gave Dojima's traders enough influence over rice prices, and by extension the wider economy, that the shogunate eventually stepped in to formally sanction and oversee the exchange in 1773, decades after the practice had already taken hold.

Galileo was seventy when he knelt before ten cardinals of the Inquisition in Rome. The formal finding was not heresy itself but that he was vehemently suspected of it, for holding that the sun stands still at the centre of the world and the earth moves. He was made to renounce the view aloud.

The sentence spared his life but not his freedom. Imprisonment was commuted the next day to permanent confinement, and after a spell with an archbishop in Siena he was allowed home to his villa at Arcetri, near Florence, where he lived watched over until his death in 1642.

Gallienus inherited a crisis he had not made when his father Valerian was captured by the Sassanid king Shapur I in 260, leaving him sole emperor of a state under attack on every frontier at once. In the west, the general Postumus broke away and set up a rival Gallic Empire covering Britain, Spain and much of Gaul, and it outlasted Gallienus entirely.

In the east, Palmyra under Odaenathus took on Rome's defence against Persia while staying nominally loyal, a loyalty his widow Zenobia would later abandon. Gallienus was killed in September 268 while besieging a usurper at Milan, cut down by his own officers after a false alarm drew him from his tent without his guard.

The General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade was meant as a stopgap. Twenty-three nations signed it in Geneva on 30 October 1947 while a much larger body, the proposed International Trade Organization, was still being negotiated among more than fifty countries. When the United States withdrew from that larger project, the stopgap became the only working framework for world trade.

GATT ran on that improvised basis for nearly half a century, through repeated rounds of tariff cuts, before it was finally given a permanent institution. On 1 January 1995 the World Trade Organization took over its functions, and the seventy six governments that had belonged to GATT became its founding members.

Delegates from a dozen European states met in Geneva in August 1864 and signed an agreement built directly on Henry Dunant's proposals from the previous year. It bound signatory armies to spare field hospitals and ambulances from attack and to treat wounded soldiers from any side without distinction once they were disabled from fighting.

Medical staff and the civilians helping them were granted protection as non-combatants, and the treaty gave the red cross on a white ground legal standing as the sign marking anyone and anything covered by these rules. It was the first multilateral treaty of its kind, and every later Geneva Convention was built as an addition to it.

The four conventions adopted in 1949 were written by people who had just read the Nuremberg and Tokyo trial records. Earlier Geneva agreements had covered wounded soldiers and prisoners of war; this revision added a fourth convention protecting civilians, the population that had suffered the war's occupations, sieges and camps with the least legal protection of all.

Together the four texts set out rules for the wounded and sick in the field, the wounded and shipwrecked at sea, the treatment of prisoners of war, and civilians under occupation. Nearly every state in the world has since ratified them, in whole or with reservations, giving them a reach that few other treaties from the period can match.

An alliance signed with the restored Byzantine Empire in 1261 was what really opened the door east: it gave Genoese merchants tax privileges in Constantinople that Venetians did not have. Genoa's ships followed the advantage into the Black Sea, founding the colony of Caffa in Crimea as a base for grain, slaves and silk arriving overland from Asia.

Further west, Genoese trading posts on Chios and Lesbos and at Smyrna gave the republic a chain of stopping points across the Aegean. None of it was formally an empire; Genoa ruled the sea lanes through scattered colonies and trading rights rather than territory, which made the rivalry with Venice as much financial as naval, fought out over decades of intermittent war.

George Floyd died in Minneapolis on 25 May 2020 after a police officer, Derek Chauvin, knelt on his neck for roughly nine and a half minutes while he was handcuffed on the pavement. A bystander filmed the arrest on her phone. Floyd told the officer more than twenty times that he could not breathe before he stopped moving.

The footage spread within hours and protests began in Minneapolis the following day, then spread to thousands of towns and cities across the United States and to more than sixty other countries over the following weeks. Estimates put total American participation at somewhere between fifteen and twenty six million people, making it among the largest protest movements in the country's history.

East Germany did not merge with West Germany as an equal partner. It dissolved itself and joined under Article 23 of the West German Basic Law, the same clause that had let the Saarland rejoin in 1957, and its territory was reconstituted into five states rather than kept as a single unit. The Unification Treaty setting out the terms was signed on 31 August 1990, and unity took effect just after midnight on 3 October.

Full sovereignty still needed the agreement of the four wartime occupying powers, settled in the Two Plus Four Treaty signed that September, which ended Allied occupation rights that had lasted since 1945. Soviet troops did not finish leaving German soil until 1994. East and West Berlin, divided for twenty-eight years, were merged in the same act and Berlin was named the capital of the united country.

The empire ended because a fleet refused to leave port. Ordered to sail against the British navy in a battle their admirals privately expected to lose, sailors at Kiel mutinied on 29 October 1918 and formed a workers' and soldiers' council, a model that spread to city after city within days.

By 9 November the unrest had reached Berlin, where Philipp Scheidemann announced a republic from a Reichstag window, reportedly without asking his own party's permission first. Kaiser Wilhelm II left for exile in the Netherlands the next morning, and the abdication he had resisted for weeks was settled within hours of the proclamation.

Austria's government ordered its own army not to resist when German troops crossed the border on 12 March 1938, so the annexation happened without a shot fired. A plebiscite held the following month returned a claimed 99.7 percent in favour, but it was run under German occupation after roughly 360,000 people were stripped of the vote and opponents arrested.

Neither Britain nor France moved to intervene. One British diplomat later recalled a common view at the time that Austrians were Germans after all, so if that was what they wanted it was not worth a war over. The lack of any response encouraged Hitler's next demands, aimed within months at Czechoslovakia.

The split traced back to a currency reform in 1948: when the Western allies introduced the Deutsche Mark in their zones without Soviet agreement, Moscow walked out of the joint governing councils and sealed off road and rail access to West Berlin, forcing a year-long allied airlift to keep the city fed. Reparations disputes had already made joint administration of Germany nearly unworkable before the blockade began.

The Federal Republic of Germany was proclaimed in the western zones on 23 May 1949, and the German Democratic Republic followed in the Soviet zone that October. The two states pursued opposed economic and political systems for the next four decades, reuniting only in 1990 after the collapse of East Germany's government.

Older histories credited the Ghana Empire's fall to an Almoravid conquest around 1076, but modern scholars question whether any such military conquest happened at all. The Almoravids' spread of Islam likely unsettled Ghana's traditional authority without a single decisive battle behind it.

The more lasting pressure was economic. Ghana's wealth had rested on controlling trade rather than mining it directly, taking the gold heading north and the salt heading south while never holding the goldfields itself. As trade shifted toward routes along the Niger and Senegal rivers, that middleman position weakened and Ghana's vassals grew stronger than its centre.

Ghana's wealth rested on a gap in the map: the empire that ruled the western Sahel's gold trade never controlled a single gold field. Its kings held the routes instead, taxing salt heading south and gold heading north as camel caravans crossed lands they did not own.

Camels, introduced into the western Sahara centuries earlier, had turned irregular desert tracks into working roads. Merchants paid duties in both directions, reportedly a gold dinar on salt entering the kingdom and two on salt leaving it, and that toll, not mined ore, built Wagadu's reputation as a land of gold.

Al-Harith ibn Jabalah spent forty years holding a desert frontier for an emperor who did not entirely trust him. As foederati, the Ghassanids fielded cavalry against Persian and Lakhmid raiders so that Constantinople rarely had to, and in return Justinian gave al-Harith the highest rank open to a client king.

The alliance still cracked over religion. The Ghassanids followed the Miaphysite church, at odds with the Chalcedonian creed Constantinople preferred, and later Byzantine emperors moved against their rulers over it. The kingdom outlasted that quarrel only until 636, when it was swept up in the Arab conquest of Syria at Yarmuk.

Giordano Bruno spent seven years before the Roman Inquisition refusing to recant a list of positions that included denying the Trinity, Christ's divinity and the virgin birth, alongside his belief that souls were reincarnated. He also taught that the universe had no centre and no edge, and that the stars were distant suns with worlds of their own circling them.

The Inquisition burned him alive in Rome's Campo de' Fiori on 17 February 1600 after he refused every chance to recant. Historians still argue over how much his death owed to the cosmology and how much to the theology, since either set of claims alone was enough to convict a man of heresy in that court.

Gorbachev had signalled the change before he even held the top job, telling colleagues in December 1984 that the Soviet system needed openness to survive. Once he became general secretary in 1985, glasnost turned that into policy: censorship eased, previously banned books returned to library shelves, and newspapers began printing accounts of Stalin era crimes that had been unmentionable for decades.

Perestroika was the harder, slower half, restructuring how factories and ministries made decisions instead of taking orders from the centre. Dissidents and legal reformers argued the changes were vague compared with the civil liberties they wanted, but for ordinary citizens the shift in what could be said out loud was immediate.

Sui China sent an army of over a million men against Goguryeo in 612, by contemporary count 1,133,800 combat troops with a supply train that may have doubled it. It was the largest single invasion force fielded anywhere in the world up to that point, aimed at a kingdom holding Manchuria and northern Korea.

It failed completely. The general Eulji Mundeok drew a detachment of roughly 305,000 men into a retreat along the Salsu river and destroyed it; some 2,700 are recorded reaching home. Total Sui losses across the campaign passed 300,000, and the failed invasions helped push the Sui dynasty toward collapse six years later.

Emperor Charles IV issued the Golden Bull at imperial diets in Nuremberg and Metz in 1356, and it did something no earlier decree had managed: it fixed exactly who could choose the next King of the Romans and how. Seven electors got the vote, the archbishops of Mainz, Cologne and Trier, and the secular rulers of Bohemia, the Rhineland Palatinate, Saxony-Wittenberg and Brandenburg.

Four votes out of seven were enough to elect an emperor, so no minority of three could block a decision forever. The electoral territories themselves were made indivisible, closing off the kind of family partition that had fragmented other German titles. The Bull said nothing about needing papal approval for any of it, a silence that quietly ended Rome's old claim to confirm the choice.

Batu Khan spent seven years leading Mongol armies across the Eastern European steppe before settling, around 1242, into ruling what he had conquered rather than expanding it further. His territory stretched from Siberia to the Danube and from the Black Sea to the Caspian, governed from a new base on the lower Volga.

Russian princes were not removed from their thrones. They kept their lands on condition that they travelled to the khan's court for confirmation of their title and paid regular tribute, a system that let a small Mongol administration control a much larger settled population without having to occupy every town itself.

American senator George Mitchell had chaired talks among Northern Ireland's parties for nearly two years before Tony Blair and Bertie Ahern pushed the deal to a close on 10 April 1998. The text split governance into three strands, a devolved assembly in Belfast, cooperation between Belfast and Dublin, and cooperation between Dublin and London, with ministerial seats shared out among unionist and nationalist parties by formula.

Voters north and south of the border ratified it separately in May 1998, in Northern Ireland by 71 percent and in the Republic by 94 percent. Paramilitary groups on both sides agreed to begin decommissioning weapons, and the deal set up an assembly that has been suspended repeatedly since, but the ceasefire it built on has held.

Konstantin Chernenko died on 10 March 1985, the third Soviet leader to die in office in under three years, and the Politburo met the same night to choose a successor. At 53, Mikhail Gorbachev was younger than most of the men voting, and some doubted his experience, but he was elected general secretary the following day, on 11 March 1985.
