He moved quickly. Glasnost loosened censorship and let citizens argue publicly about the system's failures, while perestroika began decentralising economic decisions long made in Moscow. He later pulled troops out of Afghanistan, a war he privately considered a mistake, and pursued arms reductions with Washington. None of it was designed to dissolve the Soviet state, but the openness it allowed made that outcome harder to stop.

Goryeo's peak is usually dated to the reign of Munjong, from 1046 to 1083, remembered afterward as its most peaceful and prosperous stretch. Buddhism held the status of state religion, and the capital alone supported some seventy temples by the 11th century.

The dynasty's most striking achievement survives at Haeinsa temple: the Tripitaka Koreana, a Buddhist canon carved onto roughly 81,000 wooden printing blocks. It replaced an earlier edition destroyed during the Mongol invasions, recarved between 1236 and 1251 and still intact today, alongside Goryeo's movable metal type, centuries ahead of Gutenberg.

Wang Geon did not seize the throne himself; his own generals handed it to him after they turned on their unstable ruler, Kung Ye, in 918. He renamed the kingdom Goryeo, reviving an old dynastic name, and moved its capital to his home city of Kaesong.

Unification followed gradually rather than by a single conquest: the weakened Silla kingdom submitted peacefully in 935, and Later Baekje fell the year after. The name Goryeo, already centuries old when Wang Geon revived it, is the root of the modern word Korea.

Goryeo potters did not simply copy the Chinese wares they were admired for. They developed sanggam, a technique of carving a design into wet clay and packing the grooves with contrasting white or dark clay before glazing, so the pattern showed through the finished surface rather than sitting on top of it.

The colour mattered as much as the method. Goryeo's smaller kilns fired and cooled faster than their Chinese counterparts, which kept the glaze's mineral crystals from fully forming and left a paler, greyer green known as bisaek, prized in its own right rather than judged against the deeper jade of Chinese celadon.

Gaius Gracchus, tribune of the people in 123 BCE, fixed the price ordinary Romans paid for grain at roughly six and a third asses per modius, a sum kept deliberately a little below what wheat normally fetched just after harvest. The state bought grain when it was cheap and stored it in public granaries, ready to release at the fixed price regardless of market conditions.

The scheme drew support well beyond the poor it was meant to help, since it gave Gracchus a large, grateful constituency in an assembly where votes mattered more than sympathy. The law outlived him by decades before being repealed near the century's end, only to be restored shortly afterward by another tribune.

Joseph Paxton was a gardener, not a trained architect, and he sketched the exhibition hall's design on blotting paper during a railway board meeting. His glasshouse of cast iron and glass, nicknamed the Crystal Palace, went from proposal to opening in nine months and enclosed several mature elm trees in Hyde Park rather than cutting them down.

Prince Albert had pushed for the exhibition against sceptics who feared it would draw a mob to London. Instead six million visitors came between May and October 1851, roughly a third of the population of England and Wales, and the profits later paid for the Victoria and Albert, Science and Natural History museums.

Buganda, Bunyoro and Rwanda were among several interlacustrine kingdoms that formed around the Great Lakes of East Africa, each resting on cattle-keeping and dense agriculture that could support courts, standing retinues and layered chieftaincies rather than scattered village rule.

These states shared features: a sacred kingship, tribute paid in cattle and produce, and appointed chiefs who answered upward. But they rose to power by different routes, and Bunyoro's traditions, which trace an earlier, semi-legendary Chwezi dynasty, differ from Buganda's account of a clan-based founding.

Thunberg refused to fly, so she crossed the Atlantic in a racing yacht, spending two weeks at sea from Plymouth to reach New York in time for the United Nations Climate Action Summit on 23 September 2019. She was sixteen. Her speech to the assembled leaders lasted barely four minutes and abandoned the polite tone such gatherings usually get.

The speech opened by asking the room how they dared, and accused leaders of stealing her future with empty words while ecosystems collapsed and people died. Clips of the line, delivered with a visible glare that circulated as a meme within hours, made the speech one of the most shared moments of her campaign, though the summit itself produced no binding new emissions commitments.

The Lucayans had been settling the Bahamas for around eight hundred years by the time their population peaked at roughly 40,000, living in small farming and fishing communities spread across the islands' cays. They grew cassava and cotton, fished the shallow banks, and had no reason to expect the arrival of Columbus's ships in 1492.

What followed was rapid and total. Spanish raiders carried Lucayans off to work as forced labour and pearl divers on other islands, and by 1520, when colonists tried to round up whoever remained, they could find only eleven people left in the entire archipelago. The Bahamas then stood uninhabited for roughly 130 years.

The destroyer USS Maddox exchanged fire with North Vietnamese torpedo boats on 2 August 1964. A second clash two days later, reported to Washington as another attack, is now widely doubted by historians, and declassified National Security Agency material suggests it may not have happened at all.

Congress nonetheless passed the resolution on 7 August, granting President Johnson power to use armed force in Southeast Asia without a formal declaration of war. The vote was 416 to nil in the House and 88 to 2 in the Senate. Johnson later remarked that the resolution was like his grandmother's nightshirt: it covered everything.

An anonymous letter reached a Catholic peer, Lord Monteagle, in late October 1605, warning him to stay away from the opening of Parliament because it would receive a terrible blow without seeing who struck it. He handed it to the authorities, and a search of the cellars beneath the House of Lords on the night of 4 November found Guy Fawkes guarding three dozen barrels of gunpowder hidden under firewood.

Fawkes, a soldier who had spent a decade fighting in the Spanish Netherlands, was arrested under a false name and tortured in the Tower before naming his fellow conspirators. Several, including the plot's organiser Robert Catesby, died resisting arrest at Holbeche House days later; the survivors, Fawkes among them, were convicted of treason and executed the following January.

The dynasty took its name from an obscure ruler simply called Gupta, whose kingdom around 240 was modest. Its real rise came under his grandson Chandragupta I, who took the throne around 320 after marrying Kumaradevi, a princess of the Licchavi clan. That marriage brought territory and prestige enough for him to claim the grand title Maharajadhiraja, king of kings.

What followed is remembered less for conquest than for output. Under Chandragupta's successors, the mathematician Aryabhata worked out a value for pi and described the earth's rotation, while Kalidasa wrote Sanskrit poetry still read today. None of it required a battle: the Gupta court funded scholars and let them work.

Anthony Ashley-Cooper, Earl of Shaftesbury, pushed the bill through a Parliament trying to keep the Catholic James, Duke of York, from the throne, and feared what an unrestrained monarch might do to critics in the meantime. The mechanism it strengthened was old: a prisoner could demand a writ ordering a jailer to bring them before a judge and justify the detention.

What was new was the enforcement. The Act barred jailers from shipping a prisoner abroad or shuffling them between prisons to dodge that writ, and it fined any jailer who tried, with the money going to the prisoner. It covered most criminal detentions, though not treason or felony charges, and left the writ itself as the tool later invoked against arbitrary confinement far beyond England.

Trajan died in August 117 without a clearly named heir, and Hadrian, his cousin and ward, claimed that an adoption had been arranged on Trajan's deathbed. The story was convenient enough, and Hadrian's position as a serving general in the east strong enough, that the Senate had little practical choice but to confirm him.

Where Trajan had expanded the empire, Hadrian spent much of his reign consolidating it, withdrawing from Trajan's unstable Mesopotamian conquests and touring the provinces in person. In Britain he ordered the construction of a fortified wall running roughly 73 miles coast to coast, marking a fixed northern frontier rather than a line for further advance.

Abu Zakariya Yahya governed Tunis on behalf of the Almohad caliphate until 1229, when the caliph in Marrakesh publicly renounced the doctrine the whole empire had been built on. Abu Zakariya treated that as grounds to stop obeying him and ruled Ifriqiya on his own account from then on.

He kept the modest title of amir for years before finally claiming the caliphal title of Commander of the Faithful around 1236, a direct challenge to Marrakesh. Tunis, chosen for its harbour linking the western and eastern Mediterranean rather than any inland alternative, remained the Hafsid capital for the next three and a half centuries.

Tsar Nicholas II called the conference, and it opened on 18 May 1899, his own birthday, at the House in the Wood near The Hague. Delegates from 26 states banned poison, the killing of surrendered soldiers, looting and collective punishment, and required humane treatment of prisoners.

A separate declaration outlawed dropping projectiles from balloons for five years and banned soft-nosed bullets that flattened on impact, a rule aimed at ammunition nicknamed after the Dum Dum arsenal in India. The conference also created the Permanent Court of Arbitration, the first standing body for settling disputes between states without war.

Before Emperor Wu, an official's career depended largely on birth or patronage. He founded an Imperial Academy to teach the Confucian classics and began selecting officials by their grasp of that scholarship rather than their family connections, a change aimed at pulling talented commoners into an administration the aristocracy had dominated.

The system he began was still rough by later standards, closer to sponsored recommendation than a formal examination open to all. It nonetheless set the template that Chinese dynasties refined for centuries afterward: officials chosen, at least in principle, for what they knew rather than who they were born to.

The Qin state's own capital fell within four years of the emperor's death, and out of the scramble that followed came two rival commanders, Liu Bang and Xiang Yu. Liu Bang, a commoner who had once worked as a minor local official, took the title King of Han in 206 BCE and then finished off Xiang Yu at Gaixia in 202 BCE, becoming Emperor Gaozu of a reunified China.

The dynasty he founded gave China its ethnonym, the Han people, and lasted on and off for four centuries. Under his successors it pushed the Silk Road west, standardised coinage, and produced papermaking and early seismometers. Emperor Wu later made Confucian learning the basis of the civil service, a system for selecting officials that outlasted the dynasty itself by well over a thousand years.

Emperor Wu had spent years fighting the nomadic Xiongnu along the northern frontier before he turned to a cheaper solution: making neighbouring rulers send envoys, gifts and hostages to his court instead of raiding it. States that submitted received recognition and trading rights in return, a bargain dressed up as ceremony.

The arrangement reached well beyond China's immediate borders. Envoys travelled to kingdoms in Central Asia that Han China had only recently learned existed, some missions numbering in the hundreds of people, carrying silk and receiving horses, furs and rare goods that moved as tribute in name but as trade in practice.

The Hanseatic League never had a founding ceremony, and no single document created it. What happened in 1241 was narrower: Lubeck, sitting on both the Baltic and North Sea trade routes, struck an alliance with Hamburg to protect the roads between them from robbery and tolls. The word Hanse itself would not appear in a document for another twenty six years.

Out of that arrangement grew a network that eventually took in close to two hundred towns across what are now eight countries. Hanseatic ships carried furs, wax, timber and grain west and cloth east, and Bergen's stockfish moved south in exchange for grain. By the time of the Treaty of Stralsund in 1370 the League could fight and win a war against the King of Denmark.

Amsterdam beat the Hanse at its own business. Dutch shipowners undercut the league's freight rates on the Baltic grain run, and once merchants could hire a cheaper hold, the towns of Lubeck and Bremen lost the middleman role that had funded their fleets for three centuries.

The league had no standing army, no shared treasury and no single ruler to negotiate for it, only a loose diet of towns that voted and often disagreed. Territorial princes in Germany and Scandinavia chipped away at member cities' independence, and by 1669 only a handful of delegates bothered to attend its final formal assembly.

No single treaty created the Hanseatic League. Merchant guilds in Lubeck, Hamburg, Danzig and dozens of other towns had simply found it paid to act together, protecting shared trade routes and demanding the same privileges from foreign rulers rather than negotiating alone.

Their leverage peaked around 1370, when the League beat Denmark in a war fought largely over control of Baltic herring and trade routes. The Treaty of Stralsund that year forced King Valdemar IV to grant Hanseatic merchants tax exemptions and control of key fortresses guarding the Oresund strait, making the League Northern Europe's dominant commercial power.

Harsha was still a teenager when he took power in 606, after both his father and elder brother had died in quick succession, and he spent much of his reign fighting to hold together the territory he inherited. By the time he settled his capital at Kannauj, he controlled most of the Gangetic plain across northern India.

The clearest picture of his court comes from an outsider: the Chinese monk Xuanzang, who travelled through India collecting Buddhist texts and wrote admiringly of Harsha's fairness and generosity as a ruler. Xuanzang described a capital that drew scholars and artists from distant regions, largely because Harsha personally funded monasteries and religious gatherings.

Nobody recorded exactly when Kano and Katsina began, and Hausa tradition is more useful here than any chronicle: it remembers a division of labour rather than a founding date. Kano and Rano were known for weaving and dyeing cloth, while Katsina and Daura grew as places where caravans stopped to trade rather than to make anything themselves.

That split shaped centuries of growth even before either city turned Muslim. Kano's ruler Yaji converted around the 1350s, and later rulers built mosques and schools that pulled in clerics and merchants from as far as Egypt, but the underlying pattern, textile towns feeding trading towns, had been set long before Islam arrived to formalise it.

No single founding date survives for the Hausa city-states, only a slow crystallising of walled towns across what is now northern Nigeria into a set of kingdoms that specialised rather than competed for the same trade. Kano and Rano wove and dyed cloth in indigo on a scale that earned them the title kings of indigo; Katsina and Daura instead built their wealth as market towns, the kings of the market.

Gobir, positioned furthest north, took on the role of defending the others from raids, while Zazzau supplied enslaved labour to its neighbours. Hausa traders carried cloth, leather, salt, kola nuts and gold along routes stretching across the Sahara, founding merchant quarters in distant towns to keep the network running.

Rising population, not conquest, did the early work. As Polynesian settlers moved inland from Hawaii's coasts and valleys, denser farming became necessary, and canal fed pondfields built for taro let some communities support more people than others, giving ali'i chiefs a way to turn food surplus into political authority.

That authority rested on mana, a spiritual force chiefs claimed through genealogy, and was enforced through kapu, a system of restrictions on food, conduct and land. Heiau, temple platforms built from unmortared lava rock, marked this authority in stone; the largest, reserved for chiefs and priests, hosted the most consequential rituals.

Centuries before Captain Cook ever sighted the islands, Hawaii was never one kingdom but several, each built around a single volcanic island or stretch of coastline. Oral tradition traces the split to around 1200, when the archipelago broke into rival chiefdoms centred on Hawaii, Maui, Oahu and Kauai, each under its own line of ali'i.

Rule passed through the high chiefs, the ali'i nui, who commanded lesser chiefs and commoners alike and drew authority from genealogy as much as force. Borders between these island states shifted constantly with inter clan warfare, a pattern that held for generations until Kamehameha I finally brought the islands under a single crown in the 1790s.

On the evening of 4 May 1886, a rally in Chicago's Haymarket Square was winding down peacefully when police moved in to disperse the last few hundred people still listening. Someone in the crowd threw a dynamite bomb into the advancing ranks, killing officer Mathias Degan, and a chaotic exchange of gunfire followed. Seven police officers and at least four civilians died before the night was over.

Nobody ever established who threw the bomb; the chief suspect fled the country before he could be charged. Eight anarchists were tried anyway, most for their speeches rather than their actions, and only two had even been present that night. Seven were sentenced to death; four were hanged in November 1887, one died by suicide in his cell, and Illinois' governor pardoned the survivors in 1893, calling the trial unjust.

Thirty-five states, nearly every country in Europe alongside the United States and Canada, signed the Helsinki Final Act between 30 July and 1 August 1975. It was not a treaty and carried no enforcement mechanism, only a political commitment covering security, economic cooperation and, in its most contested section, human rights.

Soviet negotiators treated the human rights clauses as a formality that cost them little for Western recognition of Cold War borders. Dissidents inside the Eastern bloc read them differently, and used the accords to found monitoring groups, among them Helsinki Watch, which later grew into Human Rights Watch.

When John of Gaunt died in February 1399, Richard II cancelled the arrangements that would have let his exiled cousin Henry Bolingbroke inherit Gaunt's lands automatically. Richard then left for a campaign in Ireland, and Henry sailed back to England claiming he only wanted his inheritance restored, gathering soldiers and support faster than the king's regents could counter him.

By the time Richard returned, Henry controlled enough of the realm to have himself crowned Henry IV instead, founding the Lancastrian line. Richard was imprisoned and died within months, aged thirty three, most likely starved on Henry's order, though an examination of his skeleton centuries later found no marks of violence.

Henry became king on 22 April 1509 at seventeen, on his father's death, and moved fast once in power. Within weeks he had Richard Empson and Edmund Dudley, his father's unpopular tax collectors, arrested, an early sign of the readiness to use execution as a political tool that would mark the reign.

He also reversed himself on marriage. Having once rejected the idea at fourteen, Henry announced soon after his father's burial that he would after all marry Catherine of Aragon, his brother Arthur's widow, citing a supposed deathbed wish of his father's. The wedding followed on 11 June 1509, with a joint coronation at Westminster Abbey less than two weeks after.

Hojo Tokimasa was never shogun, and neither was his son, grandson, or any Hojo after him. When his son in law Minamoto no Yoritomo died in 1199, Tokimasa took the title of regent, shikken, to the boy who inherited the shogunate, and by 1203 the family holding real power in Kamakura was not the one holding the office.

The arrangement outlasted Tokimasa by more than a century. Hojo regents kept a line of shoguns as figureheads, at times replacing one for a more pliable relative, and ran the Kamakura government until 1333, when a rival imperial faction finally brought the clan down.

Charlemagne had already been crowned emperor once, in 800, but that title lapsed after his line's power collapsed. When Pope John XII placed a crown on Otto I in 962, he was reviving a defunct office rather than inventing one, giving the German kings a claim to stand as Charlemagne's successors in the west.

Otto had already spent over a decade consolidating power in Germany and northern Italy before the coronation, defeating rival dukes and a Magyar invasion at the Lechfeld. The empire that took shape around his crown had no fixed capital and no single language, a loose federation of princes under an emperor that would outlast most of its neighbours by centuries.

Lincoln signed the Homestead Act on 20 May 1862, opening surveyed public land to almost anyone willing to work it. Applicants had to be citizens or intend to become one, be at least twenty one or head a household, and had never taken up arms against the government.

Five years of residence and cultivation turned a 160 acre claim into a deed. Between 1862 and 1934 the act granted about 1.6 million homesteads covering roughly 270 million acres, and a 2017 estimate put the number of living Americans descended from those settlers at around 93 million.

Britain's grip on Hong Kong had always rested on three separate deals: the island ceded outright in 1842, Kowloon added in 1860, and the much larger New Territories held only on a 99 year lease signed in 1898. That lease was due to expire in 1997, and since the colony no longer functioned without the mainland territory attached to it, Britain agreed to hand back the whole thing rather than just the leased part.

The transfer took place at midnight on 1 July 1997, at a ceremony attended by Prince Charles, Tony Blair and Jiang Zemin. China promised Hong Kong could keep its own legal system, currency and way of life for fifty years under the arrangement known as one country, two systems, a promise that continues to shape disputes over how much autonomy the territory actually retains.

The Hopewell peoples of eastern North America were never one nation, but a scatter of river-valley communities linked by exchange routes running from Lake Ontario south to Florida. What moved along those routes travelled remarkable distances for people without wheeled transport: obsidian from what is now Yellowstone turns up by the hundreds of pounds in burial mounds in Ohio.

Copper and mica came from the Great Lakes, marine shells and pearls from the Gulf and Atlantic coasts, and pipestone was carved locally into ceremonial pipes that were then traded far from where they were made. The goods moving through this network were less about daily use than about ceremony, drawing distant communities together for burials and gatherings that the objects themselves were made for.

A hospital in Montpellier gave Innocent III his model: there, he was told, the hungry were fed and orphans cared for by staff who lived as servants rather than paid officials. In 1201 he rebuilt a declining Saxon hospice on the Tiber in Rome to the same purpose, and it took the name Santo Spirito.

The new hospital also answered a specific horror Innocent had heard of: infants abandoned and drowned in the river. It installed a rotating hatch where a mother could leave a baby anonymously and have it taken in rather than left to die. Other Italian and European cities copied both the hospital's structure and the hatch over the following centuries.

Halebidu's Hoysaleswara temple was never finished. Work began around 1120 under King Vishnuvardhana and continued for decades, yet no tower was ever raised over its two shrines, only a stone plinth carved in bands of elephants, horsemen and scenes from the Ramayana and Mahabharata.

The sculptors worked in soapstone, soft enough to cut when freshly quarried and hard enough to survive centuries once exposed to air, which let a Hoysala temple carry detail harder stone would not allow. Nearby Belur's Chennakeshava temple, begun three years earlier, shows the same technique on a completed structure.

On 2 May 1670, Charles II signed away land he had never seen. The royal charter handed a group of London investors, led by his cousin Prince Rupert, exclusive trading rights over every river and stream draining into Hudson Bay, a territory that came to be called Rupert's Land.

Nobody in London had measured what that meant. The drainage basin covered close to four million square kilometres, more than a third of modern Canada, reaching into what is now the north central United States. Rupert became the company's first governor over a territory neither he nor his fellow shareholders had set foot in.

Baghdad fell to Hulagu Khan's army in February 1258 after a siege of less than two weeks, ending five centuries of Abbasid rule. The last caliph, al-Musta'sim, was rolled in a carpet and trampled by horses, a method the Mongols reserved for royal captives whose blood was not to touch the ground directly.

Hulagu, grandson of Genghis Khan, had already crushed the Nizari Ismaili strongholds in Persia in 1256 before turning on Baghdad. Out of these conquests he built the Ilkhanate, a Mongol state ruling Persia and Mesopotamia that answered nominally to the Great Khan in the east but governed as its own dynasty for the next eighty years.

The organisation did not emerge from a labour congress but from a peace treaty. Its founding report was folded into Part XIII of the Treaty of Versailles, adopted at the Paris peace conference on 11 April 1919, on the argument that lasting peace required decent conditions for workers rather than the resentment that had helped produce the war.

Its structure was unusual for the time: governments, employers and workers each sent delegates, though governments held twice the votes of the other two groups combined. The first International Labour Conference met in Washington in October 1919 and adopted six conventions at once, setting limits on working hours and banning most child labour.

Since the 1920s, US immigration law had allotted entry quotas by national origin, a system built to favour Western and Northern Europe and keep the country's population mix roughly as it already was. Johnson signed its replacement at the foot of the Statue of Liberty on 3 October 1965, and told the crowd the change was not revolutionary, expecting it to reshape little.

It reshaped a great deal. With origin quotas gone, immigration from Asia and Latin America rose sharply in the decades that followed; among those who arrived after the act, roughly half came from Latin America and a quarter from Asia. The foreign-born share of the US population, about 5 percent when the act passed, had nearly tripled by the early twenty-first century.

Andrew Johnson fired his own Secretary of War, Edwin Stanton, without asking the Senate first, defying a law Congress had passed specifically to stop him. The House impeached him for it on 24 February 1868, the first such vote against a sitting president.

The Senate trial came down to a single ballot. Thirty five senators voted to convict against nineteen for acquittal, one vote short of the two thirds needed to remove him from office, and Johnson finished his term still president.

England set an early precedent. In the fourteenth century Edward III banned the import of finished woollen cloth outright, hoping to force the trade's most profitable stage, weaving rather than raw wool export, onto English looms instead of Flemish ones.

Tudor monarchs refined the approach. Henry VIII and Elizabeth I combined tariffs with subsidies, granted monopolies and even sponsored industrial espionage to build up domestic wool manufacturing, treating trade policy as a tool for growing an industry rather than simply raising revenue.

Every year Inca officials called apupanaca travelled the provinces selecting girls of eight to ten, mostly from the families of local nobles, and sent them to live in walled compounds called acllawasi, sometimes housing as many as two hundred at once. Selection was a form of tribute the state extracted directly from conquered peoples.

Inside, the chosen women wove the finest cloth in the empire and brewed the chicha used in state ceremonies, skills valued highly enough that the results were reserved for the Inca and his court. Some were later married off to men who had served the empire well; others were kept for religious duties, and a select few were set aside for sacrifice.

Cusco was a modest hill city under siege when the Chanka, its traditional enemy, attacked and the ruler Viracocha fled rather than defend it. His son Cusi Yupanqui rallied the defenders, drove the Chanka off, and had himself crowned Sapa Inca under a new name: Pachacuti, Earth Shaker.

What followed was not conquest by the sword alone. Pachacuti summoned neighbouring chiefs to Cusco for feasts and ceremony, then converted goodwill into obligation, demanding labour and soldiers in return. His armies pushed south to Titicaca and north toward Quito, and within three generations the Cusco valley had become the largest empire the pre-Columbian Americas ever saw.

By 1493 the empire ruled from Cusco stretched north into what is now Ecuador and Colombia and south along the Andes, held together not by a single army garrisoning it but by the Qhapaq Nan, a road network reaching almost every province it controlled.

Population estimates run from six to fourteen million, a range so wide partly because the Incas kept their records on knotted cords called quipu, most of which the Spanish later destroyed. Households owed labour rather than goods under the mit'a system, which built the roads, bridges and storehouses that made the empire's size workable at all.

A quipu carried no letters. Cusco's officials, called quipucamayocs, encoded numbers into knotted cords of cotton or camelid wool: cord colour, knot position and cord order together held a decimal figure, and a trained reader could recite what it meant without ever seeing a written word.

Under expanding Inca rule the knots tracked tribute owed under the mita labour system, counted households down to infants and the elderly, and recorded stores and military musters across a state that stretched thousands of kilometres. No alphabet was needed to run an empire that size, only cords, and enough quipucamayocs trained to read them the same way twice.

Inchon's harbour had tides among the largest in the world, up to eleven metres between low and high water, which left invading ships only a narrow window each day to cross the mudflats before running aground. Many of MacArthur's own planners argued against the site for exactly that reason; he pushed it through regardless, betting that its very unsuitability meant the North Koreans would not expect a landing there.

Reconnaissance led by a naval lieutenant named Eugene Clark found that the harbour's channels had not, in fact, been mined as feared, clearing the way for the assault that began on 15 September 1950 with the capture of Wolmido island ahead of the main landings. Within a month UN forces had taken roughly 135,000 North Korean prisoners, and Seoul was recaptured before the month was out.

B.R. Ambedkar chaired the seven member committee that spent nearly three years drafting the document, sitting through eleven sessions of the Constituent Assembly before it was finished. What they produced remains the longest written constitution of any country, running to 395 articles and eight schedules by the time it took effect on 26 January 1950.

The date was chosen deliberately: 26 January had already been marked twenty years earlier as Purna Swaraj day, when the Indian National Congress first declared full independence as a goal rather than a distant hope. Rajendra Prasad took office as the republic's first president on the same day the document came into force.

A lawyer named Cyril Radcliffe, who had never set foot in India before, was given five weeks in the summer of 1947 to draw the border splitting Punjab and Bengal between two new countries. He worked from out of date maps and census returns, and the line he produced was published only after independence had already taken effect on 14 and 15 August.

Estimates of the dead from the migrations that followed range from roughly 200,000 to two million, a gap that reflects how little the movement of people across the new border was ever formally counted. Between twelve and twenty million people crossed it in one direction or the other, on foot, by cart, and by train.

Sailors did not need to fight the wind. The Indian Ocean simply reverses direction with the seasons, so ships bound east ran before the summer monsoon and returned home riding the winter reversal months later, a rhythm that let merchants cross open water instead of hugging a coastline for thousands of kilometres.

By 1200 that rhythm linked Swahili ports such as Kilwa and Mogadishu to Arabia, Gujarat and the Malay world, moving ivory, gold and mangrove timber east and cloth, beads and ceramics west. No single power ran the network; it worked because captains from different coasts kept the same seasonal calendar.

Andrew Jackson signed the act on 28 May 1830, authorising the government to trade land west of the Mississippi for tribal territory in the southeast. It did not name a single tribe, but its target was the land held by the Cherokee, Choctaw, Creek, Chickasaw and Seminole nations, whose removal Jackson framed as an exchange rather than an expulsion.

The Cherokee fought removal in the courts and won a Supreme Court ruling in their favour, which Jackson's administration simply ignored. Federal troops marched roughly 16,000 Cherokee west in the winter of 1838 and 1839 along what became known as the Trail of Tears; thousands died of cold, disease and starvation on the way, one of at least eighteen tribes displaced under the act.

Europeans had bought Indian indigo for the colour since antiquity, and the Greek word for it simply meant Indian. What changed around 1600 was the route: once Portuguese ships could sail directly to Indian ports rather than relying on overland middlemen, the dye arrived in larger volumes at lower cost.

European weavers wanted a fast, reliable blue for wool and cotton, and Indian producers scaled up to meet it, planting fields specifically for the crop rather than gathering it incidentally. Spain and other powers later tried to break the dependence by growing indigo in their own American colonies, using enslaved labour to do it.

Dutch troops held Indonesia's major cities and industrial sites for four years after the 1945 independence proclamation but could never pacify the countryside, where guerrilla resistance kept the occupation costly and inconclusive. Two rounds of negotiated agreements, at Linggarjati and Renville, broke down into renewed fighting each time the Dutch launched what they called police actions to reassert control.

What finally forced the concession was Washington, which threatened in 1949 to cut off Marshall Plan reconstruction funds to the Netherlands unless it settled the conflict. Queen Juliana signed the transfer of sovereignty on 27 December 1949, ending four years and four months of war and leaving the new republic to govern an archipelago the Dutch had ruled for more than three centuries.

Jawaharlal Nehru and Mohammad Ayub Khan signed the treaty in Karachi on 19 September 1960, alongside a World Bank official whose institution had spent nearly a decade brokering the deal. Rather than sharing each river, the treaty split the Indus system in two: India got the three eastern tributaries, the Ravi, Beas and Sutlej, while Pakistan got the larger western ones, the Indus, Chenab and Jhelum.

The split was lopsided by volume, roughly eighty percent of the combined flow going to Pakistan, but it gave each side clear control rather than a shared tap either could dispute. The treaty survived wars between the two countries in 1965, 1971 and 1999 without either side suspending it, a record that outlasted most of what else the two nations agreed that decade.

Ronald Reagan and Mikhail Gorbachev signed the treaty at the White House on 8 December 1987, after years of talks that had collapsed as recently as the Reykjavik summit the year before. It banned an entire category of weapon rather than merely limiting numbers: ground launched ballistic and cruise missiles with ranges between 500 and 5,500 kilometres, nuclear and conventional alike.

Verification mattered as much as the ban itself, since each side was for the first time allowed to inspect the other's missile sites. By the treaty's June 1991 deadline, the two countries had destroyed 2,692 missiles between them, including American Pershing II and cruise missiles and the Soviet SS-20. The United States withdrew from the treaty in 2019, citing Russian violations Moscow denied.

Frankish custom drew a line most modern law does not: ancestral farmland, called Salic land, was reserved entirely for sons, while personal belongings could still pass to a daughter. The written law spelled it out bluntly, that no portion of such an inheritance should come to a woman while any male relative survived to claim it.

Around 570 the rule bent rather than broke. If a man died with no surviving son, his daughters could now inherit the land itself, a narrow exception carved into a system otherwise built on equal division among a dead man's sons. Kingdoms across the former Frankish territories kept variations of this compromise for centuries afterward.

A ship's cargo was worth more than the ship itself, and a captain who lost both to a storm off Sardinia lost everything at once. Genoese and other Italian merchants began writing separate contracts that paid out if a voyage failed, splitting the loss away from loans on the cargo itself, in the fourteenth century.

Premiums were not set by tables but by guesswork: a broker weighed the season, the route and the reputation of pirates working a stretch of coast, then named a price. The practice spread north along the same trade routes it protected, reaching Bruges and London within a couple of centuries and outliving every fleet it once covered.

Kim Jong Un walked across the concrete demarcation line at Panmunjom on 27 April 2018, becoming the first North Korean leader to set foot in South Korean territory since the Korean War armistice of 1953. Moon Jae-in briefly stepped north in return, a gesture neither side had planned in advance.

The two leaders met at the Peace House inside the Joint Security Area, their first meeting in over a decade, and signed the Panmunjom Declaration committing to work toward denuclearisation and a formal end to the war. Two further meetings between them followed later that same year.

Franklin Roosevelt signed Executive Order 9066 on 19 February 1942, ten weeks after Pearl Harbor, authorising the military to exclude anyone from designated zones without trial or charge. Roughly two thirds of those removed were American-born citizens, and most had days to sell homes, farms and businesses before reporting to assembly points with only what they could carry.

Ten camps run by the War Relocation Authority held people behind barbed wire and armed watchtowers, mostly in remote stretches of California, Arizona, Wyoming and Arkansas. Camp hospitals recorded nearly six thousand births and over eighteen hundred deaths before the last facility closed in March 1946, months after the war that justified it had already ended.

Alaska's Thule hunters did not simply drift eastward across the Arctic. Skin-hulled umiaks large enough to tow a bowhead whale carcass, and dog sleds that extended a hunter's range over sea ice, let them follow migrating whales and seals across Canada and on to Greenland within a few centuries.

The Dorset people had occupied that same coastline for over a thousand years, and by around 1000 they were gone. Archaeologists have found almost no trace of contact between the two groups: no shared campsites, no clear record of conflict or absorption, only a change in the tools left behind.

Pope Gregory VII opened the dispute in 1075 with a document, the Dictatus papae, claiming that only the pope could appoint or remove bishops. Henry IV had been doing exactly that across his own territories for years, most recently installing his own choice as Bishop of Milan over Rome's candidate. When Henry refused to back down in 1076, Gregory excommunicated and deposed him.

The argument was never only about religion. German bishops ran much of Henry's administration and supplied troops for his armies, so control of their appointment was control of the empire's machinery, not just its churches. Losing that authority to the pope would have hollowed out royal power at its base, which is why Henry fought a fight that would run, on and off, for nearly fifty years.

Negotiations ran for nearly two years between Iran and six other powers: the United States, Russia, China, Britain, France and Germany. A framework was reached in Lausanne in April 2015, but the harder details, including inspection access, took another three months to finish in Vienna.

Under the deal signed on 14 July 2015, Iran agreed to cut its enriched uranium stockpile by roughly 98 percent and reduce its operating centrifuges from about 19,000 to just over 6,000, in exchange for relief from sanctions once inspectors confirmed compliance. The United States withdrew from the agreement in 2018.

Iraq owed Kuwait roughly 14 billion dollars from the war with Iran, and Saddam Hussein accused Kuwait of driving down oil prices and siphoning crude from a shared field. On 2 August 1990 some 88,000 Iraqi troops crossed the border and took Kuwait City within a day. Iraq installed a puppet government first, then formally annexed the country on 28 August.

The UN Security Council condemned the invasion within hours and, over the following months, passed twelve resolutions Iraq ignored. A US-led coalition of 35 nations assembled in Saudi Arabia through the autumn, and the ground war that followed in February 1991 expelled Iraqi forces from Kuwait in roughly a hundred hours.

The Anglo-Irish Treaty, signed in December 1921, gave the new state dominion status equal to Canada's rather than full separation, and the Free State itself came into being on 6 December 1922. Members of its parliament had to swear an oath naming both the state and the king, a form of words republicans found impossible to accept and refused to take.

Northern Ireland, six of Ireland's thirty two counties, used a right written into the treaty to opt straight back out the following day, leaving the Free State with the remaining twenty six. A boundary commission was meant to redraw the border afterward, though its work never produced the changes either side expected.

Oral tradition names three founders of the confederacy: Dekanawida, a peacemaker whose own people rejected him; Hiawatha, an Onondaga orator grieving a murdered family; and Jigonhsasee, remembered as the Mother of Nations. Together they carried a message of peace to five nations, the Mohawk, Oneida, Onondaga, Cayuga and Seneca, who had spent generations raiding one another.

What they built, likely around 1450 though the exact date is disputed, was governed by the Great Law of Peace and a Grand Council of fifty chiefs, one set for each clan across the five nations. The structure was described as a single longhouse stretching from the Mohawk in the east to the Seneca in the west, each nation keeping a door.

Isabella had already gambled on the throne five years earlier, marrying Ferdinand of Aragon in secret in 1469 while her half-brother Henry IV still opposed the match, crossing Castile in disguise to reach the wedding at Valladolid. When Henry died in December 1474 she had herself proclaimed queen at Segovia within a day, before rivals could act.

The crown was not settled by that proclamation alone. Opponents backed Henry's daughter Joanna as the rightful heir and married her to the king of Portugal, dragging Castile into years of war that turned only after the inconclusive battle of Toro in 1476, when Ferdinand's claim of victory broke his rivals' will to keep fighting.

Tariq ibn Ziyad landed at the rock that still carries his name, Gibraltar from Jebel al Tarik, with a force that grew from roughly seventeen hundred men to several thousand as he pushed north in 711. He was a Berber commander acting under Musa ibn Nusayr, sent to test a Visigothic kingdom already weakened by disputed succession.

At Guadalete that July, King Roderic's army was routed and Roderic himself was killed in the fighting. With no rival strong enough to rally the Visigoths, Tariq and Musa's forces pushed on and held more than two thirds of the peninsula within a few years, founding the state later Muslims called Al-Andalus.

David Ben-Gurion read the proclamation at the Tel Aviv Museum on the afternoon of 14 May 1948, and it took him sixteen minutes. The building had no name yet fit for the occasion; it is now called Independence Hall. Within hours the United States had extended recognition, and the Soviet Union followed three days later with formal diplomatic recognition.

Troops from Egypt, Transjordan, Iraq and Syria crossed into the territory the next morning, opening a war that ran into 1949. By its end Israel held about half again the land the United Nations partition plan had allotted it, and more than 700,000 Palestinian Arabs had fled or been expelled from the areas that became Israeli territory.

Two hundred thousand Italian troops crossed from Eritrea into Ethiopia on 3 October 1935 without a declaration of war. Facing a poorly equipped Ethiopian army, Mussolini's forces made repeated use of mustard gas, dropping an estimated 330 tons of it over several months in direct violation of the Geneva Protocol Italy had itself signed.

The League of Nations voted sanctions that November but left out oil, coal and steel, the materials Italy actually needed, and Britain kept the Suez Canal open to Italian shipping throughout. Emperor Haile Selassie fled into exile in May 1936 as Italian troops entered Addis Ababa, and the League's failure to stop a member state's invasion badly damaged its credibility.

The Virginia Company's settlers built James Fort on a swampy peninsula in May 1607, choosing the site for its defensible position rather than its water or soil. Both proved bad choices: a severe drought had already begun, and within the first year roughly two thirds of the original settlers were dead before a resupply fleet reached them in 1608.

The worst came later. Through the winter of 1609 to 1610, remembered as the Starving Time, colonists ate dogs, horses and boiled shoe leather, and evidence uncovered by archaeologists shows some resorted to eating the dead. Of the 214 people counted in one supply mission, only 60 survived until a relief fleet under Thomas West arrived in June 1610 and kept the colony from being abandoned.

The treaty that ended Korea's independence was signed on 22 August 1910, not by the emperor but by his prime minister, Ye Wanyong, acting alongside Japan's resident general, Terauchi Masatake. Korean law required the emperor's own signature on such a treaty; Sunjong never gave his, though the imperial seal was affixed anyway.

That gap became the basis for later argument that the annexation was never legally valid, a position Korea's government in exile and its post-war successors maintained for decades. Whatever its legal standing, Japanese rule over the peninsula lasted thirty-five years, run through a resident-general's office rather than any Korean institution.

A small explosive charge went off beside a stretch of railway track near Mukden on the night of 18 September 1931, damaging so little of the line that a train passed over it minutes later. Japanese officers had planted it themselves, then blamed Chinese saboteurs and used the incident to launch a full invasion of Manchuria.

By early 1932 Japan had installed the puppet state of Manchukuo under the last Qing emperor, Puyi, as a figurehead. A League of Nations commission concluded Japan was the aggressor and recommended Manchuria be returned to China; rather than comply, Japan simply withdrew from the League, exposing how little the organisation could do against a great power.

The Bar Kokhba revolt against Roman rule ended in 135 with Judaea devastated and its leadership broken. Hadrian barred Jews from entering Jerusalem itself, banned circumcision and the public study of Torah, and renamed the province Syria Palaestina, a name chosen specifically to sever its association with the people who had rebelled.

Most of the bans on religious practice were lifted after Hadrian's death, but the exclusion from Jerusalem held. Jewish life recentred on Galilee inside the province, while communities already settled in Babylonia and elsewhere grew into the larger and increasingly influential centres of Jewish scholarship for centuries that followed.

Across German and Swiss cities in 1349, Jewish communities were accused of causing the plague by poisoning wells, and mobs and magistrates responded with killings. In Strasbourg on 14 February, roughly two thousand Jews were burned to death in the Jewish cemetery, before the plague itself had even reached the city, and residents afterward divided up the possessions left in the ashes.

The violence was not confined to one place. Sources record around five hundred and ten Jewish communities destroyed across Europe during the wider plague years, and some victims are recorded as having taken their own lives rather than face capture. Existing prejudice against Jewish communities, combined with fear of a disease no one could explain, made the killings widespread rather than isolated.

Sima Yan, Emperor Wu of Jin, had spent years building river fleets before he sent them down the Yangtze against Eastern Wu in 280. The last of the three rival kingdoms surrendered without a prolonged siege, and for the first time since the collapse of the Han dynasty a century earlier, one court ruled the whole of China proper.

The peace did not hold. Emperor Wu's court settled into a decade of prosperity, but his death in 290 left a contested succession that broke into the War of the Eight Princes. Within a generation the unified state he had built was fracturing into the divisions that followed at Luoyang and Chang'an.

Brown expected hundreds of enslaved people to rush to join him once he seized the federal armory at Harpers Ferry, then to fight his way south through the Appalachians freeing more as he went. On 16 October 1859 his small band took the armory with little trouble, but almost no one else arrived, and he let a passing train continue on its way, carrying word of the raid ahead of him.

By the next morning local militia had cut off both bridges out of town, and Brown's men were trapped in the armory's engine house. Marines under Robert E. Lee stormed it on 18 October and captured him wounded. Convicted of treason, he was hanged on 2 December 1859, and became a martyr to abolitionists within weeks of his death.

Sent north in 1388 to invade Ming-held territory, General Yi Seong-gye decided the campaign was hopeless and marched his army back to the Goryeo capital instead. He executed King U, installed a puppet, then removed his remaining rivals one by one until nothing stood between him and the throne he claimed in 1392.

He considered keeping the old dynasty's name but faced pressure from aristocrats still loyal to it, so he chose Joseon in tribute to the ancient state of Gojoseon and secured the Ming emperor's endorsement of the new title. He also moved the capital from Kaegyong to Hanseong, the city now known as Seoul, and the dynasty he founded ruled Korea for over five centuries.

Joseon Korea's gwageo examinations, modelled on the older Chinese system, were open in theory to any man who was not enslaved or outcast. Passing them required years of study in the Confucian classics, and only families with the money to spare a son from farm labour that long could realistically afford it, so the yangban who sat them were mostly yangban sons already.

By the 1600s the class had stopped relying on the exam at all to prove itself. Families kept local registers of lineage, and status increasingly passed by descent rather than by a passing grade, while a struggling treasury let some buy low posts outright. An exam meant to open government instead entrenched the people already running it.

Charles X gambled that he could rule without an elected chamber's consent. His July Ordinances of 1830 dissolved the Chamber of Deputies, gutted press freedom and barred much of the merchant class from voting, all in one stroke, and Paris answered within two days.

Barricades went up on 27 July, and by the 29th royal troops had lost control of the city, three days that Parisians would call the Trois Glorieuses. Charles abdicated on 2 August and sailed for Britain. The men who had beaten him then bypassed his preferred heir entirely, installing Louis Philippe as a constitutional king instead of a restored absolute one.

Aguda, elected leader of the Jurchen tribes in 1113, declared himself emperor in the spring of 1115 after refusing to accept letters from the Liao court that did not address him by his new title. It was a small point of protocol that marked a real break: a subject people of the Khitan Liao now claimed equal standing.

The Jin backed the claim with a decade of campaigning, taking Liao's capitals one by one until its last emperor was captured in 1125. They then turned on their former Song allies, and in January 1127 broke into Kaifeng and carried off two Song emperors, leaving the Jurchens in control of all of northern China.

Roman law by the 6th century was a mess of centuries of overlapping and contradictory imperial rulings, and Justinian handed the problem to a jurist named Tribonian rather than trying to settle it himself. Tribonian's commission finished the Codex, a compilation of imperial enactments, in 529, then turned to sorting the writings of earlier jurists into the Digest.

The Digest, finished in 533, distilled roughly three centuries of legal opinion into a single reference, alongside a student textbook called the Institutes completed the same year. Together with the later Novellae, these four parts were meant to replace every earlier source of law outright, and they became the base that most European legal systems built on.

Minamoto no Sanetomo was walking down the shrine steps at Tsurugaoka Hachimangu after a ceremony in February 1219 when his own nephew, Kugyo, stepped out from beside the stairway and killed him. Kugyo was beheaded within hours, but the damage to the Minamoto line could not be undone.

Sanetomo left no heir, and with him the Seiwa Genji branch of the Minamoto shogunal line ended. The Hojo family, who had governed as regents behind the shoguns for years, installed a child from the Fujiwara court as the next figurehead. Real authority stayed with the Hojo regency for the rest of the Kamakura period.

The Genpei War ended in 1185 with the Taira clan destroyed at the naval battle of Dan no ura, and Minamoto no Yoritomo the last major rival standing. He did not move his government to the imperial capital at Kyoto but ruled from Kamakura, his own power base, keeping the emperor as a figurehead at a careful distance.

The imperial court granted him the title of shogun formally in 1192, though the machinery of military government, the chancellery, and the stewards he posted across the provinces to collect taxes and keep order, was already running years before that paper title arrived.

Kanem's rulers had converted to Islam in the eleventh century, and by the thirteenth the connection ran deep enough that they endowed a hostel in Cairo for their own pilgrims and students travelling to Mecca. The empire around Lake Chad reached its height under Dunama II Dibalemi, who is credited with a cavalry force reportedly numbering in the tens of thousands.

That military reach protected a trade in salt, ivory and enslaved people carried north across the Sahara, the same routes that brought back the books, craftsmen and scholars who made Kanem one of the region's centres of Islamic learning. Trade and faith travelled the same roads in both directions.

Kanem's wealth did not come from farmland around Lake Chad. It came from the Kaouar oases, a string of desert waypoints the Sayfawa dynasty absorbed in the eleventh century, giving Kanem a grip on the caravan routes crossing the Sahara toward North Africa.

Caravans paid duties to cross Kanem's territory, income the state used to buy weapons, cloth and books from the north while selling ivory, animal skins and captives to the south. By the following century, under Mai Dunama II, Kanem's reach extended as far as the Fezzan.

The new emperor was seven years old when he was enthroned in Beijing on 7 February 1661, too young to rule, so his late father had named four regents to govern in his place. One of them, Oboi, spent the next eight years accumulating power and eliminating rivals among the other three.

In 1669, with his grandmother's help, the teenage emperor had Oboi arrested and took personal control of the throne. He went on to put down the Revolt of the Three Feudatories in the south, oversee repairs to the Grand Canal, and manage flood control along the Yellow River, governing for sixty one years in total.

The Karakhanid khanate had no single ruler. Two khagans reigned at once, an eastern Arslan Qara Khaqan and a western Bughra Qara Khaqan, each with subordinate princes beneath them, a structure the dynasty kept even as its territory split and reunited across Central Asia.

After converting to Islam around 934, Karakhanid rulers added Arabic titles such as sultan alongside their older Turkic ones, and presided over a court whose culture was largely Persian while its administration still spoke Turkic. The dual kingship survived that blending largely unchanged.

Satuq Bughra Khan converted to Islam around 934, reportedly on the strength of a legal ruling that let him depose his own father, who had stayed pagan. It took another generation before the change spread beyond the ruling house: in 960, chroniclers record roughly 200,000 tents of Turkic nomads converting at once.

The Karakhanids went on to rule Transoxiana and the Tarim Basin from cities including Balasagun, Samarkand and Kashgar, holding Transoxiana independently from 999. Internal succession disputes later split the khanate into eastern and western halves in the 1040s, and it survived in that divided form into the early 13th century.

Ogedei Khan ordered Karakorum built in 1235, the year after his armies finished off the Jin dynasty, and the palace was finished within a year. A Flemish friar who visited in 1254 described a walled city with twelve pagan temples, two mosques and a Nestorian church standing within a few streets of each other.

At the centre of it stood a silver tree built by a captured Parisian goldsmith, its branches fitted with pipes that poured wine, fermented mare's milk and rice beer for the khan's guests on command. Karakorum's population of Chinese artisans, Muslim traders and Christian clergy made it, for a few decades, one of the more religiously mixed cities anywhere on earth.

Kashgar sat at the point where routes from China, India and Persia converged before crossing the Pamirs, which made it worth fighting over rather than simply trading through. In the decades around 800 the oasis changed hands between the Tibetan Empire and the Uyghur Khaganate, and whoever held it controlled the caravans passing beneath its walls.

A Chinese monk who passed through Kashgar generations earlier had already described a city of abundant crops and fine woven rugs, evidence that its market culture predated any single conqueror. What made the city durable across centuries of shifting rulers was less any one ruler's investment than its position, fixed by geography rather than by decree.

Janibek and Kerey did not defeat Abu'l Khayr Khan in battle. They simply left, taking their followers east into Moghulistan rather than accept his rule over the Uzbek Khanate, a withdrawal the steppe called qazaqliq, a life of frontier raiding and hunting for those who had lost a succession fight but refused to submit.

The migration was gradual rather than a single founding day: Kazakh tradition dates the break to 1465, while some later chroniclers place the tribes' actual settlement around 1470. Out of that drift the name qazaq stopped meaning an outcast and came to mean a people, giving the new khanate both its subjects and its name.

Frank Kellogg, the American secretary of state, and Aristide Briand, France's foreign minister, put their names to an agreement signed in Paris on 27 August 1928, in which the signing states renounced war as a tool of policy. Fifteen nations signed that day, and within a decade the number of adherents had climbed past sixty, drawing in most of the world's governments.

The pact carried no mechanism to enforce itself: it named no penalty beyond withdrawing the treaty's own benefits from a violator, and the United States Senate made clear that ratification bound the country to nothing further. States kept fighting without formally declaring war, a habit the pact did nothing to stop, though its wording later helped shape the postwar legal case against wars of aggression.

Nixon announced on 30 April 1970 that US forces had moved into Cambodia, widening a war he had promised during his campaign to wind down. Students at Kent State University in Ohio protested through the following days, and after a campus building burned, the state's governor sent in the National Guard.

On 4 May, guardsmen fired into a crowd of demonstrators and onlookers on the Commons, roughly 67 rounds in about 13 seconds, killing four students and wounding nine, one of whom was left permanently paralysed. None of the dead had been closer to the guardsmen than any of the students who survived, a detail that fuelled years of dispute over whether an order to fire had ever been given.

Malabar's pepper vines and cinnamon groves had been drawing outside traders since long before 1300, back to Roman ships that sailed the Arabian Sea using seasonal monsoon winds first charted around the first century. What kept the coast dominant into the fourteenth century was less any single product than its position: it sat at the point where Arab dhows from the Red Sea met Chinese junks from the east.

The port of Kozhikode, known to Europeans as Calicut, became the gateway through which Arab, and later Portuguese and Dutch, merchants reached South India in turn. Rulers taxed the trade rather than running it directly, letting foreign merchant communities settle and compete against each other for the same warehouses.

Yasovarman I moved his capital from Hariharalaya to a new city on Phnom Bakheng hill after winning a succession war against his own brother. He named it Yashodharapura, and building began at once: around a hundred monasteries went up within his first year on the throne.

The site he chose remained the Khmer capital for roughly six hundred years, later hosting Angkor Wat. Yasovarman also finished the great Indratataka reservoir his father had begun and had the East Baray built, an artificial lake nearly eight kilometres long.

Angkor did not fall to a foreign army so much as to its own former subjects. Ayutthaya, a Siamese kingdom that had grown out of territory once loyal to the Khmer court, marched on the capital in 1431 after a rebellion against Siamese authority spiralled into open war, and its forces looted the city.

The population that survived the sack drifted south toward Longvek rather than rebuild, and the royal court eventually followed, abandoning the temples of Angkor to jungle within a generation. Only Angkor Wat itself stayed in use, kept as a Buddhist shrine while the rest of the city that had once ruled the region emptied out around it.

Before 802, Jayavarman II had ruled as a vassal under Javanese overlordship. He climbed Mount Mahendraparvata, now known as Phnom Kulen, and had a visiting brahmin named Hiranyadama perform a rite that proclaimed him a universal monarch, a devaraja, free of any foreign claim on his throne.

The ceremony is recorded only in an inscription carved three centuries later at Sdok Kak Thom, describing his priest Sivakaivalya's family line. That gap between the event and its record is typical of the period: the devaraja rite it describes became the religious basis for the kings who later built the temple complexes at Angkor.

Under Muhammad II, who took the throne in 1200, Khwarazm swallowed the Karakhanids and the Ghurids within fifteen years and moved its capital to Samarkand. By 1218 its territory ran from the Syr Darya to the Zagros Mountains and held a population of roughly five million.

That same year, a governor at the border town of Otrar seized a merchant caravan sent by Genghis Khan and executed its members as spies. Muhammad II backed the killing and mistreated the envoys sent to demand redress. The Mongol invasion that followed took Bukhara, Samarkand and Gurganj within three years and ended the empire.

Khrushchev was on holiday at Pitsunda on the Black Sea in October 1964 when a call from Mikhail Suslov summoned him back to Moscow. He returned to a Presidium that had already agreed to remove him, angered by his erratic economic schemes and the humiliation of the Cuban missile crisis two years earlier.

The Central Committee forced his retirement on 14 October, and unlike Stalin's purges, nobody was shot: Khrushchev was simply pensioned off to a dacha. Leonid Brezhnev, his own protege, took the party leadership, with KGB chief Vladimir Semichastny among those who had helped arrange the removal from within.

Around 1100 the Khwarezmian state was still a governorship, not yet an empire. Anushtegin, a former Turkic slave of the Seljuq sultans, had been granted control of Khwarezm in the 1070s, and it was his son Muhammad who turned that governorship into a hereditary throne, becoming shah around 1097.

The trade infrastructure the region later became known for, chains of fortified waystations sheltering caravans between Central Asian cities, belonged mostly to the empire's later, larger phase in the early thirteenth century. In 1100 Khwarezm was still a Seljuq vassal finding its feet, decades away from the reach it would eventually command.

Gold mined far inland around Great Zimbabwe reached the Indian Ocean coast at the port of Sofala, and around 1170 Kilwa's sultan took Sofala from the traders who had previously controlled it. From then on almost nothing moved through that port without Kilwa's rulers taking a share, and the metal that had once simply passed the island by became the base of its economy.

Merchants from Arabia, Persia and India called at Kilwa to exchange cloth and manufactured goods for the gold and ivory Sofala supplied, and the island minted its own coins for roughly five centuries to handle the trade. The arrangement lasted until Portuguese ships began working the same coast in the early sixteenth century and broke the monopoly by force.

Kilwa's fortune traced back to around 1170, when its sultan took the mainland port of Sofala from rival traders. Sofala was the outlet for gold and ivory carried up from Great Zimbabwe and the Monomotapa kingdom, and holding it let Kilwa tax the flow of metal before it ever reached a foreign ship. The city minted its own coinage for roughly five hundred years, examples of which turned up as far away as northern Australia.

When the Moroccan traveller Ibn Battuta reached Kilwa in 1331 he called it one of the finest cities he had seen, and admired the wealth its sultan drew from the gold trade and from raids on the interior. The Great Mosque was enlarged and the sprawling Husuni Kubwa palace built during this same prosperous stretch of the fourteenth century.

Kilwa itself produced almost nothing. Its wealth came from controlling Sofala, an entrepot far to the south that funnelled gold and ivory out of the interior kingdoms around Great Zimbabwe, which Kilwa's rulers then traded onward for manufactured goods arriving from Arabia, Persia and India.

By the mid fourteenth century that gold revenue let Kilwa mint its own coinage, a rare mark of financial confidence among Swahili Coast city-states. Coins bearing Kilwa sultans' names have turned up as far away as northern Australia, evidence of just how far the trading network the city sat astride actually reached.

Ezana of Aksum learned Christianity from his childhood tutor Frumentius, a shipwrecked Syrian, and became the first Aksumite king to adopt the faith himself. He marked the change on his coinage, swapping a disc and crescent for a cross, among the earliest coins anywhere to carry a Christian symbol.

His own inscriptions describe campaigns that weakened the neighbouring kingdom of Meroe on the Nile, though scholars still argue over whether these were conquests or interventions against a local rebellion. Aksum's reach by his reign extended far enough that his coins have turned up as far away as India.

The Hebrew Bible tells the story three times over: Saul is privately anointed by the seer Samuel after going out to search for his father's lost donkeys, then publicly chosen by lot at Mizpah, then confirmed as king at Gilgal only after he leads a relief force to break an Ammonite siege of Jabesh-Gilead.

Whether any of it happened as told is disputed among historians. Some point to remains at sites such as Khirbet Qeiyafa as support for an early kingdom taking shape in this period, while others argue the united monarchy is a later literary construction with little independent evidence behind it either way.

Ibn Saud had spent three decades taking Arabia region by region, starting with his 1902 recapture of Riyadh, then Nejd by 1921 and the Hejaz, with Mecca, by 1925. Rather than merge them at once, he ruled Nejd and the Hejaz as separate kingdoms under his own crown for several years, an arrangement that kept older loyalties intact while power stayed with him alone.

On 23 September 1932 he combined the two into a single state, the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, with himself as king. The date is still marked as the country's national day. The unification gave the new kingdom control of the Hejaz's pilgrimage cities, a source of both prestige and revenue that oil would not rival for another decade.

George Carmack filed the discovery claim on Bonanza Creek in August 1896, though it was his companions Skookum Jim and Tagish Charlie who had actually found the gold; they let Carmack stand as the official discoverer because they doubted Canadian authorities would recognise an Indigenous claim. News did not reach the outside world until steamships carrying the first fortunes docked in Seattle the following July.

Around 100,000 people set out for the Yukon, most on foot over the Chilkoot Pass, where an avalanche in April 1898 killed more than sixty of them. Only some 30,000 to 40,000 completed the journey, and by the time most arrived the richest ground around Dawson City was already staked. No more than a few hundred stampeders ever became rich from it.

The kingdom began, by tradition, with a marriage rather than a battle: a union between Nima a Nzima, ruler of Mpemba Kasi, and a daughter of the neighbouring Mbata kingdom's ruler. Their son, Lukeni lua Nimi, pushed the alliance southward around 1390, absorbing smaller territories along the Congo River into a single state.

What resulted was not a loose confederation but a working government. The Manikongo ruled from the capital at Mbanza Kongo through a royal council and provincial governors drawn from noble families, with electors involved in choosing succession, a level of central administration unusual enough that later Portuguese visitors compared it to a European kingdom.

The Kingdom of Kongo took shape around 1390 out of a marriage alliance between two Kikongo-speaking peoples, and its ruler took the title Mwene Kongo, a name later Portuguese visitors rendered as manikongo, the word that stuck in most outside accounts of the kingdom.

Governance ran through appointed provincial governors who served fixed terms and could install their own subordinates down to village level, where leadership stayed locally chosen. As the manikongo's central authority grew, provinces that had once been semi-independent allies lost real power and kept only symbolic status.

Mehmed Koprulu did not accept the grand vizierate on 14 September 1656 without conditions. The Ottoman Empire was reeling from military defeat and factional chaos, and the elderly Koprulu reportedly told the valide sultan he would take the post only with total authority, free of interference even from the sultan himself. She agreed, and he held her to it.

He used that freedom to purge the officer corps and provincial administration of officials he judged disloyal or corrupt, by methods contemporaries described as violent. When fire tore through Istanbul in 1660, he directed the rebuilding himself. By steering the young Sultan Mehmed IV toward hunting rather than governing, he kept effective power in his own hands, and left the empire's finances and army steadier than he found them.

Two American colonels, Dean Rusk and Charles Bonesteel, picked the 38th parallel as a dividing line on 10 August 1945 using a National Geographic wall map, working overnight with no Korean expert in the room and little more reasoning than that it placed Seoul on the American side. Rusk later admitted that had he known more Korean history he would probably have drawn the line elsewhere; the Soviets accepted the proposal without objection.

Syngman Rhee won UN-supervised elections in the south in May 1948 and the Republic of Korea was proclaimed that August, while Kim Il Sung, installed as northern leader in December 1945, headed the Democratic People's Republic of Korea founded that same year. Each government claimed sole legitimacy over the whole peninsula, a standoff that broke into open war within two years.

Kosovo's parliament declared independence unilaterally on 17 February 2008, without a referendum and without an agreement from Belgrade, after years of UN administration that followed the 1999 war. Serbia rejected the move immediately, continuing to describe Kosovo as its own autonomous province rather than a separate state.

Recognition split along old fault lines. The United States and most of the European Union recognised the new state within weeks, while Russia and China refused, and more than eighty countries still withhold recognition today. A 2013 agreement brokered in Brussels got Serbia to accept Kosovo's institutions operating on the ground, without conceding the argument over sovereignty itself.

Tradition holds that Shyaam a Mbul a Ngoong was not born to rule the Kuba at all, but was an outsider adopted by a Kuba queen who travelled through neighbouring kingdoms studying how they were governed before returning around 1625 to unify scattered chiefdoms into one state. The king he became, called the nyim, answered to a court council drawn from every subgroup rather than ruling alone.

That council system came with elected offices and separated judicial and military functions, an unusually formal structure for the region at the time. Competition among titled courtiers for the king's favour poured wealth into raffia textiles, carved cosmetic boxes and palm wine cups, turning everyday objects at court into some of central Africa's most prized surviving artworks.

The Kuba Kingdom took shape in the Congo basin around 1625, when a man named Shyaam a-Mbul a Ngoong seized power from a local ruler and pulled a scatter of chiefdoms under one crown. What followed was unusually prosperous: American crops such as maize and cassava, arriving through Atlantic trade networks, improved food supply enough to fund an aristocracy known for its patronage of textile art.

Raffia cloth, woven from palm fibre and often embroidered in geometric patterns, was the Kuba's best-known craft and doubled as a store of value across the region's markets. A king who could tax and redistribute cloth on that scale was also demonstrating the reach of his government, since the raffia trade ran through networks his officials controlled.

Kublai Khan's officials counted the population of Yuan China not as one people but as four ranked categories: Mongols at the top, various non-Chinese subjects from Central and West Asia below them, then northern Chinese who had lived under the earlier Jin state, and southern Chinese, former subjects of the defeated Song, at the bottom.

The ranking was not symbolic bookkeeping. It set who paid what tax, who could hold which office, and who owed which labour service, with southern Chinese carrying the heaviest burden despite being the empire's largest group. Villages were organised into units of fifty households answerable for local order, a structure built for extracting revenue that also bred the resentment later Yuan rulers never fully contained.

Kumaragupta I held together the empire his father and grandfather had built for four decades, from about 415, without losing territory that historians can point to. His coins and inscriptions turn up across a vast stretch of northern India, and he performed the ancient horse sacrifice, a ritual claimed only by rulers secure enough to stage it.

Buddhist pilgrims later credited a king called Shakraditya with founding monasteries at Nalanda, and most historians identify him with Kumaragupta, though the link rests on circumstantial evidence rather than a direct inscription. Trouble seems to have gathered only near the end of his reign or after it, when his successor's records speak of restoring fortunes that had slipped.

Kanishka I ruled a territory stretching from what is now Uzbekistan down to Mathura in northern India, a reach that put the Kushan Empire astride every land route connecting the Mediterranean, Persia, India and China at once. His coins carried Greek lettering on one face and Buddhist and Iranian imagery on the other.
