That mixture was not decoration but description: goods, pilgrims and ideas all passed through Kushan territory together. Kanishka's patronage of Buddhism helped carry it north along the same roads that carried silk and glass, out of India and eventually into the oasis towns bordering China.

Kanishka I ruled from Peshawar and Mathura, but the Rabatak inscription records his authority reaching from Central Asia and the Tarim Basin down to Pataliputra on the Ganges, an unusually direct written claim rather than a later legend. His empire sat astride the roads linking India, Iran and China.

He never converted to Buddhism himself, but he is said to have presided over a great Buddhist council in Kashmir and patronised both major schools of Buddhist art, Gandhara and Mathura. His coins carried images of the Buddha, an early use of currency to spread a religious image, and Chinese pilgrims later described a stupa he built at Peshawar as several hundred feet tall.

The Primary Chronicle claims that feuding Slavic and Finnic tribes around Novgorod invited a Varangian warband to rule them in 862, and that its leader, Rurik, accepted. Little else about him is verifiable, and even his ethnicity is disputed by historians who read the tale as later political myth making.

Rurik's kinsman Oleg extended this rule south, taking Kiev around 882 and folding it into a loose federation of Slavic and Finnic peoples along the river routes to Byzantium. Its name outlived it: Russia, Ukraine and Belarus all trace a founding claim back to the same chronicle.

Delegates in Kyoto argued for eleven days in December 1997 before adopting a protocol that gave industrialised countries specific, binding targets for cutting greenhouse gas emissions, ranging from an eight percent cut for the European Union to an allowed increase for Australia. Developing countries, including fast-growing emitters like China and India, took on no binding targets at all.

The United States signed in 1998 but never ratified it, after the Senate voted 95 to nothing against any climate treaty that exempted developing nations. The protocol needed countries responsible for 55 percent of 1990 emissions to ratify before it took effect, a threshold Russia's ratification finally cleared in February 2005.

From their capital at al-Hira in lower Mesopotamia, the Lakhmid kings of the Banu Lakhm answered to the Sassanid court while ruling the Arab tribes on Persia's desert flank in its stead. That arrangement let the Sassanids watch a long, thinly populated frontier without stationing their own troops along it, and Lakhmid commanders fought in Persian campaigns against Byzantium's own Arab client kingdom in Syria.

The kingdom ended abruptly around 602, when the Sassanid emperor Khosrow II had the last Lakhmid king, al-Nu'man III, put to death rather than continuing to rule through him. Persia replaced a workable buffer with direct control it could not really sustain, and within decades Arab armies moving up from the peninsula overran the province the Lakhmids had once guarded.

Lampang survives in the record mainly under names later chronicles stopped using, Wiang Lakon and Khelang Nakhon, a sign of a settlement older than the sources that describe it. It sat among Mon and Khmer principalities in the river basins of what is now northern Thailand before Tai speaking rulers pushed south from Chiang Saen and Chiang Rai.

Its own history thins further where Chiang Mai's chronicles take over, since Lampang was rarely the seat of government. What breaks the silence is the 1770s, when a local leader named Nan Thipchang drove Burmese forces out of the city, a rebellion still remembered as the moment Lampang re-entered its own story.

Mangrai's first choice of capital, Wiang Kum Kam, founded in 1294 on the Ping River, kept flooding. Construction on its replacement began in 1296, some kilometres to the northwest at the foot of Doi Suthep, on ground already fortified by the local Lua people, whose defences Mangrai simply built onto rather than starting over.

He named the new city Chiang Mai, meaning new city, and it has remained capital of the northern Thai region more or less continuously since. The Lanna kingdom it anchored kept its own distinct language, script and Buddhist traditions for centuries even after later rulers in Bangkok absorbed it into a unified Thailand.

Archaeologists know the people who made this pottery only by the style itself, since nothing else survives of who they were. Between roughly 1600 and 1200 BCE, potters working near the Bismarck Archipelago pressed toothed stamps into wet clay to leave rows of tiny geometric dots and a distinctive cross in circle motif, then fired the pots at low heat.

Fragments of that same stamped ware turn up on islands more than 4,000 kilometres apart, from the Solomons to Fiji, Tonga and Samoa, alongside obsidian and stone tools that were never local to where they were found. That spread is the clearest evidence that these communities were sailing open ocean routes between islands out of sight of each other, carrying goods as well as the pottery style with them.

On the night of 1 October 2017, a 64 year old gambler named Stephen Paddock broke two windows of his 32nd floor suite at the Mandalay Bay and fired down on the crowd at the Route 91 Harvest country music festival below. He fired more than a thousand rounds across roughly 490 metres in about ten minutes. Sixty people were killed and hundreds more wounded before he stopped.

Police found Paddock dead in the suite from a self inflicted gunshot, surrounded by an arsenal of rifles, some fitted with bump stocks that let a semi-automatic weapon fire almost as fast as a machine gun. Investigators combed through his finances, his medical records and his relationships for months afterwards and never settled on a motive, closing the case without one.

Puyi was five years old and had no idea what was happening. On 12 February 1912 his regent, the Empress Dowager Longyu, signed the abdication edict on his behalf, a deal brokered by general Yuan Shikai between the collapsing court and the republicans of the Xinhai Revolution.

The new republic let Puyi keep his title and stay inside the Forbidden City with a household and an annual subsidy, and for some time nobody told him his reign had actually ended. He believed himself emperor still, a fiction the palace maintained until his eventual eviction in 1924, twelve years after the edict he never understood he had signed away.

Spain's grip on its American colonies had been slipping for a decade before 1821, ever since Napoleon's invasion of Spain itself left the crown too weak to govern from across the ocean. In Mexico, a former royalist officer named Agustin de Iturbide switched sides, joined forces with insurgents under the Army of the Three Guarantees, and marched into Mexico City that September without a final battle.

Elsewhere the fighting had been much harder won. Simon Bolivar and Jose de San Martin had spent years campaigning across the Andes and the northern coast, and by the early 1820s most of Spanish South America had followed Mexico out of the empire. Spain kept Cuba and Puerto Rico for another seven decades, but its mainland American empire was effectively gone within a few years of Mexico's break.

Le Loi began the Lam Son uprising in 1418 with a handful of men sworn to a secret oath and little else against an occupying Ming garrison. Nine years of guerrilla fighting from mountain bases followed, including a surprise capture of the Nghe An citadel in 1424 that forced the Ming commander to fall back north.

The decisive battle came at Tot Dong and Chuc Dong in October 1426, after which Ming forces began withdrawing rather than face another campaigning season. By 1428 Le Loi was crowned Le Thai To, and Ming China accepted his rule under a tributary arrangement rather than reoccupying Vietnam, ending sixty years of Ming presence there.

The alliance signed at Cambrai in December 1508 called itself a crusade against the Ottomans. Its real purpose sat in secret clauses: France, the Holy Roman Empire, Aragon and the Papal States had agreed to carve up Venice's mainland territory between them, alarmed by how far the republic's holdings had spread across northern Italy.

It did not survive its own success. Once Venice had been badly beaten in the field, Pope Julius II grew more worried about French power in Italy than about Venice, and switched sides in 1510. Aragon followed him into a new Holy League against France, and by 1512 the emperor made his own truce with Venice, leaving the coalition that had formed against it in ruins.

Philip II did not need to persuade the Greek cities so much as defeat them first. After crushing Athens and Thebes at Chaeronea in 338 BCE, he called the survivors to Corinth and offered terms that looked generous on paper: each city kept its own constitution, free navigation, and a promise of no interference in internal affairs, all guaranteed by a common oath.

The guarantee came with Macedonian garrisons at Corinth, Thebes, Ambracia and Pydna, which made refusal difficult. The League's council named Philip supreme commander for a planned invasion of Persia, a campaign his assassination in 336 BCE prevented him from leading. His son Alexander inherited both the title and the war.

Woodrow Wilson had pushed hardest for it at the Paris peace talks, and its covenant was largely drafted by two other men, Britain's Lord Robert Cecil and South Africa's Jan Smuts. The League came into being on 10 January 1920 with an Assembly, a Council and a permanent secretariat based in Geneva.

Wilson won the Nobel Peace Prize for the idea, then watched his own Senate refuse it. Republican opponents led by Henry Cabot Lodge kept the treaty short of the two thirds majority it needed on 19 March 1920, and the United States never joined the organisation its own president had designed.

Franklin Roosevelt signed the act on 11 March 1941, letting the president lend or lease arms and supplies to any nation whose defence he judged vital to American security, rather than sell them outright and demand cash up front. Britain, already stretched thin on foreign reserves under the old cash and carry rule, was the first beneficiary; China followed within weeks, and the Soviet Union after the German invasion that June.

Congress had no simple way to price a loan of destroyers or aircraft, so most of it was never repaid in the ordinary sense. Roosevelt likened it to lending a garden hose to a neighbour whose house was on fire. By the war's end the United States had supplied roughly fifty billion dollars in aid, nearly two thirds of it to Britain and its empire and a large share to the Soviets.

A merchant travelling from Florence to a fair in Champagne could carry a letter instead of a chest of coin: an instruction from his own banker asking a correspondent abroad to pay the bearer on presentation. Italian trading houses built networks of such correspondents across Europe, turning a written promise into money a stranger would honour.

The practice reduced the need to move silver and gold along roads plagued by bandits and tolls, and it depended entirely on reputation: a house whose letters were routinely honoured could lend its name across a continent. That trust in paper over metal became one of the foundations Italian banking families later built fortunes on.

The plebeians had walked out of Rome before, in earlier centuries, to force concessions from the patrician class. In 287 BC they did it again, withdrawing to the Janiculum hill amid debt disputes, and the dictator Quintus Hortensius was appointed to settle it. Ancient writers blamed debt and conscription; some modern historians think rural plebeians were really after a say in distributing land recently won in the Third Samnite War.

Whatever the trigger, the law that ended the standoff removed the Senate's power to veto decisions of the Plebeian Council. Resolutions passed there, called plebiscita, became binding on all Romans without needing senatorial approval. It closed a conflict between the two orders that had run, on and off, for roughly two centuries.

The American Colonization Society had been shipping free and freed African Americans to the Pepper Coast since 1822, an arrangement that suited slaveholders who wanted free Black people out of the country as much as it suited the settlers seeking a fresh start. By the 1840s the society could no longer fund or govern the colony, and Liberia's settlers had to decide whether to go it alone.

They declared independence on 26 July 1847, becoming the continent's first republic, with a constitution modelled closely on the one used in the United States. The Americo-Liberian settlers who led the new state held political power over a much larger indigenous population that had not been consulted about any of it.

John Adams signed the legislation on 24 April 1800, setting aside five thousand dollars for books a moving government would need once it left Philadelphia for the new capital. The whole collection fit into a room in the Capitol: 740 volumes and three maps, ordered from London for members of Congress to consult.

It did not survive the decade intact. British troops burned the Capitol in August 1814 and destroyed most of what had been bought, leaving only a single account book that an officer took as a souvenir and that was not returned to the United States until 1940. Thomas Jefferson sold Congress his own library, nearly 6,500 books, to rebuild the collection the following year.

Neither man was running for president. Stephen Douglas held an Illinois Senate seat that Abraham Lincoln wanted, and since state legislatures still chose senators before the seventeenth amendment, the two campaigned by arguing directly with each other across seven towns between August and October 1858.

Douglas defended popular sovereignty, letting each territory vote on slavery for itself, a position he had built into law with the Kansas-Nebraska Act. Lincoln pressed him on whether that could ever be reconciled with the Supreme Court's Dred Scott ruling. Douglas kept his Senate seat, but newspaper coverage of the debates made Lincoln a national figure within two years.

The treaty was a fallback. Its predecessor, a proposed EU constitution, had been rejected by French and Dutch voters in 2005 referendums, so negotiators stripped out the symbolic language, kept most of the substance, and called it an amending treaty instead of a constitution to avoid another referendum fight.

Signed on 13 December 2007 and in force from 1 December 2009, it created a standing President of the European Council to replace the rotating six-month chair, and a High Representative to speak for the bloc on foreign policy, roles meant to give the EU a more consistent voice abroad.

Lithuania signed the Union of Lublin in 1569 out of weakness, not strength. Its armies were losing ground to Moscow in the Livonian War, and Polish nobles would not send reinforcements without something in return. The price was several Lithuanian provinces, including Kiev and Volhynia, handed over to Poland as part of the deal.

What emerged was one crown worn by one elected monarch over two states that each kept their own army, treasury and law courts, joined by a shared parliament in which Polish deputies outnumbered Lithuanian ones three to one. At roughly 400,000 square miles and eleven million people, the resulting Commonwealth was one of Europe's largest states, and it held together for over two centuries before partition erased it from the map in 1795.

Governor Orval Faubus called out the Arkansas National Guard on 4 September 1957, saying they would keep the peace outside Central High School. Their real job was to block nine Black students from entering, and for weeks they succeeded, turning the teenagers away at gunpoint while a crowd jeered.

President Eisenhower stripped Faubus of control over the Guard by federal order on 23 September and sent the 101st Airborne Division instead. Paratroopers escorted the nine students inside on 25 September, and soldiers stayed at the school through the rest of the year, standing outside classroom doors while lessons continued.

Seven governments negotiated at Locarno in October 1925: Germany, France, Belgium, Britain, Italy, Poland and Czechoslovakia. The core deal bound Germany, France and Belgium to accept their shared borders as fixed by Versailles, with Britain and Italy standing as guarantors. Germany would not extend the same acceptance eastward, leaving its frontiers with Poland and Czechoslovakia open to future revision.

The arrangement also committed Germany to keep the Rhineland demilitarised. It held for barely a decade: on 7 March 1936 German troops marched back into the zone, and the other signatories issued verbal protest but took no military response. The treaties stayed nominally in force, but the Rhineland's remilitarisation had already made them dead letter.

Cardinal Mazarin had run France's government for eighteen years, and courtiers assumed the twenty-two-year-old king would simply appoint a successor. Instead, days after Mazarin's death in March 1661, Louis told his ministers he would govern alone, ordering that nothing be signed or sealed without passing through him first.

He inherited a treasury near collapse. Within months he had Nicolas Fouquet, the finance minister he judged too rich and too independent, arrested, and by 1665 replaced him with Jean-Baptiste Colbert. The move began seven decades of rule in which Louis kept the high nobility close at court and out of independent power.

Robert Livingston and James Monroe went to Paris in 1803 with instructions to buy New Orleans, nothing more. French treasury minister Barbe-Marbois instead offered the entire territory west of the Mississippi. Napoleon had lost interest in a New World empire after an army sent to crush a slave uprising in Haiti was decimated by fighting and disease.

The Americans settled on fifteen million dollars for roughly 828,000 square miles, under three cents an acre, doubling the size of the country without a shot fired. The deal left the new republic with a stake in a struggle it refused to acknowledge: when Haiti declared independence the following year, the United States would not recognise it and backed a trade embargo instead.

Historians cannot agree when the Luba kingdom of the Congo basin began. Congolese and Western scholars have proposed founding dates ranging from the eighth century to the eighteenth, and the region around its old capital in Kabongo has never been fully excavated, so the gap is archaeological as much as historical.

Its own account is a myth of overthrow: a hunter king named Kalala Ilunga is remembered as having toppled a predecessor called Kongolo Mwamba and introduced iron forging to the Luba. Every later ruler, or mulopwe, claimed descent from him and was treated as divine after death, with the village he had ruled from turned into a shrine kept by officials called men of memory.

The Lunda state grew out of a marriage story: a Luba hunter named Ilunga Tshibinda married Lueji, a ruler of the local Lunda people in the southern Congo basin, and their son took the title Mwaant Yaav, founding a new ruling line. Later kings such as Naweej built on that base, adding a queen mother's office and a formal heir apparent to steady succession.

Rather than conquering and absorbing its neighbours outright, Lunda grew as a confederation: local chiefs kept their own authority so long as they sent tribute to the centre. Muslim traders brought weapons and advisers from towns further east, and Lunda's reach eventually stretched from roughly 150,000 square kilometres of territory to double that at its height.

Lunda power grew less by conquest for its own sake than by absorbing the peoples along its trade routes into a single political system. Chiefs who accepted the mwata yamvo's authority kept local rule but paid tribute upward, a structure flexible enough to stretch from the upper Kasai river deep into what is now Angola and Zambia.

Muslim traders from towns on the upper Congo supplied Lunda rulers with firearms and military advisers, evidence of how far the network reached even before European traders arrived on the coast in numbers. That reach let Lunda intermediaries control goods moving between the Atlantic and Africa's interior for generations.

Twelve foreign and finance ministers signed the treaty in the Dutch town of Maastricht on 7 February 1992, after talks that folded together separate negotiations on political union and monetary union into one document. It renamed the European Community the European Union and set out a three pillar structure covering the internal market alongside new areas of shared foreign policy and justice cooperation.

The treaty entered into force on 1 November 1993, after Danish voters, who had rejected it in a first referendum, approved a revised version with opt-outs. It also fixed the path toward a single currency, with convergence criteria on debt and inflation that member states would have to meet before adopting what became the euro.

Portugal's foothold in Macau began in 1557 with an annual rent of 500 taels of silver paid to local Chinese authorities, a lease that outlasted the Portuguese empire that granted it and nearly every other European colony in Asia.

The formal handover came at midnight on 20 December 1999, two years after Hong Kong's return to China under a similar arrangement. Macau became a Special Administrative Region under a promise of separate laws and a market economy for fifty years, the same model applied across the border.

Nobody signed Magna Carta. King John pressed his seal into wax at Runnymede on 15 June 1215, since a medieval king authenticated a document that way, not with a signature. A council of twenty five barons was set up to make sure he kept to it. He did not, and within ten weeks Pope Innocent III had annulled the charter, tipping England into the First Barons' War.

The document that mattered was not the one at Runnymede. It was reissued in 1216 stripped of its sharpest clauses, again in 1217 as part of a peace settlement, and again in 1225 by Henry III in exchange for a new tax grant. Edward I confirmed it as statute law in 1297, and it was that later, revised text, not John's, that entered English law.

Simon de Montfort had beaten and captured King Henry III at the Battle of Lewes in May 1264, and ruled England in Henry's name through a council he controlled. To shore up support beyond the barons who had backed him, he summoned a parliament in January 1265 that went further than any before it.

Alongside the earls and bishops, Montfort called two knights from every county and, for the first time, two burgesses from selected towns, ordinary citizens sitting in the same assembly as the nobility. The arrangement did not survive its architect: Montfort was killed at the Battle of Evesham that August, but the practice of summoning elected townsmen to parliament outlived him.

Gajah Mada rose to become Majapahit's chief minister in 1336, and swore that he would take no rest, no spices, no fruit and no pleasure until the archipelago was united under his queen. The oath became the empire's guiding ambition for the next three decades, as fleets and tribute demands reached out from Java toward Sumatra and beyond.

Direct rule, though, never stretched much past Java and Bali. The roughly ninety further territories recorded as tributaries in the court chronicle Nagarakretagama were bound in by trade monopolies and the threat of naval reprisal rather than resident governors, a looser structure than the record's proud tally of dependencies suggests.

Raden Wijaya founded Majapahit on 10 November 1293, on land granted to him by a Mongol invasion force he had first courted as an ally and then turned on once it had done the work of driving out his rivals. The kingdom he built on that betrayal grew, under his descendants and the minister Gajah Mada, into a network of tributary states that the 1365 court poem Nagarakretagama counted at around ninety-eight.

It was the last major Hindu-Buddhist state to hold power in the archipelago before Islamic sultanates rose in its place, and its reach is still used as a rough template when Indonesia's modern borders are discussed. The empire's own decline began after 1389 and it collapsed in 1527, conquered by the Sultanate of Demak.

Gajah Mada was a chief minister under Queen Tribhuwana who reportedly swore not to taste palapa, a seasoning or a period of rest depending on the reading, until he had brought the scattered islands of the archipelago under one crown. Chroniclers list the places he named in that oath, from Bali and Sunda to Tumasik, the settlement that would later become Singapore.

The campaigns that followed pushed Majapahit's reach across Sumatra, Kalimantan, the Malay peninsula and eastward through the Moluccas, making it the largest maritime power Southeast Asia had seen. The empire never ruled this expanse as a single administered state; distant territories were bound to Java mainly by trade and tribute rather than garrisons.

From its inland capital at Trowulan on Java, Majapahit built its influence less through direct rule over distant islands than through control of the sea lanes that connected them. Its fleets, described in chronicles as including hundreds of large jong trading ships alongside smaller rowing and barge craft, gave it the naval reach to police those routes and enforce a claim on the trade passing through them.

The empire's territories from Sumatra to New Guinea were held together mainly by tribute and commercial ties rather than garrisons, which historians describe as a sea-based, or thalassocratic, form of power. Outer regions supplied goods and acknowledged Majapahit's authority in exchange for access to the trade network Java's rulers oversaw, rather than being administered as a single unified state.

Parameswara arrived at the mouth of the Bertam River with nothing left to rule. He had already lost Singapura and fled north through Muar and Ujong Tanah, one exiled king among refugees, before he stopped at a fishing village and, according to legend, watched a mouse deer fend off a hunting dog under a tree he then named his settlement after.

The village he founded around 1400 sat where monsoon winds reversed twice a year, letting traders from India wait out the season alongside those from China. Malacca grew rich on that timing alone, drawing Muslim, Hindu and Buddhist merchants who had scattered from other fallen ports, and within decades it outgrew every kingdom Parameswara had lost.

Mansa Musa's death left Mali without his authority, and the rulers who followed him were, by most accounts, weak, short-lived or outright cruel. Real power increasingly sat with the kankoro-sigui, an official who governed from behind the throne while the empire's grip on distant provinces loosened.

Tuareg raiders took Timbuktu in 1433 and Oualata three years later. The rising Songhai Empire then absorbed territory Mali had held for generations, capturing Mema by 1465 and seizing Timbuktu itself from the Tuareg in 1468. Mali tried appealing to Portugal for support in 1487, without effect, and the empire kept shrinking into a scatter of chiefdoms.

Sundiata Keita had spent part of his youth in exile, a crippled prince written off by rivals at his own father's court. He returned at the head of an alliance of Manden chiefdoms and met the Sosso ruler Soumaoro Kante in battle at Kirina around 1235.

The Sosso forces broke, and the assembled chiefs declared Sundiata mansa over twelve kingdoms, the alliance that became the Mali Empire. A charter agreed among the victors, the Kouroukan Fouga, is remembered as having set out how the new state's peoples and clans would deal with one another. Sundiata's generals spent the following years pushing its borders further across West Africa.

Thomas Malthus published his essay anonymously in 1798, arguing that population, left unchecked, doubles roughly every twenty five years while food supply grows only by fixed amounts each cycle. The gap between the two, he wrote, would always be closed eventually by famine, disease or war, whatever policies tried to prevent it.

Darwin later credited the essay directly: reading it in October 1838, he wrote, it struck him at once that favourable variations would tend to survive such pressure and unfavourable ones to perish. Alfred Russel Wallace reached a similar conclusion from the same book, and both built natural selection on Malthus's arithmetic of scarcity.

The men who took Egypt's throne in 1250 had been bought as boys, trained as soldiers, and owed loyalty only to the sultan who armed them. When the last Ayyubid sultan died, his widow and his Mamluk officers moved to keep power within the regiment rather than let it pass to a rival dynasty, ending a family line the Kurdish general Saladin had founded.

For a decade afterward the Franks in the Levant barely noticed them as a threat. That changed at Ain Jalut in 1260, where the Mamluk general Baibars feigned a retreat to draw the Mongol army into a trap and Sultan Qutuz closed it with a flanking charge, the first time a Mongol force had been stopped for good rather than merely delayed.

Japan's Kwantung Army had seized Manchuria by force through 1931, and on 1 March 1932 it proclaimed the territory an independent state, Manchukuo, with its capital at Changchun, renamed Xinjing. To give the new state a face other than a Japanese general's, it installed Puyi, the last emperor of the Qing dynasty, first as regent and later, in 1934, as emperor under the name Kangde.

Puyi signed decrees and held ceremony, but the Kwantung Army's commander doubled as Japan's ambassador and could veto him outright, while Japanese vice-ministers embedded in every department made the actual decisions. Manchukuo issued its own currency and stamps and joined no meaningful international body; only a handful of states, chiefly Japan's allies, ever recognised it.

Mandela was one of eight defendants convicted at the Rivonia Trial, named for the farm where police had seized documents on a planned armed campaign against apartheid. The prosecution accused him of recruiting people for sabotage training and soliciting funds abroad, charges heavy enough that the state had weighed asking for death.

The judge instead handed down life imprisonment on 12 June 1964. Walter Sisulu, Govan Mbeki, Denis Goldberg and four others received the same sentence alongside him, while a further co-defendant, Lionel Bernstein, was acquitted. Mandela would spend the next twenty-seven years in prison, most of them on Robben Island.

The word for a Maori tribe, iwi, literally means bone. Genealogy did the work a written land register might do elsewhere: an iwi traced itself back through whakapapa to a founding ancestor, and that lineage, not a survey line, was what made a territory, or rohe, belong to it.

Below each iwi sat smaller hapu, the working political units of daily life, and above them, loose clusters called waka grouped iwi that shared descent from the same migration canoe. No central authority bound the system together, and a rohe's boundary was rarely fixed: two iwi could claim the same ground through different ancestors without either version being wrong.

Maori iwi trace descent from the Polynesian voyagers whose traditions describe arriving from Hawaiki, and over time each iwi came to hold a recognised territory, a rohe, though the boundaries between neighbours often overlapped rather than running as clean lines on a map.

Below the iwi sat hapu, smaller kin groups that handled most day to day authority, and below those again sat individual whanau households. The layering meant an iwi was less a single government than a federation of hapu who could act together in war or ceremony and apart the rest of the time.

New Zealand had no farmed land at all until Polynesian voyagers reached it, and iwi organised what they found from nothing: forests, coastlines and unfamiliar soils divided among tribal groups by shared ancestry rather than by fences or deeds. Smaller hapu held and worked land within that wider tribal territory.

Resource limits were enforced through tapu and rahui, restrictions backed by spiritual sanction rather than force, closing a fishing ground or forest patch so it could recover. Because these rights ran through whakapapa, genealogy, rather than title, land use shifted as hapu grew, split, or lost standing relative to their neighbours.

Spanish forces expected the same swift conquest south of the Bio Bio river that they had achieved further north, and it did not come. Mapuche communities, organised in family and territorial groupings with no single ruler in peacetime, had already been electing war leaders called toqui since the 1550s to unite bands against Spanish incursions.

That practice of electing wartime leadership, without surrendering local autonomy in peace, let Mapuche groups keep fielding armies decade after decade rather than collapsing after one defeat. The frontier along the Bio Bio held for generations, and Spain never conquered the territory south of it by force.

Mapungubwe's hilltop capital, above the Limpopo river, had grown rich brokering gold and ivory to Swahili coast traders. Around 1300 it was abandoned, and no single cause explains why: the likeliest culprit is that Indian Ocean trade shifted north toward Sofala and the goldfields of the Zimbabwean plateau, leaving Mapungubwe's merchants without the imported goods that had underpinned their authority.

Without those goods to redistribute, the bond between rulers and subjects that had held the kingdom together seems to have frayed. Its people scattered rather than regrouping elsewhere, but the political model they left behind, a sacred king ruling from a hill above his subjects, resurfaced soon after at Great Zimbabwe.

Mapungubwe, not Great Zimbabwe, was the first state south of the Zambezi built on a gold economy. From a hill above the meeting of the Limpopo and Shashe rivers, its rulers controlled ivory and gold bound for the Swahili port of Sofala, trade that made Mapungubwe wealthy roughly a century before Great Zimbabwe took over the same route.

The clearest evidence is a burial find: a small rhinoceros carved from wood and covered in gold foil, unearthed with other royal grave goods in the 1930s. At its height the capital held several thousand people, evidence of a hierarchy built on controlling trade rather than farming alone.

A king needed a coronation to be a king, not merely a warlord who held forts, so on 6 June 1674 Shivaji staged one at Raigad, with Vedic priests performing rites that had lapsed for a Hindu ruler in the Deccan for generations. He took the title Chhatrapati, lord of the royal umbrella, before a crowd said to number in the tens of thousands.

The ceremony was itself a political claim: Shivaji had spent years as a nominal vassal within Mughal and Bijapuri politics, and crowning himself declared he answered to neither. The kingdom he founded that day outlasted him by more than a century, eventually contesting Mughal power across much of the subcontinent.

Marcus Aurelius came to power in 161 on the death of his adoptive father Antoninus Pius, and insisted the Senate name his adoptive brother Lucius Verus as co-emperor alongside him, an arrangement without much precedent. He was already known as a serious student of Stoic philosophy, a habit he kept up through years of war on the Danube and Euphrates frontiers.

His private notebooks, written in Greek during military campaigns and addressed to himself rather than any audience, survived to become the Meditations. He is counted as the last of the rulers later called the Five Good Emperors, a label invented long after his death; his own son and successor, Commodus, broke sharply with the pattern by ruling as an unchecked autocrat.

Facing a shortage of soldiers for the war against Jugurtha in Numidia, the consul Gaius Marius in 107 BC enrolled volunteers from the capite censi, citizens too poor to meet the property qualification that had traditionally governed army service. It was a practical fix for an immediate manpower problem rather than an announced overhaul of the military system.

Later Roman writers credited Marius with far more: redesigning the javelin, making the eagle the sole legionary standard, and reshaping the legion around the cohort. Modern historians doubt most of this, finding little evidence any of it was new or permanent under Marius. What is clear is that opening the ranks to the landless tied soldiers' loyalty to whichever general could reward them with land and pay, a change Marius had not intended.

The core idea behind the Rhodian Sea Law is older than any surviving text of it: if a captain ordered cargo thrown overboard to keep a sinking ship afloat, the loss should not fall on whichever merchant's goods happened to go over the side first. Instead every owner whose cargo made it to port shared the cost, a principle later jurists called general average.

Roman emperors are said to have ratified the custom rather than invented it, folding a much older Mediterranean shipping practice, plausibly Phoenician in origin, into their own legal code. Byzantine compilers eventually wrote the law down in the form that survives, covering crew pay and salvage disputes alongside the jettison rule.

Isabella, heir to Castile, married in secret on 19 October 1469, without the consent of her half brother King Henry IV. She slipped away from court claiming to visit a tomb in Avila while Ferdinand, heir to Aragon, crossed Castile disguised as a servant to reach her at the Palacio de los Vivero in Valladolid.

As second cousins the pair needed papal dispensation, which they secured through a bull whose authenticity was later questioned, arranged with help from the future Pope Alexander VI. Henry IV denounced the match as a breach of an earlier agreement, but Isabella took Castile's throne in 1474 and Ferdinand inherited Aragon in 1479, and their joint rule became the basis of a unified Spain.

George Marshall chose a Harvard commencement, not a press conference, to announce American aid for Europe on 5 June 1947. He spoke for under twenty minutes and named no figures, leaving the detail to Congress, which eventually voted through roughly twelve billion dollars over four years once Truman signed the programme into law the following spring.

Stalin briefly weighed joining before Molotov walked out of the Paris talks that would have committed the Soviet Union to open its books to American oversight. Moscow then barred the Eastern Bloc from accepting any aid and answered with its own Molotov Plan, calling Marshall's programme a scheme for the economic enslavement of Europe.

Mataram began as a small inland domain under Pajang's overlordship, until Senopati broke away and started fighting his way down the Solo river toward the Java coast. City after city fell to him through the 1590s, Madiun and Kediri among them, and by the mid 1590s the coastal states of Cirebon and Galuh had been forced to accept him as their overlord too.

Not everything went his way: an attempt to take Banten in 1597 failed outright, and Surabaya, the strongest of his rivals, held out for decades after his death in 1601. His son and later Sultan Agung kept up the pressure, and by the 1620s Mataram ruled most of central and eastern Java from the interior he had first secured.

Stephen was captured at the Battle of Lincoln in February 1141, dismounted and fighting on foot after his cavalry broke. With her rival in chains at Bristol, the church declared Matilda Lady of England and Normandy, and the Bishop of Winchester handed her the royal treasury, though Stephen's crown was nearly all that remained in it.

Her triumph lasted five months. Besieging the bishop at Winchester that July, she was encircled by Stephen's queen and reinforcements from London, and her army broke in the retreat. Robert of Gloucester was captured covering her escape to Devizes, and the two sides swapped prisoners: Stephen free again, Matilda's claim to the throne never recovered.

Ashoka had already conquered Kalinga and, by his own later account, been sickened by the slaughter it cost. He answered by carving his changed policy into stone, on pillars raised across northern India, in a plain script ordinary travellers could read rather than the priestly language reserved for scholars.

The major pillar edicts, cut late in his reign around 237 to 236 BCE, urge mercy, truthfulness and care for animals and the poor rather than any single creed. Versions in Greek and Aramaic appear on frontier pillars in what is now Afghanistan, aimed at subjects who read neither Brahmi nor Kharoshthi. No other ruler of his era left instructions to his people in stone on this scale.

Chandragupta's rise began as a war on the Nanda dynasty of Magadha, a kingdom accounts describe as widely resented by its own subjects, guided by his advisor Chanakya. Their forces stripped away the Nanda's outer territories first and advanced on the capital, Pataliputra, only once the ground had been prepared, roughly between 322 and 319 BCE.

Alexander the Great had died in 323 BCE leaving Greek governors in the Indus valley, and Chandragupta turned on them next, pushing Greek authority out of northwestern India. A later marriage alliance with the Seleucid ruler Seleucus, sealed around 305 to 303 BCE, handed him the western Indus territories outright, and campaigns south and into Gujarat left him ruling more of the subcontinent than any king before him.

Little about Chandragupta's rise is independently confirmed. Buddhist, Jain and Hindu sources agree that he overthrew the Nanda dynasty around 322 BCE with the help of an advisor, Chanakya, but historians treat much of the detail as legend grown up around a real conquest rather than a reliable record.

What is clearer is the scale of what followed: Chandragupta pushed Greek garrisons left behind by Alexander out of the Punjab, then fought his way toward the Nanda capital at Pataliputra, taking territory and installing garrisons as he advanced. The empire he founded eventually stretched from Afghanistan into the Deccan, the first to unify most of the Indian subcontinent under one ruler.

No single catastrophe ended the southern Maya lowlands. Palenque, Copan and Tikal declined at different times across the eighth and ninth centuries, abandoning temples and plazas that were never reoccupied, and construction had almost stopped across the central Maya area by 830.

Tree ring and lake sediment studies point to a severe, decades long drought, with some years showing rainfall reduced by as much as seventy percent. Deforestation and soil erosion compounded the shortage, and rival city states kept fighting each other even as their water reserves failed.

The league that bound the great Yucatan cities together was never a peaceful partnership. Chichen Itza, Uxmal and Mayapan had shared power under a loose confederacy, but the arrangement leaned on the Cocom lineage, who governed the western lands and pressed rival cities to accept their authority.

A Cocom leader named Hunac Ceel is said to have claimed divine favour after surviving a ritual plunge into a sacred cenote, using that survival to justify Cocom dominance over the league. The confederacy held for generations, but the resentment it stored up eventually broke it: in 1441 the ruler of Uxmal turned on the Cocom family and destroyed them, splitting Yucatan into rival provinces.

The Mayflower had been chartered for Virginia, but storms pushed it to Cape Cod instead, well outside the territory its passengers had permission to settle. Some of the non-Puritan passengers on board, travelling for their own reasons rather than religious ones, argued that landing outside the agreed patent released them from any obligation to obey Pilgrim leadership.

To head off that argument, 41 of the men on board signed a short compact on 21 November 1620, agreeing to form a body politic and submit to whatever just laws it later passed for the colony's good. It pledged loyalty to James I in the same breath, and gave Plymouth a working government before a single building had been raised ashore.

No founding charter survives for the school at Salerno; a later legend credits four teachers, a Latin, a Greek, an Arab and a Jew, meeting by chance and deciding to teach together. What is certain is that by the eleventh century the town trained physicians who valued experience over theory.

Its curriculum drew on Hippocrates and Galen alongside Arabic texts translated by Constantine the African. Salerno also produced women physicians, among them Trotula, whose writing on women's medicine circulated across Europe for generations after her death.

Giovanni di Bicci de' Medici broke away from a relative's bank in Rome and set up on his own in Florence in 1397, starting with around 10,000 gold florins of capital. Rather than run one firm out of a single office, he structured each branch as its own legal partnership, so that a failure or lawsuit in one city could not pull the others down with it, an arrangement since compared to a modern holding company.

The bank's Rome office managed papal finances so extensively it became known as God's bankers, while branches in Venice, London, Bruges and Geneva moved money through bills of exchange that sidestepped the Church's ban on interest. Combined with wool, silk and alum trading, this network made the Medici the continent's most respected bank within two generations, and funded the family's rise in Florentine politics.

Several older Florentine banking families had just collapsed when Giovanni di Bicci de' Medici split from his nephew's Roman bank in 1397 and set up on his own in Florence with 10,000 gold florins. The timing left a gap in the market that a cautious new house could fill.

Rather than run one central partnership, the Medici incorporated each branch, Rome, Venice, Geneva, Bruges, London, separately under Florentine ownership, so a failure in one city could not drag down the rest, a structural flaw that had ruined the earlier Bardi and Peruzzi banks. Surviving ledger fragments from the Bruges branch also show the firm keeping careful double-entry books, tracking debits against credits rather than one running total.

Two kings had already abandoned wives and remarried before the Fourth Lateran Council met in 1215, and the bishops gathered in Rome meant to close the loophole that let them do it. Canon fifty addressed marriage impediments through kinship and ordered that engagements be publicly announced ahead of the wedding.

The point of the announcement was practical rather than ceremonial: a public banns period gave a congregation time to object if the couple were secretly related, already married, or otherwise forbidden to wed. Clergy were expected to preside and record the union, moving marriage away from a private arrangement between families and toward something the wider parish could verify.

Behind the restoration lay the domains of Satsuma and Choshu, rivals turned allies who had watched foreign warships force open Japanese ports and decided the shogunate could not be trusted to answer them. On 3 January 1868 their forces backed a declaration that political power was returned to the Imperial House, ending the Tokugawa shogunate that had ruled Japan since 1603.

Emperor Meiji, still a teenager, became the nominal centre of a government run largely by the domain leaders who had put him there. Within a few years the samurai class was dissolved, the old domains replaced with prefectures, and a programme of rapid industrialisation and Western-style institutions was under way.

Gold and silver, in the thinking that dominated European treasuries by the mid seventeenth century, were the only real measure of a state's strength, and the way to get more of them was to sell abroad far more than a country bought. Governments answered that logic with tariffs on foreign manufactures, bans on carrying gold or silver out of the country, and colonies forbidden to trade with anyone but their own mother state.

England's Navigation Acts, beginning in 1651, and France's later reforms under Louis XIV's minister Jean-Baptiste Colbert put the doctrine into practice on a national scale, organising industries into state-favoured monopolies and subsidising exporters. The writer Thomas Mun captured the creed in one line: the balance of foreign trade was the rule of a nation's treasure.

Jean-Baptiste Colbert ran French finances for over two decades and treated trade as a war conducted with tariffs instead of soldiers. He organised industries into guilds bound by more than a thousand state directives, imported foreign artisans to build up domestic crafts, and taxed goods crossing into France while cutting the tolls that slowed trade within it.

Roads and canals paid for by the crown moved that domestic trade faster, and French industrial output grew substantially under his direction. He never matched the Dutch or English at overseas trade itself, but the doctrine he applied, that a nation's wealth was measured in exports and precious metal kept at home, dominated European economic policy for another century.

A ship holding a fixed compass bearing traces a curve on the globe, but on ordinary maps of the time that same course was drawn as a bent line, forcing a captain to keep replotting it. Gerardus Mercator solved this in 1569 by stretching the spacing between lines of latitude further apart the closer they came to the poles, so that any constant bearing became a straight line on paper.

The trade off was size: regions near the poles were inflated far beyond their true area, a distortion still visible in modern classroom maps. Sailors were slow to adopt it, but within a few generations Mercator's projection became the standard chart for ocean navigation, and it still underlies most digital world maps in use.

Kush moved its capital south from Napata to Meroe centuries before the kingdom's later prime, drawn by a stretch of the Nile with better rainfall and, crucially, abundant iron ore and timber. Furnaces there produced enough surplus iron to trade rather than merely to arm the kingdom's own soldiers, alongside gold and ivory sold on to Rome.

Meroe also produced its own script, adapting Egyptian signs into an alphabet used for both everyday records and royal inscriptions. Scholars can read the letters aloud but still cannot translate most of what they say, because the underlying Meroitic language remains only partly understood even now.

Independence came not from the insurgents finishing what they started but from a former royalist officer switching sides. Agustin de Iturbide, who had spent years fighting the rebels, joined forces with insurgent leader Vicente Guerrero in 1821 under the Plan of Iguala, and their combined army swept the exhausted colonial government aside within months.

Spain's viceroy signed the Treaty of Cordoba on 27 September 1821, formalising the split. Iturbide then crowned himself emperor of a new Mexican monarchy, a role that lasted barely two years before a republican revolt replaced it with a federal constitution in 1824. Spain did not recognise any of it until 1836.

Paul Allen and Bill Gates had never actually run their BASIC interpreter on the Altair 8800 microcomputer before flying to Albuquerque to demonstrate it to the machine's maker in March 1975. Allen wrote a simulator to test it on a different computer, and the program worked the first time it touched real Altair hardware.

The two formed a partnership that April, and Allen suggested the name Micro-Soft, a contraction of microcomputer software that the hyphen would later drop. Albuquerque was chosen only because that was where the Altair's manufacturer, MITS, happened to be based, and the company moved to Washington state within a few years.

Zhu Yuanzhang began as a penniless peasant and a Buddhist monk before joining the Red Turban rebels in 1352, during a wave of uprisings against Mongol Yuan rule brought on by heavy taxation and Yellow River flooding that the Yuan government had left unmanaged. He took Nanjing in 1356 and spent the next years crushing rival rebel leaders, most decisively Chen Youliang at the Battle of Lake Poyang in 1363.

With his rivals gone he marched north in 1368, and the last Yuan emperor fled the capital rather than fight. Zhu declared the Ming dynasty and took the era name Hongwu, meaning vastly martial. His rise ended roughly a century of Mongol rule over China and restored a Han Chinese imperial house for the first time since the Song.

Silver at Potosi had been running short since the easy surface ore ran out in the 1560s, leaving deeper deposits too poor in silver for the old smelting methods to bother with. Viceroy Francisco de Toledo's answer was to seize the mercury mines at Huancavelica for the Spanish crown and ship the mercury to Potosi, where it could pull silver out of that low grade ore through amalgamation instead of fire.

Toledo called it the marriage of the mountain of Huancavelica to the mountain of Potosi, and the numbers bore him out: output at Potosi roughly quintupled between 1571 and 1575. The labour behind that jump was overwhelmingly forced, drawn from Andean communities under the mita system to work both mountains at once.

Around 2000 BCE, Knossos was already a crowded town, its population estimated to have grown to some 18,000, and sites across Crete including Phaistos and Malia were undergoing major building work as their populations surged. The grand palace complexes people now associate with Knossos followed soon after, going up in the following century or so.

Cretan traders were reaching Egypt, Cyprus, the Levantine coast and Anatolia by this period, carrying goods and styles across the eastern Mediterranean. Later centuries would see that reach grow further still, but the population growth and construction of the centuries around 2000 BCE marked the point at which Cretan society moved from scattered towns toward the networked island culture historians call Minoan.

Bernadette Soubirous was fourteen, illiterate and gathering firewood near Lourdes on 11 February 1858 when she said a woman in white appeared in a grotto at Massabielle. She returned to the site repeatedly over the following months, reporting eighteen apparitions in total, and on one visit in March the figure identified herself as the Immaculate Conception.

During the visions Bernadette uncovered a spring that pilgrims soon credited with healings, and a local bishop formally recognised the apparitions in 1862. Lourdes grew into one of the largest pilgrimage sites in the world, drawing several million visitors a year, and Bernadette was canonised a saint in 1933.

Ernesto Miranda was arrested in Phoenix in March 1963 over a kidnapping and rape case, and after two hours of police questioning he signed a confession. He had not been told he could remain silent or ask for a lawyer before the interrogation began, and his conviction rested on that confession alone.

The Supreme Court overturned it on 13 June 1966, ruling that anyone in police custody must be warned of the right to silence and to counsel before questioning starts, or the resulting statements cannot be used at trial. The wording the Court prescribed became the Miranda warning, recited by police officers in the United States ever since.

Cahokia had once housed as many as fifteen thousand people around its central plaza near the Mississippi, with tens of thousands more in the farmland around it, a population North America would not see gathered in one place again for centuries. People began leaving in larger numbers from the late 12th century, and by the mid 13th the city had lost roughly half its residents.

No single cause explains the emptying. Archaeologists point to flooding of the surrounding bottomlands, deforestation and overhunting that strained the land, and nutritional problems from a diet leaning heavily on maize, alongside signs of internal conflict: burned villages and defensive stockades built around the same period. By 1350 the site that had briefly rivalled contemporary European cities stood abandoned.

Three droughts struck the Mississippian heartland between 1150 and 1275, the last severe enough to strain a civilization whose cities depended on maize surpluses to feed thousands of people packed around ceremonial mounds. At Cahokia, the largest of them, roughly half the population is thought to have left for other regions, including new settlements around present-day Nashville.

The result was not collapse so much as fragmentation. By 1300 ceremonial centres such as Moundville had lost much of their surrounding population even as their elite core persisted, and power scattered into a wider field of smaller, competing chiefdoms across the Southeast. New religious practices, including the Datura ritual complex, spread through the region as the old, single-centred order broke down.

Spiro, a ceremonial mound centre in what is now Oklahoma, pulled in copper worked at Etowah in Georgia and stone palettes carved at Moundville in Alabama, objects that had crossed most of the eastern half of the continent before reaching a single burial deep inside an earthen mound.

None of it moved by wheel or draft animal. Canoes and human portage carried marine shell from the Gulf coast, copper from the Great Lakes and mica from the Appalachians between mound centres hundreds of kilometres apart, an exchange that drew several thousand people to major sites for trade and ceremony alike.

Missouri's request to join the Union in 1819 threatened to tip the Senate's careful balance between slave and free states. The deadlock broke only when Illinois senator Jesse Thomas added a separate provision: Missouri would enter as a slave state, Maine would be carved off from Massachusetts and enter free, and the balance would hold at twelve states each.

Thomas's clause did the lasting work. It banned slavery from the rest of the Louisiana Purchase territory north of the 36 degree 30 minute line, leaving Missouri itself as the one exception north of that mark. The line held for over three decades before the Kansas-Nebraska Act unraveled it in 1854, and the Supreme Court struck it down as unconstitutional in the Dred Scott case of 1857.

Monte Alban had stood mostly abandoned for two centuries when Mixtec families began returning to its terraces around 1200. They came not to rebuild the Zapotec city's pyramids and ballcourts but to bury their own dead inside the tombs already cut into the hillside.

One of those tombs, reused and resealed by later burials, still held gold, turquoise mosaics and carved jaguar bones when archaeologists opened it in the twentieth century, among the richest funerary troves found anywhere in the Americas. The builders had been gone for generations, but the mountain kept being useful for the one purpose that mattered to their successors.

Edward I called the Westminster assembly of November 1295 mainly to pay for war, against France, against Scotland, and against unrest in Wales, not out of any theory of representation. He told the summoned lords, clergy and commoners that what touches all should be approved by all, an argument for consent to taxation rather than a plan for a new institution.

The gathering brought together roughly 49 lords and clergy with 292 commoners, two knights from each county and two representatives from each city and borough, a formula later parliaments largely repeated. Historians William Stubbs and Frederic Maitland gave it the name Model Parliament centuries afterward, and it was this assembly's representatives who pressed to trade grants of money for the hearing of grievances.

The first production Model T left Ford's Piquette Avenue plant in Detroit in August 1908, priced around 825 dollars, a stiff sum for most families. What changed that was not the car itself but the factory: from October 1913 Ford ran the chassis past workers on a moving line, cutting assembly from roughly twelve and a half hours to about ninety minutes.

Prices fell as output climbed. A Model T that cost 825 dollars in 1909 sold for 440 dollars by 1914 and 260 dollars by 1925, even as wages rose. Over nineteen years Ford built more than fifteen million of them, the same black car with the same mechanical layout, changed only by how cheaply the line could turn it out.

Cloves and nutmeg grew nowhere else on earth but a handful of small islands in eastern Indonesia, which made the Moluccas worth fighting over out of all proportion to their size. Portugal had held the upper hand there since taking Malacca in 1511, and a 1529 treaty with Spain fixed a line through the Pacific and paid Portugal 350,000 gold ducats to keep Spanish ships out of the spice islands themselves.

The line did not stop Spanish ambition, only redirect it: unable to touch the Moluccas without provoking Portugal, Charles V turned his attention to the nearby Philippines instead, reasoning that an archipelago with no spices was not worth a Portuguese quarrel. Local sultanates such as Ternate kept resisting Portuguese control throughout, and the contest ran on for decades after any treaty had supposedly settled it.

Mombasa was trading long before 1400. The Arab geographer al-Idrisi already described it as a wealthy port in 1151. By the fourteenth century the city sat within the wider Kilwa Sultanate, one of a chain of Swahili coast towns moving goods between the African interior and the Indian Ocean.

When Vasco da Gama arrived in 1498 searching for a route to India, Mombasa gave him a hostile reception, unlike its neighbour Malindi further up the coast. The city's old ties to Kilwa did not survive contact with the Portuguese, who imposed direct rule over Mombasa from 1593.

The Mon were the first people in mainland Southeast Asia to receive Theravada Buddhist missionaries arriving from Sri Lanka, and Mon kingdoms in lower Burma carried that tradition onward rather than originating it. Their script, adapted from Pallava writing used in southern India, survives in a cave inscription near modern Saraburi dated to around 550.

That inheritance travelled further than the kingdoms that first held it. Later Burmese rulers who conquered Mon territory adopted the religious culture rather than replacing it, and Theravada Buddhism carried by Mon communities continued to shape belief across the wider region long after their own kingdoms had been absorbed.

A grant of land to a monastery was a gift that never had to be repeated. Kings and nobles endowed religious houses with estates as an act of piety and, often, as a way of keeping land out of the hands of rival families, and because monasteries rarely sold what they were given, those holdings only grew across generations.

Louis the Pious, Charlemagne's son, put real effort into refounding monasteries that had lapsed and endowing new ones, adding to a pattern already under way. By the height of Carolingian rule some monastic houses controlled estates worked by thousands of tenants, run by administrators answerable to an abbot rather than to any count.

A former Roman official named Cassiodorus gave up politics in the 530s and built a monastery at Vivarium with a library at its centre, instructing monks to copy manuscripts as a form of religious labour alongside farming and prayer. The Rule of Saint Benedict, written around the same decades, made reading part of a monk's daily obligation rather than a private pursuit.

Copying was slow and the losses were real, but works of Aristotle, Plato and other classical writers survived the collapse of Roman schooling chiefly because monks kept recopying them. The curriculum that grew around this habit, blending scripture with the old trivium and quadrivium subjects, later fed directly into the first medieval universities.

Monet painted a hazy sunrise over the harbour at Le Havre in 1872 and needed a title for the catalogue when it went on show two years later. Asked what to call it, he shrugged that it could not really pass for a view of the port and told the organisers to just put Impression.

The critic Louis Leroy seized on that word to mock the whole exhibition in a review for Le Charivari, coining the term Impressionists as an insult. Painters who had shown alongside Monet, including Renoir, Pissarro and Degas, kept the label anyway, and it stuck to their movement rather than to him alone.

Ruling China as a conquering minority meant Kublai Khan could not simply govern as his grandfather Genghis had on the steppe. He kept a Mongol military elite at the top but staffed much of the bureaucracy underneath with Chinese and Central Asian officials, adopting the Chinese practice of a central secretariat to draft policy while provincial branch secretariats carried it out at a distance.

The population was sorted into ranked categories, Mongols first, then various non-Chinese subjects, then northern and finally southern Chinese, each facing different tax and legal treatment. Villages were grouped into units of fifty households responsible for local order and labour duties, a structure built to extract revenue and manpower from a population many times the size of the conquerors themselves.

When Genghis Khan died in 1227 his empire was already twice the size of the Roman Empire at its height. His successors kept expanding it for another two generations. Kublai Khan finished the conquest of Song China in 1279, folding the richest and most populous country on earth into a realm that already ran from Siberia to the edge of Eastern Europe.

By 1294 the Mongol domain covered roughly 23.5 million square kilometres, still the largest contiguous land empire ever assembled under one family. It was never one government for long: within decades of Kublai's death it had split into rival khanates that fought each other as readily as they had once fought outsiders.

A message could cross the Mongol Empire, from Korea's border to Persia, faster than any European courier could cross a single kingdom. The yam worked through relay stations spaced roughly twenty to forty miles apart, each stocked with fresh horses, food and shelter so a rider never had to slow his own mount to rest it.

Riders handed documents to a waiting courier at each station rather than continuing themselves, letting the message travel at a horse's freshest pace for the whole route: two hundred to three hundred kilometres in a day was achievable. Ogedei Khan expanded a rougher version his father Genghis had used into this empire-wide network, and after the Golden Horde's collapse Russia kept the system running as its own postal service.

The Khalkha Mongols did not submit to the Qing out of admiration. In 1688 the Dzungar leader Galdan invaded their territory from the west, and the Khalkha nobles, unable to hold their own grazing lands, turned to the Kangxi Emperor for protection rather than face conquest by a rival Mongol power.

That appeal cost them their independence in return for their safety. Kangxi extended Qing protection and, with it, Qing authority, formally binding the Khalkha leadership into the empire as vassals, a status that folded Outer Mongolia into Qing administration for the rest of the dynasty's rule.

Reports that Bill Clinton had a relationship with a 22-year-old White House intern surfaced online in January 1998, days before he denied it on television with a line that would define the saga: he had not had sexual relations with that woman, Miss Lewinsky. He held to that denial in public for seven months.

In August 1998 he told a grand jury he had in fact had an improper physical relationship with Lewinsky. The House of Representatives impeached him that December on charges of perjury and obstruction of justice. The Senate acquitted him in February 1999; the vote to convict fell well short of the two-thirds majority needed to remove him from office.

President James Monroe delivered the line in his annual message to Congress on 2 December 1823, but the wording was chiefly the work of his secretary of state, John Quincy Adams. It declared the Americas closed to further European colonisation and warned that any attempt to extend a European monarchy's system into the hemisphere would be treated as a threat to the United States itself.

Adams had pushed for a unilateral statement rather than a joint declaration with Britain, wanting the United States to speak for itself even though its navy could not yet have enforced the warning against a determined European power. The doctrine had little practical effect for decades, and it was later presidents, not Monroe, who invoked it to justify direct intervention across Latin America.

The European Union set the bar deliberately high before the vote could count: 55 percent of ballots cast in favour, with turnout above 50 percent, a threshold proposed by EU envoy Miroslav Lajcak specifically to head off a result too narrow to be accepted by both sides. On 21 May 2006, Montenegro cleared it by barely a point and a half, with 55.5 percent voting to leave.

Montenegro's parliament formally declared independence on 3 June, ending the loose federation of Serbia and Montenegro that had replaced Yugoslavia only three years earlier. Serbia responded by declaring itself the union's legal successor state, inheriting its seat at the United Nations while Montenegro started fresh as the newest member.

Rosa Parks was not the first Montgomery rider arrested for refusing a bus seat that year, but local organisers judged her case the one to build around. She was detained on 1 December 1955, and within four days a boycott began that would run for 382 days, sustained by a citywide carpool network rather than by simply walking.

Jo Ann Robinson and the Women's Political Council printed the leaflets that got the boycott moving overnight, and E.D. Nixon lined up the legal case. Martin Luther King, then twenty-six, was chosen to lead the new Montgomery Improvement Association partly because he was too recently arrived to have made enemies. The boycott ended after the Supreme Court upheld a ruling against bus segregation in Browder v. Gayle on 13 November 1956.

Diplomats agreed the Montreal Protocol on 16 September 1987 to phase out chlorofluorocarbons and halons, the refrigerant and aerosol chemicals then widening the hole in the ozone layer over Antarctica each spring. It came into force in 1989, and unlike most environmental agreements it set binding, scheduled cuts rather than voluntary targets, later tightened several times as evidence of the damage grew.

It became the only United Nations treaty ever ratified by every recognised state, with 198 parties. Kofi Annan called it perhaps the most successful international agreement to date, and measurements since have found the ozone layer slowly recovering as roughly 98 percent of the targeted substances were phased out worldwide. A 2016 amendment agreed in Kigali extended the same mechanism to CFC replacement gases.

France had exiled Sultan Mohammed V to Madagascar in 1953, hoping a more compliant relative would quiet nationalist unrest. It had the opposite effect: his removal turned him into the movement's rallying figure, and by late 1955 France judged it safer to bring him back than to keep fighting his popularity.

Mohammed V returned in November 1955 and negotiated independence from France without further war, formalised in March 1956; Spain ceded its northern protectorate shortly after. He resumed the throne not as sultan but as king, a title chosen to mark a monarchy remade rather than merely restored.

Aurangzeb did not wait for his father to die. When Shah Jahan fell ill in 1657 and named his eldest son Dara Shikoh as heir, Aurangzeb marched instead, won the battles of Dharmat and Samugarh in 1658, and declared his father unfit to rule. Shah Jahan spent his last eight years confined in Agra Fort, tended by his daughter Jahanara.

Dara was executed the following year on a charge of apostasy, and a second brother, Murad, was arrested and put to death in 1661. Under the emperor who had removed them, Mughal territory eventually covered nearly the whole Indian subcontinent, and by some estimates its economy briefly outweighed Qing China's.

Ibrahim Lodi brought roughly 100,000 men and a thousand elephants to Panipat in April 1526. Babur brought perhaps a twelfth of that number, but he had cannon and a Central Asian encirclement tactic called the tulugma, and he used both to trap and break the Sultan of Delhi's line. Ibrahim Lodi died on the field, ending the Lodi dynasty outright.

Babur rode into Delhi and Agra within days, but holding what he had won was harder than taking it. Many of his own Afghan and Turkic followers wanted to go home rather than settle in India's heat, and the Rajput ruler Rana Sanga still stood against him. He fought on, and the dynasty he had just founded outlasted every one of those objections by centuries.

Shah Jahan's path to the throne was not gentle. When his father Jahangir died in October 1627, he moved quickly to eliminate rival claimants, executing his chief male relatives before his coronation at Agra Fort on 14 February 1628. His reign went on to see the Deccan sultanates brought to heel, with Golconda submitting in 1635 and Bijapur the following year.

The building programme that defines his reputation began with grief rather than ambition. His wife Mumtaz Mahal died in June 1631 giving birth to their fourteenth child, and accounts describe him as paralysed by mourning for weeks. The mausoleum he commissioned for her, along with the Red Fort and the Jama Masjid, marked the high point of Mughal architecture, a golden period that ended in 1658 when his son Aurangzeb deposed and imprisoned him.

In 1327 the sultan ordered Delhi's population marched over 700 miles south to a new capital at Daulatabad, arguing the site would let him govern the north and south together. A road was laid with shade trees and rest stations, but food and water ran short on the way, and by 1335 rebellion and plague forced him to send everyone back to a depopulated Delhi.

Three years earlier he had tried to fix a shortage of silver by issuing brass and copper coins valued as if they were gold or silver. Without controls on minting, counterfeits flooded the markets until the currency was, by one account, worth no more than stone. Traders refused it, and by the time Ibn Battuta arrived in 1334 the scheme had already been dropped.

El Dorado began as a title, not a place. Spanish colonists heard of a chief who covered himself in gold dust and rowed onto Lake Guatavita to wash it off, an investiture rite for a new Muisca ruler, and turned the gilded one into rumours of a golden city that lured expeditions for two centuries.

The confederation it distorted was real: four groupings, centred on Bogota, Tunja, Duitama and Sogamoso, each led by a chief who bound smaller capitanias through personal alliance rather than direct rule. Muisca traders exchanged salt, emeralds and cotton across the highlands until Spanish conquest ended the system in 1537.

Hitler burst into a Munich beer hall on the night of 8 November 1923 with armed men and announced, from a table he had climbed onto, that the Bavarian government was deposed. He had recruited the retired general Erich Ludendorff to lend the coup military credibility, along with Ernst Rohm, Rudolf Hess and Hermann Goring.

The next morning around two thousand marchers met a police line at the Feldherrnhalle. Shots were exchanged, killing sixteen Nazis, four police officers and a bystander, and the putsch collapsed within minutes. Hitler was arrested two days later and sentenced to five years for treason, of which he served about nine months, using the time at Landsberg prison to dictate Mein Kampf.

Great Zimbabwe was not conquered so much as walked away from. Its farmland exhausted, Karanga families drifted north onto the Zimbabwean plateau, and an elephant hunter named Mutota is remembered as the one who turned that drift into a kingdom by founding a new capital and drawing surrounding chiefdoms under it.

Gold is the metal people now associate with Mutapa, but it was never the base of the economy, which rested on farming and cattle. Gold production from the empire's mines actually peaked before about 1500, then declined as outlying regions such as Manyika broke away in the following century, well before Portuguese traders arrived expecting an empire built on it.

Long before Homer's Greeks besieged Troy, a real Bronze Age culture was building hilltop citadels with walls so thick that later Greeks credited them to one-eyed giants. Mycenaean civilisation grew out of the local mainland Bronze Age, shaped heavily by contact with Minoan Crete, rather than arriving as an outside conquest.

Its palaces at sites such as Pylos and Knossos ran tightly managed economies, tracking textiles, land grants and tax owed in a syllabic script called Linear B, the earliest form of written Greek known. Deciphered only in the 1950s, the clay tablets turned out to record inventories and accounts rather than literature, the paperwork of a bureaucracy rather than an epic.

A white mob rampaged through Springfield, Illinois in 1908, burning Black-owned homes and lynching two men within walking distance of Abraham Lincoln's tomb. The outrage pushed journalist William English Walling, social worker Mary White Ovington and Henry Moskowitz to call a meeting in New York that January.

Sixty prominent Americans signed the founding call, among them W. E. B. Du Bois, Ida B. Wells and Mary Church Terrell. The group formed on 12 February 1909, timed to the centenary of Lincoln's birth. Boston attorney Moorfield Storey, who was white, became its first president, while Du Bois ran publicity and edited its magazine.

George H. W. Bush, Carlos Salinas de Gortari and Brian Mulroney each signed the agreement in their own capital on 17 December 1992, having negotiated it as outgoing or soon-departing leaders. Bill Clinton, who inherited the ratification fight, added side agreements on labour and the environment before pushing it through Congress the following year.

It took effect on 1 January 1994, immediately removing tariffs on roughly half of Mexico's exports to the United States and phasing out most of the rest over the following decade. The deal replaced a patchwork of separate trade rules among the three countries and became the template for the later United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement.

South Africa had administered Namibia under a League of Nations mandate and then simply refused to give it up after the UN declared the occupation illegal in 1969. Guerrilla fighting by the South West Africa People's Organisation ran from 1966, and it took a 1988 accord tying Namibian independence to the withdrawal of Cuban troops from Angola to unlock a settlement.

UN peacekeepers under UNTAG supervised elections in November 1989, and Namibia became independent on 21 March 1990 with Sam Nujoma as president. The transition closed one of the last colonial-era disputes on the continent, settled not by a single treaty but by a chain of regional bargains among South Africa, Angola and Cuba.
