Napoleon sailed from Toulon in May 1798 aiming not at France's usual enemies in Europe but at Egypt, hoping to cut Britain off from its trade routes to India. He brought over a hundred scholars and scientists along with his army, intending to study the country as thoroughly as he conquered it.

The campaign turned quickly. On 1 August 1798, Horatio Nelson's fleet caught the French ships at anchor in Aboukir Bay and destroyed most of them, stranding Napoleon's army in Egypt. The scientists stayed on regardless, and among their finds was a slab of inscribed basalt near Rosetta that would eventually unlock the reading of hieroglyphs.

The agency did not start from nothing. Eisenhower folded an existing body, the National Advisory Committee for Aeronautics, which had studied flight since 1915, into a new civilian organisation rather than hand spaceflight to the military, a deliberate choice meant to keep the programme separate from weapons development.

The National Aeronautics and Space Act became law on 29 July 1958, and the renamed agency opened for business that October. The decision followed within a year of the Soviet Sputnik launch, when American officials worried publicly that the country was falling behind in a contest that had, until then, barely existed.

Twelve countries signed the North Atlantic Treaty in Washington on 4 April 1949, building on an earlier and smaller pact among Belgium, France, Luxembourg, the Netherlands and Britain. The new treaty pulled in the United States and Canada alongside Portugal, Italy, Norway, Denmark and Iceland, countries with little in common beyond a shared unease about Soviet intentions in Europe.

Its core clause, Article 5, commits every member to treat an attack on one as an attack on all. The wording was deliberately vague about what a response must involve, a compromise that let the United States join a peacetime European alliance for the first time in its history without binding Congress to any automatic declaration of war.

English merchants had a Dutch problem in 1651. After Spain lifted its trade embargoes on the Dutch in 1647, Dutch shippers, with their efficient entrepot system, had come to dominate the Baltic, Mediterranean and colonial carrying trade that English merchants wanted for themselves. Parliament's answer was a law requiring goods from Asia, Africa or America to arrive in England only on English-owned, English-crewed ships.

The Act barely disguised its target. It banned foreign vessels from bringing in goods that had not originated in their own country, closing the loophole through which Dutch traders had been reselling the world's cargo to England. The Dutch protested but could not have it repealed, and the resentment it stoked is usually counted among the causes of the First Anglo-Dutch War the following year.

Foreign ministers Vyacheslav Molotov and Joachim von Ribbentrop signed a non-aggression pact in Moscow, dated 23 August 1939, between two governments that had spent years denouncing each other as mortal enemies. In public the treaty promised only that neither side would attack the other.

A secret protocol, denied for decades afterward, carved Poland, Finland, Estonia and Latvia into German and Soviet spheres, with Lithuania added to the Soviet side weeks later. Germany invaded Poland from the west on 1 September 1939; the Soviet Union invaded from the east on 17 September, and the two armies met and divided the country between them.

Neanderthals were the first hominins to make Europe a permanent home, present from roughly 243,000 years ago until their disappearance around 40,000 years ago, with a last refuge in Gibraltar perhaps lasting longer still. Their toolkit, known to archaeologists as the Mousterian industry, relied on flaked stone points and scrapers suited to hunting large game.

They kept fire, ate whatever was locally abundant, mostly big game alongside plants and mushrooms, and bore the scars to prove it: their skeletons show frequent fractures from animal attacks and rough terrain. Some groups buried their dead, as at Shanidar Cave in Iraq, though nothing in the graves shows a belief in an afterlife. Their population stayed small throughout, with signs of inbreeding in the surviving remains.

Nero was sixteen when his mother Agrippina, having married the emperor Claudius and arranged for her son to be adopted ahead of Claudius's own son Britannicus, saw Claudius die in October of the year 54. The Praetorian Guard proclaimed Nero emperor that same day, before Claudius's death was even announced to the wider public.

His early years were guided by advisers including the philosopher Seneca, and were later remembered as comparatively restrained. That did not last: Nero had his mother killed in 59, his first wife in 62, and eventually turned on Seneca as well. He died by his own hand in 68 as army commanders turned against him, the last of the Julio-Claudian emperors.

Franklin Roosevelt took office on 4 March 1933 with roughly a quarter of the workforce unemployed and the banking system seizing up under runs. Within days his Emergency Banking Act closed every bank in the country for inspection, reopening only the solvent ones under Treasury oversight, a pause that stopped the panic almost immediately.

Over the following hundred days Congress passed programme after programme: the Civilian Conservation Corps put young men to work planting trees and building trails, the Agricultural Adjustment Administration paid farmers to cut production and raise prices, and the Tennessee Valley Authority began wiring electricity into a region that had gone without it. The pace of that spring gave the whole decade of legislation that followed its name.

Ernst Rohm had built the Sturmabteilung into a paramilitary force several times the size of the German army, and he wanted it absorbed into that army with himself in command. Generals feared him, business leaders distrusted his talk of a second revolution, and Hitler needed both groups on side.

Over 30 June and 1 July 1934, SS squads shot Rohm and dozens of other SA leaders, along with unrelated old enemies such as former chancellor Kurt von Schleicher. The government later admitted to 85 deaths, though historians think the true toll ran into the hundreds; the purge left the SS, not the SA, as the dominant force behind Hitler.

Nixon had built his career on hard anti-communism, which made him an unlikely candidate to fly to Beijing. He arrived on 21 February 1972 for a week of talks with Mao Zedong and Premier Zhou Enlai, ending twenty-three years in which Washington and the People's Republic had had almost no direct contact.

The visit produced the Shanghai Communique on 27 February, a statement in which both sides acknowledged deep differences, particularly over Taiwan, while agreeing to work toward normal relations. Full diplomatic recognition did not follow until 1979; what the trip achieved in 1972 was simply reopening a conversation that had been closed since 1949.

Nixon set out the policy almost offhand, at a press conference on Guam on 25 July 1969 while touring Pacific allies, rather than in a prepared address. The context was Vietnam, where American casualties and domestic opposition were forcing a search for a way to stay committed to allies without keeping hundreds of thousands of troops in the field.

The doctrine held that the United States would keep its treaty commitments and its nuclear shield, but that an ally facing a conventional threat should supply the manpower for its own defence, with America providing money and materiel rather than soldiers. Nixon formalised the reasoning in a November 1969 speech on withdrawing US forces from Vietnam.

Ahmad Nizam Shah's ancestors were Brahmin Kulkarnis from Pathri, a lineage that had converted and entered Bahmani service generations before he governed Bijapur's districts as Malik Ahmad. His break came after he beat back a far larger force under Sheikh Muaddi Arab in a night attack, proof enough of his own strength to act alone.

On 28 May 1490 he declared independence and founded the Ahmadnagar sultanate, ruling first from Junnar before starting a new capital at Ahmednagar in 1494. By 1499 he had taken the fortress of Daulatabad, giving his breakaway state the ground to hold what he had claimed.

Leaders gathered in Belgrade on 1 September 1961 for the first Conference of Heads of State or Government of Non-Aligned Countries, drawing on principles the Bandung Conference had set out six years earlier. Yugoslavia's Josip Broz Tito hosted; Egypt's Nasser, India's Nehru, Ghana's Nkrumah and Indonesia's Sukarno were among the leaders who shaped the founding agenda.

None of the five had any interest in taking orders from Washington or Moscow, and Tito in particular used the movement to keep Yugoslavia's communism independent of Soviet control. The movement never became a formal bloc with binding rules, but it gave dozens of newly independent states a shared platform for arguing against alignment with either Cold War superpower.

China's Eastern Jin dynasty did not fall to an outside invader. In 420 one of its own generals, Liu Yu, deposed the last Jin emperor and founded the Liu Song dynasty in the south, while the Xianbei rulers of Northern Wei finished uniting the north by 439, leaving two rival courts facing each other for close to two centuries.

Despite the border, the two sides intermarried more than the rivalry suggests. Over half of Northern Wei's Xianbei princesses married into the families of Han officials who had defected north, and one Northern Wei emperor later ordered his court to adopt Han dress, language and surnames, blurring the line the split was meant to draw.

The union broke over a small procedural refusal: when King Oscar II would not approve a separate Norwegian consular service, and then would not appoint a new Norwegian government at all, the Storting voted unanimously on 7 June 1905 to declare the union dissolved. No shots were exchanged; a referendum that August confirmed the decision by 368,208 votes to 184, a margin close to unanimous.

Rather than accept a Swedish prince, Norwegians chose Prince Carl of Denmark, who insisted on a further referendum to confirm popular support for keeping a monarchy at all before he would accept the crown. Nearly 79 percent backed a king over a republic. Carl arrived that November and took the regnal name Haakon VII, weeks after Oscar formally renounced his claim to the Norwegian throne.

In theory the veche, an open assembly of the city's free men, held supreme power in Novgorod and elected the posadnik who ran daily government, the military official known as the tysyatsky, and even the archbishop. No prince ruled by inheritance here; several were invited in and expelled again when the assembly judged them unfit.

In practice the boyar and merchant families who dominated the veche's proceedings ran what one historian called an oligarchy wearing a republic's clothes. That same merchant class profited from Novgorod's position as the Hanseatic League's easternmost post, where German traders kept a permanent depot, the Peterhof, to handle furs and wax moving west.

Kush had been trading with Egypt and fighting it for centuries before it went the other way. King Kashta pushed Kushite control north to Thebes around 750 BCE, and his successor Piye finished the job, marching down the Nile against Egypt's fractured local rulers and taking both Upper and Lower Egypt by 727 BCE.

Piye's own account of the campaign survives on a stone stela he had carved at the temple of Amun in Napata. His dynasty, the twenty fifth, ruled Egypt for roughly seventy years and restored temples and monuments before an Assyrian invasion under Esarhaddon drove Kushite rule back south in 671 BCE.

Only five states had tested nuclear weapons when the treaty opened for signature in 1968, and the deal it offered was uneven by design. Recognised nuclear powers kept their arsenals for now; everyone else promised not to acquire any, in exchange for help with peaceful nuclear technology and eventual disarmament talks.

It entered into force on 5 March 1970 and now binds 191 states, more than almost any other arms agreement. India, Pakistan, Israel and, later, North Korea never accepted its terms or withdrew from them, and each went on to build a nuclear arsenal outside the treaty's reach.

Two laws were rushed through in a matter of days and announced at the Nazi party's rally in Nuremberg on 15 September 1935. The Reich Citizenship Law restricted full citizenship to those of German or related blood, leaving Jews as subjects of the state rather than citizens with rights.

The companion Law for the Protection of German Blood and German Honour banned marriage and sexual relations between Jews and non-Jewish Germans, and barred Jewish households from employing German women under 45. A decree that November set out who legally counted as Jewish by counting grandparents, and later amendments extended similar restrictions to Roma people.

Judges delivered verdicts on 1 October 1946 against 22 defendants tried at Nuremberg, of the 24 originally indicted; Martin Bormann was tried and sentenced in his absence, Robert Ley had killed himself before the trial began, and industrialist Gustav Krupp was ruled too ill to stand trial at all. Twelve men, including Hans Frank and Julius Streicher, were sentenced to death; three were acquitted outright.

Hermann Goering, sentenced to hang, swallowed a smuggled cyanide capsule in his cell hours before his scheduled execution on 16 October. The other ten condemned men were hanged that morning, and the tribunal separately ruled the SS, the Gestapo and the Nazi Party leadership corps to have been criminal organisations.

An estimated 1.8 million people packed the National Mall on 20 January 2009, the largest crowd ever recorded for an event in Washington. Partway through the oath, Chief Justice John Roberts and Barack Obama stumbled over each other's words, misplacing a phrase, and the two quietly retook the oath the next evening at the White House with no audience and no Bible present.

His inaugural address avoided grand promises for a country in the middle of a financial crisis, calling instead for what he termed a new era of responsibility. He was also the first president to name nonbelievers alongside the country's religious traditions in an inaugural speech, describing a nation of Christians, Muslims, Jews, Hindus and those with no faith at all.

At noon on 22 April 1889, a cannon or a bugle, accounts differ, sent settlers racing on horse, wagon and foot to stake claims across roughly two million acres that had until then been reserved as Indian Territory. Whoever planted a stake first on a given plot could keep it, which turned the opening minutes into a scramble measured in seconds rather than hours.

The rush gave the language two new words. An 'Eighty-Niner' meant a veteran of that first run, worn as a badge of honour for decades after. A 'Sooner' meant someone who had slipped past the army patrols and hidden out to claim land before the signal sounded, a form of cheating common enough that Oklahoma eventually adopted the nickname for itself anyway.

A hofje is a courtyard ringed with small almshouses and closed off by a single gate, a design the Dutch used to shelter their elderly poor from the seventeenth century onward. Wealthy citizens and guilds funded them privately, so a place inside often depended on more than just age: applicants also had to match the founder's religion and prove they were genuinely poor.

From the 1600s a resident typically needed to be at least fifty, and most hofjes took in women rather than men, since widows without income were the group city authorities worried about most. Several dozen of these courtyards still stand in Amsterdam, Delft, Haarlem and Utrecht, some still used for their original purpose four centuries later.

Around 400 BC, the eastern half of the Olmec heartland began emptying out, and no war or invasion explains it. Researchers point instead to environmental collapse: rivers shifting course, farmland silting up, and possibly volcanic activity that made the region unfit for the large farming population it once supported.

The Olmec had no name for themselves that survives; the word comes from a much later Aztec term for 'rubber people'. Sites such as Tres Zapotes kept parts of Olmec culture alive after the heartland emptied, and later Mesoamerican peoples, the Maya included, inherited the ballgame, bloodletting rituals and early calendar systems some trace to Olmec practice.

Farming villages had worked Mexico's Gulf lowlands since roughly 5000 BCE, and it took thousands of years for that slow start to sharpen into something recognisably Olmec. Traces at El Manati push Olmec presence back to around 1600 to 1500 BCE, well before the culture is usually said to have arrived.

By about 1400 BCE, at the site of San Lorenzo Tenochtitlan, that gradual build up had produced an elite able to command jade, obsidian and magnetite hauled in from hundreds of kilometres away, and organised ceremonial centres that mark the first clearly Olmec settlements in Mesoamerica.

Five nations spread across what is now upstate New York agreed to stop fighting each other and formed a confederacy remembered as the Haudenosaunee, or the League of the longhouse. The Oneida were one of the five founders alongside the Mohawk, Onondaga, Cayuga and Seneca, each keeping its own council while sending representatives to a shared one.

The league's own oral tradition credits a peacemaker figure with persuading the warring nations to bury their weapons under a symbolic tree, an account later oral historians and some scholars place well before European contact. The Oneida held a specific role within that council as one of the two junior nations, a status that shaped how their voice was weighed in shared decisions.

Egypt and Syria attacked Israeli-held territory on 6 October 1973, and when Washington began resupplying Israel with weapons, Saudi Arabia's King Faisal led the Arab members of OPEC in cutting production and cutting off oil sales to the United States and its allies altogether. The embargo, which ran into March 1974, eventually widened to include the Netherlands, Portugal, Rhodesia and South Africa.

Crude that had sold for about three dollars a barrel was fetching close to twelve by 1974, and petrol stations across the United States and Western Europe began rationing supply by licence plate number and day of the week. The shock ended two decades of cheap postwar oil and pushed several importing economies into recession.

Delegates from Iran, Iraq, Kuwait, Saudi Arabia and Venezuela met in Baghdad from 10 to 14 September 1960 and agreed to found the organisation on the final day. The trigger was blunt: multinational oil companies had cut the posted price of crude in 1959 and again that August, without asking the countries the oil came from.

The five founders were answering a market dominated by a handful of Western firms known as the Seven Sisters, who set prices largely on their own terms. OPEC's early role was coordination rather than control; it took over a decade, and several more members joining, before it could move prices by acting together rather than merely comparing notes.

Exit polls on 21 November 2004 gave the opposition candidate Viktor Yushchenko an eleven point lead. The official count, announced hours later, gave the win to Viktor Yanukovych by three points instead, and it was that gap between the two numbers, not the result itself, that sent hundreds of thousands into the streets of Kyiv wearing his campaign's orange.

The protests held for weeks through winter cold until Ukraine's Supreme Court did something unusual for the region: it examined the fraud allegations and ordered a rerun. Yushchenko won the December revote with around 52 percent of the vote and was inaugurated in January 2005, a peaceful reversal decided in a courtroom rather than a street.

American expansionists had been chanting for the whole of the Pacific Northwest up to the line of 54 degrees 40 minutes, coined as the slogan 'Fifty-Four Forty or Fight'. Britain and the United States had jointly occupied the territory since 1818, and neither government wanted the argument to become a second war.

The treaty, signed on 15 June 1846, split the difference at the 49th parallel instead, the line that already marked the border further east. Vancouver Island stayed entirely British even though the parallel cuts through its southern tip, a compromise that left the boundary running cleanly along the mainland.

On 5 June 1883 the train pulling out of Paris was not yet heading to Constantinople at all. Its first journey ran only as far as Vienna by way of Munich, a route chosen because the rail links further east were still incomplete, patched together with a ferry crossing and connecting trains that later editions of the service would smooth over.

The extension to Bucharest and on to Constantinople did not arrive until October of that year, four months after the inaugural run. Once the full route settled, the Paris to Istanbul crossing took roughly two days and twenty hours, a schedule fast enough that European newspapers treated the journey itself as the story rather than the cities at either end.

Secret talks in Norway between Israeli academics and PLO officials produced a framework neither side's government had put on the table publicly. On 13 September 1993 Yitzhak Rabin and Yasser Arafat shook hands on the White House lawn as Shimon Peres and Mahmoud Abbas signed the actual document, with Bill Clinton presiding.

The accord set up the Palestinian Authority to govern parts of Gaza and the West Bank and scheduled a five year transition toward a permanent settlement, deferring the hardest questions, Jerusalem, refugees, borders and settlements, to later talks. Israel recognised the PLO as representing the Palestinian people, and the PLO recognised Israel's right to exist, but the deferred issues remain unresolved.

Osman I did not inherit an empire. He led a small band of Turkic warriors, the Kayi, in a border region of northwestern Anatolia that his father Ertugrul had held before him, and for years his ambitions ran to capturing individual fortress towns from Byzantine garrisons rather than founding a dynasty. His victory at Bapheus in 1302 was the beylik's first major win against Byzantine forces.

Osman never took Bursa, the city that became his son Orhan's capital in 1326, and he was dead by the time it fell. What he left behind was a working state with its own administration and a reputation for alliances that crossed religious lines, foundations solid enough that his descendants built an empire on them that lasted into the twentieth century.

Suleiman took the throne on his father Selim's death in September 1520 and spent his first two years proving he could hold it, taking Belgrade in 1521 and Rhodes in 1522. At Mohacs in 1526 he crushed the Hungarian army and killed its king, splitting Hungary three ways between Ottoman, Habsburg and Transylvanian rule.

The advance stalled outside Vienna in 1529, where an overstretched siege failed and set the border of Ottoman Europe for a century of skirmishing with the Habsburgs. Suleiman ruled for 46 years, longer than any other sultan, over an empire that by his death held roughly 25 million subjects.

A timar was a grant of tax revenue, not of land itself. The sultan kept title to the ground; a cavalryman, a sipahi, received the right to collect its taxes in place of a wage, an arrangement given its Ottoman form under Mehmed I after 1413 and expanded greatly once Constantinople fell in 1453.

The grant carried duties. A sipahi who skipped campaigning for seven years running lost his timar, and holders also policed their district and were expected to protect the peasants working it. Officials resurveyed the empire's land repeatedly to keep the registers of who held what current.

The Alaafin of Oyo was not a free king. He was chosen by a council of seven senior officials, the Oyo Mesi, led by a prime minister called the Bashorun, and he had to descend from a specific royal line and ward to qualify at all. It was a throne with a built-in check rather than an absolute one.

That check had teeth: if the Oyo Mesi judged an Alaafin's rule unacceptable, they could present him with an empty calabash or parrot's eggs, a formal instruction to take his own life. The structure is usually dated later than the empire's early rise, taking clearer shape after a Nupe occupation around 1535 and Oyo's seventeenth century recovery.

Most Yoruba states fought on foot, but Oyo sat in open savannah where horses could be bought from traders to the north, and its rulers built a mounted force other city states simply could not match. Heavy cavalry carried bows for open battle while lighter riders armed with clubs harried retreating enemies, a combination that let Oyo campaign far beyond its own borders.

After recovering its original territory from Nupe occupation, Oyo moved its capital to Oyo Igboho and pushed outward under a string of aggressive rulers, one of whom is credited with conquering nearly all of Yorubaland. Horses bred poorly in the humid south, so Oyo's dominance rested on a supply line for mounts that its rivals could never fully replicate.

The plain at Bagan eventually held more than ten thousand Buddhist temples, stupas and monasteries, over two thousand of which still stand. The building was not the work of one reign but generations of kings competing to leave something durable in brick, each structure a private act of merit as much as public architecture.

The kingdom's political and territorial peak came under Narapatisithu, who ruled from 1174 to 1211 and pushed its borders to their widest extent. Later dynasties studied Bagan's temples as a standard to match, and none, by most accounts, ever quite managed it.

Anawrahta took the throne at Pagan in 1044 and spent three decades turning a small city-state on the Irrawaddy into Burma's first unified kingdom. He abandoned the Ari Buddhism his predecessors had followed and adopted Theravada Buddhism, reportedly after contact with Mon monks from the south.

Later Pagan kings kept building on his foundation until the plain around the capital held over ten thousand temples and stupas, of which more than two thousand still stand. In 1071 Pagan helped restore Theravada practice in Ceylon, reversing the direction of an older religious debt.

The Palas had endowed Nalanda and Vikramashila, the great Buddhist monastic universities, for generations before a Kaivarta vassal named Divya led a rebellion in the eleventh century that stripped the dynasty of control over its own subordinate rulers. Later kings clawed back territory, but the central authority never fully recovered.

In the early twelfth century the Sena dynasty, Hindu rather than Buddhist, took Bengal from the weakened Palas under Vijayasena. Their victory closed the last major line of Buddhist imperial patrons on the subcontinent, a shift in state religion rather than a single conquest, and one felt most in the monasteries that had depended on Pala grants.

Palenque was in the middle of a succession crisis when a twelve year old named K'inich Janaab Pakal took the throne on 27 July 615, following the deaths of the previous ruler and his intended heir. A regent, likely his mother, is thought to have governed on his behalf during his early years as king.

He went on to rule for 68 years, among the longest confirmed reigns of any monarch in recorded history, and used that time to rebuild Palenque's standing through military victories, marriage alliances and a construction programme that greatly enlarged the royal palace. Two of his sons later inherited the throne he had spent nearly seven decades securing.

The Pallavas had ruled part of southeastern India since the 3rd century, but it was Mahendravarman I and his son Narasimhavarman I, reigning across the early and mid 7th century, who turned them into the dominant power over the Telugu country and northern Tamil lands. Narasimhavarman I briefly occupied the rival Chalukya capital at Vatapi in 642.

Their court also shifted temple building from carving into rock faces to raising freestanding stone structures, seen in the monolithic rathas and the Shore Temple at Mamallapuram, now a UNESCO World Heritage Site. The dynasty kept fighting the Chalukyas, Cholas and Pandyas for the next two centuries before the Cholas finally ended their rule.

Palmares grew from the 1605 by people who had escaped slavery in Pernambuco's sugar plantations and built settlements deep in the forested interior, out of easy reach of Portuguese patrols. It survived through farming, raiding and, at times, negotiation, under a line of leaders rather than one founder.

Its best known leader, Zumbi, took over in 1678 after rejecting a peace deal his predecessor Ganga Zumba had struck with the colonial authorities. Portuguese expeditions failed repeatedly through the 1680s before a force finally breached the main settlement in 1694. Zumbi was captured and killed the following year.

Colombia's senate had just rejected a treaty granting the United States canal rights, so Panamanian conspirators led by Jose Agustin Arango, financed by French engineer Philippe Bunau-Varilla, organised a secession instead. When Colombian troops landed at Colon in November 1903 to put the revolt down, railway officials sympathetic to the plotters kept the soldiers from their commanding officers long enough for the revolt to succeed unopposed.

Theodore Roosevelt sent the USS Nashville and recognised the new republic within days, though he avoided endorsing the plot outright. Fifteen days after independence, Bunau-Varilla, acting as Panama's envoy despite being French, signed a canal treaty in Washington that no Panamanian had drafted or reviewed. It gave the United States a perpetual lease over the canal zone.

Roman coins and pottery keep turning up at Korkai, the Pandya port where the Tambraparni river meets the sea. That is how a dynasty ruling from inland Madurai is known to have shipped pearls and silk as far as the Mediterranean, long before any Tamil chronicle mentions the trade in writing.

By the early 600s a Pandya king named Sendan had pushed west into Chera country, spreading the network past the coast toward the Arabian Sea side of the peninsula. Alagankulam grew up as a second port to handle the overflow, and Sri Lanka sat close enough across the strait to be both a trading partner and a rival for the same pearl banks.

King Somesvara of the Hoysalas died in battle against the Pandyas, and with him went one of the last checks on Jatavarman Sundara Pandyan's ambitions. From around 1251 the Pandya armies pushed north into Telugu country as far as Nellore and south through Kerala, undoing generations of Chola supremacy in one reign.

The campaign reached across the strait as well. Pandya forces took northern Sri Lanka and carried off the island's most sacred object, the Tooth Relic said to belong to the Buddha, a raid that mixed plunder with a deliberate blow to Sinhalese royal legitimacy, since possession of the relic was tied to the right to rule.

A Philadelphia railroad went into receivership on 20 February 1893, and the collapse spread outward: gold reserves were draining, farmers were defaulting on loans, and confidence in paper currency was failing. On 5 May the National Cordage Company went bankrupt and the Dow fell 24 percent in a single session. Within months over five hundred banks and 15,000 companies had failed.

The Northern Pacific, Union Pacific and Atchison, Topeka and Santa Fe railroads all went under, taking the jobs of the men who had built and staffed them. Unemployment reached 43 percent in Michigan and 35 percent in New York; nationally, close to one worker in five was out of a job at the worst of it. The slump was declared over within eight months, but a second panic in 1896 kept hardship running into 1897.

The papacy needed rescuing before it could be granted anything. When the Lombards seized the Byzantine-held Exarchate of Ravenna in 751, the Duchy of Rome was cut off from Constantinople with no army of its own to call on, leaving Pope Stephen II to look for protection elsewhere.

He found it in Pepin, the Frankish king whom Stephen's predecessor had already crowned in place of the powerless Merovingian line. Pepin marched into Italy, defeated the Lombards, and in 756 handed the former Ravenna territories to the pope rather than keeping them for himself, a grant that gave the papacy direct rule over central Italian land for the next eleven centuries.

Coins were heavy, and a tea merchant carrying strings of them from the provinces to the Tang capital risked robbery on the road. From around 804, merchants began depositing cash with agents in the capital and carrying home a paper certificate instead, redeemable at a regional office for a small exchange fee.

The government took notice and by 812 had accepted the certificates as valid itself, routing them through its own revenue and salt monopoly offices. The notes never replaced coin outright, but the Song dynasty that followed built true government banknotes on the same method, a change that later brought its own lesson in inflation.

The Paris conference in December 2015 succeeded partly by avoiding the mistake of its predecessor: instead of imposing binding emissions cuts from above, as the failed 2009 Copenhagen summit tried, each country submitted its own voluntary pledge and agreed to report progress and revise targets every five years.

Delegates from 196 parties adopted the text on 12 December 2015, committing to keep warming well below two degrees Celsius above pre-industrial levels, with an aspiration of 1.5 degrees. The agreement entered into force less than a year later, in November 2016, faster than most multilateral treaties manage.

It began with students at Nanterre objecting to crowded dormitories and university discipline, a grievance small enough that nobody expected it to spread. Police closed the campus on 2 May 1968 and moved against demonstrators at the Sorbonne days later, and the sight of officers beating students in the Latin Quarter drew workers into the streets in solidarity.

By mid-May roughly ten million people, about two-thirds of the French workforce, were on strike, and President de Gaulle briefly flew to a French military base in West Germany to confirm the army's loyalty before returning. Negotiators offered wage rises through the Grenelle agreements, de Gaulle called fresh elections, and his party won them decisively as the strikes wound down through June.

Four parties signed in Paris on 27 January 1973: the United States, North Vietnam, South Vietnam and the Provisional Revolutionary Government representing the Viet Cong. The deal set a ceasefire, required American forces out within sixty days, and allowed prisoner exchanges, but it also let North Vietnamese troops already in the South stay where they were.

That last concession undid the rest. Both sides broke the ceasefire almost immediately, and by March 1973 fighting had resumed in full. Washington did not intervene again; North Vietnamese forces expanded their hold over the next two years and took Saigon in April 1975, ending the war the accords had claimed to settle.

Mithridates II pushed Parthia's borders from Syria and the Caucasus to Central Asia and India, absorbing Mesopotamia, Armenia and Bactria along the way. It was the largest the empire would ever be, and it put Parthia within reach of two other great powers at once.

In 96 BC he opened Parthia's first formal contact with Rome, sending an envoy named Orobazus to meet Sulla, a meeting the Romans managed so as to make Parthia look like the weaker party; Orobazus was later executed over it. Around the same years, Chinese envoys reached his court, and within a year the routes later called the Silk Road were carrying goods between the two empires.

Poland-Lithuania had no army capable of stopping what came next. After the Bar Confederation's rebels lost their fight against Russian influence, Russia, Prussia and Austria simply agreed among themselves to take slices of the commonwealth rather than let any one of them seize it all. Poland's own diet was left to ratify losses it had no power to refuse.

Prussia took Royal Prussia and land along the Notec river, Austria took Galicia along with the salt mines at Bochnia and Wieliczka, and Russia took Polish Livonia and part of eastern Lithuania. Between them the three powers took roughly 30 percent of the commonwealth's territory and about half its population, a first cut that two further partitions would finish within twenty-three years.

A man remembered as Merah Silu converted to Islam, took the name Malik al-Salih, and in 1267 founded a sultanate at Pasai on Sumatra's northern coast. The timing followed the collapse of Srivijaya's regional trade dominance, which left an opening for merchants passing through the Strait of Malacca to seek new ports willing to deal with them.

Pasai's gold, pepper and forest products drew traders from across the Indian Ocean, and its rulers built one of the first durable Islamic courts in Southeast Asia; a royal tomb from 1297 carries an inscription entirely in Arabic. When the traveller Ibn Battuta reached Pasai in 1345, he described it as the furthest edge of Dar al-Islam, the Islamic world, with no Muslim-ruled territory beyond it.

A single ruling family controlling territory from Korea to Hungary meant a merchant could, in theory, travel the whole distance under one set of rules and one system of relay stations rather than crossing dozens of hostile borders. Historians call this stretch of relative order the Pax Mongolica, and it lasted from the early 13th century into the mid 14th.

Silk, spices and textiles moved west while silver and manufactured cloth moved east, and with the goods came techniques: printing, papermaking and Chinese banking methods spread along the same roads. Venetian traders like the Polo family used exactly this security to reach the Mongol court in China, a journey that would have been unthinkable a century earlier without the safety the Mongols enforced along it.

Peace is a generous word for it. Augustus's own reign still saw wars on the Rhine and in Spain and the destruction of three legions in Germany's Teutoburg Forest in 9 CE. What the Pax Romana meant in practice was the end of the civil wars that had torn the Mediterranean apart for a century, not an absence of fighting at the empire's edges.

Inside those edges, though, trade moved with unusual freedom: roads, a common currency and a single legal system connected Britain to Egypt without a border crossing between them. Historians generally count the peace as lasting until Marcus Aurelius's reign in the late second century, roughly two hundred years in which no rival claimant tore Rome itself apart.

The settlement of 1555 ran on a single principle, cuius regio, eius religio: whichever faith a prince held became the official religion of his territory, and subjects who could not accept it were free to leave with their property rather than face persecution. It ended years of armed standoff between Charles V and the Lutheran princes without either side conceding the theological argument.

It protected exactly two churches. Article 17 shut out everyone else by name, so Calvinists, Zwinglians and Anabaptists gained no legal standing at all and remained open to punishment. That gap stayed unresolved for almost a century, until the Peace of Westphalia in 1648 finally extended recognition to Calvinism.

Signed in April 1559, the treaty closed six decades of intermittent war between France and Spain over Italy. France gave up its claims to Naples, Sicily and Milan and pulled out of Piedmont, while Spain handed back the northern French fortresses it had taken at Saint-Quentin and elsewhere. France kept Calais, seized from England the year before, and the Three Bishoprics of Toul, Metz and Verdun.

The peace was sealed with two royal marriages, and it was the wedding celebrations that killed a king. Jousting in Paris that July, Henry II took a splintered lance through the eye from Gabriel de Montgomery and died ten days later, leaving France under a fifteen-year-old and heading into decades of religious civil war.

Kennedy signed the order creating the Peace Corps on 1 March 1961, six weeks into his term, and put his brother-in-law Sargent Shriver in charge of building it from nothing. The idea was partly a counter to Cold War suspicion of Americans abroad, and partly a bet that idealism could be organised like an agency.

The first volunteers left for Ghana and Tanganyika that August after Kennedy addressed them from the White House lawn. Within six years the programme had placed over 14,500 volunteers in 55 countries, mostly teaching, farming or building, on two-year postings with a living stipend rather than a wage.

After nine years of near continuous war, Britain and France signed a treaty at Amiens on 25 March 1802 that handed back most of the colonies each side had seized from the other. Britain kept Ceylon and Trinidad but agreed to restore Malta to the Knights Hospitaller as a neutral territory, and France pulled its troops out of the Papal States and Naples.

The peace held barely a year. Britain accused Napoleon of expanding his influence in Switzerland and Italy and of stalling on the Malta withdrawal, and declared war again on 18 May 1803. It was the only stretch of general peace in Europe between 1793 and 1814, and both sides had used it mainly to rearm.

The sticking point was money. France agreed to drop its support for Portugal and gave up its claim to Catalonia, while Spain ceded Roussillon and Artois and handed over a string of Flanders towns including Arras and Gravelines. The border it drew still runs along the crest of the Pyrenees, with one accidental gap: no one specified which side of a ridge Llivia sat on, so it stayed Spanish, an enclave inside French territory.

The peace was sealed by marrying Louis XIV to Maria Theresa, daughter of Philip IV of Spain, who renounced her claim to the Spanish throne in return for a dowry. Spain never paid it. Louis later cited the missing dowry as grounds to invade the Spanish Netherlands, launching the War of Devolution in 1667.

Charles II did not grant Pennsylvania out of admiration for Quakers. He owed sixteen thousand pounds to William Penn's late father, an admiral who had financed naval refits the treasury would not pay for, and handing over a colony in America settled the debt more cheaply than cash.

Penn called the result his holy experiment. The charter of 1681 promised laws to preserve Christian and civil liberty and, in Penn's own dealings, free trade with the indigenous population and liberal property rights. His annual rent to the crown was set at two beaver skins a year.

Daniel Ellsberg had helped compile a classified Pentagon history of the Vietnam War while working for the RAND Corporation, and in March 1971 he passed copies to a New York Times reporter he trusted. The study showed that Truman, Eisenhower, Kennedy and Johnson had each misjudged or misrepresented the war to Congress and the public, including a plan to widen the conflict while Johnson publicly promised restraint.

After three instalments ran in June 1971, the Nixon administration won a court order halting publication, so the Washington Post picked up the story instead. The Supreme Court ruled six to three on 30 June that the government had not met the burden required to justify blocking a newspaper before publication, and the papers kept running.

The assassination of opposition senator Benigno Aquino on the Manila airport tarmac in 1983 had already turned public opinion against Ferdinand Marcos. A snap election on 7 February 1986 gave him the pretext of a mandate, but thirty election commission technicians walked out over what they said was open vote rigging, and Cardinal Jaime Sin called on Filipinos to defend the count.

From 22 to 25 February, more than two million people filled Epifanio de los Santos Avenue in Manila, and soldiers sent to disperse them defected instead of firing. With his own army no longer reliable, Marcos and his family left for exile in Hawaii on 25 February. Corazon Aquino, the assassinated senator's widow, was sworn in as president the same day, after twenty years of Marcos rule.

Pepin held the real power in Francia for years before he held the title. As Mayor of the Palace he ran the kingdom while Childeric III sat on the throne as a figurehead, so in 751 Pepin put a question to Pope Zachary: whether it was right that the man without royal power should be called king. Zachary answered no.

Childeric was shaved of his long Merovingian hair, the dynasty's mark of kingship, and sent to a monastery. Three years later Pope Stephen II travelled to Paris to anoint Pepin in person, the first time a pope had crowned a European ruler. The favour bound the new Carolingian dynasty to Rome from its first year.

A caravan carrying frankincense from southern Arabia had to cross hundreds of kilometres of desert before it reached a market, and Petra sat at the point where nearly every route through that desert converged. Nabataean control of the wells and cisterns along the way meant a caravan effectively paid a toll simply to survive the crossing.

From Petra, roads ran to Gaza on the Mediterranean, to Damascus in the north, and down to the Red Sea port of Leuce Come. The city built cisterns and channelled dams to hold water through the dry months, and that engineering, as much as its position, is what let a desert settlement become rich enough to carve monuments into the surrounding cliffs.

Salerno's medical school drew on Latin, Greek, Arabic and Jewish medicine at once, unusual for a Christian town of its size, and it is credited with the Antidotarium Nicolai, a list of standard drug recipes that circulated across Europe for centuries as a reference for what a remedy should actually contain.

The split from general medicine hardened slowly rather than at a single moment. It was not until 1231 that Emperor Frederick II's Constitutions of Melfi put the school's authority into law, requiring anyone practising as an apothecary to hold a licence and to be of honest character, a rule that treated dispensing medicine as its own trade.

When Charles IV died in 1328 leaving no son, the nearest male relative was his nephew Edward III of England, through Edward's mother Isabella. French assemblies instead invoked Salic law to bar inheritance through a woman, and crowned Philip of Valois, a grandson of Philip III in the male line, on 29 May 1328.

Edward initially accepted the ruling, and the quarrel that followed grew out of Aquitaine rather than the crown itself. In 1337 Philip declared Edward's French duchy forfeit for harbouring his enemy Robert of Artois. Edward answered by reviving his claim to the French throne outright, a challenge to Salic law that opened the Hundred Years' War.

Homer Plessy was seven-eighths white by the census categories of the day, and he boarded a whites-only railway carriage in New Orleans in June 1892 deliberately, as part of a planned legal challenge to Louisiana's segregation law arranged with a civil rights committee. He was arrested within minutes, exactly as the plan required, to produce a test case for the courts.

The Supreme Court ruled against him seven to one in May 1896, holding that separate facilities did not violate equal protection as long as they were nominally equal. Justice John Marshall Harlan alone dissented, writing that the Constitution 'is color-blind, and neither knows nor tolerates classes among citizens.' The ruling stood for nearly sixty years until Brown v. Board of Education dismantled its logic in 1954.

By 1618 the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth covered roughly a million square kilometres and held some twelve million people, making it one of the largest states in Europe at a time when its king could not simply issue an order and expect it obeyed. The nobility elected each monarch and bound him in advance with charters that limited what he was allowed to do once crowned.

The Warsaw Confederation of 1573 had guaranteed a degree of religious freedom unusual for the period, so Catholics, Protestants, Orthodox Christians and Jews lived under the same crown with fewer legal disabilities than elsewhere in Europe. That mix of huge territory, an elected throne and comparative tolerance made the Commonwealth unlike any of its neighbours.

Pompey came home in 60 BC expecting the Senate to ratify the settlements he had negotiated across the eastern provinces and to grant farmland to the soldiers who had fought for him. Senators led by Cato the Younger and Metellus Celer blocked both, unwilling to hand a single general that much lasting influence.

Unable to move the Senate on his own, Pompey struck a private bargain with Julius Caesar and Marcus Crassus, an alliance historians later called the First Triumvirate. It had no legal standing and no name at the time, but Caesar used it to push Pompey's veterans' land bill through and to secure his own command in Gaul.

Pilate's title was prefect, not governor in the later sense: a post that implies his duties were mostly military, backed by judicial and tax authority over a small, restive province. He held it for roughly a decade, one of the two longest tenures of any Roman official in Judea.

His record outside the gospels is a string of clashes with Jewish custom. He hung gilded shields in Herod's old palace and moved military standards bearing the emperor's image into Jerusalem, both provoking crowds large enough to force him to back down. He was eventually recalled to Rome after ordering troops against armed Samaritans near Mount Gerizim.

Indigenous peoples across the Americas had no prior exposure to smallpox, influenza or plague, diseases that arrived with European ships from 1492 onward and spread faster than the newcomers who carried them. In parts of Mexico, epidemic waves through the sixteenth century killed by most estimates between half and four fifths of the population.

A pre-contact population once estimated in the tens of millions collapsed to a fraction of that figure within a few generations. Historians still argue over how much weight to put on disease alone against war, forced labour and the destruction of food systems that followed conquest, and some now describe the combined toll as genocide rather than accident.

Between roughly 1000 and 1340, estimates put Europe's population growing from around forty million to seventy million, without any single event behind it. Milder summers across much of the continent lengthened growing seasons, and farmers pushed into forest and marsh earlier generations had left uncleared.

The heavy plough and the horse collar let one team break tougher, wetter soils than an ox alone could manage, and a shift from two-field to three-field rotation kept two-thirds of a village's land producing crops each year instead of only half. More food meant more surviving children, and more hands to clear still more land.

King Manuel II had been on the throne barely two years, having succeeded his father after gunmen shot King Carlos I and the crown prince dead in a Lisbon square in 1908. Republicans, organised since a congress the year before, rose on 3 October 1910 and fought through the capital for two days while army units switched sides or simply stood aside.

Manuel fled first to Mafra, then met his mother and grandmother at Sintra, and sailed for exile in England as the republic was declared on 5 October. Behind the immediate collapse lay a state that had run through seven governments in two years and never recovered from the 1890 British ultimatum forcing it out of central Africa.

Winston Churchill did not see the conference through. He arrived on 17 July 1945, left mid-talks to await the results of a British election, and returned to learn he had lost. Clement Attlee took his seat at the table for the final week, with Ernest Bevin as his new foreign secretary, while Stalin and Truman remained the whole time.

Truman used the meeting to tell Stalin, obliquely, that the United States had a powerful new weapon. Stalin, who already knew of the atomic bomb through Soviet espionage, showed little reaction and said he hoped it would be used against Japan. The three delegations also fixed Germany's occupation zones and moved its eastern border to the Oder-Neisse line.

In 690 Wu Zetian did not seize the throne from a rival. Her own son, Emperor Ruizong, was made to yield it to her after years in which she had already ruled as regent. She then took the title huangdi in her own name, founding the short lived Zhou dynasty and breaking the Tang line she had married into decades earlier.

Ruizong was not killed or exiled. He was kept inside the palace, absent from court and public life, while his mother governed for fifteen years. In December 705 a palace coup removed her from power a few months before she died, and the Tang dynasty she had interrupted was restored under the son she had once set aside.

The Volstead Act defined any drink over half a percent alcohol as illegal, and it came into force at one minute past midnight on 17 January 1920. Enforcement started immediately: in New York a Brooklyn cafe owner was arrested for selling brandy just four minutes into the new law, and Indianapolis made an arrest within five.

Around 1,520 federal agents were assigned to police the entire country, a force too small to stop the bootlegging and speakeasies that followed within months. The law banned manufacturing and selling alcohol but never made drinking itself a crime, a gap that shaped how the following thirteen years played out.

Alexander the Great died without naming a successor, and his generals spent the next two decades carving his empire into rival kingdoms. Ptolemy, one of his officers, had already secured Egypt as governor by 323 BC. In 305 BC he took the title of king outright, breaking with any pretence of ruling on behalf of Alexander's heirs.

Ptolemy built his capital at Alexandria rather than an old Egyptian centre, and mixed Greek administration with Egyptian religious symbolism, styling himself pharaoh to his Egyptian subjects. The dynasty he founded lasted nearly three centuries, longer than any other Hellenistic kingdom, ending only when Cleopatra VII died in 30 BC and Egypt became a Roman province.

A gunman opened fire inside the club just after 2am on 12 June 2016, then held hostages during a three hour standoff before police breached the building with an armoured vehicle. He was shot dead by officers at 5:17am. Forty nine people were killed and dozens more wounded, most of them young and gay or Latino, on what was Latin Night.

During emergency calls made from inside the club, the gunman pledged allegiance to the Islamic State group and cited recent American airstrikes in Iraq and Syria. Investigators found no operational link to the group beyond that claim. For sixteen months it was the deadliest mass shooting by a single gunman in American history, until the Las Vegas concert attack surpassed it in October 2017.

Twenty-three years of fighting over Sicily ended not on a battlefield but at the negotiating table, once Carthage's fleet had been broken and the island's cities had run out of reasons to keep resisting. The Treaty of Lutatius in 241 BCE forced Carthage out of Sicily entirely, handed Rome all prisoners, and set an indemnity of 3,200 talents of silver, payable over ten years.

Rome was not finished squeezing afterward. A few years later, while Carthage was distracted putting down a mercenary revolt, Rome demanded Sardinia and Corsica as well, along with another 1,200 talents, and Carthage gave way rather than fight a war it could not yet afford. The resentment this left behind fed directly into the far larger war that began in 218 BCE.

Boris Yeltsin resigned on New Year's Eve 1999, handing the presidency to a little-known former KGB officer he had made prime minister only months earlier. Vladimir Putin's rise had been startlingly fast: a deputy mayor of St Petersburg in the mid-1990s, he headed the FSB by 1998 and was prime minister within a year.

As acting president he called an early election for March 2000, giving rivals little time to organise, and won comfortably in the first round. He was inaugurated that May and, through subsequent elections, a term as prime minister and a return to the presidency, has held power in Russia for over two decades since.

The New Model Army had just won the civil war and did not know what to do with the victory. Meeting inside St Mary's church in Putney over two weeks in late 1647, officers and elected soldier representatives argued over who should get a vote once the king was gone, working from a draft called the Agreement of the People.

Thomas Rainsborough put the radical case bluntly: the poorest man in England has a life to live as much as the greatest, and so should have a voice in choosing his government. Henry Ireton answered that only men with a permanent stake in the kingdom, meaning property, had any right to a say. The king's escape on 11 November cut the argument short.

Shang Yang never ruled Qin. He advised its duke as chief minister from 356 BC, and his reforms worked by stripping away privileges the old aristocracy had relied on: noble rank no longer came from birth but from a soldier's tally of enemy heads taken in battle.

The same laws that built Qin's military machine executed Shang Yang. After his patron died in 338 BC, the new ruler had him torn apart by chariots and his family killed. Qin kept his reforms anyway, and the state he had built went on to conquer the rest of China within little more than a century.

Seven warring states had used seven currencies, seven scripts and seven sets of weights, and conquest alone would not make them one country. Qin Shi Huang ordered the Qin state's own seal script simplified and imposed everywhere else, so an official in the old state of Chu could suddenly read an order sent from the old state of Qi.

Coinage was unified around the round bronze Ban Liang piece with its square hole, replacing the knife- and spade-shaped monies particular states had minted. Cart axles were fixed to a standard width so wheel ruts on one road matched wheel ruts on the next, letting grain wagons move between regions without changing wheels. The measures survived the Qin dynasty's own rapid collapse by a wide margin.

King Zheng of Qin spent nine years finishing what generations of Warring States rivals had failed to do. Han fell in 230 BCE, then Zhao, Wei, Chu and Yan in turn, and by 221 BCE the last holdout, Qi, had surrendered. Zheng took a new title, Qin Shi Huang, first emperor, rather than remaining just another king among equals.

Conquest was the easy part; holding the result together was the project that followed. With his minister Li Si, he forced the former rival states onto one script, one currency, the Ban Liang coin, and standard weights and measures, even fixing the width of wagon axles so carts built anywhere could use the same roads. The empire he built lasted barely fifteen years after his death, but the administrative unity outlived it.

Beijing fell twice in two months in 1644. Rebel forces took it in April and the last Ming emperor, Chongzhen, hanged himself rather than be captured. The Manchu regent Dorgon then allied with the Ming general Wu Sangui, who had been guarding the Shanhai Pass and turned against the rebels after they seized his father and his household.

Wu and Dorgon crushed the rebel army at Shanhai Pass in May and marched into Beijing days later. Rather than present themselves as conquerors, the Manchus held a formal funeral for Chongzhen and styled themselves heirs to the fallen Ming, a claim to legitimacy that eased the takeover of a much larger population by a much smaller one.

By 1897 Victoria's arthritis kept her from leaving her carriage even for the thanksgiving service outside St Paul's Cathedral, so the ceremony was held on the cathedral steps while she remained seated in the open landau that had carried her six miles through London crowds. She wrote afterward that no one, she believed, had ever received such an ovation.

Eleven colonial prime ministers rode in the procession, and troops from across the empire marched behind them, from Canada to Cyprus to Borneo. Beacons were lit in a chain across Britain, three English cities received new charters that week, and that year's Epsom Derby was renamed the Jubilee Derby in her honour. The scale was a deliberate display of imperial reach rather than a private family occasion.

Sultan Quli had come to the Deccan from Hamadan in Iran and risen through the service of the Bahmani sultans before that kingdom broke apart into five rival states. In 1518 he declared himself independent at Golconda, taking the title Qutb Shah and turning a provincial command into a throne.

Golconda's later wealth came from diamonds mined nearby and cut and traded in the city, a business so dominant that the name became a byword for a fortune found rather than earned. The dynasty Sultan Quli started held the fort for 171 years, until the Mughal emperor Aurangzeb finally overran it in 1687.

Ragusa, the city now called Dubrovnik, could not stop the plague at its harbour, so in 1377 its council ordered every arriving ship and traveller held for thirty days, usually on a nearby island, before anyone was allowed into the city. Officials called the period a trentine, and it worked well enough that other Adriatic ports copied it.

The word quarantine itself came later. In 1448 the Venetian Senate lengthened the isolation to forty days, a quarantena, and that Venetian term rather than Ragusa's original thirty-day trentine is the one that survived into every modern language.

Rajput identity was not, as colonial era historians once argued, inherited from foreign invaders such as Scythians or Huns absorbed after the Gupta Empire's collapse. Modern scholarship instead traces most Rajput clans to peasant and pastoral communities, a far less romantic origin than the warrior lineage the clans themselves later claimed.

The transformation happened gradually rather than in a single conquest. From the seventh century, local strongmen across northwestern India built fortified settlements and kin based landholdings, and by the twelfth century the term rajaputra had come to mean this whole class of regional rulers rather than a single bloodline.

Honorius moved his court out of Milan in 402, choosing a town ringed by swamp and marsh rather than a city built for grandeur. An attacker could not simply march on Ravenna: the wetlands slowed any approach, and a canal link to the Adriatic kept the port open for supplies and messages even under threat.

The move also kept Ravenna within easier reach of Constantinople by sea, useful as the western and eastern courts leaned on each other for support. The marshes did not save the city forever; over the following centuries Ravenna itself changed hands more than once, but it remained the seat of what was left of Roman power in the west.

Henry Dunant was a Swiss businessman travelling to see Napoleon III on unrelated matters when he arrived at Solferino in northern Italy on 24 June 1859, the day of the battle, and found some 40,000 wounded and dying men with almost no medical care between them. He organised local villagers to tend soldiers of both sides under the motto tutti fratelli, all are brothers, and wrote up the experience in a short book, A Memory of Solferino.

That book reached the Geneva Society for Public Welfare, which on 9 February 1863 approved Dunant's proposal for a permanent relief organisation. A five-member committee held its first meeting on 17 February 1863, the date now treated as the founding of what became the International Committee of the Red Cross.

Pliny the Elder complained in the first century that India, China and Arabia between them drained one hundred million sesterces a year from Rome, and the complaint is the best evidence of how large the traffic had grown. Ships left the Egyptian ports of Myos Hormos and Berenice by the hundred, timed to catch the monsoon winds across to India.

The Kingdom of Aksum, on the African shore opposite, grew wealthy as a middleman in the same network, taking in Roman glass and wine and passing on ivory and incense. A Greek merchant's handbook, the Periplus of the Erythraean Sea, recorded which ports would buy what, port by port, for sailors making the crossing.

Old Sarum sent two members to Parliament from an empty hill; Manchester and Birmingham, with hundreds of thousands of residents between them, sent none. The 1832 Act swept away that arrangement, abolishing 56 of the smallest boroughs outright and cutting representation in thirty more.

It took a bank run to get the bill through the Lords. Reform unions organised mass protests through the 'Days of May' in 1832, and depositors pulled well over a million pounds from the Bank of England in fear of unrest. The Act that followed lifted the English electorate from around 400,000 to 650,000, still a fraction of adult men and no women at all.

Deng Xiaoping had no formal title as head of state or government when he set China on a new economic course at the Third Plenum of the Eleventh Central Committee on 18 December 1978. He used his standing within the party to steer it away from Maoist collectivism without ever holding the top job himself.

Farmers were allowed to sell surplus produce after meeting state quotas under what became known as the household responsibility system, and coastal cities such as Shenzhen were opened as special zones offering tax breaks to foreign investors. Agricultural output rose sharply through the following decade as the changes spread beyond their original testing grounds.

Popes needed money moved across Europe without carts of coin crossing bandit country, and Florentine families worked out how to do it with paper. The Bardi and the Peruzzi built networks of branches from the Middle East to London, using bills of exchange and credit to shift funds for the papacy and for kings, turning what had been a wool and textile fortune into an international finance business.

The two houses grew large enough that a single royal default could ruin them: Edward III of England's failure to repay war loans later helped sink both companies. In the mid 13th century, though, they stood near the height of a business built on trust in a signature rather than a sack of coin, a model other Italian cities soon copied.

On 7 March 1936, German troops crossed into the Rhineland, a strip of their own territory that Versailles and then Locarno had bound Germany to keep free of soldiers and fortifications. France's general staff had the stronger army on paper but told the government that pushing the Germans back out would mean full mobilisation, at a cost officials judged the treasury could not bear.

Britain's cabinet took the same view, one official noting a Commons mood so sympathetic to the German case that few there wanted to risk war over it. Neither government moved beyond a diplomatic protest, and William Shirer later described this moment as the last point at which Western Europe could have stopped Hitler's rearmament cheaply.

Louis XIII made Armand-Jean du Plessis, Cardinal Richelieu, his chief minister on 12 August 1624, after the arrest of the previous holder of the post. Richelieu's first target was not a foreign rival but the French nobility: in 1626 he abolished the office of Constable of France and ordered noble castles razed, removing the fortresses that lords had used to defy the crown for generations.

He turned next on the Huguenots, personally directing the year-long siege of their stronghold La Rochelle, which surrendered in 1628. The Peace of Alais the following year stripped French Protestants of their fortified towns and political privileges, though it left their right to worship intact. Richelieu also bypassed unreliable local nobles by governing through crown-appointed intendants, a system that outlasted him.

Once Constantine had defeated his last rival in 324 and ruled alone, he chose to build his new capital not at Rome but at Byzantium, an old Greek trading town commanding the strait between Europe and Asia. He rebuilt it on a scale to match Rome itself and had it declared New Rome, though it soon took his own name instead.

The choice put the imperial court closer to the frontiers that mattered most, the Danube and the Persian border, and further from a western Senate whose influence Constantine had little interest in indulging. Constantinople stayed an imperial capital for over a thousand years, long enough that later writers gave the eastern Roman state that outlived Rome itself a separate name, Byzantine, taken from the city's old Greek one.

The South Sea Bubble had just wrecked half the cabinet when Robert Walpole took over the Treasury on 3 April 1721. He had used his political skill to shield two senior lords from ruin during the scandal's inquiry, a favour that earned him the nickname the Screen and the debts of gratitude that put him in office.

Walpole held the Treasury, the Exchequer and leadership of the Commons together for twenty one years, longer than anyone since. He never accepted the title of prime minister, which had no formal existence yet, but the way he combined those offices around the crown's shrinking power became the model later holders of the job followed.

Rome's census sorted citizens by wealth, not birth, which is what made it more than a headcount. Property was reckoned in asses, a bronze currency unit, and a man's class ran from the richest tier at 100,000 asses down to a fifth class at 11,000, below which he owed no regular military service at all.

The scheme is credited to King Servius Tullius, traditionally reigning from 578 to 534 BC, though modern historians doubt any single king built it in one reign. What it settled was concrete: how much armour a soldier had to buy himself, how much tax he owed, and how much weight his vote carried in the assembly.

Octavian did not call himself king or emperor. After beating Mark Antony at Actium in 31 BCE and taking Egypt, he handed his extraordinary powers back to the Senate in 27 BCE, in a staged gesture the Senate answered by handing most of them straight back, along with a new name: Augustus, the revered one.

He kept the tribune's powers, control of the army and most of the provinces, while consuls and the Senate carried on meeting as if the Republic still ran itself. That fiction, government dressed as restoration, is what historians call the principate, and it is the arrangement that later emperors inherited rather than a single dramatic coronation.

The story Romans told themselves is a rape and a suicide. Sextus Tarquinius, son of the king Tarquin the Proud, assaulted a noblewoman named Lucretia, who killed herself after naming her attacker. Her kinsman Lucius Junius Brutus is said to have raised Rome against the monarchy in response, expelling the king in 509 BCE.

Most modern historians treat that account as legend layered over a much less dramatic event, probably an aristocratic power shift within Tarquin's own family, or the end of an Etruscan occupation of the city. What followed is better attested: royal power passed to two consuls elected annually, each able to veto the other, a structure meant to prevent any one man from ruling as king again.

The uprising began not in the capital but in Timisoara, where on 16 December 1989 members of the city's Hungarian minority protested the eviction of a dissident Reformed pastor. Security forces fired on the crowds, and unlike the peaceful transitions already underway elsewhere in the region that autumn, the unrest in Romania spread as an armed confrontation between the army, secret police and civilians.

Nicolae and Elena Ceausescu fled Bucharest by helicopter on 22 December as the revolt reached the capital, but were caught within hours. A military tribunal tried them on 25 December on charges including genocide, and paratroopers executed the couple by firing squad the same day. They were the last people ever put to death in Romania before capital punishment was abolished.

Delegates from more than 150 countries spent five weeks in Rome arguing over how much power any new court should have over sovereign states before adopting the statute on 17 July 1998 by a vote of 120 in favour, seven against and 21 abstaining. No official record named which countries opposed it, though the United States, China and Israel were among the states that raised objections during the talks.

The statute needed sixty ratifications to take effect, a threshold ten countries crossed together at a single United Nations ceremony on 11 April 2002. The International Criminal Court opened in The Hague that July with jurisdiction over genocide, war crimes and crimes against humanity, though several major powers, including the United States, have never joined it.

Jean-Jacques Rousseau published his treatise in 1762, opening with the claim that force alone creates no right and that obedience is owed only to legitimate power. Rather than a ruler holding authority handed down from subjects, Rousseau argued that the people remain sovereign, governing through what he called the general will.

The book was banned within weeks in both Geneva and Paris, and an arrest warrant sent Rousseau fleeing to Switzerland. Its idea that government rests on consent, not inheritance or conquest, later fed directly into the language of the French Revolution and the American founding, distinguishing his theory from the older accounts of Hobbes and Locke.

Twelve men left a lecture at Gresham College on 28 November 1660 and decided to formalise what they had been doing informally for years: meeting to watch each other's experiments. Christopher Wren, Robert Boyle and John Wilkins were among them, and they named their new body a college for promoting experimental learning.

They chose as their motto Nullius in verba, take nobody's word for it, a rebuke to argument from ancient authority. Charles II granted a royal charter in 1662, and in 1665 the society began publishing Philosophical Transactions, the first journal devoted purely to science, which introduced the practice of having other scientists check a paper before it appeared.

Changamire Dombo built his power on cattle and conquest rather than inheritance. Leading a breakaway Rozvi group, he pushed into the Kingdom of Butua on the southern Zimbabwean plateau and conquered it around 1683, carving out territory that the older Mutapa and Torwa states could not hold onto.

Portuguese traders who had pushed inland chasing gold found Dombo's forces unwilling to tolerate their forts and expelled them from the plateau's interior in the 1690s. The state he founded, the Rozvi Empire, went on to control the region's most productive gold-bearing land for roughly a century after Great Zimbabwe's older centres had long fallen quiet.

Abd al-Rahman ibn Rustam was a Persian convert who followed Ibadi teaching, a branch of Islam that rejected hereditary claims to leadership in favour of an elected imam. Followers who had fled persecution elsewhere in North Africa gathered around him, and in 777 they built him a walled capital at Tahert, in what is now Algeria.

Tahert grew into a trading centre with its own fortress, gardens and reliable water supply, drawing merchants of other faiths as well as Ibadi settlers. Rustamid traders carried goods and books south across the Sahara for well over a century, until the Fatimids conquered the city in 909 and scattered its community toward Ouargla and the Mzab valley.

Rwanda's kingdom began as one hill among many. Oral tradition places its origins on Gasabo, where a small chiefdom took shape sometime between the fourteenth and sixteenth centuries and only gradually absorbed neighbouring chiefdoms around Lake Muhazi rather than conquering a region in one campaign.

Historians still disagree on who deserves credit for the first true kingship, with some naming Ruganzu Bwimba and others Ruganzu II Ndoli generations later. What is clearer is the pace: the territory that became central Rwanda was not fully absorbed into the expanding kingdom until the sixteenth century, long after Gasabo's first chiefs.

Ismail was fourteen when Turkoman fighters called the Qizilbash carried him to power in 1501, having rallied around him as the spiritual heir to a Sufi order his family had led for generations. Within the year he took Tabriz and had himself crowned shah of a Persia that had not been ruled as a single state for centuries.

He then reversed the region's religion by decree. Iran and Azerbaijan had been largely Sunni, and Ismail made conversion to Twelver Shia Islam compulsory, exiling or executing scholars who resisted while importing Shia clergy from further afield and rewarding them with land. The realignment held, and Shia Islam has remained Iran's state religion ever since.

The Safavids had held the fortress city of Kandahar since 1554, and it sat on the route into India that both empires needed to control, so envoys shuttled between the Mughal and Safavid courts far more often than open war broke out. Akbar eventually pried the city loose by diplomacy rather than force, gaining it in 1595 after decades of this uneasy back and forth.

The peace never held for long. When Akbar died, the Safavid shah Abbas sent an army to besiege Kandahar, and only reinforcements from the new emperor Jahangir forced a retreat. Control of the city kept changing hands between the two courts for another half century, each side treating the other as a rival to be managed rather than an enemy to be destroyed.

The last of the sakoku edicts fell on the Portuguese, who had traded with Japan for nearly a century. The order was blunt: the whole community, along with their mothers, nurses and dependants, was to be banished to Macao. It followed the Shimabara rebellion of 1637 to 1638, which the shogunate blamed partly on Catholic missionaries and used as justification for cutting off Catholic Europe entirely.

One door was left open. Dutch merchants, who had shown no interest in proselytising, were confined to Dejima, an artificial islet in Nagasaki harbour connected to the city by a single guarded bridge. For over two centuries it was Japan's only officially sanctioned channel to the West, until Commodore Matthew Perry's ships forced the country open again in 1853.

Between February 1692 and May 1693, more than two hundred people in Massachusetts were accused of witchcraft. Nineteen, fourteen women and five men, were hanged. Giles Corey refused to enter a plea at all and was pressed to death under stones for his silence.

The unravelling began with doubt, not remorse. Clergy started questioning whether a victim's claim to see an accuser's spectre was proof of anything, and when accusations reached respected citizens, Governor William Phips halted the court. The following year courts stopped accepting spectral evidence, convictions collapsed, and Massachusetts formally annulled them in 1711.
