Philip VI made the gabelle a permanent royal tax in March 1341, turning salt, something every household needed to preserve food, into a state monopoly sold at fixed prices from royal granaries. Rates varied wildly by province: centuries later a measure of salt cost a few sous in Brittany and twenty times as much in Berry, and smugglers who moved salt between the two could be sentenced to the galleys.

The inequity, not the tax itself, was what generations of peasants resented most, since exempt regions and privileged classes paid nothing while others bore the full weight of it. The National Assembly abolished the gabelle in 1790, only for Napoleon to reinstate a version of it in 1806; France did not remove it from law entirely until 1945.

Salt from Saharan mines such as Taghaza moved south by camel caravan while gold moved north to meet it, an exchange so lopsided in local scarcity that at Timbuktu the two were, by some accounts, traded close to weight for weight, salt for gold.

Sijilmasa on the Sahara's northern edge, and Timbuktu and Gao further south, anchored the route. Carrying costs alone could run to a large share of the salt's original price by the time it reached buyers, who paid a further markup, while the gold, in bars, blanks and dust, travelled on north to be minted into coin.

Talks that began in Helsinki in November 1969 dragged on for two and a half years before Richard Nixon and Leonid Brezhnev signed anything in Moscow. What they produced on 26 May 1972 was less a disarmament deal than a freeze: existing numbers of strategic missile launchers were locked in place rather than reduced.

A linked Anti-Ballistic Missile Treaty, signed the same day, limited each side to two missile defence sites, later cut to one. SALT I did not touch bomber fleets or the accuracy of warheads, and both sides kept building within its limits, but it was the first agreement in which Washington and Moscow accepted outside constraints on their nuclear arsenals at all.

Jimmy Carter and Leonid Brezhnev signed SALT II in Vienna's Hofburg Palace on 18 June 1979, extending the limits their predecessors had agreed on missile launchers into a fuller cap on delivery vehicles and warheads. It was meant to buy time for a more ambitious follow-up treaty.

That follow-up never came. The Soviet invasion of Afghanistan that December, and the discovery of a Soviet brigade in Cuba, killed any chance of Senate ratification, and Carter withdrew the treaty from consideration in January 1980. Neither side ever ratified it, yet both largely kept to its limits until it lapsed at the end of 1985.

War against the Xiongnu had emptied the treasury of the Han court, and Emperor Wu's finance minister, Sang Hongyang, proposed a fix: the state itself would produce and sell salt and iron, goods everyone needed and nobody could do without. Private ironmasters and salt boilers were shut out of a trade that had made some of them wealthier than provincial officials.

The state ran the mines and boiling pans directly, or licensed favoured operators, and pocketed the margin instead of taxing it after the fact. Officials also bought and sold ordinary goods to smooth price swings and add further revenue. Confucian critics later argued the policy squeezed peasants through inflated prices, but later dynasties kept reviving the same monopoly whenever war emptied their own treasuries.

Before the federal Civil Marriage Act, same-sex marriage was already legal in most of Canada by court order: provincial and territorial rulings had extended it province by province from 2003 onward, so the 2005 law mainly made uniform a right most Canadians already held.

The Act passed on 20 July 2005, making Canada the fourth country to recognise same-sex marriage nationwide, after the Netherlands, Belgium and Spain, and the first outside Europe. Members of Parliament were allowed a free vote rather than one bound by party line.

Samoan governance never centred on a single monarchy in the European sense. Authority instead rested with matai, chiefly titleholders chosen by their extended family to represent it, hold its land and speak for it in village councils, a system known as fa'amatai that still structures Samoan life today.

This structure grew out of centuries of settlement across the archipelago, with village and district councils negotiating status and precedence between competing chiefly lines. Titles could be combined or contested, and the resulting hierarchy of matai gave Samoan society a form of complex, distributed political organisation without a fixed capital or single ruling house.

The killing of newspaper editor Pedro Joaquin Chamorro Cardenal in January 1978 did more to end the Somoza dynasty than decades of guerrilla war had managed alone. Riots followed, then a general strike that closed roughly four in five businesses in Managua, and Washington cut off aid over human rights abuses. A coalition of students, farmers, priests and a small number of Marxists found itself, briefly, on the same side.

Anastasio Somoza Debayle resigned on 17 July 1979 and flew to Miami; Sandinista fighters entered Managua two days later. The Frente Sandinista de Liberacion Nacional, which had fought as a guerrilla movement since 1961, formed a five member Junta of National Reconstruction and began redistributing land and running literacy campaigns under a declared state of emergency.

Adam Lanza, 20, shot his mother dead at their home on the morning of 14 December 2012 before driving to Sandy Hook Elementary School in Newtown, Connecticut, armed with her rifle. He forced his way past a locked entrance and killed twenty children, all aged six or seven, along with six staff members, before shooting himself as police arrived.

Connecticut's legislature responded within months, passing a law in April 2013 that expanded background checks, banned high-capacity magazines and created the country's first registry for people convicted of dangerous weapons offences. A parallel federal effort to expand background checks failed in the Senate that same month by a handful of votes.

Ardashir began as a minor ruler in Pars, in Persia's southwest, and spent years demanding submission from neighbouring princes before the Parthian king Artabanus IV moved to stop him. The two met in battle at Hormozgan, where Artabanus was killed, removing the one man positioned to check Ardashir's ambitions.

Ardashir pressed on into the former Parthian west and was crowned at Ctesiphon in 224 as king of kings, a title his dynasty would hold for over four centuries. He and his successors framed the new order as a restoration of older Persian kingship rather than a break from it, reviving court rituals and religious authority that the Parthians had let slacken.

Five countries, Belgium, France, West Germany, Luxembourg and the Netherlands, had signed an agreement on a boat moored near the Luxembourg village of Schengen back in 1985, but it took a decade of technical work on shared visa rules and police cooperation before anyone actually removed a border post. The agreement finally came into force on 26 March 1995 among seven states.

Land border checks between the participating countries ended that day, letting drivers cross what had been international frontiers without stopping. The zone has since grown to cover most of the European Union plus Iceland, Norway, Liechtenstein and Switzerland, making it one of the largest areas of unrestricted travel in the world.

John Scopes had not necessarily even taught the lesson he was charged over. The American Civil Liberties Union wanted a test case against Tennessee's new Butler Act, which banned teaching human evolution in public schools, and Scopes, a substitute science teacher in Dayton, agreed to be indicted so the law could be challenged in court.

The July 1925 trial drew Clarence Darrow for the defence and three time presidential candidate William Jennings Bryan for the prosecution, and reporters by the hundred. Scopes was found guilty and fined 100 dollars, a verdict thrown out on appeal because Tennessee law reserved fines over 50 dollars for a jury, not a judge, to set.

Eight earls and thirty one barons put their seals to a letter addressed to Pope John XXII on 6 April 1320, asking him to recognise Scotland's independence and to press England toward peace. Robert the Bruce, excommunicated for killing a rival at the altar in Dumfries, needed the papacy's blessing as much as his kingdom needed England's recognition.

The letter's boldest line claimed that if Bruce himself ever submitted to England, the Scots would depose him and choose another king to defend their freedom, an argument that independence belonged to the people rather than the crown. The Pope urged peace but did not concede the point, and Scotland's independence was only formally recognised eight years later, at Edinburgh.

Turnout on 18 September 2014 reached 84.6 percent, the highest recorded in any UK-wide vote since before women could cast a ballot at all. Scots answered a single question, whether Scotland should be an independent country, and the ballot for the first time extended the franchise to sixteen and seventeen year olds.

No won by a wider margin than pre-vote polling had suggested, 55.3 percent to 44.7, out of more than 3.6 million votes cast. Pollsters afterwards traced much of that gap to a late swing among voters weighing what currency an independent Scotland would actually use, since keeping the pound had been the campaign's most disputed unresolved question.

Reagan used a televised address on 23 March 1983 to ask American scientists to make nuclear weapons obsolete, not just outnumbered. The Strategic Defense Initiative proposed lasers, particle beams and space based interceptors that would shoot down incoming missiles before they hit their targets, abandoning decades of doctrine that had relied on the threat of retaliation to keep both sides from firing first.

The nickname arrived within a day. Senator Edward Kennedy mocked the plan in a speech that same evening as a reckless Star Wars scheme, and a Washington Post story picked up the phrase the next morning. Reagan disliked the label, but it stuck to the programme for the rest of its life and coloured how sceptics judged its odds of ever working.

Eight countries signed the Southeast Asia Collective Defense Treaty in Manila on 8 September 1954: Australia, France, New Zealand, Pakistan, the Philippines, Thailand, the United Kingdom and the United States. Only two of the eight, Thailand and the Philippines, were themselves in Southeast Asia. Its headquarters opened in Bangkok the following February.

SEATO never built the joint command NATO had. Pakistan quit in 1973 after losing its eastern half to Bangladesh, France stopped paying its share in 1975, and South Vietnam, which the treaty had been built to protect, fell that same year. The organisation held a last military exercise in February 1976 and dissolved in June 1977.

Louis-Napoleon had been elected president of the Second Republic in 1848, but the constitution barred him from a second term. Rather than step down in 1851, he staged a coup on the night of 1 December, occupying the printing office and key buildings while his troops dissolved the National Assembly.

A plebiscite endorsed the coup by a large margin, and a second vote a year later asked whether the republic should become an empire. An implausible 97 percent said yes, and on 2 December 1852, exactly a year after the coup, Louis-Napoleon was proclaimed Napoleon III, Emperor of the French.

Julius Caesar's assassins had fled Rome, and none of the men left behind, Octavian, Mark Antony and Lepidus, could beat them alone. On 27 November 43 BC a tribune passed the lex Titia, giving the three men joint power to issue binding edicts and override provincial governors for five years, with no right of appeal against them.

They used that power first against their own enemies at home. Proscription lists went up naming roughly three hundred senators and equestrians, whose property was confiscated and whose killers could claim a reward; Cicero, once an ally of Octavian, was among those hunted down. The triumvirs then turned east to fight Caesar's assassins at Philippi, and the alliance itself lasted only as long as its members needed each other.

Pope John XXIII called the council to bring the Church up to date, a project he termed aggiornamento, and opened it in Rome on 11 October 1962 before more than two thousand bishops. He died the following June, and Pope Paul VI carried the sessions through to their close in December 1965, three years after they began.

The council produced sixteen documents that reshaped Catholic practice: Mass could now be said in local languages rather than only Latin, bishops gained a collegial share of authority alongside the pope, and the Church committed itself to dialogue with other Christian churches and non-Christian faiths. Recognition of religious liberty as a matter of human dignity was among its most debated conclusions.

Seleucus had been a lesser figure among Alexander's officers, given the unglamorous cavalry command rather than a province when the empire was first divided. By 305 BC, after years of shifting alliances among the Diadochi, he controlled a vast stretch of territory running from Anatolia through Mesopotamia to the Indus, and took the royal title alongside his rivals.

He never controlled the whole of it securely. In 305 BC he traded his easternmost claims, including territory in India, to the Mauryan ruler Chandragupta in exchange for war elephants he later used against Antigonus. The empire he founded remained the largest of the Hellenistic successor states, ruled from new Greek-style cities such as Antioch and Seleucia rather than from Babylon.

The Seljuk Empire began not as one man's creation but a family enterprise. Two brothers, Tughril and Chaghri, led their Turkic followers out of Central Asia into Khorasan in 1037, with their uncle Musa Yabghu reportedly sharing command in an arrangement closer to a triumvirate than a single throne.

Their authority firmed up gradually rather than at a single founding moment. In 1040 they broke the Ghaznavid sultan Mas'ud I at Dandanaqan, and by 1046 the Abbasid caliph al-Qa'im had formally recognised Tughril's rule over Khorasan. Baghdad itself fell to the Seljuks in 1055, by which point their lands stretched from Persia toward Anatolia.

The Seljuk chief Tughril did not have to fight his way into Baghdad in 1055; the Abbasid caliph al-Qa'im invited him, wanting help removing the Buyid dynasty that had controlled the caliphate from behind the throne for a century. Tughril arrested the last Buyid ruler, and after brief clashes with the population his troops looted parts of the city before he ordered order restored.

The caliph asked him to release the deposed Buyid ruler and his companions; Tughril freed some prisoners but refused to let that one go, showing where authority now actually sat. He took the title King of the East and the West, and the Abbasid caliph kept his religious standing while Tughril's family held the real power behind it, a pattern that lasted for generations.

About six hundred people set out from Selma on 7 March 1965 to walk the fifty miles to Montgomery over the denial of Black voting rights. State troopers and mounted possemen met them at the Edmund Pettus Bridge and beat them back with clubs and tear gas; seventeen marchers needed hospital treatment, and organiser Amelia Boynton was photographed unconscious on the roadway.

Televised footage of that day, remembered as Bloody Sunday, pushed President Johnson to address Congress within the week, where he set Selma alongside Lexington and Appomattox. A third, protected march finally reached Montgomery on 25 March, and the Voting Rights Act became law that August, banning the literacy tests and other devices used to keep Black voters off the rolls.

Ottoman troops had garrisoned the Belgrade fortress since 1826, the last physical sign of the sultan's authority over Serbia, until an 1867 order withdrew them. Full independence still needed a war: Serbia fought the Ottomans twice between 1876 and 1878, the first conflicts of its modern history.

Those wars settled little on their own, and it took the great powers meeting in Berlin to make the outcome permanent. On 13 July 1878 the Treaty of Berlin recognised Serbia as fully independent, though it also handed neighbouring territory to Austria-Hungary rather than to Serbia itself.

Serfdom did not begin with a law. A free peasant hit by war, a bad harvest or debt could place his hands in a lord's and accept protection in exchange for labour, a private bargain known as bondage. Over time these individual deals hardened into an inherited status few could escape.

A bound serf owed his lord fixed days working the lord's own fields, plus taxes paid in produce rather than coin. He could not leave the land without permission, and his children were born into the same obligation, whatever their own choices might have been.

Michael Servetus argued that the Trinity was a Greek philosophical addition with no basis in scripture and called infant baptism a device of the devil. He had said as much to John Calvin years earlier by post, and Calvin had already written to a friend that if Servetus ever came to Geneva, he would not leave it alive.

Servetus arrived anyway in 1553 and was arrested. Calvin pressed the council toward a death sentence, asking only that Servetus be beheaded rather than burned; the council, led by Ami Perrin, chose burning instead, and Servetus died at the stake on 27 October 1553, still refusing to recant.

Ohio senator John Sherman wrote the bill that carries his name, and Congress passed it almost without dissent: 52 to 1 in the Senate, unanimous in the House. President Benjamin Harrison signed it on 2 July 1890, giving the federal government its first statute against monopolies and the cartels then known as trusts.

For its first years the law mostly disappointed the people who had pushed for it. Courts moved slowly, and in 1894 the Supreme Court ruled a sugar-refining monopoly outside its reach entirely, reading the statute narrowly. It took until 1904 and the breakup of Northern Securities Company for a case to show the act could actually dissolve a trust, fourteen years after it was signed.

Only one family stood between Tokugawa Ieyasu and an uncontested dynasty: the Toyotomi, led by Hideyori under his mother Yodo-dono's influence. Ieyasu had already taken the title of shogun by 1603, but as long as Osaka Castle sheltered a rival with a claim to the old Toyotomi legacy, that title rested on force rather than settled succession.

The castle fell in 1615 after a second siege that year. Hideyori and Yodo-dono died in the final assault, and Ieyasu's men later executed their son. With the last serious challenger gone, the Tokugawa shogunate went unchallenged by any comparable rival for roughly two and a half centuries.

Bantu-speaking farmers had lived on the Zimbabwe plateau since roughly 150 BC, but it was their Shona-speaking descendants who began raising dry stone walls there in the eleventh century, without mortar, fitted stone on stone. The building went on for three hundred years, growing from modest enclosures into a city.

By the time it was a royal capital, the Great Enclosure's walls stood eleven metres high, and the settlement held perhaps ten to eighteen thousand people. Its wealth came from controlling gold moving toward the Swahili coast, along with cattle, salt and copper, and its stoneworkers also turned gold into beads and ornaments for their own rulers.

Outside a church in Palermo on Easter Monday, 1282, a French sergeant assaulted a young Sicilian woman and her husband stabbed him dead. As the bells rang for vespers, the crowd turned on the French garrison around them, and by nightfall thousands of French men and women in the city were dead, reportedly picked out by demanding suspects say the word ciciri, a sound French speakers could not manage.

The killing spread across the island within weeks, ending Charles of Anjou's rule there almost overnight. The rebels then invited Peter III of Aragon, married to a Hohenstaufen heir, to take the crown, turning a single riot into a war between Aragon and the Angevins that dragged on for two decades.

Constantinople had sat astride the overland trade routes between Europe and Asia for over a thousand years before Ottoman forces took the city in 1453. What followed was not a closed border but a change of landlord: the Ottomans began competing for control of those routes against other powers, and tariffs and tolls made the old land passage more expensive to European merchants.

Rather than pay that new cost, European traders started looking for a sea route around it entirely. Portuguese and Spanish expeditions pushed down the African coast and out across the Atlantic in the following decades, a search for an alternative that helped open what became known as the Age of Discovery.

Zhang Qian set out around 138 BCE to find allies against the Xiongnu and was captured by them instead, spending roughly thirteen years among his captors before he finally reached the lands he had been sent to. He came home having found no ally, but with detailed reports of kingdoms in Central Asia that China had never known existed.

Emperor Wu sent embassies west on the strength of those reports, some several hundred strong, carrying Chinese silk out and bringing horses and unfamiliar goods back. Zhang Qian's journey did not create trade between China and the Mediterranean by itself, but it is the point at which the routes stopped being rumour and started being mapped.

By 1100 the network stretched over four thousand miles, and no single merchant travelled its length. Goods passed hand to hand through relay trade: silk and porcelain moving west, glass from Egypt and pistachios from Persia moving east, each leg handled by traders who rarely saw the route's far end.

Religion moved with the caravans as readily as cargo. Buddhism, Christianity and Judaism all spread along these roads and mixed with local belief as they went, picking up new forms in each oasis town they passed through. The same corridors that carried brocade and dye would later carry plague westward, a cost nobody who traded here could have foreseen.

Zhang Qian was not sent to open a trade route. In 138 BC Emperor Wu dispatched him west to find military allies against the Xiongnu, the nomadic power blocking Han China from the lands beyond it. The Xiongnu caught him almost immediately and held him for thirteen years, during which he married and had children among his captors.

He escaped, reached Central Asia, and found the alliance he sought was no longer wanted, the people he had been sent to court having settled into peace. What he brought home instead, in 125 BC, was detailed knowledge of wealthy kingdoms to the west. Later missions to those kingdoms turned that intelligence into the caravan routes historians later named for silk.

The overland routes later called the Silk Road were never one road but a shifting mesh of caravan tracks across Central Asia, kept moving for centuries by Sogdian merchants whose language became the common tongue of trade between China and lands to its west.

Along these routes silk, tea and porcelain travelled west out of China, while horses, camels, glassware, wine and gold moved east, exchanged hand to hand through a chain of oasis cities rather than carried start to finish by any single trader. Song China's wealth by the turn of the millennium kept demand for the exchange high on every side of it.

Silla's bone rank system, likely codified into law under King Beopheung in 520, sorted the aristocracy by how closely related they were to the royal line. Only those of sacred bone status could take the throne; those of true bone rank could reach ministerial office but no higher.

Rank governed more than politics: the colour of a person's clothing and the size of their house and carriage were fixed by birth. Marriage was strictly controlled too, since a child needed both parents of true bone status to inherit that rank, a rule that pushed the aristocracy toward marrying within itself.

A single objection was enough. The Hwabaek, Silla's council of high-ranking nobles, settled matters like royal succession and war only by unanimous agreement, so one dissenting noble could stop a proposal that every other member supported.

Kings had once sat in on these deliberations directly, but from 531 leadership passed to an official called the Sangdaedeung while monarchs stepped back from the room. The council's power was not merely ceremonial: it once deposed a reigning king, Jinji, whom its members judged unfit to rule, though royal authority later reasserted itself and pushed the Hwabaek toward the margins.

Silla could not beat Baekje and Goguryeo on its own, so Queen Seondeok sent an envoy to the Tang court asking for troops. The strategy that followed, credited to King Muyeol, was to break the enemy alliance apart first: take Baekje in 660, then turn combined Silla and Tang forces on a weakened Goguryeo.

Goguryeo held out until its powerful minister Yeon Gaesomun died in 666 and the kingdom split into rival factions. Tang and Silla armies exploited the collapse, besieging and taking Pyongyang on 22 October 668. The Three Kingdoms period was over, though Silla would spend the following years fighting to push Tang forces back out of the peninsula it had just helped conquer.

Singapore had joined the Federation of Malaysia only in 1963, and the merger did not settle much. Trade disputes, disagreements over race-based policy and communal riots in 1964 left the two governments barely on speaking terms within two years of union.

Secret talks between Kuala Lumpur and Singapore produced a separation agreement, and on 9 August 1965 the Malaysian Parliament voted 126 to 0 to let Singapore go. Lee Kuan Yew, who had campaigned for merger, became prime minister of a country he had not sought, with no natural resources and a population he once doubted could survive alone.

More than a thousand economists signed a joint letter begging Herbert Hoover to veto the bill before he signed it on 17 June 1930. Henry Ford reportedly called it economic stupidity in person, and the head of J.P. Morgan later said he had nearly gone down on his knees to plead with Hoover against it.

Named for Senator Reed Smoot and Representative Willis Hawley, the act raised duties on thousands of imported goods. Canada, France, Italy and half a dozen other trading partners answered with tariffs of their own; American exports to the countries that retaliated fell by roughly a third, and world trade as a whole collapsed by around two thirds over the next four years.

Edward Snowden spent months exchanging encrypted messages with a documentary filmmaker and a journalist before flying to Hong Kong in May 2013 to hand over the files in person. The first story ran in The Guardian on 5 June, describing a program called PRISM that gave the National Security Agency direct access to user data held by Microsoft, Google, Facebook, Apple and several other major companies.

Once his identity became public days later, Snowden fled toward Latin America but got no further than Moscow, where a cancelled passport left him stranded at the airport for weeks before Russia granted him asylum. He remains there today, having become a Russian citizen in 2022, while the journalists who reported his leaks shared a Pulitzer Prize.

Roosevelt signed the Social Security Act on 14 August 1935, creating a federal pension funded by a payroll tax on current workers rather than by savings each person had set aside. Alongside old-age benefits it set up state-run unemployment insurance and aid for families headed by a single mother, the first time the federal government had underwritten either.

The original law left large groups out: farm labourers, domestic servants and most government employees were not covered, a gap that fell hardest on Black workers in the rural South, where a majority of them worked in excluded jobs. Congress extended coverage to most of these groups only in later decades.

Rome's Italian allies supplied soldiers for its wars without receiving Roman citizenship or a vote in Roman assemblies. In 91 BC, after the reformer Marcus Livius Drusus was assassinated and his proposals to extend citizenship collapsed with him, several allied peoples, including the Marsi and Samnites, rose in revolt rather than wait any longer.

The fighting was costly enough that Rome, mid war, began offering citizenship to communities willing to lay down arms, hoping to split the rebellion rather than defeat it outright. It worked: citizenship was extended across Italy over the following years, though a bitter argument over which of Rome's voting tribes the new citizens would join outlasted the war itself and fed directly into the political violence of the following decade.

Socrates was convicted by a jury of 501 Athenians, and the vote was close: 280 for guilty, 221 for acquittal. The charges were impiety and corrupting the young; among his former students had been Alcibiades and Critias, men many Athenians blamed for the city's recent slide into war and oligarchy.

Offered a chance to propose his own lesser sentence, Socrates reportedly suggested the city award him free meals for life, which only angered the jury further. He drank the hemlock himself at about seventy, and Plato later wrote that the poison crept upward from his legs while his mind stayed clear to the end.

The dozens of small states later grouped as Busoga never shared one ruler. Each chiefdom governed its own patch of hills and swamp around Lake Kyoga, in what is now eastern Uganda, built up by Bantu-speaking settlers who crossed the Nile and mixed with Nilotic peoples already living there.

A single Busoga kingdom is a later idea. Britain installed the first paramount ruler, the Kyabazinga, in 1906, welding the separate chiefdoms together for colonial convenience, and a formal coronation followed only in 1939. Before that, Busoga's political history ran county by county, not crown by crown.

A watchtower in Gansu preserved a letter, dated to 313, from a Sogdian trader warning colleagues that the route east had gone bad. It is one of the earliest direct records of a merchant network that by the 6th century ran the full 1,500 miles from Sogdiana to China, rather than handing goods off between oasis towns.

Their language became the trade tongue of Central Asia and the court language of the Turkic Khaganate that protected their caravans. Along with silk and metalwork, Sogdian traders carried Zoroastrianism, Manichaeism and Buddhism eastward, and Nestorian Christianity followed the same roads into China.

Other Central Asian traders were sometimes simply called by the Sogdians' name, a measure of how thoroughly Sogdian colonies had come to run Silk Road commerce by 600. Their settlements stretched from their Central Asian homeland to garrison towns deep inside China, each one staffed by merchants who spoke the local language alongside their own.

That fluency, not just goods, was the real export. Sogdian became the working language of trade and diplomacy across the region, used at the Turkic khagan's court as readily as in market towns, letting Sogdian intermediaries broker deals between Chinese, Turkic and Persian parties who otherwise shared no common tongue.

By the 6th century Samarkand sat behind four rows of walls and four gates, an organised city rather than a caravan stop, positioned exactly where routes from China, Persia and the lands beyond met. That position, more than any single ruler, made it the Sogdian civilisation's principal centre.

Around 550 the Western Turkic Khaganate took the region from the Hephthalites and struck marriage alliances with Samarkand's rulers, giving merchants there the political cover to keep trading through a change of overlords. Sogdian traders based in the city carried goods, and their own language, along the routes their city commanded.

The strike began over the firing of a crane operator, Anna Walentynowicz, at the Lenin Shipyard in Gdansk. By the end of August 1980 the government had agreed to let the workers organise outside party control, and on 17 September delegates from across Poland registered Solidarity as a single national union, with Lech Walesa as its chairman.

Membership reached nearly ten million within a year, roughly a third of Poland's working population. Martial law shut the union down in December 1981 and jailed its leaders, but it survived underground until round table talks with the government in 1989 led to elections that ended communist rule in Poland.

The Horn of Africa's Red Sea coast had been a Muslim trading region for centuries before Adal took shape as a state, its ports linking the Ethiopian highlands to Arabia and India. Camel caravans and coastal dhows exchanged gold, ivory and enslaved people for glass, cotton and Chinese porcelain, wealth that later gave Adal's rulers the means to build an army.

That trade also fed a long rivalry with the Christian kingdom of Abyssinia, which controlled the highland interior Adal's merchants depended on for goods to sell. The conflict was fought over caravan routes and tribute as much as religion, and it eventually drew in Ottoman and Portuguese muskets on opposing sides.

The traveller Ibn Battuta reached Mogadishu around 1331 and called it an exceedingly large city, ruled by a sultan, Abu Bakr ibn Shaikh Umar, who spoke Somali at home and Arabic in business. Its merchants were rich enough to impress a man who had already crossed half the Islamic world.

Ships arrived from Aden and from Cambay in India carrying spices and cloth, and left loaded with gold, ivory and beeswax. The city wove its own export cloth, toob benadir, cut for buyers as far off as Egypt and Syria, a sign of how tightly Mogadishu's economy was bound to markets it never saw.

Zeila had no river and little farmland of its own. What it had was a harbour on the route between the Red Sea and the Gulf of Aden, and that was enough to make it a capital: by the twelfth century it anchored trade between Ethiopia's interior and the Islamic world, later the seat of the Ifat and then Adal sultanates.

Caravans brought gold, ivory, incense and enslaved people down from the Ethiopian highlands to be shipped out through its harbour, while cloth and other imports travelled back inland. Zeila's fortunes declined only when Adal's capital moved inland and, centuries later, French built Djibouti took over its shipping.

The world's first paper money began as a private workaround in Chengdu, where merchants tired of hauling heavy strings of coin issued paper receipts instead. Sixteen of the city's largest merchant houses eventually pooled their notes into one standardised system, charging a small exchange fee for the convenience.

The government took the idea over in 1023 and printed its own standard notes the following year, complete with anti-counterfeiting seals and a fixed lifespan of two or three years before a note had to be redeemed or reissued. It worked well enough to outlast the dynasty's caution, and by the twelfth century over-printing had driven the currency into the inflation the original merchants had never faced.

Zhao Kuangyin did not seize power through open rebellion but through a staged mutiny. His own soldiers, the story goes, draped a yellow robe over him at Chenqiao in 960 and refused to march further under anyone else, forcing the boy emperor of the Later Zhou to abdicate in his favour. He took the name Taizu and spent sixteen years subduing the remaining kingdoms to reunify China.

The dynasty he founded is remembered less for its army than for what it printed, financed and built. Song China issued the world's first paper banknotes, developed movable type printing, fitted ships with a compass for true north, and fielded gunpowder weapons including fire lances, all inside a state that also recruited its officials through competitive written examinations.

Sichuan's coinage was the problem. The province used heavy iron cash, so much of it that any sizeable transaction meant hauling strings of metal by the sackload, and Chengdu merchants began issuing paper receipts, jiaozi, redeemable for coin so the coin itself never had to travel between hands.

Private jiaozi houses kept failing, and in 1023 the Song government created an office to take over issuance itself. The first standardised government notes, with fixed denominations and a set exchange fee, appeared the following year, the earliest paper currency printed by a state rather than a merchant.

Wang Anshi's civil service overhaul split the imperial academy into three colleges: outer, inner and superior. A student who tested into the top grade of both internal examinations could be appointed directly to office, bypassing the palace examination other candidates still had to sit.

Anshi's chancellorship ran from 1069 to 1076, and the system he built specialised students in a single Confucian classic alongside arithmetic or medicine, rather than the broad classical education examinations had rewarded before. Critics said the narrower path mainly helped officials' own sons, who could afford the tutoring it required.

Askia Muhammad had taken the Songhai throne by force, overthrowing Sonni Ali's son, and he governed nothing like his predecessor. Sonni Ali had ruled through conquest and local custom; Askia replaced it with centrally appointed governors answerable to Gao rather than hereditary chiefs left to their own devices.

He built out ministries for finance, justice, protocol and even waters and forests, staffed largely by relatives, made sharia the basis of law and Islam the religion of the ruling class, and set standard weights, policed trade routes and organised taxation. A conquest state became, under him, something closer to a bureaucracy.

A special convention met in Columbia on 17 December 1860, then moved to Charleston to finish its work. On 20 December delegates voted 169 to nothing to dissolve the state's union with the rest of the United States, the first such vote by any state.

Four days later the convention issued a declaration explaining itself, and it did not equivocate: it named the election of a president hostile to slavery and northern refusal to return escaped slaves as its grievances. Six more states left within weeks, and by February a rival confederacy had formed around them.

The South Sea Company existed to manage government debt, not to trade much, but its directors spread extravagant rumours of riches from Spanish American markets it barely touched. Shares that traded at £128 in January 1720 hit £1,000 by August, bought on credit the company itself was lending out.

The scheme could not survive selling pressure, and by autumn the price had fallen back below £150, wiping out thousands of investors. A parliamentary inquiry found fraud reaching into the cabinet: the chancellor of the exchequer went to prison, two ministers died in disgrace, and Robert Walpole oversaw the confiscation of most of the company directors' wealth to repay victims.

Mikhail Gorbachev had called the occupation a bleeding wound as early as 1986, and by mid-1987 announced the army would leave entirely. The Geneva Accords, signed by Afghanistan, Pakistan, the United States and the Soviet Union in April 1988, set the terms and timetable for a pullout that had taken years of quiet argument inside the Kremlin to agree.

Soviet troops began leaving under that timetable and the last column crossed the Amu Darya into the Uzbek SSR on 15 February 1989, ending a war that had drained the Soviet military, economy and political standing for nine years. The communist government left behind in Kabul fought on alone until 1992, when Moscow's financial support stopped following the Soviet Union's own collapse.

Francisco Franco died on 20 November 1975 after ruling Spain for thirty six years, and two days later Juan Carlos was sworn in as king under the very laws Franco had designed to keep the dictatorship intact after him. Instead the new king backed reform, appointing Adolfo Suarez as prime minister in 1976 to dismantle the system from within.

Suarez legalised the previously outlawed Communist Party in April 1977, a step his own cabinet warned could provoke the army, and held Spain's first free elections that June. A new constitution followed in a December 1978 referendum, and the transition survived its sternest test in 1981 when the king publicly opposed an attempted military coup.

A royal charter granted in 1602 gave the VOC powers no ordinary trading company held: it could raise its own armies, build forts and sign treaties with Asian rulers in the name of the Dutch republic. On Ambon, Dutch forces allied with local Muslim groups to push out the Portuguese and secured the sole right to buy cloves from Hitu.

Where diplomacy failed, the company used force. Its governor Jan Pieterszoon Coen had much of the Banda Islands' population killed or deported in the 1620s and replanted the islands with nutmeg groves worked by enslaved labour, driving prices paid to remaining growers down to whatever the company chose to set.

Cloves and nutmeg grown only in the Maluku Islands travelled thousands of kilometres before reaching a European kitchen. Ships carried them first to Indian ports such as Kozhikode, then on through Sri Lanka toward the Arabian Sea, a chain nobody at either end controlled in full.

Arab sailors, many descended from Yemeni and Omani traders, dominated this Indian Ocean network by 1400, moving cargo onward through Hormuz and Jeddah toward the Near East. Jewish merchant networks carried goods the final stretch into Europe, so a jar of cloves on a Venetian table had usually passed through the hands of four or five separate trading peoples.

Earlier traders had crept along the coast from the Red Sea to India, trading through middlemen at ports like Aden and taking months to do it. Once Roman sailors worked out how to ride the summer monsoon straight across the open Arabian Sea and the winter monsoon back, a return voyage to India's Malabar coast became a single season's trip instead of a hazard-strewn crawl.

The geographer Strabo reported that around 120 ships a year sailed for India from the Egyptian port of Myos Hormos under Augustus, against a handful under the Ptolemies before Rome took Egypt. Pepper, cinnamon and other spices flowed west in such volume that pepper warehouses were later built in Rome itself, while Roman gold coin flowed east in exchange, turning up in hoards across southern India.

Srivijaya did not fall in a single conquest. Chola fleets from southern India raided its ports after 1025, and the maritime state that had once taxed shipping through the Malacca Strait shrank for generations afterward, its authority passing piecemeal to the Melayu kingdom based at Jambi.

By the time Chinese records stopped naming a Sumatran power called Sanfoqi, the region's trade had already reorganised around newer courts. Majapahit rose in Java and Malacca on the strait itself, both later claiming the old routes Srivijaya had once controlled from a capital whose exact site is still debated by archaeologists.

The oldest evidence for Srivijaya is not a chronicle but a stone. The Kedukan Bukit inscription, dated 16 June 682 and found near Palembang on Sumatra, records a ruler assembling an army and fleet. A Chinese monk named Yijing had already described visiting the kingdom a decade earlier, in 671.

Srivijaya held the Strait of Malacca less through conquest of land than through control of the sea lanes running through it. Its fleet regulated which ships passed and where they had to put in, turning a stretch of water into a toll route between India and China and building a trading economy on the fees.

Parliament passed the Stamp Act on 22 March 1765, requiring that colonial newspapers, legal documents, playing cards and even dice carry an embossed revenue stamp bought with British coin rather than colonial paper money. It took effect that November, the first direct tax Britain had levied on the American colonies rather than a duty on trade.

Colonial assemblies petitioned against it, and delegates from nine colonies met as the Stamp Act Congress that October. Mobs intimidated the appointed stamp distributors into resigning, so the tax was never effectively collected anywhere. Parliament repealed it on 18 March 1766, but the argument it provoked, that taxation required representation, did not go away with it.

John D. Rockefeller incorporated Standard Oil in Ohio in 1870 with a million dollars of capital, alongside his brother William, chemist Samuel Andrews and four other partners. What set the firm apart at first was not size but thrift: while rival refiners dumped the heavy waste from kerosene production, Rockefeller found buyers for it.

A railroad deal in 1868 had already given his earlier company a shipping rate far below what competitors paid, and he used the margin to undercut them on price and then buy them out. By 1904 Standard controlled roughly nine tenths of American oil refining.

Talks over cutting long-range nuclear arsenals had dragged on for nearly a decade, stalled repeatedly by disputes over verification and which weapons to count. George H. W. Bush and Mikhail Gorbachev finally signed the Strategic Arms Reduction Treaty in Moscow on 31 July 1991, the first agreement to cut rather than merely cap the two superpowers' strategic arsenals.

The treaty capped each side at 6,000 deployed warheads and 1,600 intercontinental missiles and bombers combined. The Soviet Union collapsed five months later, and ratification had to be renegotiated among Russia, Ukraine, Belarus and Kazakhstan before the reductions it set out were actually carried through.

Before 1710, printing rights in England belonged to the Stationers' Company, a guild that had held a near-permanent monopoly on what could legally be published since the previous century. The Statute of Anne broke that hold by putting copyright into law for the first time and, crucially, giving it to authors rather than the printers who set their type.

The term was modest by later standards: fourteen years from publication, with a second fourteen-year renewal if the author was still alive when it expired. Works already in print got twenty-one years. Once the clock ran out, the text became free for anyone to print, a deliberate limit that later copyright law kept extending but never dropped.

Before 1931, an act passed at Westminster could bind Canada, Australia or the other dominions whether or not their own parliaments agreed to it. The Statute of Westminster ended that: it barred any future UK law from applying to a dominion unless that dominion had asked for it, turning a legal hierarchy into a group of equals bound only by shared allegiance to the Crown.

Canada, the Irish Free State and South Africa took the statute's effect immediately in 1931; Australia, New Zealand and Newfoundland delayed formal adoption for years afterward. It followed directly from the Balfour Declaration of 1926, in which Britain and the dominions had already agreed, in principle, that none stood subordinate to another.

Before there was a building for it, there was already a market. When the VOC issued shares in 1602, Amsterdam merchants began reselling them informally out of the company's own headquarters, since the charter let holders transfer stock to a third party rather than lock it away until the venture paid a dividend.

That informal resale grew formal enough to need a dedicated home, and in 1611 Amsterdam opened a purpose-built exchange designed by Hendrik de Keyser. Official bookkeepers recorded each transfer in a capital ledger, giving buyers confidence that a share was really theirs and turning VOC stock into something that could be traded almost like cash.

Sudan had been ruled since 1899 as an Anglo-Egyptian condominium, nominally shared between Cairo and London but administered in practice much like a British colony. That arrangement began to unravel after Egypt's 1952 revolution, whose leaders, including the half-Sudanese Muhammad Naguib, pressed for British withdrawal from both Egypt and Sudan.

Sudan became fully independent on 1 January 1956, ending both British and Egyptian authority at once rather than transferring power from one to the other. A parliamentary government took office in Khartoum, though the new state inherited a divide between the Arab-majority north and the south that would erupt into civil war within months.

Sukhothai did not begin as a nation but as one local ruler's grab for a single city. In 1238, Bang Klang Hao took Sukhothai from its Khmer-aligned governor with help from his brother in law, and afterward adopted the regnal name Si Inthrathit and founded the Phra Ruang dynasty.

Later generations, especially under the king Ram Khamhaeng at the end of the century, credited Sukhothai with giving the region a Thai script and establishing Theravada Buddhism as state religion, which is why it is remembered as the first Thai kingdom. Modern historians treat that title cautiously, noting the city rose out of a mixed Mon and Khmer landscape rather than a purely Thai one.

Islamic religious law, the sharia, stood outside any sultan's power to alter, but a separate body of secular decree called kanun was entirely his to shape. Suleiman gathered up the scattered rulings of the nine Ottoman sultans before him, stripped out contradictions and duplication, and issued a single unified code covering land tenure, taxation on trade and produce, and criminal punishment.

That criminal section notably cut back the number of offences carrying death or mutilation as a penalty. Ottoman subjects came to call him Kanuni, the Lawgiver, for the work, and the code he assembled stayed in force for more than three hundred years after his death.

Sulla had been given command against Mithridates in the east, then had it stripped from him by a political manoeuvre in Rome favouring his rival Marius. Rather than accept it, in 88 BC he marched his legions on Rome itself, the first Roman general to lead an army against the city. He won that round, left for his eastern campaign, and returned in 83 BC to fight a second civil war against Marius's allies.

Sulla had himself made dictator in 82 BC, not as a temporary emergency office in the old sense but with no fixed term, and published proscription lists naming enemies who could be killed for a reward. He resigned the dictatorship after roughly two years and retired from politics, but the precedent he set, that a general's personal army could decide who ruled Rome, outlived him.

Sharif ul-Hashim came from Johore as a religious scholar rather than a conqueror, settling at Buansa in the Sulu archipelago and becoming its first sultan. Sources differ on whether this happened in 1405 or decades later in 1457, but either way he brought Sunni Islam to a region that had previously followed Hindu-influenced local beliefs.

The archipelago was already a trading crossroads, pulling in merchants from southern China and across Southeast Asia from the fourteenth century onward. Sulu began as a vassal of the powerful Bruneian Empire and only became fully independent in 1578, after which it grew into a maritime power stretching toward Mindanao and northeastern Borneo.

Monsoon winds made the Swahili coast a hinge between Africa and Asia: ships rode them south in one season and north in the other, and the estuaries at Kilwa and Mombasa gave them somewhere sheltered to load. By the thirteenth century Kilwa had taken over the gold trade routed north from Zimbabwe through Banadir, and taxed every shipment that passed through its harbour.

What came back on those same ships was silk and porcelain from China, cotton from India, black pepper from Sri Lanka, exchanged for the coast's own ivory, timber and gold. The wealth built coral stone mosques and merchant houses still standing at Kilwa, evidence of a trading network that reached the whole rim of the Indian Ocean.

Stone towns along the East African coast, from Mogadishu to Kilwa, grew wealthy as middlemen between the African interior and the Indian Ocean. Ivory, along with timber, animal skins and gold, was carried down to the coast and loaded onto dhows bound for Arabia, India and China, where it was worked into combs, inlays and ornaments unobtainable from any other source.

In return, Swahili merchants brought back silk and porcelain from China, cotton and spices from India, and pepper from Sri Lanka, goods that moved on into the African interior along the same routes ivory had travelled outward. The exchange left behind Chinese porcelain shards that archaeologists still dig out of ruined coastal towns today.

Kilwa sat on an island off the East African coast, a modest position that became commanding once its rulers took the mainland port of Sofala around 1170. Gold and ivory carried up from the interior kingdoms around Great Zimbabwe passed through Sofala, and Kilwa taxed and resold it to merchants from Arabia, Persia and India who called at its harbour.

By around 1300 the city was minting its own coinage, examples of which have since been found as far away as northern Australia, alongside cloth, spices and incense moving through its markets. The wealth this trade generated paid for coral stone mosques and palaces that later travellers, arriving within a few decades, judged among the finest they had seen on the whole coast.

Mombasa's oldest surviving stone mosque, the Mnara, dates to around 1300, physical evidence of a town that had by then converted decisively to Islam and built in coral stone rather than timber. Ivory, gold and spices moved through its harbour on the way to markets as far as India and China, carried on dhows that timed their crossings to the monsoon.

Mombasa's fortunes at this stage were tied to Kilwa rather than opposed to it: the island city to the south drew Mombasa into its sphere from the early fourteenth century, and Mombasa did not become fully independent until Kilwa's own sultanate began to unravel around 1502. Its harbour, though, was the asset that outlasted every shift in who controlled it.

The document dated 1291 says nothing about crossbows or apples. It is a defensive pact among three valley communities, Uri, Schwyz and Unterwalden, promising mutual help and a peaceful way to settle disputes among themselves, mainly to keep their mountain trade routes free of outside interference. The famous oath on the Rutli meadow, tied to the William Tell story, is a later tradition, dated by a sixteenth century chronicler to 1307.

The three Forest communities fought off a Habsburg army in 1315 and pledged, from then on, not to make outside alliances without each other's consent. Other valleys and cities joined over the following centuries, and the loose alliance that grew from this original charter became modern Switzerland, which still marks 1291 as its founding date.

Mark Sykes and Francois Georges-Picot spent the winter of 1915 into 1916 drawing a line across a map of Ottoman territory neither man had much reason to think he owned yet. Britain took the southern strip running toward the Gulf and a claim on Mediterranean ports; France took the north, covering Syria, Lebanon and what is now southeastern Turkey; Palestine was set aside for international control.

None of this squared with promises Britain had separately made to Arab leaders about postwar independence. The arrangement stayed secret until the new Bolshevik government, hostile to the old tsarist alliances, published the text in Moscow in November 1917; the Manchester Guardian reprinted it days later, and Arab trust in British assurances never fully recovered.

Pachacuti did not simply conquer, he redrew the map. He split his growing realm into four suyus radiating from Cusco: Chinchaysuyu to the northwest, Antisuyu into the Amazon fringe, Kuntisuyu southwest and Qullasuyu southeast, each under a governor answerable to the Sapa Inca at the centre.

Below the governors, local kurakas kept running conquered communities much as before, while the sons of defeated rulers were brought to Cusco to be schooled in Inca custom before being sent home to govern. The empire spread its own administrators thin and let existing chiefs do the daily work of ruling.

The ancestors of the Taino began the journey centuries earlier, out of the Amazon basin and up the Orinoco into what is now Venezuela, then island by island through the Lesser Antilles toward Cuba and the Bahamas. Genetic evidence traces pottery-making farmers moving into the Caribbean along that route roughly two and a half thousand years before they reached Hispaniola.

Once settled, Taino communities grew cassava on raised mounds of earth called conucos, a technique that drained the soil and kept it fertile between plantings, alongside maize, beans and sweet potato. Society was organised under a cacique, with nobles, priests and commoners beneath, and leadership passed down through the mother's line.

Afghanistan's capital had already endured four years of factional shelling among former anti-Soviet militias when Taliban fighters entered Kabul on 27 September 1996. Former president Mohammad Najibullah had been sheltering inside the UN compound since his government fell in 1992; the Taliban dragged him out, tortured him and killed him the same night, then hung his body from a traffic post.

The new authorities announced the Islamic Emirate of Afghanistan and imposed a strict reading of sharia within days: women were barred from most work and schooling, television and music were banned, and men were required to grow beards. The takeover ended the civil war among the mujahideen factions but replaced it with a new and isolated government.

Li Yuan did not plan a dynasty so much as survive one collapsing around him. As a Sui official and cousin of the reigning emperor, he watched Sui rule disintegrate into revolt, and in 618, after Emperor Yang was murdered by his own officers, Li Yuan declared himself emperor rather than wait to be swept away with the regime he had served.

His rebellion had an unusual figure at its edge: his daughter, Princess Pingyang, who raised and personally commanded her own troops during the fighting. Once established, the dynasty's second ruler, Li Shimin, pushed Tang territory past the old Han borders and drew up a legal code that Chinese dynasties kept copying for centuries.

Wood does not usually survive two thousand years, but teak from an ancient Egyptian port on the Red Sea has, identified by archaeologists among cargo linked to the Indian Ocean trade. Its resistance to rot and fungus made it valuable long before any European buyer arrived to bid for it.

That same durability made teak the timber shipwrights wanted most once European trading companies began building and repairing fleets in Asian ports. Forests in Burma and Siam supplied hulls that could survive tropical shipworm far longer than European oak, so builders sought it out for vessels meant to spend years at sea.

Tejen sits on a river that never reaches the sea; it dies out in the Karakum desert after watering a strip of farmland barely wide enough to keep a town fed. That strip was still worth crossing for merchants moving between Persia and the oasis cities of Central Asia, and Tejen took its place among the stops that made the desert passable at all.

Its larger neighbour Merv, a few days' travel north, drew most of the caravans and nearly all of the chronicles, leaving Tejen's own medieval history thin by comparison. What survives is mostly geography: a river oasis positioned exactly where thirsty travellers needed one, on a road with few alternatives.

On the morning of 20 June 1789, deputies of France's Third Estate arrived at their usual hall to find the doors locked and guarded on the king's order. Fearing they were about to be dispersed by force, they followed a suggestion from Joseph-Ignace Guillotin and moved to a nearby indoor tennis court at Versailles instead.

There, led by the astronomer Jean Sylvain Bailly, 576 of the 577 deputies present swore not to separate until France had a written constitution. Only Joseph Martin-Dauch refused, saying he would obey no decision but the king's. The oath turned a locked-out assembly into a body claiming to speak for the nation.

The Soviet Union, the United Kingdom and the United States signed the treaty in Moscow on 5 August 1963, less than a year after the Cuban Missile Crisis had shown how close the two superpowers could come to disaster. It took effect that October and well over a hundred further countries eventually joined it.

Negotiators had originally hoped for a complete ban but gave up on covering underground tests, since verifying them without intrusive inspections proved technically hard and politically unwelcome to Moscow. What the treaty did stop was atmospheric, underwater and space detonations, ending the practice of venting fallout directly into the air that people breathed.

A two-thirds Senate majority for annexation could not be found, so President Tyler took a shortcut: a joint resolution needing only a simple majority in each house. Congress passed it in March 1845, and Texans ratified it that autumn, ending nine years as an independent republic that Mexico had never recognised.

Mexico had warned that annexation meant war, and it did. The Mexican minister broke relations before the ink was dry, and fighting began the following spring over the disputed border with Mexico. In Washington the deeper argument was slavery: adding one more slave state threatened the careful balance Congress had held in the Senate for a generation.

By 1834 around 30,000 Anglo-American settlers in Texas outnumbered Mexican-born residents there by roughly four to one, and Santa Anna's decision to scrap Mexico's 1824 constitution and rule by central decree cost Texas the local autonomy that had made the imbalance tolerable. Fighting broke out at Gonzales in October 1835 over a single cannon the Mexican army wanted back.

The Alamo fell on 6 March 1836 after a thirteen day siege, with almost every defender killed, William Travis and Davy Crockett among them. Six weeks later Sam Houston's army caught Santa Anna's force by surprise at San Jacinto, routed it in under twenty minutes, and captured the general himself, who bought his life by ordering Mexican troops out of Texas.

A winter of strikes across public services, remembered as the Winter of Discontent, had left the Labour government of James Callaghan looking unable to govern. Thatcher, who had led the Conservative Party since beating Edward Heath for it in 1975, won the general election of 4 May 1979 and took office that day as the first woman to hold the post in Britain.

She arrived promising to curb the power of trade unions, sell off state-owned industries and pull the state back from managing the economy directly, a break from the postwar consensus both parties had largely shared. Unemployment and industrial disputes marked her early years in office before the policies associated with her name became shorthand for the decade, a term applied to her governments rather than one she coined herself.

Theodoric took Italy from a man he had been sent to remove. Emperor Zeno ordered him against Odoacer, the general who had deposed Rome's last western emperor, and after years of campaigning the two agreed in February 493 to rule Italy jointly.

The peace lasted ten days. At a banquet marking Theodoric's entry into Ravenna, he raised a toast, then drew his sword and cut Odoacer down himself. He went on to settle around forty thousand Ostrogoths across Italy and rule it for over three decades, keeping Roman administration largely intact under Gothic kings.

Nobody had organised Roman law in over a century when Theodosius II ordered the job done in 429. Imperial rulings since Constantine's reign, more than 2,500 of them scattered across a hundred years of edicts, letters and rescripts, were gathered, sorted by subject and stripped of anything obsolete or contradictory.

The finished code was published in February 438 and took effect across both halves of the empire, east and west, on the first day of the following January, with Valentinian III agreeing to enforce it in Ravenna as well as Constantinople. It gave later compilers, including Justinian a century afterward, a model to build on rather than start from scratch.

On 11 December 220, the last Han emperor, Xian, abdicated to Cao Pi, who had inherited his father Cao Cao's grip on the north and now took the throne himself. Xian had reigned for three decades as a figurehead while warlords fought over the empire behind him; he was allowed to live out his life with a noble title rather than executed.

Within a year two rivals answered by declaring their own emperors: Liu Bei in the southwest and, later, Sun Quan in the Yangtze south. The three courts, Wei, Shu and Wu, fought and allied in shifting combinations for six decades until Jin absorbed the last of them in 280. Storytellers turned the period into China's most retold cycle of war and betrayal long before any of it was called history.

Caravans crossing Central Asia had a choice north of the Taklamakan Desert: skirt the desert's edge through oasis towns, or run along the northern foot of the Tian Shan mountains through Turpan and on toward what is now southeastern Kazakhstan.

The mountains themselves produced almost nothing merchants wanted; their value was as a wall that forced traffic into a predictable band of passes and springs. Towns such as Kashgar grew rich simply by sitting where routes around the range converged.

Roman law had long capped how much public land any one citizen could hold, a limit the wealthy had simply ignored for generations. As tribune in 133 BC, Tiberius Gracchus revived the cap and proposed redistributing the surplus to landless citizens, bypassing the Senate by taking the bill straight to the popular assembly.

Seeking re-election to push the law through, Tiberius was confronted at a crowded voting site by a mob led by his own cousin, Scipio Nasica. He and many supporters were beaten to death with clubs and stones, and their bodies were thrown into the Tiber rather than buried. His land commission survived him and distributed over a million iugera of land, but the killing showed that Roman political disputes could now be settled with violence.

Timbuktu began as a place Tuareg herders left their belongings while they grazed animals elsewhere, becoming a permanent settlement only in the early twelfth century. Its location, a few miles from the Niger and at the desert's edge, made it a natural exchange point between river traffic and camel caravans.

The city's real growth came later, after Mansa Musa passed through on his way to Mecca around 1325 and brought scholars back with him. By 1300 it already held some ten thousand people; by the 1500s, under Mali and then Songhai rule, that had grown fivefold, and gold, salt and books had made it as much a university town as a market.

Before settling on a name, Briton Hadden and Henry Luce nearly called their new venture Facts, to signal how brief it would be. The first issue reached newsstands on 3 March 1923 under the title they chose instead, with the slogan Take Time, It's Brief printed under the masthead.

Its formula was not more news but less: a week's events condensed into short, brisk items organised by section, written in a clipped, opinionated house voice. Covers put a single face on the front rather than a headline event, a choice that made the magazine's founders, still in their twenties, the template for a century of American newsweeklies.

Timur's empire nearly did not survive him. When he died in February 1405, his chosen heir Pir Muhammad held the throne barely two years before a grandson, Khalil Sultan, seized Samarkand and ruled in his place, and it took Timur's son Shah Rukh several more years of fighting to impose order on the fragments.

Shah Rukh then governed for some thirty-five years, and under him the dynasty turned from conquest toward patronage. Persian poets, miniature painters and astronomers worked at courts in Herat and Samarkand, a period historians call the Timurid Renaissance, built on the wealth Timur's campaigns had violently assembled a generation earlier.

By around 800, Tiwanaku near Lake Titicaca covered roughly four square kilometres and held between ten and twenty thousand people, sustained by an agropastoral economy rather than by markets: goods moved through elite redistribution instead of trade for profit.

Its builders raised the Akapana, a terraced platform 257 metres wide, alongside the Pumapunku's megalithic stonework and the Kalasasaya's astronomically aligned courtyard. The city drew pilgrims as much as it governed territory, and its artistic style spread across the southern Andes through contact with the neighbouring Wari.

Tiwanaku had been growing in the Titicaca basin since roughly 200, but it reached its peak of influence between 500 and 600, when its reach stretched well beyond the altiplano into Peru's Moquegua valley, where settlements built in Tiwanaku's own architectural style appear far from the capital.

The state relied less on conquest than on elite gift-giving and llama caravan networks, images of loaded pack animals turn up on portable objects traded across the region. Its capital near Lake Titicaca grew to hold over ten thousand people and produced the massive stonework of the Akapana platform and the Gateway of the Sun.

The shells themselves came from one place: deep water off Vancouver Island, harvested chiefly by the Nuu-chah-nulth using long barbed rods to bring up the narrow tusk-shaped dentalium. From there they moved through a chain of coastal and inland peoples, the Tlingit among the northernmost, who received and passed them on rather than gathering them.

Strung into lengths, the shells travelled as far as the Great Plains, the Great Basin and central Canada, valued for adornment and as a medium of exchange well beyond the waters they came from. A network that long meant a shell's worth could be judged by length alone, a portable, counted standard in places that never saw where it was harvested.

Tobacco reached Spain as seeds in 1559, carried back by the royal chronicler Francisco Hernandez de Toledo, and within decades the habit had spread across a continent that had never seen the plant before. Early promoters, including the English writer Thomas Harriot, claimed it opened the body's pores and warded off disease.

The crop then became the reason for Virginia's survival as an English colony. Jamestown settlers, struggling to grow anything else worth shipping home, planted tobacco and used it as currency, and demand for it in Europe helped drive the expansion of enslaved labour across the Caribbean through the seventeenth century.

The largest of the Tarim Basin's oasis states, Kucha, is thought to have held some eighty thousand people, ringed by desert on every side and kept alive by irrigation drawn from the surrounding mountains. Its rulers spoke a language related to no neighbour, an Indo-European tongue that had somehow ended up isolated deep in Central Asia.

That language survives only in manuscripts, thousands of them, written centuries after these kingdoms' peak using an alphabet borrowed from Indian Brahmi script. The oases themselves existed to keep caravans moving between China and the west, and it was through them that Buddhism, carried along the same roads, first reached Chinese-speaking lands in force.

Shogun Tokugawa Iemitsu did not shut Japan's ports with a single order. Between 1633 and 1639 his government issued a sequence of edicts, each tightening what the last had left open, restricting where Japanese ships could sail and funnelling foreign trade through officials the shogunate controlled. The aim was less to keep foreigners out than to keep domain lords from building independent wealth and weapons through overseas contacts.

Christianity gave the policy its sharpest edge. Missionaries were increasingly viewed as agents of destabilisation, and after the Shimabara uprising of 1637 to 1638, in which persecuted Christians and peasants rose against local authorities, the shogunate treated the religion itself as a threat to be stamped out rather than merely regulated.

Tokugawa Ieyasu had already won the decisive battle three years earlier at Sekigahara, ending a century of civil war among Japan's regional lords. In 1603 he took the title of shogun and ruled from Edo Castle, in what is now Tokyo, leaving the emperor in Kyoto as a figurehead while real authority sat with him and the daimyo who answered to him.

The isolation the shogunate became known for took decades to close in fully. Ieyasu banned Catholicism outright in 1614, and by 1635 his successors barred Japanese subjects from leaving the country and shut the ports to everyone but China, Korea and the Dutch, a policy that held with little change until the mid-1800s.

Toledo's own Muslim ruler, al-Qadir, asked Alfonso VI of Castile for help putting down an uprising against him. Alfonso obliged, then kept the city for himself, and after a long siege it fell on 25 May 1085. Al-Qadir was compensated with a lesser throne in Valencia, where he was killed a few years later.

Alfonso first let Toledo's Muslims keep their great mosque and property, and even took the title emperor of the two religions. The concession did not last: while he was away, the newly appointed archbishop, Bernard of Sedirac, seized the mosque with the queen's backing and consecrated it as a cathedral.

Almost everything told about the Toltecs comes down through the Aztecs, who arrived in central Mexico centuries after Tula had emptied. They described a golden age of master builders and craftsmen, and some historians now suspect that story served Aztec rulers who wanted the prestige of claiming Toltec descent.

What survives independently at Tula, in the modern state of Hidalgo, is a city of pyramids, ball courts and four Atlantean stone warriors, each over four metres tall, once holding up a temple roof. Obsidian workshops there fed trade routes across Mesoamerica, evidence of a real city behind the later legend.

The Tuʻi Tonga dynasty had once projected power across a vast stretch of the Pacific, its authority acknowledged as far as Samoa, Futuna, Rotuma and Niue, carried by double-hulled canoes fitted with triangular sails that could cross open ocean between island groups other polities never linked.

By the turn of the eighteenth century that authority was splitting rather than growing: a separate Tuʻi Haʻatakalaua line had already taken over secular rule generations earlier, and a third title, the Tuʻi Kanokupolu, was drawing power away from the original Tuʻi Tonga line even as its ceremonial prestige endured.

Tonga already had a paramount king, the Tu'i Tonga, when a younger line was created to govern more directly. Ngata, a junior son sent to rule the western district of Hihifo on behalf of his family, founded what became the Tu'i Kanokupolu title, meant as a subordinate post rather than a new throne.

Over succeeding generations that junior line absorbed more of the practical authority the senior Tu'i Tonga once held, splitting into rival branches along the way. By the time Europeans began charting the Pacific in numbers, the Tu'i Kanokupolu had become the title that actually ran Tongan affairs.

A peasant's son ended a century of Japanese civil war by starving out the last holdouts rather than storming them. At the siege of Odawara in 1590, Hideyoshi ringed the Hojo clan's castle and kept his own camp entertained with musicians and acrobats while the defenders watched supplies run out below.

Two years earlier he had ordered a sword hunt, stripping peasants of weapons and melting the metal into fittings for a giant Buddha statue in Kyoto, a policy that removed the threat of armed uprising for a generation. He followed it with nationwide land surveys that fixed tax obligations village by village, though in at least one province the surveyors' arrival provoked open revolt.

Nerva, an elderly senator installed as emperor after Domitian's assassination, had no son and needed a successor the army would accept. In 97 he adopted Trajan, a general commanding legions on the Rhine, and when Nerva died in January 98 Trajan succeeded him without contest, the first emperor born outside Italy, in the Roman province of Hispania.

Trajan spent much of his reign on campaign rather than in Rome, annexing Dacia and, late in his rule, pushing into Mesopotamia against the Parthians. Under him the empire reached its largest territorial extent, stretching from Britain to the Persian Gulf, though the eastern gains proved impossible for his successor to hold and were abandoned soon after Trajan's death in 117.

The Ly dynasty did not fall to an invading army but to a wedding. Court official Tran Thu Do arranged a marriage between the child empress Ly Chieu Hoang and his seven year old nephew, then had her abdicate the throne to her new husband. The Tran dynasty began on 31 December 1225 without a battle fought.

Tran Thu Do secured the new regime by forcing the deposed emperor to suicide and moving against surviving Ly relatives. The dynasty he installed by intrigue went on to defeat three separate Mongol invasions later in the century, culminating in a naval victory on the Bach Dang River in 1288 that broke Yuan ambitions in Vietnam for good.

Camels had crossed the Sahara since the 3rd century, but regular caravan routes only formed once Islam began spreading through West Africa in the 7th and 8th centuries, giving traders on both sides a shared law and language to trade under. Gold moved north from Wangara toward Sijilmasa in Morocco, then on to Mediterranean ports.

Salt moved the other way, and at Timbuktu it changed hands for close to its weight in gold. Timbuktu, Gao and Djenne grew rich as staging posts on that exchange, and the trade in gold, salt, slaves and kola nuts along the Taghaza and Walata trails ran at that scale into the early 17th century.

Salt was worth close to its weight in gold, almost literally: at markets like Timbuktu, blocks mined at Taghaza traded near weight for weight against gold dust carried up from the forest edge. Camel caravans made the crossing possible, moving salt south and gold north along routes that had already operated for centuries.

The trade carried people too. Alongside salt, gold, kola nuts and cowrie shells, captives taken farther south were marched north to Mediterranean and Egyptian markets, sold as domestic servants, concubines or soldiers. Control of these routes was what turned inland West African rulers into some of the wealthiest men of their age.

Britain handed the French fortress of Louisbourg back to France in exchange for Madras, a trading post in India that a French fleet had captured three years earlier. British and American colonists who had bled to take Louisbourg were furious to see a European negotiator swap it for a foothold on another continent entirely.

Every major power signed the 1748 settlement and almost none of them liked it.
